#3517. Stacey Abrams in Conversation With Ta-Nehisi Coates

When I first met Stacey Abrams in 2015, she passed on to me the message that she was then passing on to anyone who’d listen: Someday soon, Georgia would be blue. This struck me as unlikely. But three years later Abrams ran for governor, and shocked the country by coming within two points of winning. Then two years later, when Joe Biden sealed his presidential election in 2020 with a win in Georgia, and Raphael Warnock and Jon Ossoff won Senate seats, Abrams looked prophetic. Now, Democrats have gone beyond Georgia, penetrating into the deepest reaches of the South—Mississippi, South Carolina, Texas. To understand how the GOP’s Solid South grew brittle, I could think of no better person to talk to than Abrams.

The following conversation has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Ta-Nehisi Coates: My recollection of our first meeting goes back to 2015, when I was promoting Between the World and Me. You interviewed me for the book. We had a wonderful discussion. My family was actually in the audience, because, like all Black folks, I have family in Atlanta. They were so excited. I was talking to Stacey Abrams—Minority Leader Stacey Abrams. And one of the things you said backstage was, “We’re going to make Georgia blue.” And I don’t know that I scoffed at you. I like to think I wasn’t quite that rude.

Stacey Abrams: Your eyebrow arched a bit.

I confess to the eyebrow arching. And so the eyebrow arched and you made the case. Can you tell me what you saw?

I’d gone through redistricting, and one of the component pieces of redistricting, of course, is that it’s predicated on the census. The US census is a tool that is incredibly powerful and deeply inexact. It was the first time Republicans had power to draw the lines since Reconstruction. And I took a posture in my caucus, and it was this: “If you vote for their maps, I will come after your seats.” And I was not only unequivocal in saying it, I wrote it down because I didn’t want anyone to misquote me.

In order to take that posture, I had to read the maps myself. And what I saw was that Republicans were placing bets that, by drawing the lines a certain way, they were going to give themselves 124 of 180 seats. So 67% of the seats, even though they’d only won the election by 57%.

But I looked at those same maps and I’m like, In this place, in this part of Paulding County, there is a new subdivision that is predominantly Black. And in this part of Gwinnett County, there is a burgeoning Korean population that is now going into its second generation, which means a lot of those will be eligible voters. And down in South Georgia, you have third-generation migrant farm workers who are Latino, but who have decided to plant their roots here and raise their families here. When you looked at those numbers, the maps had a very different story to tell about Republican dominance: They could win for a decade. They could not win for a generation.

We tell ourselves stories about the information we get, and people repeat stories without ever reading it themselves. There are a lot of people who can quote Tom Sawyer who’ve never read the book. And so in our politics, that happens a lot, that the story that becomes popular doesn’t ever get traced back to its origin or to the original text.

What I saw in Georgia is true in Louisiana, in Mississippi, in Tennessee, in Alabama, in South Carolina. We just saw it happen in North Carolina.

So when you saw this wave of redistricting happening around the country this year, did you see a similar opportunity?

Oh, absolutely. I was in Tennessee the day that they passed the maps and what stuck out for me was Raumesh Akbari, who’s the Senate minority leader, she asked to see the bill, and the Republican chair of the committee said, “Well, we don’t have a bill yet, but we know what it’s going to say.” They planned to vote on it even though they did not have the text of the bill.

The Republicans were moving so fast because they thought they understood what they were pulling together. Justin Pearson didn’t pick up the seat he wanted, but they were at risk of losing a seat they thought was going to be theirs because they misread the topography, but they didn’t do a deeper dive into exactly what was laying in the crevices. And that’s where opportunity for us is born.

There are not enough Black people to win any single seat outright on their own in most legislative districts, and no statewide elections, especially post–Louisiana v. Callais, but there are coalitions that can be built. And what I saw from the very beginning was the possibility of coalition.

What I see for the South, what I think the South proved on Tuesday, is the possibility of coalition, but coalition does not happen without conflict. It does not happen without conversation, and it does not happen when we have convinced ourselves of the permanence of our second-class citizenship and our subjugation. What we saw on Tuesday was a moment where people realized that the power to improve their own lives had become so desperately thin that they had to use it or lose it. We cannot rely on that for the next two years.

What I hear you saying is that the last two years created an emergency. But that can’t be depended on. It can’t be “The Most Important Election of Our Lifetime” every two years. Desperation is not enough.

It can’t be. Desperation gets you one moment. There’s a whole body of medical research on people that have heart attacks and they get saved. And what it shows is that they are exercise fiends for about six weeks and then they fall back into their patterns because it’s a normalcy bias.

If we constantly feel on the edge of danger, we cannot function. And so we reorient our understanding of normal to survive. And therefore our responsibility in this moment is to look at the opportunity that was revealed on Tuesday, but not read into it that that opportunity either requires desperation or it requires this milquetoast approach, because our default is not just normalcy, but the most banal form of normalcy we can imagine.

I know you have some concerns about some of the narratives emerging out of the midterms. Would you talk a bit about that?

I saw something on Axios that I think was well-intentioned and it essentially said that the threats to our democracy were overblown, that our courts held, that our Congress held, that our presidency wasn’t overreaching, and that for normal people, things were fine. How have we reached the place where we think it is normal that the capital city in the United States of America is under military occupation? How is it okay that the courts held when it permits the incarceration of children in Dilley, Texas, and the kidnapping of people of color because of race and the language that they speak? There is something aggressively privileged about this idea that democracy is not in jeopardy because those who are the most protected don’t feel harm.

But Tuesday was a repudiation of this idea that things are normal. You saw turnout at extraordinary levels from a cross section of communities, almost all of whom have been directly impacted by the harms of this administration. Not just the economic harms that hit everyone, but harms that were amplified and refined for their cruelty.

At the same time, there’s a worry that I have that, because we won control of Congress for the patriots—and that’s how I frame it, I no longer think it’s just Democrat versus Republican, it’s patriots versus authoritarians—even though the patriots may have gained more purchase in Congress, we still have a Supreme Court that gutted the last vestiges of protection for the Voting Rights Act. We still have a Supreme Court that stripped women of their bodily autonomy. We still have a Supreme Court that has said that protections that are afforded by DEI are somehow suspect. And when those are true, then the successes of Tuesday don’t signal that we’ve won. They signal that we have to work even harder because the harms have not dissipated, they just haven’t penetrated.

You said something a few months back that’s stuck with me—that our elections are ripe for entertainment. As a sports fan, I think it’s not a coincidence that so many sports figures are now commenting on politics because the way they appear on TV is actually quite similar to the way sports appears. You have these long campaigns, which is like your season. Then you have primaries, which are like your playoffs, and then you have this big Super Bowl that happens on Tuesday. And so, it’s an entertainment and ratings bonanza. And I think, as I recall, you were cautioning against that as a view of politics. Can you speak a little bit more about that?

Yeah. When you think about politics, if you think about elections as an event, and to extend your analogy, if the elections are the finals, if the elections are game seven, if it’s the Super Bowl, when that happens, then the day after, you go home, the game is over. But the challenge I have is that it’s not just that we treat it as a sporting event, it’s that we treat politics as though we are spectators at a sporting event. And when we look at the other party, it’s like we are spectators watching a very disciplined, seasoned team that practices in the off-season, that travels together, that plays overseas. They’re constantly engaged and we are on and off. We think of politics, again, as entertainment as opposed to the job.

How did we end up with this entertainment narrative?

Theodore White did this series where he examined elections 1960, 1964, 1968, 1972. And when you read it, as someone who is reading it in the 21st century, the arc of how we have viewed politics changed dramatically, specifically in 1960 with the advent of television, because the election contest between John Kennedy and Richard Nixon hinged in no small part on that televised debate. And I think for you and me and for anyone who wasn’t old enough to see it, I did not realize that it was one of the most watched programs in American history. We take for granted how many people are going to watch the debates these days, but with that first debate, it was one of the most watched programs in the world because it had never happened before. And the moment it became a television spectacle, it became entertainment because you were watching, you picked winners and losers, you picked your villain and you picked your champion.

It’s human nature, we put things into these narrative arcs. As someone who writes comic books, you understand this. As someone who writes thrillers, I think about this. You create a villain, you have a protagonist, an antagonist, you have to have a storyline, you have to have complications, and when television became the medium, it added a layer and a texture to what had long been the mechanics of politics. Then you add into it the drama of Black and brown people getting to participate. And then you layer on top of that “blue state versus red state,” and the sharp division, and the attribution to entire regions of a value system and a personality based on a single day.

What would it mean to remain engaged beyond elections? When I think about the conservative movement, I think about the degree to which the religious right is engaged. I think about Trump rallies. I think people were baffled by this at first—the clothes, the trucks, the boats. But what I would say is those are markers of community. They aren’t my politics. But they seem part of something larger than a particular bill or policy.

There’s a lot of talk in organizing about going for belief first, or belonging first. On the left, we are often accused of belief, that you have to be in line with all of our ideas, our values, our ideologies, but also the tactical, practical ways of exercising them, and that because we say you have to believe first, we filter out people who haven’t had time to understand or adapt or even decide what they believe. The right uses belonging. They say, “Come and be a part of us, and we’ll tell you what we are.” So you get the jersey, you get the cap, you get the red, you get to use the language, even if you haven’t decided that you actually believe all they believe, which is why you have people who are suddenly surprised that this is what happened.

We have to shift. Not to say that we don’t have beliefs, but we have to give people time to grow into those beliefs. I come at this from my time as minority leader. I had a caucus of 60 members in a chamber of 180, and my members included suburban white mothers and rural Black pastors and everything in between. We were the most racially diverse caucus. We were geographically diverse. And I had no power. I was the minority leader. My job was to help harmonize their approach. I could not lead with belief, because people were entitled to their beliefs, but my job was to bring them into belonging first because they were members of the caucus. And then my second job was to make sure that anyone who needed them to believe something had the platform to offer the tutelage.

That’s the place where I think we are failing. We don’t do the tutelage. We say, “There has been a conversation, this is now our truth. And if you don’t adopt that truth, you are somehow opposed to it,” as opposed to, “You haven’t adopted the truth because you don’t know what it means and you don’t understand it and you haven’t experienced it. Let me give you time and space to come in,” or, “You have legitimate disagreement, and maybe on this, we will not be in alignment, but your disagreement should not lead to hostility against my community.”

The Democratic Socialists of America have attracted a lot of attention recently, but one thing they seem to do is this “belonging” piece. I can’t say I understood this before, but I was talking to someone for a story, and then mentioned the social environment. So here in New York, when people go out to canvas, afterwards, they all go out for beers. The beers are not really the point, but making people feel like they belong to something is.

Yeah. I mean, what they are doing is what works in most effective social movements. During the Vietnam War, one of the most effective protest waves happened at coffee shops. You brought people together around the table, they got to vent about what they were upset about, they went out and protested and then they came back together. People like being liked.

In terms of belief, how does one do that and not make those who are in that coalition who are particularly vulnerable feel abandoned? Obviously, I mean, this is not the only case, but I’m thinking about the tremendous amount of negative attention brought on the trans community. What do you do when the “belonging” comes in conflict with actually protecting the members of your coalition?

My first position is, if you have a faith that tells you it is okay to cause harm because you feel uncomfortable, I need to understand where your faith lies. Our first responsibility is the protection of difference. And it is to say you don’t have to embrace, but you cannot lift up pitchforks. You cannot demonize, you cannot revile, you cannot scapegoat because all of those are hostile actions of cruelty that not only cause harm to the victim, they diminish your ability to learn. So the worry I have is that too often we sacrifice that education piece because it’s uncomfortable and because it requires defending those you may not be in complete alignment with, and it’s an easier thing to just jump on the bandwagon.

In my caucus, when I was a minority leader, another issue I had was abortion, and I had two members who were pastors. I was not going to be able to change their ideological position and I wasn’t going to try. But I had these members walk off the floor, instead of voting, on abortion bills. And there were some who got mad and they’re like, “Oh, we should know their position.” I said, “A yes vote on this bill causes harm, and no vote is a help. Not voting is the same as a no vote. So why do you need them to make a declaration when their declaration of refusing to do harm is progress?” So there’s a complexity that we often elide because we failed to measure what harm looks like, and the path from good to harm is a lot shorter than we want to believe.

Did you work with Angie Nixon during her race?

I feel like she excited a certain element of the base in a way that we haven’t really seen before.

I contributed and then I went down to Florida, actually did an event at Florida A&M University and did one at Cafe Resistance. I got to know her mama. I knew of her as a state representative. And when I decided to support her campaign, it was because she has always put the work of serving people first. She has built networks, but more importantly, she solves problems.

When Florida started banning books, she started a bookstore for banned books. That kind of tactical response with strategic intention is often lacking and it has been part of how I try to operate. We’ve got people who are good at being diagnosticians and we’ve got folks who can offer prescriptions and we’ve got people who can actually administer the medicine. And we need more people who are willing to do all three. You need people who are specialists; I’m not saying you don’t, but what she has demonstrated is the capacity to do the three.

Have you heard some of the negative commentary after the election about her campaign? I’m thinking about James Carville, for instance—this notion that somehow she was a poor fit for Florida or was a bad candidate. It’s not great. Have you seen any of this?

Well, I have thoughts on the fact that we keep thinking the solution to the problem is the thing that failed before. And I believe in experimentation. If you look at my history, I have never been top of mind as the solution to problems. And some of it is timing, some of it is capacity, and some of it is helping change the public imagination, but we’re never going to get what we need if we only use what we’ve always had.

I just find it interesting that she is attracting negative commentary, from certain quarters, in a way that David Jolly is not, even though they both lost and the margin wasn’t that much between the two of them. She came very, very close to winning, in a state Democrats really didn’t expect to compete in two years ago. And look, I just have to say, you are somebody who in 2018 came really, really close too. You’re both Black women. I just wonder what you make of the critique.

The critique is easy because Angie Nixon is different. She’s different than what they are used to, and she is different than 250 years of expectation has led us to presume is right. I am excited about Juliana Stratton and Angela Alsobrooks and Lisa Blunt Rochester being in the US Senate. That is an extraordinary thing. Adding Angie Nixon would’ve been an amazing, amazing addition. But for pundits whose sense of success is grounded in past history, she strains the imagination.

David Jolly ran a smart race. Angie Nixon ran a smart race, and we know that because they came close to winning, but you are never entitled to victory. You are entitled to effort. And this notion that there is some magical formula for what wins in the South got completely obliterated yesterday when Scott Colom won a seat that we haven’t held since 1874. We know that what can win is a combination of a smart candidate, an invested campaign, and an electorate who sees and hears themselves in the story told.

Angie didn’t get that opportunity because she had a late primary and no resources. And to judge her using a metric that was never designed for her is deeply problematic. And it’s not just about her being a Black woman, it’s about how do we win an evolving electorate if all we know is to do what we’ve always done? And so my argument for the Democratic Party is that our notions of electability have to evolve with the democracy that we deserve and that we design, and it cannot be anchored to these sometimes antiquated notions that the only thing we can do is not lose as opposed to let’s try really hard to win by meeting the moment. And I think Angie Nixon did an incredible job of meeting the moment.

And what about you—do you still have ambitions for public office?

Do you worry that some of the work you do as a kind of public political strategist (like in this interview, frankly) will conflict at all? When I think about people seeking office, they often try to say as little as possible.

Politics is a tool. It is not an identity for me. It’s a tool. And that’s different. And there are people for whom this is what they do and we need those people. This is not a disparaging comment about others, but for me, it is a tool. It is one of the ways to do the work I believe needs to be done. I think that poverty is immoral. I think it is solvable. I think it is economically inefficient. And for most of my life, the work for me has been about how do you solve this economic poverty? When I got deep in the work, I realized that we also had a moral poverty that we had to contend with, and we have this poverty of imagination. And the problem is you cannot convince people to believe that their problems can be solved if you won’t talk about them.

And in the South, silence is protective. It has been a way to nibble around the edges, but the only people who could be loud about it were the people who could afford volume. And politicians rarely can afford volume. I want things to be better and I’m not willing to forgo any tool that will make that happen. But I’m also not willing to protect my future opportunities by rejecting my current responsibilities.

#3516. Boxer Lee Reeves Dead at 31 After Suffering Brain Injury During Fight

Pro boxer Lee Reeves has died at the age of 31, months after he suffered a traumatic brain injury during a fight.

Reeves had been in a coma since a bout against Gary Cully in Dublin on August 1. He died at University Hospital in Limerick, Ireland, on Monday, November 16.

The boxer lost consciousness during the 10th round of his fight against Cully, 30. Reeves received medical attention in the ring and was then taken to a nearby hospital, where he was described as being in “critical but stable condition.”

Reeves was transported from Dublin to Limerick in October in an effort to get him closer to his family. He died “with loved ones by his side,” according to The Athletic.

The late boxer’s trainer, Jonathan O’Brien, shared a series of emotional social media posts after Reeves’ death.

“Goodbye son sleep tight you fought so hard till the end,” O’Brien shared via Instagram on Monday. “We love you so much rest in peace with your mam and brother waiting at the heavenly gates look over your sisters and your father give them the strength to get true this we love you Lee 🥹💔🥹🙏🫶🏼.”

In another post on Tuesday, November 17, O’Brien wrote, “I’ll see you again Son 🥹.”

O’Brien’s wife, Emma, also remembered the late boxer on social media.

“We will never forget you 💔,” she shared via Instagram on Monday, adding, “I’ll miss seeing your beautiful face pop up on my phone, I’ll miss hearing your wise powerful and always positive words 😔 You fought your hardest and you did yourself and everyone proud 💯 like you always have 💪🏼 El Champo your legacy will live on forever 🇮🇪.”

Cully, the boxer who Reeves was fighting, offered his condolences after news of his former opponent’s death.

“We shared the ring back in August but we [had] been going back for years,” Cully shared via Instagram on Monday. “I still remember the stadium days when I used to watch Lee in the nationals the weight above me and always be impressed by his fights and his flashy gear 😂.”

He added, “What a character and a gent. It’s never been nothing [but] love between us champ can’t really believe I’m writing this but RIP brother ❤️.”

Queensbury Promotions founder and promoter Frank Warren called Reeves’ death “heartbreaking.”

“Lee was a fine young man and a credit to the sport,” Warren wrote via X on Monday. “He will be sorely missed, and my thoughts and prayers are with his family and all who loved him.”

#3515. Ocarina Of Time Is 2026’s Best-Selling Physical Game In The US, But GTA 6 Is Coming

Nintendo's The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake for Switch 2 is the best-selling physical game of 2026, according to Circana, but GTA 6 is coming out soon and could topple that record.

Circana's Mat Piscatella said the Ocarina of Time remake for Switch 2 was the first game to surpass 1 million physical units sold in the US for its launch week since 2023's The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom.

Ocarina of Time for Switch 2 released on November 5, and Circana's reporting period ended on November 7, so the achievement was actually accomplished in just two days, not even a full week.

Ocarina of Time's physical edition, which includes a cartridge, sells for $70, compared to $60 for its digital counterpart.

GTA 6 launches on November 19, and while the game is fully digital, Rockstar is releasing a "physical" version of the game at brick-and-mortar retailers. Buyers don't get a disc--only a code for the game.

In any event, for Circana, code-in-a-box games are considered new physical game sales, so GTA 6 is no doubt going to topple Ocarina of Time's record.

Ocarina of Time's remake for Switch 2 sold more than 5 million copies over its first four days globally. The latest sales data for GTA 6 pre-purchases show that the game has passed 16 million units sold worldwide.

#3514. Windows Laptops Just Closed a Major Gap With the MacBook Neo

To say the MacBook Neo disrupted the laptop market would be an understatement. When the Neo dropped, former Apple CEO Tim Cook said Apple had its best-ever launch week for first-time Mac customers, and the company is reportedly planning on doubling the MacBook's sales for 2027. It's not hard to see why the MacBook Neo is such a hit: Apple is offering the essential Mac experience at a fantastic price point. You no longer need to spend $1,000 or more for a MacBook, so long as you're okay making some sacrifices to get there—which, it seems, many customers are.

While the MacBook Neo has been a boon for Apple and Apple fans alike, I can only imagine the stress it brought to PC manufacturers—especially those with budget or midrange machines. Windows PCs have long won the price war against Apple. While MacBooks have their passionate customers, buyers looking for the best value have had to weigh expensive Apple laptops against many far cheaper options from companies like Dell, HP, ASUS, and Lenovo. But with the Neo, suddenly a MacBook was competing in this space, and well.

Part of the issue for PC manufacturers was Apple's control over its own ecosystem. Unlike most PC makers, which only produce the hardware for each machine, Apple makes both the hardware and the software for its MacBook lineup. As such, the company has the advantage of optimizing that hardware. It can design macOS to run more efficiently on weaker hardware, in a way that companies like Dell or ASUS can't. You might be comparing the MacBook Neo against a Windows laptop with similar specs, or even better specs, but because Microsoft makes Windows, not the laptop manufacturer, it's possible the Neo ends up with the better overall experience. While that might still be the case, Microsoft may have just closed that gap in a meaningful way.

This week, Microsoft announced key upgrades to memory-management efficiency, particularly for machines with 8GB of RAM. This is the amount of memory the MacBook Neo has, as well as many budget and midrange Windows laptops. That's not much memory for 2026, regardless of platform, but Apple seems to have squeezed a lot out of it for the Neo. Now, Microsoft may have just done the same for PCs, as Windows is reportedly 20% more responsive, with 40% faster multitasking.

In its blog post, Microsoft highlighted improvements that users with 8 GB of RAM can expect from Windows going forward. First, Microsoft says it focused on better utilizing the RAM your machine already has. The company compares its memory management to a desk: Anything on the "desk" is stored in RAM; anything in your "drawer" is stored in your drive. As you use your PC, Windows used to move more of your apps and tabs to your drawer to free up more RAM for other things, meaning you'd need to reload those items whenever you returned to them. Going forward, the company says that Windows can keep up to 2GB more of your active data in RAM instead of moving it to slower storage elsewhere. That means apps and tabs should refresh less frequently when you leave and return to them.

Microsoft also says that small actions should be faster across the board. When you open the Start menu, search across your PC, right-click, open Settings, launch the Snipping Tool, and open File Explorer, those actions may be up to 20% faster than they were in January. Microsoft Edge may open up to 33% faster, while Teams can enable Efficiency Mode by default on 8 GB machines, which means it can launch up to 20% faster too. Microsoft put together an interesting stress test to compare multitasking performance between today and January. It opened 20 tabs in Edge, a 4K video, large Word, PowerPoint, and Excel files, then Outlook and File Explorer, all without closing any windows. That experience was 40% faster following this latest update.

Microsoft says it also improved the memory efficiency in its apps: The company claims it reduced committed-memory growth by up to 900 MB, and saved up to 360 MB in RAM across Word, PowerPoint, Excel, and Outlook. That extends to third-party apps as well: Microsoft says that WhatsApp has double-digit memory improvement now. Widgets also only load when you open the app, which saves 200 MB of RAM when the app is closed, while Edge tabs go inactive after 15 minutes instead of two hours.

Microsoft isn't making these upgrades in a vacuum. Hardware costs, particularly for RAM, have skyrocketed in the age of AI. Microsoft knows that people are likely going to hold onto existing hardware for longer than they usually do, or that they'll opt for less-expensive configurations, including, perhaps, machines with 8 GB of RAM.

PCMag's Chris Hoffman was adamant before this latest Windows update that buyers should steer clear of PCs with 8 GB of RAM. Now, he's pulling back a bit. In his testing, Hoffman noticed improvements when multitasking on an 8 GB PC when compared to similar tests from months ago. He could run multiple Chrome tabs, a Microsoft Word window, and Spotify without bogging down the computer much. Hoffman isn't a lightweight user, so he still wouldn't personally choose an 8 GB machine, but he admits, "If I were an average PC buyer looking for a reasonable desktop experience and could save hundreds of dollars by opting for 8GB of RAM, I might be happy with the performance."

To that point, I think this new Windows update makes 8 GB PCs competitive, especially against the MacBook Neo. We'll still need direct comparisons to know how well this new Windows experience holds up across the board, but these updates are promising. Users with 8 GB machines just got a free, valuable update overnight; new customers can opt for a more affordable PC without feeling like performance will take a nosedive just because they opened one too many Edge tabs.

As Hoffman says, 8 GB of RAM is not ideal for any user looking for serious multitasking or professional workflows, regardless of whether they choose a Mac or PC. But for the average computer customer looking for a solid machine without breaking the bank, I no longer see the Neo as necessarily the default choice. After all, Apple has slowly raised its price, too, from $599 to $699. If you're platform-agnostic, or even prefer Windows to macOS, these updates from Microsoft are quite promising. If you're in the market, check out PCMag's excellent list of budget laptop recommendations.

Landman is making quite the splash down in Texas right now, as people saw the show being filmed at a Texas Christian University game over the weekend. Then, not long after that, Ali Larter posted a photo dump from filming, and it featured one person I never expected to see: Glen Powell.

Of course, I’m well aware that Glen Powell is dating Michelle Randolph, Larter’s on-screen daughter and a veteran of Taylor Sheridan’s shows. He’s also famously from and lives in Texas, which is where Landman is filmed. So, it’s not illogical for him to be around the set of this popular Paramount+ show. However, I was still surprised to see him in the final slide of Larter’s photo dump. Take a look:

In that final slide, you can see Larter posing for a photo with her co-stars, Billy Bob Thornton and Michelle Randolph, as well as Glen Powell.

Now, Landman has actually been filming at Texas Christian University since October, per the university. However, it made headlines over the weekend because Randolph was spotted with the cheerleaders on Saturday during the game against the Kansas State Wildcats.

In Landman, she plays Ainsley Norris, the daughter of Thornton’s Tommy and Larter’s Angela. She’s a student at TCU, and a big part of her storyline has to do with her joining the cheer team. It would seem it will be an even bigger part of her arc in Season 3, seeing as not only was Randolph seen filming at this game, but Larter and Bobbi Salvör Menuez, who play Paigyn, were there too.

To top it all off, Glen Powell was also spotted at the game. As you can see in the third image of this carousel TCU uploaded, the Twisters actor was on the sidelines – which is also where his girlfriend happened to be.

A post shared by TCU (@texaschristianuniversity)

Rumors that Powell and Randolph were dating picked up in late 2025, and the actors went Instagram official in July of this year. Since then, they’ve posted pictures of each other here and there, and the Running Man star’s dog, Brisket, even made a cameo in one of the 1923 actress’s photo dumps.

Speaking of Brisket, Powell’s dog also gives him another tie to Landman. In early 2025, Brisket met up with Demi Moore’s pup, Pilaf. Man, it’s really a small world, and maybe I shouldn’t be shocked that he now has a connection to another star of this Taylor Sheridan show.

Overall, it was very cute to see the Top Gun: Maverick star pop up in a photo dump all about Landman. Clearly, he’s being a supportive partner and cheering Randolph on as she literally cheers on TCU. I also bet it’s pretty cool to just say you get to hang out with her, Ali Larter, Billy Bob Thornton, and Sam Elliott.

Now, I think the question becomes: Could we get Glen Powell on Landman? Taylor Sheridan has a tendency to hire A-listers for his shows, so I don’t think it’s out of the question. Plus, these images make it clear that the Chad Powers star is already literally very close to the production.

#3512. New Ubisoft Boss Wants Studio To Become “A24 Of Video Games”

Ubisoft recently hired games industry veteran Christoph Hartmann to become the general manager of Creative House 2, which is now known as Massive Entertainment. In a new interview, Hartmann talked about his hopes for the unit, saying his dream would be for it to become "like the A24 of video games."

He told Variety that what he means by this is that Massive can be like A24 in that it can make games that are both critically and commercially successful. A24's biggest hit ever was this year's Backrooms, which made more than $400 million worldwide against a reported budget of $10 million and was received positively by fans and critics.

Some of A24's other recent big critical and commercial hits have included Marty Supreme ($192 million), Everything Everywhere All at Once ($148 million), The Drama ($135 million), and Civil War ($127 million).

Saying Ubisoft's Massive could aim for what A24 is doing is certainly an ambitious goal, and it's not the first time that Hartmann has made such a bold claim about what he's working on. When he was at Amazon, Hartmann said his objective was to help Amazon become “the Disney of the future,” with gaming standing alongside TV, film, music, and retail.

Massive covers franchises like The Division, Ghost Recon, Splinter Cell, and March of Giants (which Ubisoft bought from Hartmann's previous company, Amazon). "Hartmann’s role is to oversee strategic direction and development of the studios and brands under Creative House 2 [now Massive]," Ubisoft said.

Hartmann told Variety that he wants Massive to "definitely not" be a place that only makes shooter games.

"I want us to be a label which really looks after the core gamer. And what I mean by that, it’s almost easier to describe what we’re not going to do. So I’m not going to do a racing game. I’m not going to do sports. I’m not going to do a casual kids title. But could we do an RPG one day? Could we do MMO? Could I maybe do even a strategy game? Sure, it’s all coming down to the right talent," he said.

Hartmann also discussed why he left Amazon, saying the company is focused on the AI buildout right now and "games just can't be their prime focus right now." Prior to Amazon, Hartmann worked at 2K for decades.

#3511. Sony Wants to Give You Up to $400 for Your PS5

Companies usually want you to buy something from them. They might cut prices to make their products more enticing, or introduce perks and upgrades to make stagnant prices (or even price hikes) more appealing. But rarely do I see companies encourage customers to sell their products.

Such is the case with Sony and its PlayStation console. This week, the company began reaching out to some customers with an odd prompt: Rather than buy a new PS5 or PS5 Pro, you can sell your existing PS5 console for up to $400. There are stipulations there, of course: Your console needs to be in good working order, and, apparently, come with two controllers—even though Sony only includes one in the box. The price could also fluctuate depending on your console model, storage capacity, and included accessories. But, still, the company says it'll help you net up to $400 for your existing PS5.

It's a bizarre deal, especially when you consider who you're trading your console to. Sony isn't necessarily accepting trade-ins itself. Instead, it's partnering with BackMarket. The thing is, you can trade in your PS5 directly through BackMarket and get a better value than Sony is offering through its direct link. When I try to trade in my standard PS5 with one controller, BackMarket offers $435, $35 more than Sony's highest offer. If I add a second controller to that deal, BackMarket bumps up the total to $455.

You might also be wondering why Sony would do this. Not only is it weird for a company to encourage you to sell one of its products, but the PS5 is about to have a big moment. Grand Theft Auto VI is finally about to launch, and it'll likely be one of the biggest video game launches, if not the biggest video game launch, of all time. Why, then, would Sony encourage users to jump ship?

While Sony doesn't say, the answer likely has to do with how expensive it is to pick up a PS5 right now. Even though the console launched back in 2020, units are few and far between, jacking the price up to unreasonable levels. Sony raised international prices due to tariffs last year, but the current shortage is more probably tied to the ongoing memory crisis that's putting a strain on all tech, including game consoles. A new PS5 on Amazon will easily cost you over $800. If you want to find a PS5 Pro, don't be surprised to find it well over $1,000. Sony likely wants players who aren't using their consoles to sell them, so that active players (who will also buy games like GTA VI) will pick them up. It's not just Sony, either: Microsoft has been offering similar deals to inactive Xbox gamers this year.

If Sony reached out to you directly, you can take advantage of the deal without issue—just click the link in the email. But if you never received such an offer, you still have options. For one, that BackMarket deal is live for anyone. That links takes you to the deal for the standard PS5, but you can also head to this link to enter the info for your specific PS5 model. GameStop, of course, will happily take your PS5 off your hands, but it doesn't seem as generous as BackMarket. Right now, it seems you can get up to $275 in store credit, or $192.50 in cash for a standard PS5.

#3509. An NES Power Glove Just Became The Most Dangerous Weapon In Pro Wrestling

All Elite Wrestling's recent Full Gear event had no shortage of great moments, but Austin Creed stole the show with a move straight out of Street Fighter. After teaming up with his Next Level partner Kofi Kingston and Swerve Strickland to take on Bandido, Hangman Adam Page, and Brody King in a Texas Death Match, anything went in this brawl — including vintage NES accessories.

Looking the worse for wear at King's hands, Creed busted out an NES Power Glove and landed a Shoryuken uppercut that exploded in a shower of sparks, knocking his burly foe flat on his back. The moment quickly went viral, and Creed's team would eventually triumph, emerging as the AEW World Trios Champions.

Creed is no stranger to video games; during his run with WWE, he ran the Up Up Down Down YouTube channel, where he competed with fellow performers in a wide variety of games. Wrestling and video games have formed a symbiotic relationship over the years, with top performers like Kenny Omega referencing games like Street Fighter and Final Fantasy 7 for his signature moves. Video games have also positively influenced professional wrestlers, with top WWE star Roman Reigns saying it's a popular downtime activity with his fellow wrestlers and better than some of the "extracurricular" exploits of previous generations.

In another video game crossover, former WWE champion Cody Rhodes played Guile in the live-action Street Fighter movie, which was released last month, and he even cosplayed as the character at WWE SummerSlam. Sadly, the film wasn't a big box-office hit, making only $100.7 million worldwide during its run (via Box Office Mojo). In comparison, the other Capcom-based movie, Resident Evil, was far more successful, generating over $416 million worldwide and making it the highest-grossing Resident Evil movie of all time.

#3508. GTA 6 Has A Lot Of Different Bird Species, Here’s How Many

Rockstar's Grand Theft Auto 6 has a lot of details and depth, including dozens of different bird species for people to find. If you're a birder, you're in for a good time.

According to The Guardian, Rockstar confirmed that there are 62 types of birds that players can spot. Players can whip out binoculars to "study" birds and animals like they could in Rockstar's last game, Red Dead Redemption II.

As PC Gamer reminds us, Florida is home to more than 500 bird types, so GTA 6 will have just a fraction of the different kinds of birds people can find in real Florida. GTA 6 was never going to replicate every single bird, of course.

Some of the birds that are found in Florida, and probably GTA 6 as well, include flamingoes, spoonbills, wood storks, egrets, kites, terns, and scrub jays. Florida is also home to bald eagles, and we'd expect them to show up in GTA 6.

Inclusive of birds, GTA 6 has more than 170 animal types, including cane toads, alligators, manatees, and rhesus macaque monkeys.

GTA 6 launches on November 19 for PS5 and Xbox Series X|S. The game launches at midnight local time, so it will be playable for people in New Zealand and Australia very soon. You can switch your Xbox region to New Zealand to play early, if that works.

For more on GTA 6, including preload information, preorder bonuses, and release times, check out our Grand Theft Auto 6 guides hub.

#3507. No, We Aren’t All Eating 'Too Much' Protein

If you’ll permit me a rant—I promise to make it fact-filled and interesting—I am sick of the articles that seem to pop up every few months claiming that we are all eating “too much” protein. They convey an inaccurate picture of how the body uses protein, and they demonize perfectly healthy meals that happen to be high in protein. It’s time to set the record straight.

It is true that most of us eat more than the RDA (recommended daily allowance) of protein, but that's a good thing—the RDA is meant as a minimum. It's true that protein-boosted foods are trendy, and that they're not necessarily great dietary choices in the big picture. It's also true that you can eat a healthy diet with little to no meat, but meat is not synonymous with protein. Let's look at what we actually know about the role of protein in a healthy diet, and how to tell if you're eating too much or too little.

As a refresher, protein is one of the three calorie-containing macronutrients (fats, carbs, protein) that make up most of the food we eat. Proteins are made of amino acids, and these amino acids are required for the growth, repair, and functioning of our bodies.

We can get protein from a variety of sources. Meats are particularly protein-dense; a chicken breast contains about 35 grams of protein. Other animal products, like milk and eggs, are also rich in protein. Plant-based foods tend to have less protein than animal products, but it’s not hard to meet or exceed protein requirements even on a vegan diet. Beans, grains, and soy products like tofu contain significant amounts of protein, for example.

If you’d like a cheat sheet on how much protein you’re supposed to eat based on your activity level, you can find one here. And that’s a good place to start dissecting this “too much protein” myth, because before we can declare an amount of protein to be “too much,” we need to understand how much is “enough.”

The government communicates targets for different nutrients to encourage us all to eat a healthy, balanced diet. These targets are the basis for the “% daily value” labels on the back of packaged foods, and for the nutrient makeup of school lunches. The RDA, or recommended daily allowance, is defined as “the average daily dietary intake level that is sufficient to meet the nutrient requirement of nearly all (97 to 98 percent) healthy individuals in a group.”

In other words, if 100% of us were to eat the RDA of protein, at least 97% of us would be getting enough protein—we'd be meeting the minimum to be healthy. That's right, this number is a minimum to avoid malnutrition, not a maximum, and not a recommendation for optimal health.

By the way, if you're wondering how that number is determined? For protein, it is based on nitrogen balance. Humans break down proteins, as part of our body’s daily function, and we excrete nitrogen as a result. If you eat enough protein (which contains nitrogen), the amount of nitrogen you excrete will be the same as, or more than, the amount you eat. In other words, if you aren’t breaking your own body proteins down (in excess of what you eat), then whatever you’re eating must be, in some sense, enough.

In this way of thinking, the RDA is the minimum to stay healthy. More is fine; less would mean that you may not be getting enough. For some nutrients, there is also an UL, or upper limit, telling you that more than a certain amount is too much. Upper limits are calculated for vitamins and minerals; there is no upper limit defined for protein.

Therefore, there is no official definition for “too much” protein. If somebody eats more than the RDA, they’re not eating too much; they’re just eating more than the minimum. You’re supposed to eat more than the minimum.

The RDA for protein is set at 46 grams per day for a 125-pound woman, and at 56 grams per day for a 154-pound man. (The USDA chose those as their examples.) That’s based on an RDA of 0.8 grams of protein per kilogram bodyweight, which works out to 0.36 grams per pound. So a 200-pound person would need 72 grams of protein per day.

This USDA report found that most adult men average roughly 90 to 100 grams of protein per day, although men aged 70 and up only get about 80 grams of protein per day. Women tend to average around 70 grams per day, with those aged 70 and up averaging 62 grams.

Above the RDA? Yes. Too much? I don’t see any way of arguing that. And before you say that we’re getting almost double the recommendation, let's check the math. Those RDA numbers are for 125- and 154-pound people. On the other hand, the averages for what we eat are based on actual people, not ideals. The average American man is 200 pounds, and the average American woman is 171 pounds. So, to compare the numbers:

The average woman is 171 pounds, so her RDA would be 62 grams per day. (Women, on average, eat 70 grams of protein per day.)

The average man is 200 pounds, so his RDA would be 72 grams per day. (Men, on average, eat 90 to 100 grams of protein per day.)

Again, there’s no need to stick to the minimum; going 8 grams over, or even 28 grams over, is fine. It’s probably better to go over than to just scrape by, and many of us arguably don’t get enough. Let me explain.

Let’s start with older adults. Not only does protein intake tend to decrease with age, older adults are vulnerable to issues that stem from a loss of muscle mass. People tend to lose 3-5% of their muscle mass per decade starting at age 30, but strength training and protein intake can support maintaining our muscle, and thus likely prevent or reduce that decline.

The Dietary Guidelines include a note that “About 50 percent of women and 30 percent of men 71 and older fall short of protein foods recommendations.” Meanwhile, a study found that older adults who don’t meet the recommendations are “more likely to be limited when stooping, crouching, or kneeling, standing or sitting for long periods, walking up 10 steps, preparing meals, and walking for a quarter mile.”

So even if it’s true that the average adult gets more protein than recommended, there are clearly a lot of elderly folks who don’t. These are the same people who have more issues functioning in everyday life. This may be a chicken-and-egg situation—was the functional decline a cause or an effect of the change in their diet?—but this sure does not seem to be a group of people who should be eating less protein.

There’s another large group of people who benefit from more, not less, protein: people who are pregnant or lactating. Instead of 0.36 grams of protein per pound of body weight (62 grams for a 171-pound person), the RDA for people who are pregnant or lactating is 0.5 grams/pound (so, 86 grams of protein per day).

When you’re pregnant, you also have higher caloric needs, so the increased total amount of food makes it easier to get the higher protein amount. Still, it makes more sense to spend your energy on making sure you’re getting enough protein, rather than worrying about getting too much.

You knew we were heading in this direction (I say between reps of barbell squats, wiping protein shake off my lips): People who exercise should get more protein than just the RDA.

While the fear-mongering “too much protein” articles sometimes mention that bodybuilders or elite athletes need their protein, they tend to hand-wave this away as a special concern that doesn’t apply to normal people. But I think it’s worth a closer look—and honestly, this situation applies to a lot more people than just a few athletes.

Officially, there isn’t an RDA for athletes; people who exercise can stave off malnutrition with the same 0.36 grams per pound as everyone else. But that doesn’t mean that the RDA is the best target to aim for.

The International Association of Athletics Federations, which governs track and field competitions, recommends that most athletes who are maintaining or gaining weight eat 0.59 to 0.77 grams of protein per pound of bodyweight per day. That’s 101 to 131 grams for the average 171-pound woman, and 118 to 154 grams for a 200-pound man.

A group of organizations, including the American College of Sports Medicine, largely agrees, recommending a range from 0.54 to 0.9 grams per pound for all athletes whose weight is stable or gaining. That includes people who do endurance training like distance running, as well as strength athletes whose exercise involves mainly lifting weights. Those ranges would go as high as 153 grams for our 171-pound woman, and 180 grams for our 200-pound man.

You don’t need to be an Olympian to consider yourself an “athlete” in this sense. If you’re training for a half marathon, you’re doing plenty of distance running, and should fuel accordingly. And if you’re “just” lifting weights in the gym, but taking it seriously enough that you’re training regularly and working hard, you should consider eating in these ranges as well.

Dieting to lose weight is not only a popular American pastime, it’s also arguably good for at least some people's health. If you’ve been on a diet recently, or if you’re planning to go on one, you aren’t a person who should settle for the RDA either.

Research shows that protein intake (and strength training—they go together!) is important to maintain muscle mass when we’re losing weight. After all, you’re aiming for fat loss, not trying to get your muscles to waste away. Muscle loss is especially a concern with weight-loss drugs like Ozempic, but any dieter should be aware of this issue.

For example, this study found that diets ranging from 0.48 to 0.72 grams of protein per kg of body weight (that’s 82 to 123 grams for our 171-pound woman, 96 to 144 for our 200-pound man) resulted in less weight regain after the diet, and helped people to maintain muscle mass and feel more full while they were dieting.

And if you’re losing weight and exercising? The IAAF recommends that athletes who are “undertaking high-quality weight loss” need at least 0.72 grams per pound of bodyweight, and possibly as much as 1.09 grams per pound. That would be 186 grams for a 171-pound athlete, or 218 grams for a 200-pound athlete. Most people won’t need to go that high, and it’s unclear whether athletes need to go that high. But I’m including these numbers so you see how high the ranges actually go.

Ultimately, weight loss is widely understood to be more effective and have healthier results with higher protein intakes rather than lower ones. When people focus on just eating less, without thinking about what their diet actually consists of, it’s easy to forget about protein. But the evidence suggests that you should increase protein when you’re decreasing overall calories.

The idea that protein causes weight gain is a common talking point in those articles about “too much” protein, and it’s sort of true—but it also doesn’t mean what you think it means.

When you eat more food than your body needs, your body can store it as fat. That’s true no matter what the excess is made of—protein, carbs, fat, or even alcohol. The protein you eat gets used for many different things in your body. You can build it into muscle tissue, use it for growth and repair of different kinds of cells, and so on. You can also use it for energy—basically, burning it for the calories.

So if you were eating a perfectly balanced diet, and then decided to add an extra 100 grams of protein per day, then sure, a lot of that protein would be used for energy, and since we’d have excess energy, it would get stored as fat.

But if you ate more protein, but that protein replaced other foods in your diet, then there would be no excess calories to store. Nobody is saying you should chug a couple of protein shakes on top of your regular diet. They’re saying (I’m saying) that you should plan your meals and snacks to include more protein.

For example, if your regular lunch is a turkey-and-cheese sandwich with a side of chips, you could improve the protein content of your diet by adding more turkey to the sandwich and replacing the chips with an apple. Same total calories, but more protein. As long as your total calories for the day aren’t in excess of your needs, the “extra” protein won’t get stored as fat.

In general, high protein diets don’t have any serious health consequences. There’s a major exception, though: in some medical conditions, you may be told to limit your protein intake to protect your health.

For example, people with chronic kidney disease are often advised to use the RDA (0.36 grams per pound of body weight) as a maximum rather than a minimum. Your kidneys play a role in processing protein for excretion, so a lowered protein intake reduces the amount of work that a damaged kidney has to do. That said, once a person with chronic kidney disease begins dialysis, they may be advised to increase their protein intake for better health now that their body has help to handle the higher levels.

People with certain other disorders, like phenylketonuria and homocystinuria, may also be advised to eat a low-protein diet. Obviously, if you have one of these conditions, you should be getting your dietary advice from your medical team (ask for a referral to a dietitian!) rather than from general articles on the internet.

Besides those known medical issues, the occasional findings about eating “too much” protein tend to fit into the “X is good for you/X is bad for you” ricochet news cycle. They’re not holistic assessments of protein in general on health in general, but rather specific research questions that are still being figured out.

For example, this 2017 study found that a high-protein (and high-fiber) diet seemed to slightly worsen one measure of insulin resistance, but it also improved metabolic health and body composition. The researchers concluded that the subjects’ body chemistry was probably just responding appropriately to the changed nutrient content of their diet. A few years later, a study of high-BMI women with insulin resistance saw improvements to their insulin resistance on a high-protein diet.

Or to take another example, a study in 2024 found a link between high-protein diets and atherosclerosis. But if you look at what the researchers were actually studying, they were looking at how leucine (one amino acid found in protein) affects the mTOR biochemical pathway in certain types of white blood cells. By the way, that mTOR pathway is involved in a lot more body processes than atherosclerosis, and does a lot of good things too.

So are these results interesting, and worth further study? Definitely. Worth changing protein recommendations? Only if this effect turns out (1) to actually lead to worse health outcomes, and (2) to outweigh the known benefits of higher protein. The body of evidence doesn’t yet support lowering protein recommendations, nor adding an upper limit.

So if protein is good for us, and most of us can’t really get “too much,” why are so many people arguing that we’re overdoing it? I think part of the reason is just misunderstanding (the writers don’t tend to have a background in nutrition and especially not in sports nutrition), but more often, I think they’re talking about a different issue entirely.

Often the “too much protein” stuff is just a way of talking about the environmental effects of meat consumption or dairy farming. People making this argument are trying to pry the double cheeseburgers out of our hands and reassure us that we’ll be okay. I don’t think an attack on protein is an appropriate way to make that point, since plant-based proteins exist and are a fine alternative. But I understand where they’re coming from.

Ultimately, if you’re trying to make the argument that we’re eating “too much” protein for our health, you really can’t do that without some evidence that we’re eating so much protein that it’s harming our health on a widespread level. And that evidence just doesn’t exist.

#3506. RHOSLC’s Jen Shah Reacts to Seeing Elizabeth Holmes' New Documentary

The Real Housewives of Salt Lake City alum Jen Shah is ready to see even more about her former prison pal Elizabeth Holmes.

“Thank you, @A24, for hosting a private screening of You Can See Everything for me and my guests on Friday,” Shah, 53, wrote via Instagram on Monday, November 16. “I watched it through the lens of my own friendship with Elizabeth. For everyone who’s been asking what I thought, consider this a little preview. You’ll hear from me soon. 🎬#YouCanSeeEverything.”

Holmes, 42, and her partner, Billy Evans, were the subjects of a nearly three-hour film, which followed their family in the 34 days leading up to the start of her federal prison sentence in May 2023.

In January 2022, Holmes was found guilty of three counts of wire fraud and one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud against investors.

She is currently serving time at the Federal Prison Camp in Bryan, Texas, which is the same facility where Shah served nearly three years for her role in a nationwide telemarketing scheme. (The former Bravo star pleaded guilty in 2022 and was released in December 2025. Shah finished her home confinement in August.)

Previously, Shah’s rep shared a glimpse into how his client built a relationship with Holmes behind bars.

“They’re friends. They’re both rehabilitating and have bonded over being on this journey of positive change,” Chris Giovanni told People in September 2023. “Their situations brought them together, and they have a good understanding of one another. They’re getting through it together.”

Giovanni continued, “Jen’s given her a lot of advice. Jen gets all the ladies together, and they rally behind her while she teaches them fitness moves, and Elizabeth has been there right along with them.”

While watching You Can See Everything, Shah sported a yellow dress with a faux fur coat. She completed the look with knee-high leopard-print boots and a matching clutch.

“Movie night 🎬🖤 Thank you, @A24,” she wrote via Instagram while posing with her friends at the VIP screening. “#YouCanSeeEverything.”

After Shah served her time, some fans may be wondering if the reality star could ever return to RHOSLC.

According to original cast member Lisa Barlow, it may not make the most sense because Shah isn’t the closest with the current group of ladies.

​​“I want her to be happy. I want her to be thriving. I want her to be with her children and her husband and her mother and everybody else,” Barlow, 51, said during a July episode of the “Therapuss” podcast. “I think that’s important. I think she’s really sorry. She did restitution, and she’s paying for her mistake.”

“I think she talks to Meredith [Marks] every now and then,” Barlow continued. “She’ll call Meredith randomly, or Meredith will check in with her. But I don’t think anyone has a deep friendship with her.”

#3505. Ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Breaks His Silence, Says He Would Come Back

Jensen Huang, the co-founder of Nvidia who was recently ousted as CEO after he admitted to having an affair with someone that US intelligence believes could by a spy for China, has now said he is open to returning to the company.

In his first public statement since his resignation from Nvidia, Huang told The Wall Street Journal that he is aware of the "outpouring of calls" from Nvidia employees, investors, business partners, and customers for him to come back as CEO. He would come back, if asked.

"If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO," he said.

This statement came a day after a source told CNBC that the Nvidia board is not considering bringing Huang back as CEO.

Huang released his statement on social media, saying, "Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me."

His statement added: "I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen is one of the greatest gifts and proudest moments of my life. Nvidia has been my life’s work. Building it into the company it is today alongside my colleagues has been a privilege and an honor. Nowhere but in America could a company like Nvidia be possible. I love our country, and I love Nvidia."

Huang acknowledged that he "did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at Nvidia" and owned up to making "serious mistakes in my personal life." He said he created problems for Nvidia's Board of Directors and he said he "deeply" regrets that. "I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation," he said.

Nvidia was the world's biggest company by market cap until the company's stock price began to crash in October, and it fell further after the controversies came to light, including multiple affairs beyond the one with the alleged spy.

To be sure, Nvidia remains a juggernaut--it's currently the No. 2 biggest company in the world, with a market cap of $3.75 trillion. Only Apple, with a market cap above $4 trillion, is bigger than Nvidia.

The New York Times and other media outlets reported that Huang had a romantic relationship with the former CEO of the AI company Megaspeed, Alice Huang (no relation). US intelligence sources claim that Alice Huang was a spy for China's Ministry of State Security, though China officially denies this narrative and says it's an effort by the US to smear China.

Megaspeed, for its part, said Alice Huang left the company in 2025 and denied any wrongdoing in the Nvidia scandal.

The Nvidia controversies have led to turmoil in the stock market, in part because Nvidia is one of the "Mag 7" companies that are driving growth in the US. Some of the information coming to light suggests that Nvidia's accounting and export control compliance are not buttoned up, and this has fueled further concerns about the growth potential and returns on investment for the AI trade. Numerous other technology and AI stocks have dropped in value significantly since the Nvidia news broke.

Nvidia's interim boss is CFO Colette Kress, who is expected to lead Nvidia's earnings call today, November 17. The earnings report will be closely watched and highly scrutinized--keep checking back with GameSpot for the latest.

Is Season 30 of The Voice making me a little bit country?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Spoiler alert! This story discusses the Live Shows' Y2K Week on The Voice Season 30, which aired November 16. Episodes are available to stream the day after they air with a Peacock subscription.

The Voice Live Shows are in full swing on the 2026 TV schedule, and have been narrowing down Season 30’s incredible talent to the Top 10. In the latest episode of NBC’s long-running singing competition, they continued to pay tribute to the hits of the late ‘90s and early 2000s with Part 2 of Y2K Week with Team Riley and Team Kelly. From the Goo Goo Dolls hit “Iris” to The Chicks’ tune “Cowboy Take Me Away” to Keane’s indie rock track “Somewhere Only We Know,” there was a blend of musical genres that traveled all over the map and gave a glimpse into how challenging it will be to continue to cut singers, moving ever closer to the winning coach and star. I need to talk about the country music.

While veteran coach Kelly Clarkson knows firsthand what it takes to win, having taken the title four times in nine seasons, including during her first season as a coach, The Voice newbie Riley Green should not be deterred, as Season 30 is proving to be anyone’s game. Take it from this rock music fan, who’s quickly being won over by one of Team Riley’s country singers. Sure, Kelly has 14-year-old and 16-year-old powerhouse singers on her team – Brianna Cameron, who sang “Reflection” by Christina Aguilera, and Koumba Diallo, who sang the Alicia Key’s hit “Fallin’” – but it’s the teenager on Team Riley that is making the best case for crooning his way to the finals.

Country singer Joe Henley (not to be confused with Joe Hendry) is only 19 and had never played a gig before auditioning for The Voice, which only makes his journey on the show more impressive. After grabbing the attention of Kelly Clarkson and Riley Green during the Blind Auditions, making it through the Battle Rounds, and hands-down reclaiming his spot on Team Riley for Cut Week, he took on Lee Ann Womack’s “I Hope You Dance.”

It's one of those country tracks that has crossed over into the mainstream, with deeply emotional lyrics that I’ve personally connected with and that always pull on my heartstrings when I hear it. It was an unexpected choice to hear the #1 hit covered by a male, but Joe crushed it, reinforcing the possibility that he really could win it all in Season 30.

For a rock girlie to be saying that is a big deal! Just saying!

Sure, Team Adam and Team Kelly have the numbers advantage, with three singers still left on each of their teams while the other coaches only have two. I can’t believe I’m still on the country train, but I actually think that Team has a very good chance of winning in his first season, whether that’s with Joe Henley or the duo Ferryn & Brinkley. He’s proven to have an excellent ear for talent and has given great advice and guidance to his team as their performances have only gotten stronger.

While we already know the competition series will be shaking things up with Season 31’s The Voice: Celebrity, we won’t learn who will take it all in Season 30, and if that could be country singer Joe Henley, until December. So, be sure to keep tuning in to NBC on Mondays at 8 p.m. ET until then.

#3503. All The Game Awards 2026 Nominees Revealed

It's almost time for The Game Awards to kick off a night of trailers and appreciation for the 2026 gaming year, but right now, it's time to see who's in the running to earn some well-deserved kudos. The 2026 Game Awards will be livestreamed from the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles on December 10, and nominees for the best games across several categories have been announced.

Like previous years, the nominees have been chosen by a global jury of media publications and creator outlets--including GameSpot--and were announced through a dedicated livestream.

Leading the nominations is Grand Theft Auto 6 with eight nominations, Control Resonant and Resident Evil Requiem with six nominations each, and Phantom Blade Zero has earned an impressive five nominations. Big Walk, 007 First Light, and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake have also earned plenty of nods, with four nominations each.

Here's a closer look at which games are in the running for several of the biggest prizes at The Game Awards this year.

Game of the Year

The best of the best for 2026, the game that excelled across multiple creative and technical fields.

  • 007 First Light
  • Control Resonant
  • Grand Theft Auto 6
  • Phantom Blade Zero
  • Resident Evil Requiem
  • The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time

Best Game Direction

For the game that was built with an outstanding creative vision and executed it through polished direction and design.

  • Control Resonant
  • Grand Theft Auto 6
  • Phantom Blade Zero
  • Pragmata
  • Resident Evil Requiem

Best Narrative

Awarded to the game that not only offers the best story of the year, but also delivers its with exceptional storytelling skills.

  • 007 First Light
  • Control Resonant
  • Grand Theft Auto 6
  • Resident Evil Requiem
  • The Blood of Dawnwalker

Best Art Direction

Video game graphics have come a long way over the years, and this award recognizes the 2026 game that featured incredible artistic design and animation.

  • Control Resonant
  • Grand Theft Auto 6
  • Mouse P.I. For Hire
  • Phantom Blade Zero
  • The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time

Best Score and Music

Great game visuals also need equally good audio, and this award is for the best music in a game, pulled from its score, original songs and/or a licensed soundtrack.

  • Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve
  • Grand Theft Auto 6
  • Mixtape
  • Phantom Blade Zero
  • The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time

Best Audio Design

Sticking with sound, this award goes to the game with the best in-game audio and sound design.

  • Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve
  • Control Resonant
  • Grand Theft Auto 6
  • Resident Evil Requiem
  • Star Wars: Galactic Racer

Best Performance

We've also seen the rise of video game thespians in modern gaming, and this award honors the individual for their voice-over acting and performance capture.

  • Patrick Gibson -- 007 First Light
  • Angela Sant'Albano --  Resident Evil Requiem
  • Liam McIntyre -- Marvel's Wolverine
  • Manni L. Perez -- Grand Theft Auto 6
  • Rahul Kohli -- Saros

Games for Impact

Video games are capable of delivering profound messages, and the Games for Impact award is handed out to the one title that gave players a thought-provoking experience.

  • Big Walk
  • Cairn
  • Forever Ago
  • Life is Strange Reunion
  • Lily's World XD
  • Mixtape

Best Ongoing Game

Live-service games have continued to be a big draw throughout 2026, and the Best Ongoing Game award is handed out to the title that has shown outstanding development of ongoing content for its players.

  • Arc Raiders
  • Final Fantasy 14 Online
  • Fortnite
  • No Man's Sky
  • The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt

Best Community Support

In recognition of the game and studio that has provided excellent community support and transparency.

  • Crimson Desert
  • Helldivers 2
  • No Man's Sky
  • The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt
  • Warframe

Best Independent Game

The top prize for indie games at The Game Awards, this one is for the smaller, risky projects that found critical acclaim in 2026.

  • Big Walk
  • Cairn
  • Denshattack
  • Mewgenics
  • Mina the Hollower

Best Debut Indie Game

Another big prize for indie developers, Best Indie Debut Game is awarded to the independent studio that produced and shipped its first game in 2026.

  • Dressmaker
  • Esoteric Ebb
  • Orbitals
  • Replaced
  • Silver Pines

Best Mobile Game

Exactly what you expect, this is the award for the best game that's playable on a mobile device.

  • Arknights Endfield
  • Monster Hunter Outlanders
  • Neverness to Everness
  • Pokemon Champions

Best VR/AR game

Likewise, this award goes to the best game that's playable across virtual, mixed or augmented reality, irrespective of platform.

Best Action Game

It's all about action with this award, which focuses on the fine art of crafting exhilarating combat.

Best Action/Adventure Game

This prize goes to the game that not only offers polished combat, but also slick traversal and puzzle-solving.

Best Role-Playing Game

Another genre favorite, the award for Best RPG recognizes the game that gave players rich character customization and progression across their journey, and it also includes nominees for MMORPGs.

For the game that was appropriate for family play, irrespective of genre or platform.

Given to the best traditional or non-traditional sports and racing game of the year.

Best Multiplayer Game

Awarded to the game that nails online multiplayer gameplay and design--including co-op and massively multiplayer experiences.

  • Big Walk

Best Adaptation

Whether it's a movie, TV series, or podcast adaptation of a video game, the award for Best Adaptation will recognize it for how creatively and authentically the source material is adapted as a piece of entertainment.

Best User Creation

Innovation in Accessibility

Most Anticipated Game

Set engines to hype! The award for Most Anticipated Game--which is for a game coming after December 10, 2026--recognizes the upcoming release that has fans excited for the future and how the video game medium could possibly be pushed forward to new heights.

Best Esports Game
