#3502. Five Race-Day Smartwatch Hacks Every Marathon Runner Should Know

I love my Garmin Forerunner 970, but the fact is, most runners don't need all the features it has to offer. In fact, for most road races, you can get by with whatever smartwatch you already own—as long as you know how to use it. If you've got a marathon or half-marathon coming up, these five tricks will only take a few minutes to set up, and they can save you from one of many of the small-but-avoidable disasters that can derail a good race.

Nothing spikes pre-race anxiety like standing in a corral of hundreds of people watching your watch fail to latch onto a signal. Tall buildings, crowded starts, and a sea of other devices make the first minute of GPS unreliable, which can leave your opening mileage pace wildly off.

The fix is simple: start the GPS search early. Step outside, into the open, as soon as you've dropped your bag, and select your run activity at least 10 to 15 minutes before the starting gun. If your watch supports multi-band or dual-frequency GPS, turn it on in the activity settings, since it's noticeably better in dense downtown starts. Then, don't press start until the gun goes off (or you cross the line, if you want chip-accurate pacing).

Bonus tip: If you're in a start corral with a long wait, you can lock the signal and then pause the activity screen. Just remember to hit start when you actually take off.

Multiple data screens are great for training, but overwhelming during a race. Too many numbers invite overthinking, and seeing the "wrong" number at mile two can lead you into a very stressful mile ten.

My recommendation is to build a dedicated race screen with three to four fields at most:

Lap pace or average lap pace (not instant pace, which jumps around constantly with GPS)

Distance or lap distance, so you know where you are relative to the mile markers

Heart rate, especially in the early miles when adrenaline tempts you to go out too fast

Elapsed time, for splits against your goal

Keep it clean and stripped down, and avoid the temptation to add cadence, power, vertical oscillation, and everything else. You can always review those stats during your cool-down.

A text from your boss at mile 14 is nobody's idea of a good time. Before race day, switch your watch to Do Not Disturb or Airplane mode, or turn on a dedicated activity mode that blocks notifications. This also saves battery, which matters if your marathon is going to take you four-plus hours.

After blocking the outside world, you can set race-specific alerts, like a high heart-rate alert to keep you honest in the first half. I also know runners who set a recurring time or distance alert for fueling—say, every 30 to 40 minutes, or every 5 miles—so remembering to down a gel or a sports drink doesn't depend on your fading brain.

Here's one thing I learn the hard way, every time: Your watch will almost always say you've run farther than the race course says you have. Race courses are measured along the shortest possible route, but along the way, you'll weave around people, take wide turns, and generally add extra distance. I've run marathons where my watch reads closer to 26.6 miles (nearly an extra half mile), so my "on pace" watch is actually behind my chip time.

The hack: Ignore the watch's auto-lap and press the lap button manually at each mile marker (or at every kilometer marker, if that's what the course uses). This gives you pace data aligned to the official course, not the satellite's best guess. It also gives you a quick mental check against your plan. If you've set up your watch for it, display average lap pace, then glance at it a few hundred meters after each marker to see how you're tracking. And don't panic if your watch beeps for a mile before you pass the marker—trust the course and your lap presses, and do your best to ignore the mismatched distance adding up.

Rain, sweat, high-fives, and a hasty cup grab at an aid station can all trigger accidental taps on a touchscreen watch. Few things are worse than discovering at mile 18 that you accidentally paused, ended, or switched screens on your activity. So before the race, turn on your watch's screen lock, so a stray touch doesn't do anything.

If your watch has a configurable wake gesture, consider turning it off to save battery, and set the backlight to a short timeout. While we're talking watch-wearing protocol, remember to wear it snugly, one finger-width above your wrist bone, for a better heart-rate reading as you sweat. Finally, if your watch has one, use the post-race auto-save reminder. (Otherwise, do your best to hit stop after you cross the finish line.)

Again, you don't need the most premium running-specific watch ahead of race day. If you have time, test these hacks on a long run, so that you're not wasting any precious mental energy during the big day.

#3501. Meghan Markle's Dad Faces Child Abuse Charges in Philippines After Arrest

Meghan Markle’s estranged father, Thomas Markle Sr., is facing child abuse charges in the Philippines.

Thomas Sr., 82, has been charged with two counts of offering, distributing, selling, exporting or importing any form of child sexual abuse or exploitation material and one count of possessing such material, according to ITV.

Meghan’s half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr., alleged in October that he found storage boxes containing suspected child sexual abuse material (CSAM) at his father’s home in the Philippines. Thomas Jr. told The Sun at the time he turned over the material to local authorities. Thomas Sr. denied the allegations, calling them “sick.”

Earlier this month, Thomas Sr. was arrested in Florida on a federal charge of possession of child pornography. He was released on bond the same day.

The Central District of California U.S. Attorney’s Office claimed at the time that investigators found material depicting child sexual abuse in two storage units registered to Thomas Sr. in Los Angeles. The material allegedly contains photographs of a man believed to be Thomas Sr. with a young nude girl.

“The FBI and our partners have arrested Thomas Markle Sr. after an FBI investigation revealed he was in possession of Child Sexual Abuse Material (CSAM),” FBI Director Kash Patel claimed in a statement.

Patel continued, “Mr. Markle allegedly targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his criminal actions. Working with our Justice Department partners, our agents moved quickly, identified and located the explicit material, and arrested Mr. Markle in Florida. This FBI will use every single resource at our disposal to protect innocent kids — any predator who targets children will have zero safe haven in this country or anywhere they try to hide.”

Thomas Sr. was arrested again earlier this month after he cut off his ankle monitor.

“At a hearing today in Tampa, U.S. Magistrate Judge Lindsay Saxe Griffin of the Middle District of Florida ordered Thomas Wayne Markle detained (jailed without bond),” a spokesperson for the Department of Justice confirmed to Us in a statement. “Markle cut off his ankle bracelet at 1:45 a.m. EST today. Federal law enforcement arrested him later today. Markle is in federal custody.”

Meghan, for her part, revealed in a statement last month that she initially learned about the allegations against Thomas Sr. in 2018. (The pair have been estranged since her wedding to Prince Harry that same year.)

“In 2018, a letter was sent to the Metropolitan Police and Royalty and Specialist Protection. That letter was subsequently shared with me. It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated,” Meghan said.

She continued, “I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children was for one reason: to protect them. I trusted that the authorities were doing the same for other families.”

If you or someone you know is experiencing child abuse, call or text Child Help Hotline at 1-800-422-4453.

The second half of November is usually quiet for several reasons when it comes to new game releases–and one other big reason–but Xbox Game Pass subscribers can look forward to several new titles to close off the month--and eight games will also be leaving Game Pass on November 30.

Microsoft has announced a handful of new additions to the Game Pass library, including a kid-friendly game to kick things off and a sneak peek at some sporty fun for the first week of December. Other highlights this month include Call of the Elder Gods for a Lovecraftian puzzle-adventure, High on Life 2 joining Game Pass Premium, and Roadside Research, which is all about aliens trying to run a gas station while poorly disguised as humans.

If you're looking for action, Sniper Ghost Warrior Contracts 2 is worth checking out. All the thrill of long-distance sniping, with a surprising amount of close-quarters stealth gameplay as well. Also recommended is Motorslice, where you'll get to parkour through the ruins of a brutalist megastructure, climb massive bosses in tense fights, and hunt down living construction equipment.

Starting in December, you can get Freestyle Football 2, which is an online multiplayer soccer game built around 5v5 matches. We already have that game in the form of Rematch from Sifu developer Sloclap, but if you want a different spin on that soccer idea, take a quick look.

#3498. Brad Pitt and GF Ines de Ramon Hold Hands During Rare Red Carpet Appearance

Brad Pitt and his girlfriend, Ines de Ramon, couldn’t contain their smiles while walking the red carpet.

The couple stepped out on Monday, November 16, to attend the premiere of Netflix’s The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth in Los Angeles, which Pitt, 62, stars in as the titular character. Pitt and de Ramon, 33, held hands on their date night.

For the event, Pitt opted for a navy sweater and pants with a double-breasted coat and accessorized with a pair of sunglasses. De Ramon, for her part, stunned in a cream dress with cutouts at the waist and a plunging neckline. She styled her hair down in loose curls as she beamed with pride at the world premiere.

Pitt and de Ramon have been linked since 2022 when they were first spotted joining friends Cindy Crawford and Rande Gerber at a Bono concert at the Orpheum Theatre in Los Angeles. Two years later, Pitt and de Ramon debuted their romance at the British Grand Prix. Pitt, for his part, has denied that the 2024 appearance was part of a planned promotional event for his 2025 film F1.

“No, dude, it’s not that calculated,” he recalled to GQ in a May 2025 profile. “If you’re living … oh, my God, how exhausting would that be? If you’re living with making those kinds of calculations? No, life just evolves. Relationships evolve.”

The pair have since given glimpses of their relationship, with Pitt opening up about how he and de Ramon enjoyed a date-night at Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce’s star-studded wedding in July.

“You mean, the wedding of the century? Let me tell you, that was such an amazing night,” Pitt told Entertainment Tonight in September when asked about the phone-free event. “I think we were there [for] 10 hours, maybe 12.”

Pitt and de Ramon matched in coordinating black formalwear at the event, which was held at New York City’s Madison Square Garden.

“It was so thoughtful and well-planned and really moving and great fun,” Pitt gushed. “But it was big, and at one point, I lost her in the melee on the dance floor.”

But the pair reunited quickly. “Not long. There’s always someone to go, ‘That way,’” he said, pretending to point in opposite directions.

Prior to his relationship with de Ramon, Pitt was previously married to Jennifer Aniston from 2000 to 2005 and later to Angelina Jolie, with whom he shares six children, from 2014 to 2019.

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

The Roborock Qrevo Edge 2 robot vacuum and mop is down to $799.99 from $1,299.99 in an early Black Friday deal, saving you $500 and bringing it to its lowest price to date. Much of its appeal comes from a slim 3.1-inch profile that lets it reach under beds, sofas, and other low furniture where taller robot vacuums often can’t fit. It manages this with a feature Roborock calls RetractSense, which checks the clearance as the robot approaches a tight gap and lowers the laser navigation tower into the body, leaving a camera with a 100-degree field of view to guide it underneath.

Beyond its low profile, the Qrevo Edge 2 pairs 25,000Pa of suction with a split DuoDivide main brush that guides hair toward the suction opening, so long strands and pet fur are less likely to end up wound around the roller. Edges get extra attention too, since its FlexiArm Arc side brush reaches out into corners while its mop module swivels to get closer to walls, with the two mop pads spinning at 200 RPM as they work. It also adjusts its cleaning based on whether it encounters dry or wet dirt, boosting suction for dust and lifting its main brush over spills. For all that adaptability on the floor, getting between rooms can be trickier—the robot lacks an adjustable chassis to lift itself over obstacles, so it can struggle with thresholds higher than 0.8 inches.

Once a cleaning run wraps up, most of the upkeep happens at the dock, which washes and dries the mop pads and empties dust into a bag rated for up to 65 days. That said, its onboard water tank is relatively small at 2.3 fluid ounces, potentially requiring extra trips to the dock during larger mopping jobs. There's also no dedicated cleaning solution tank, meaning you'll have to add approved cleaning additives manually to the fresh water. The rest of the fine-tuning happens in the Roborock app, where you can set cleaning schedules, adjust suction power and water flow, and choose how the robot handles carpets.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, Nov. 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by Dec. 2, 2026.

Yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, and we vet our deals to make sure they’re the best ones. You can also refer to guides like our live blog that have already done all of the vetting for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

#3495. What Does It Take For World Of Warcraft To Be Nominated At The Game Awards?

The nominees for 2026's The Game Awards have been revealed, and just like every year before it, there is a glaring omission in the Best Ongoing Game Category: World of Warcraft.

This year's nominees are Arc Raiders, Fortnite, No Man's Sky, The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt, and Final Fantasy 14 Online. Of particular note is Square Enix's MMORPG, which has been nominated in the category every year since 2021. Developer Blizzard's MMO, on the other hand, is nowhere to be seen. 

WoW is among the most popular live-service games in industry history and has been for 22 years. Blizzard releases new expansions for its MMORPG every other year like clockwork and has done so for over two decades. It reintroduced the old-school version of the MMO, WoW Classic, in 2019 to huge acclaim from the game's passionate community.

In the years that followed, it continued to add new expansions to the modern version of WoW, adding highly requested features like account-wide unlocks and new endgame solo content. For WoW Classic, it re-released past expansions, added official servers and support for a permadeath mode popular among the game's community, and ran experimental seasons that added new content to the classic version of the game. Taken all together, the various versions of WoW have millions of players.

Earlier this year, Blizzard released Midnight, the latest expansion for modern WoW that added player housing to the MMO for the first time. A few weeks ago, it released WoW: Forever, the third major version of the MMO. Built on the bones of WoW Classic, Forever is intended to be an ongoing game that will add new content and changes to the old-school version of WoW, existing alongside the modern game. Forever was the biggest launch in WoW history in terms of concurrent players, Blizzard said.

Yet, since 2017, WoW has never even been nominated in Best Ongoing Game, a category that serves to put a spotlight on titles that continue to receive new content and evolve the experience over time--something Blizzard wrote the book on with WoW.

WoW being omitted this year in particular is more baffling than any time before, as Blizzard not only released a brand-new expansion, but also an entirely new version of the game that players have dreamed about for years. On the other hand, Final Fantasy 14's new expansion, Evercold, doesn't release until 2027, even if the game has received significant content updates over the course of the year. 

Even other Blizzard games have been nominated in this category multiple times over the years. Overwatch won Best Ongoing Game in 2017 and was nominated again in 2018. Diablo 4 earned a nomination in 2024 with the release of its first expansion, Vessel of Hatred. 

Meanwhile, it seems like nothing WoW does is enough to warrant attention. There is, of course, a simple answer to why this seems to be the case--nobody, or at least very few, on the The Game Awards voting jury plays, or keeps up to date, with WoW.

That's a shame, because if there was any year where WoW deserved to be nominated, it's this year. Forever is the culmination of an entire community's dream of having an ongoing, new version of classic WoW, and Midnight continues the philosophy of player-friendly changes first added in 2024's The War Within expansion. There are now more ways to play WoW than ever before, each receiving unprecedented support and updates. In fact, players in the modern version of WoW have been complaining that there's perhaps too much to do and that content updates are maybe too frequent. 

This is all to say that it feels like WoW deserves just a little recognition. It's been running for over two decades at this point, and in that time has in many ways defined what an "ongoing game" is and can be. 2026 has been a banner year for WoW, and its future is looking brighter than ever. It deserved a moment in the spotlight. Maybe next year (though I wouldn't bet on it).

#3494. Everything You Missed at Vanity Fair's Screening Room Los Angeles

Not even a nationwide FAA ground stop could prevent movie stars from descending upon Los Angeles for the Governor Awards and Vanity Fair's first annual Screening Room this past weekend. Hosted at LACMA's brand-new Steve Tisch theater, actors including Matt Damon, Penélope Cruz, Pedro Pascal, Andrew Garfield, John Leguizamo, and Andrew Scott joined Q&As to discuss their films and pressing topics in the entertainment industry. AI was a major theme throughout the weekend, and not just at the screening for Artificial, as actors and directors spoke about the desire to continue making things that feel “real” and “made by humans.” Following each screening, talent mingled with guests to continue the conversations.

The weekend began with a screening of Wild Horse Nine, director Martin McDonagh's dark comedy starring John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell as CIA agents behind the plan to overthrow the Chilean government in 1973. Following the showing, VF's Senior Hollywood Correspondent Rebecca Ford led a Q&A with McDonagh, Malkovich and Mariana di Girolamo, who also stars in the film.

Next up was Elsinore, which tells the story of Scottish actor Ian Charleson (played by Andrew Scott) who attempts to perform Hamlet at the National Theatre while secretly living with AIDS. In conversation with VF's Rebecca Ford, Scott, his costar Billie Piper, and writer Stephen Beresford, Scott discussed what it was like to tell Charleson's story. “I think … why the film is so moving is because [Charleson’s] not wallowing at any point. He was insanely courageous,” he said.

Come Friday night, audiences gathered for a screening of the acclaimed Spanish language drama La Bola Negra, which follows several gay men whose lives are bound together by their identities, love and loss, and the looming presence of the Spanish Civil War. It stars Miguel Bernardeau, Álvaro Lafuente Calvo (the singer known as Guitarricadelafuente) in his first major acting role, Carlos Gonzalez, Milo Quifes and Penélope Cruz.

After the film, Ricky Martin moderated a panel conversation featuring directors Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo, and stars Cruz, Guitarricadelafuente and Bernardeau. Calvo talked about how they are all riding high on the film's positive reception. “Creating this sense of community and hearing people saying, ‘This movie changed me. It really made me understand things about me.’ The power that art has, we forget it, but then this happens and … the rest is a dream. The rest we're living is a dream.”

Saturday's slate of programming began with a live recording of Vanity Fair's “Notes on a Scene” with Matt Damon, John Leguizamo and Himesh Patel, who recounted what it was like to film The Odyssey with director Christopher Nolan. Next, Seth Rogen joined Screening Room for “Scene Selection,” taking the audience through what it was like shooting Freaks and Geeks, Knocked Up, The Studio and more.

Later that afternoon, Pedro Pascal and Tony Gilroy joined the festivities following a screening of their new film Behemoth!, which tells the story of a prodigal cellist who returns to Los Angeles and to score films after decades performing symphonic work around the country. In conversation with VF's West Coast Editor John Ross for Behemoth!, Pascal spoke about how making the film gave him “a tremendous amount of hope.” “We weren't making money on this movie. Nobody was. And you had the most expensive people involved in this film because of their talent and their experience. So there was just this purity of love in the work from every single department, and that was incredibly contagious," he said.

Come Saturday night, guests were eager to see Luca Guadagnino's Artificial, which follows the rise of OpenAI and a few of its pioneers: Sam Altman, Elon Musk, Ilya Sutskever and Mira Murati. Guadagnino was joined by cast members Andrew Garfield (who plays Altman), Yura Borisov (who plays Sutskever) and Monica Barbaro (who plays Murati) for a post-screening conversation with VF's Global Editorial Director Mark Guiducci. “It's important to try to understand because as Luca said, these are the kids that have the reins of the future and we've somehow allowed them to just hold onto them. And we've kind of given our autonomy over or it's been taken from behind our backs,” Garfield said.

On Sunday, Cruz joined director Florian Zeller for a screening of the film Bunker, a timely film about a famous architect, played by Javier Bardem, and his wife Sofia, played by Cruz, who is asked to build a bunker for a tech giant. This sparks a rift in their marriage as the couple examines how success and monetary gain have affected their lives. Cruz, who is having a huge year with The Invite and La Bola Negra alongside this film, expressed her excitement that younger audiences are coming back to theaters and are looking for films that don't “over-explain."

The inaugural edition of Vanity Fair’s Screening Room paired this year’s most compelling films with a slate of programming that included post-screening panels and conversations with actors and filmmakers. Following the program in Los Angeles, Vanity Fair’s Screening Room will arrive in New York, where screenings and events will take place at Cherry Lane Theatre from December 4–6.

#3493. Man Killed Ex-GF and New BF in Murder-Suicide Following History of Abuse

A heartbroken mother shared details about her daughter’s abusive relationship with her ex-boyfriend after police said he allegedly killed her and her new boyfriend in a horrific murder-suicide.

Verchna Philippe and her boyfriend, Darnell McLean, were fatally shot by her ex Scloiwen Jean-Baptiste while they were driving in Miami Gardens in the early hours of Sunday, November 15. Investigators said that after Jean-Baptiste, 27, pulled up to their vehicle in an Uber, he shot Philippe, 25, and she crashed into a fence. McLean, 25, then tried to run away, but Jean-Baptiste chased him and shot him.

Jean-Baptiste returned to the car and shot Philippe a second time before he died by suicide.

McLean and Jean-Baptiste died at the scene, while Philippe was taken to Aventura Hospital for treatment before she died from her injuries.

“She was my right hand, my everything,” Philippe’s mother, Nadege Jean Pierre, told NBC Miami of her late daughter.

Jean Pierre explained that she had waited all night for her daughter to come home, and she didn’t learn what happened until detectives reported to her home the next morning.

“I asked, ‘Is she dead? What happened to my daughter? Where is Verchna?'” she recalled.

Jean Pierre went on to reflect on her daughter’s relationship with Jean-Baptiste, whom police said had a criminal history that dated back to 2015.

“He is a psychopath; he is a maniac,” Jean Pierre said, claiming that Jean-Baptiste has threatened Philippe in the past. “He was obsessed with my daughter.”

Police said that he threatened to kill her in 2024 and also stabbed her during a 2025 incident, according to the outlet.

Jean Pierre said that the stabbing incident happened when Philippe was getting into an Uber and Jean-Baptiste jumped in behind her. “She tried to take the knife from him, but he refused, and he stabbed my daughter,” she said.

McLean’s mother, who asked to not be publicly named, also opened up about the tragedy while speaking to the outlet. “I don’t have words to say how deep it hurts,” she said. “You took my life when you took my son’s life.”

The 75-inch Hisense U6SF Pro has dropped to $747.97 from $1,399.99 ahead of Amazon’s Black Friday sale—bringing it to its lowest price to date. The rest of the U6 Pro lineup is discounted as well, so you can pick up the same TV in sizes from 55 inches to a massive 100 inches, for anyone with the room for something closer to a home-theater-sized screen. Whichever size you choose, you’ll get free delivery to the room of choice—a service that normally costs $19.99. As for the TV itself, it’s a 2026 model that sits below the U7SG (also on sale for $1,297.99, from $1,999.99) in Hisense's lineup as the brand's entry point into Mini LED, pairing a 4K panel and local dimming with a matte, anti-reflective coating meant to cut down on glare, notes this PCMag review.

For a budget set, the U6 Pro gets a lot right when it comes to picture quality—its high peak brightness helps it hold up during a sunny afternoon in a living room with big windows, so a daytime football game or cooking show won’t look washed out, while its excellent contrast and effective local dimming keep dark scenes looking deep when you settle in for a movie at night. It also does a good job cleaning up lower-quality content, which is useful for older cable broadcasts or compressed YouTube videos—and its Fire TV interface makes it easy to jump between those kinds of content and the major streaming services without needing a separate streaming device.

The U6 Pro also brings plenty to the table for gaming, with HDMI 2.1, VRR, ALLM, and a 144Hz refresh rate that PC gamers can push to 240Hz at a lower 1080p resolution. That said, the panel’s slow response time and poor motion performance can reportedly make fast-moving scenes look noticeably blurry. Viewing angles are limited too, with the picture losing quality fairly quickly when you move off-center—and its built-in speakers aren’t particularly impressive either, so a soundbar could be worth budgeting for.

#3491. This GTA 6-Inspired Keycap Set Will Make The Wait For A PC Version Slightly Easier

Grand Theft Auto 6 is now just a couple of hours away in some parts of the world. That is, if you're planning to play on either Xbox or PlayStation. The wait for a PC version is still ongoing, with Rockstar yet to indicate when it plans to release that port. In the meantime, however, you can start ensuring that your setup is at least ready for when it arrives.

High-end keycap manufacturer GMK has revealed a new set that is clearly inspired by GTA 6 and Vice City, without explicitly mentioning either. The new set, named Neon Vice, features black keycaps with an array of colored alphas and numerical keys, all drawing from the pink, orange, and purple colors of Rockstar's impending sequel. Novelty keycaps include images of speedboats across choppy water, palm trees, and alligators, and the Vice City skyline.

Like most GMK sets, the keycaps are constructed from double-shot ABS plastic, which should ensure fantastic legibility with use over time. What isn't normal is the price, however. GMK keycap sets are priced at a premium, and Neon Vice is no exception. Expect to pay $170 for the base kit, and an additional $45 if you want the novelty keys on top of that. Preorders open for the kit today across multiple vendors around the world.

That's a lot more than the game itself, so if you haven't been bitten by the custom keyboard bug, it's probably best to just continue waiting. Thankfully the gap between console and PC versions for GTA 6 might not be as large as previous Rockstar titles, with a report suggesting that it might arrive in early 2027. If you are playing on console you can pre-load the game right now ahead of its launch, which will start for lucky players in New Zealand very soon.

What does the future hold for DC Studios?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

To say that DC Studios is in the midst of a big change would be a major understatement. It was announced a little over a week ago that in the aftermath of the Warner Bros./Paramount merger, James Gunn and Peter Safran would step down as co-CEOs of the studio. As a result, film producer (and Marvel Studios alum) Jeremy Latcham will lead the brand moving forward. There may, however, now be reason to believe that DC may be leaving WB and by extension, parent company Skydance. This is all due to some recent rumors.

A common claim that’s been reported in the aftermath of the Gunn/Safran news is that Skydance has acquired a lot of Warner Bros.-amassed debt following the merger. It’s been said that a number of DC Studios’ projects were particularly pricey for the company. In a wide-ranging piece, Page Six mentioned sources who alleged that Supergirl, which flopped at the box office earlier this year, lost WB $135 million. With that, X user @entylawyer alleges that Skydance wants to unload the superhero brand for monetary purposes:

The comic studio heads were fired. They didn't quit. Their boss wants to sell off the entire comic book universe to help get rid of some of that $100B debt.

Of course, all of this should be taken with a massive grain of salt, as Skydance’s David Ellison has not indicated that the company plans to sell DC Studios. If that were to actually happen, though, it would result in the availability of a major asset. If Ellison and co. were to sell it, it could theoretically draw some significant interest on the open market.

I’m honestly just not sure who would seek to acquire DC Studios if Skydance were to theoretically choose to sell it. There’s also the matter of which entertainment company would actually have the money to do it. One of the first brands that comes to mind is obviously The Walt Disney Company, which acquired Marvel Entertainment back in 2009 for $4 billion. However, another brand that should be considered as a hypothetical buyer is Netflix,the company that was set to acquire WB before Paramount made a higher bid.

All of that is just speculation but, of course, James Gunn’s DC exit is real, with him and Peter Safran officially stepping down on December 1. News of Gunn’s departure has generated disappointment from those who were all in on his DC plans, and some have expressed concerns about the future of his DCU continuity. As for the actual decision to part ways with Safran and Gunn, a source for Page Six alleged that their bosses had been in talks with Latcham for weeks ahead of the announcement despite publicly saying otherwise:

It was a little bit strange to have it be so publicly stated that [Gunn and Safran] were safe, and during that time, the [Latcham] process had already been kicked off. They were saying one thing, and then they were actively doing another thing.

Naturally, there are a lot of unknown variables here, and it’s currently unclear as to it or when Skydance might confirm or deny the rumor that DC Studios will be sold. In the meantime, there are still film projects from the brand that are in different stages of development as James Gunn’s Man of Tomorrow is set to hit theaters on July 9 amid the 2027 movie schedule. Matt Reeves’ The Batman: Part II is also filming right now and will hit theaters on February 18, 2028.

#3489. Timothée Chalamet Came Over for Lunch—and a Cover Story

The history of actors appearing in Vanity Fair goes back about as far as the movies themselves. Making a studio-orchestrated, Edward Steichen–captured debut in the pages of this magazine was a milestone in the careers of Gary Cooper, Gloria Swanson, Anna May Wong, and dozens of others, many of whom never made it to Technicolor.

On more than one occasion, the idea of Timothée Chalamet as the last male movie star has been a debate here at the office, usually ending in uneasy agreement: He is one of very few left, maybe the only one of his generation. He is in the tradition of Marlon Brando and Leonardo DiCaprio in that his knowability runs inverse to his fame. Like other endangered species, his extreme rarity makes him celebrated and isolated in equal measure. And with each of these stars, one rule usually holds true: The bigger they get, the less they open their mouth.

All of which is why we are thrilled to have Chalamet on our cover as he sets out to open the final, breathtaking installment of Denis Villeneuve’s Dune trilogy. He and our team, led by photographer Aidan Zamiri, fashion editor Taylor McNeill (with whom I was an assistant at this magazine in 2010), and VF global creative director Jennifer Pastore, trekked to Iceland for a multiday shoot to capture his cover story “A Star on Planet Earth.” Everyone involved—including and especially Timothée—approached it more like a film, or maybe a music video, than a typical cover, and there is a spiritual quality that runs throughout the pictures. “I love that being on the edge of a cliff in Iceland,” Timothée tells me, “you get the same feeling as being in Grand Central.”

Timothée also had the idea that I write the cover story myself, and while I was reluctant, I eventually thought, Why not mix it up? He came over to my apartment in early October for a conversation about Dune; his career; the careers of other actors, musicians, and painters; and especially the careers of the New York Knicks. I took away from our meeting that he may be a movie star, sure, but he approaches everything as an artist. The writing process is a humbling one, though—okay, it’s agony—and since filing the cover story, I have come to believe that every editor really should write a feature now and again to make us more understanding of our writers. Perhaps once a year. Consider it a new rule at Vanity Fair.

Timothée and I were both reading Kevin Roose’s The AGI Chronicles when we met up, and he pointed out that the first several chapters of the book might as well have been the source material for Artificial, Luca Guadagnino’s new film starring Andrew Garfield and Yura Borisov. The film presents a villain origin story of OpenAI’s cofounders, particularly CEO Sam Altman. It is the natural inheritor to David Fincher and Aaron ­Sorkin’s 2010 film, The Social Network, which similarly helped answer the how-did-we-get-here question for another quite recent era of technology.

In case you missed it, Altman was recently on the cover of Vanity Fair, sitting atop our revived New Establishment list. It inspired a torrent of furious reader feedback, including a few death threats. I understand that those messages were rooted in genuine fear of this technology and ire toward its Dr. Frankenstein founders (and me, by extension, for covering them). But reporting on the powerful—whether power is granted by elections or equities or zettaflops of compute—has always been the mandate of this magazine and will continue to be. We’ll keep the movie stars too.

#3488. These Are Some Of The Biggest Snubs At The Game Awards 2026

The nominees for The Game Awards have been announced. Some of the biggest games--and those that aren't out yet--make appearances on the list, including Grand Theft Auto 6 and Phantom Blade Zero, but some of the games could've--and maybe should've--been nominated in multiple categories. So, let's go over some of the biggest snubs at this year's TGAs.

Let's start with the big one: Game of the Year. You've got six games nominated here: 007 First Light, Control Resonant, Grand Theft Auto 6, Phantom Blade Zero, Resident Evil Requiem, and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. All of them are fabulous and well-deserved, but a couple of games are missing: House House's co-op adventure Big Walk and Rebel Wolves' vampire RPG The Blood of Dawnwalker. They appear elsewhere, sure, but I think they deserve GOTY contention, as well.

Let's move onto Best Performance. You've got some stellar voice work here: Angela Sant’Albano as Grace Ashcroft in Resident Evil Requiem, Liam McIntyre as James "Logan" Howlett in Marvel's Wolverine, Manni L. Perez as Lucia Caminos in GTA 6, Patrick Gibson as James Bond in 007 First Light, and Rahul Kohli as Arjun Devraj in Saros. Not taking anything away from these incredible voice talents, but Nick Apostolides as Leon Kennedy in Resident Evil Requiem, Sean Durrie as Dylan Faden in Control Resonant, and Will de Renzy-Martin as Coen in The Blood of Dawnwalker deserve some recognition, too.

Marathon could've easily been nominated for Best Art Direction and Best Action Game. Overwatch and WoW/WoW: Forever would've made sense in the Best Ongoing Game category. Denshattack's soundtrack is too good not to be nominated for Best Score and Music. And Castlevania: Belmont's Curse could slot into a number of categories, including Best Action/Adventure Game, Best Art Direction, and Best Narrative.

There are probably many others that have come out this year that maybe could--and maybe should--have been nominated but weren't for one reason or another. (Note: GameSpot is among the publications that contribute to the nomination process.)

Regardless, we won't have to wait too long to learn what games win what categories, as The Game Awards will air live on December 10 at 4:30 PM PT / 7:30 PM ET.

#3487. ChatGPT's New GIF Generator Is Fun, but Won't Replace Us Humans (Yet)

Khamosh Pathak is a freelance tech journalist with over 13 years of experience writing online. An accounting graduate, he turned his interest in writing and technology into a career. He holds a specialization in user experience design from ISDI Parsons in Mumbai, where he sought to deepen his understanding of UX, consumer devices, and interplay between software and technology.

Khamosh has written thousands of how-tos and guides on every major platform (iOS, macOS, Android, and Windows). He got started writing how-tos and guides for Guiding Tech, where he also published several e-books. His work has also been seen at MakeUseOf, How-To Geek, and PCMag. He is truly passionate about brewing good coffee.

When it comes to generating AI images, both Gemini and ChatGPT do a passable job. In most cases, the results will look AI-generated, but they likely won’t have glaring spelling issues or missing limbs. Now, OpenAI is trying something new, introducing GIF support for ChatGPT. It's the company's first "moving images" feature since OpenAI shut down Sora, and while you can generate hyper-realistic videos in Gemini, this new ChatGPT feature is trying to fill in the gap, in a small way.

OpenAI is pitching the new feature as an animation tool, not exactly as a way to create looping videos—though that’s how I ended up using it. You give ChatGPT a prompt, as detailed as you can make it, and the chatbot produces a GIF in just a few seconds. You can start with your own drawings or images, too. ChatGPT uses sketches as the base for animations, though it can turn any still image into animated GIFs. Like other AI editing tools, you can edit it if ChatGPT didn't quite get it right: You can ask ChatGPT to make the GIF longer or shorter, remove certain objects, change the style, slow down transitions, among other edits.

AI art can be quite sterile, but I was surprised by how adding motion and animation to the mix makes generating images a lot more fun. Unlike traditional GIFs, which usually pull from existing video clips, you can turn anything you want into a GIF, which is especially cool if you're using your own art. In my testing, I found this to be the most rewarding part. It’s not always possible to one-shot a GIF with a single prompt. But after a few rounds of edits, I ended up creating some GIFs that I actually wanted to share in my WhatsApp groups.

That being said, I think human-made GIFs are still the gold standard here. For example, I asked ChatGPT to generate a video of someone brewing a pour-over, with a gooseneck kettle, showing the coffee blooming process. It did okay, but it’s nothing like actually making a pour-over. The kettle doesn’t move in circles, the water doesn’t rise evenly, there are no bubbles, and the steam is all over the place.

Compare that to the GIF below, which comes from a royalty-free video. Even though it’s a compressed, low-quality, and noisy GIF, it still shows the movement of the pour, the water rising, and even the bubbles. The details captured by a real video just aren’t there in ChatGPT GIFs. If that’s what you’re expecting, you will be disappointed. But I don't think that's the point of this feature anyway.

I found that ChatGPT excels when you’re making something fun, and you don’t look into the details too much. It pulled off a loop of a cat playing with a ball, and it was great at making a festive GIF for Diwali. It even made a GIF based on a photo. I asked it to create a fun promotional GIF for my JBL Bluetooth speakers, and it did the job quite well. At first, the transitions were too jarring, and the movement just made no sense. After some editing, though, I got it to a decent place.

Still, the main issue with ChatGPT GIFs is that complex movement and transitions aren’t nailed down. A hand shifts position weirdly between frames, and colors and objects appear out of nowhere. But if you can get over these issues, you can make some fun, lighthearted GIFs and memes to share with your friends on Instagram or WhatsApp.

#3486. 007 First Light Might Be The End Of The Line For James Bond’s Favorite Watch

After months of searching and numerous potential frontrunners, Robert Pattinson has been cast as the next James Bond. It's lead to some questions about whether he's too famous or too old for the role, whether or not he looks like Bond, and just how different his portrayal might be to those that came before him. For some others, however, the questions is far more direct: What watch is he going to wear?

James Bond has long had recognizable brand associations, but one that has endured has been the partnership with luxury watch maker Omega. Bond was first seen wearing an Omega in 1995's GoldenEye, and was mostly recently seen sporting the latest iteration of the Seamaster Diver 300m in this year's 007 First Light. Although not a new film in the series, First Light still featured its own unique take on the Seamaster, the first ever created for a videogame, with Omega adding it to its bursting 007 collection that it makes available for purchase.

So given that it's been three decades, why could First Light be the last iteration of James Bond wearing an Omega? Simply put, Robert Pattinson doesn't wear one, and has very recently become a brand ambassador for one of Omega's Swiss competitors, Jaeger-LeCoultre. There's no confirmation that Pattinson's obligations will directly influence a brand deal between Omega and new Bond owners Amazon, but the omission of any watch at all in the announcement trailer sure has cause some speculation.

Daniel Craig, during his tenure as Bond, was Omega's chief ambassador, often wearing unreleased models to drum up interest for imminent releases. That might not be the case with Pattinson, which could suggest a change for what timepiece his Bond decides to switch to.

If Bond were to jump from Omega to JLC, it would be somewhat fitting. The watch maker manufactures some extremely elegant pieces with a rich history associated with each line. But none makes as much sense as the rectangular Reverso. The watch is distinct in its design, allowing the wearer to rotate the face and flip it 180 degrees, with a variety of designs on the back. Initially created for polo players to protect their prized wristwatches, you can clearly see a lot of potential for some weird and creative Bond gadgetry to intersect with a design like this.

Or maybe Pattinson will arrive on the block with yet another Seamaster Diver 300m, and all of this would've been wishful thinking. But if he doesn't, and this truly is the last we'll see of Bond with Omega, at least First Light introduced one of the better entries in the entire collection.

#3485. Below Deck's Chef Ben Robinson Defends Joao Franco After Arrest

Below Deck’s Chef Ben Robinson is coming to the defense of his costar and friend João Franco after he was arrested in Turkey following a fatal fight.

“I’m so sorry to hear this,” Ben, 45, commented via an Instagram post on Monday, November 16. “Clearly, João was trying to de-escalate the problem. Now he faced five aggressors upon him, and it was clearly self-defense. So unfortunate that this minor lost his life.”

João, 36, and his brother, Karlos Franco, were reportedly arrested in Turkey following a brawl that left a 17-year-old dead.

The pair were seen engaged in a verbal dispute with the employees of a clothing store in the Bodrum district of Muğla on November 7, according to CCTV footage obtained by Page Six.

Although João seemingly attempted to break up the fight multiple times, he eventually appeared to swing a fist at one employee, causing the person to fall to the ground. The fight ended moments later.

The individual who fell to the ground was a 17-year-old employee who hit his head on some stairs, according to local outlets. He later died at a hospital, per the reports. (Us previously reached out to reps for Bravo and João for comment.)

Ben and João starred together on season 4 of Below Deck Down Under, which premiered in February on Bravo.

Colin Macy-O’Toole, who worked with João on season 3 of Below Deck Mediterranean in 2018, also came to his costar’s defense.

“Having seen the video footage, my impression is that João appeared to be trying to defend himself and de-escalate an already escalating situation,” Colin, who was not present for the incident, told Page Six on November 11. “From what is visible, it doesn’t look to me like he was looking to start a confrontation. It looks like he was reacting to what was happening around him.”

Colin, 39, continued, “Knowing João, I think it’s important that people take the full context of the footage into consideration before jumping to conclusions or assigning blame. This is an incredibly tragic situation, and I hope the facts are allowed to come out before anyone rushes to judgment.”

João first appeared on Bravo’s Below Deck Mediterranean season 3 in 2018 as a lead deckhand under Captain Sandy Yawn before returning to the show during season 4 in 2019 as a bosun.

He later appeared on Below Deck Down Under seasons 2 and 4 as a second officer/bosun under Captain Jason Chambers.

Despite the show’s success, João previously announced that he would not be returning to the franchise.

“The show neatly mirrored my real-world career progression. Across the four series, I moved from deckhand to lead deckhand, bosun and finally captain,” he told the Mallorca Daily Bulletin in May. “I never wanted to be a deckhand forever. The goal was always the bridge, so I spent every spare moment doing courses to move up.”

I had stocked up on a variety of beer and tea, can offer a coffee or a cocktail, but Chalamet wants New York City tap water, please, no ice.

Custom jacket by Haider Ackermann for Canada Goose; pants by Roa Hiking; backpack by Montbell.

I live in a one-bedroom in the East 60s, the second floor of an 1870 town house. The walls are white, the floors are black, and there are flowers from the bodega on the coffee table.

Chalamet is in earth-toned gorpcore, from the sand-colored Gnuhr puffer all the way down to a tawny pair of Roas, and would look equally at home camouflaged on the streets of Manhattan or trekking in the Dolomites, which he has recently done with his father. Both ears are pierced. Except for a navy blue novelty tourist cap which reads, in a comically fancy font, “Hvar, Croatia”—another recent vacation destination, with girlfriend Kylie Jenner—Chalamet’s color palette is pure Arrakis.

THE PROPHECY Timothée Chalamet, who will reprise his role as Paul Atreides – the chosen one – in Denis Villeneuve’s Dune: Part Three, photographed in Iceland. Shirt by Prada.

He’s just come from the Fiorello H. LaGuardia High School of Music & Art and Performing Arts, his alma mater located directly across the park, where he spoke with a group of drama students. Tonight he’s going to a Yankees game with his mom, the former New York City Ballet prima ballerina, and his sister, Pauline.

Late lunch concluded, he relocates to the sofa. “Ahhh,” he says, taking a big seat and resting his right arm along the back.

He glances down at the old issues of Vanity Fair on my coffee table and comes to a stop on one in particular: June 1995. Courtney Love is on the cover, photographed by Herb Ritts, wearing massive white-feathered wings in homage to the Nike of Samothrace at the Louvre. Inside, there’s a Ritts portrait of a toddler Frances Bean.

OUTDOOR VOICE Timothée Chalamet and photographer Aidan Zamiri spent three days in Iceland for this shoot, code-named Caladan—the planet where Chalamet’s Dune character, Paul Atreides, was born.

“This wasn’t the crazy one,” I say, guessing at what he’s thinking.

Three years prior to this cover, in the September 1992 issue of Vanity Fair, Lynn Hirschberg profiled Love and quoted her saying that she used heroin before and at the beginning of her pregnancy. The story sparked a crisis for the young Cobain family that resulted in an investigation by the department of children and family services and Cobain threatening Hirschberg and her dog. In the annals of celebrity profiles, it goes down as one of the most scalding of all time.

Chalamet knows all about that story because he’s seen Montage of Heck, the Cobain documentary that features the Vanity Fair article. “It was mind-blowing to me because Lynn has only ever been to me just a figure of warmth...” Chalamet says, trailing off.

He puts the magazine back slowly, like it might burn him.

I’ll be honest with you: That’s not what’s about to happen here today. I’m not that scary, and he’s not using heroin. Nevertheless, this guy’s jumpy.

It’s dangerous business for a movie star to open his mouth these days. Chalamet knows that better than anyone. At 30, he’s been famous his entire adult life. He’s dating one of the most visible women in the world. And he is acutely aware how a single comment in Vanity Fair could ricochet around the pinball machine of the internet. Earlier this year, during a no-holds-barred Oscar campaign for Marty Supreme, an offhand remark comparing the film industry to ballet and opera was met with outsize outrage, as some saw an opportunity to take Hollywood’s boy wonder down a peg. Those aware that he’s from a performing arts family knew what he meant. (“Is he wrong?” New York Times’ dance critic, Gia Kourlas, asked.) He doesn’t want to revisit that with me, perhaps because as he enters another awards season, he’s cautious in a way that only comes with experience.

In our 90 minutes together, Chalamet is both earnest and also reluctant to be profiled. He is by turns generous and guarded, confident and careful. He prefaces answers to no fewer than seven different questions by saying that he doesn’t want to sound “pretentious.” Truthfully, he never does. He’s protective of his personal life and will not discuss his girlfriend, nor much outside of filmmaking. “I wish I didn’t have to talk too much,” Chalamet says. And yet here he is, all across Iceland in our cover shoot, and now on my blue velvet sofa.

Like every conversation in late 2026, ours starts with AI. “Thou shall not make a machine in the likeness of a man’s mind,” Chalamet reminds me, is one of the opening lines of Dune, Frank Herbert’s seminal 1965 sci-fi novel. The story takes place in a world where computers are banned long after an AI apocalypse like the ones that are presaged by current-day tech CEOs and causing so much societal agita.

COLD MOUNTAIN Chalamet formed a community while making the first two Dune films. The third was “a more claustrophobic, isolated experience.” Boots by Timberland; scarf by Norlha; vintage pants by Arc’teryx Pro.

Chalamet tells me he’s reading The AGI Chronicles, tech journalist Kevin Roose’s new book that maps out the sprint to reach artificial general intelligence. He points out that the first four chapters of the book track the plot of Artificial, referring to Luca Guadagnino’s new Sam Altman biopic. “This is five seconds ago.” He recommended the book to Marty Supreme director Josh Safdie, who later tells me Chalamet “found it to be not only informative, it’s helped with anxiety. The more you know, the less anxious you are about it.”

Just when everyone seems at least a little bit anxious about the end of the human species, along comes Dune’s computer-free vision of the future that is, as Chalamet puts it, “strangely superhuman, strangely very human.”

LIFE ON MARS “The whole thing is daunting,” says Chalamet about working on a franchise like Dune. Coat and shoes by Prada; pants by Stone Island.

You don’t need to have seen the conclusion of Denis Villeneuve’s trilogy to understand a few things about it. First of all, that it is enormous. Its scale is even bigger than The Odyssey’s. The grand vision of Villeneuve’s intergalactic war drama actually makes the adaptation of the West’s first epic poem (and presumed best picture front-runner so far) look like an exercise in restraint.

The production design of Dune: Part Three, set 20,000 years in the future, is largely inspired by the pangeographical past. There are aesthetic references as far-ranging as the samurai and SEAL Team 6, the Roman Empire by way of the Third Reich, Islamic extremism and the Russian Orthodox Church, the Bedouins and the Asaro mud men of Papua New Guinea, and perhaps more than any other single culture, ancient Egypt. And like the pyramids themselves, the visual effect of the film is mystical rather than technological, even though both obviously are technical achievements. (No AI was used in the making of Dune: Part Three.)

Chalamet gives Villeneuve all the credit for what he calls the “titanic” scope of the film, constructed on the foundation of the first two over the course of a decade. “It seems like he just kept building and becoming more ferociously in control of it,” he says. “Much like how Paul gets good at riding the sandworm, Denis took hold of these films.” The movie makes it easy to see how Star Wars—and particularly Anakin Skywalker’s character arc—is often considered derivative of Dune. (For the real heads: The story of Dune: Part Three is roughly equivalent to Star Wars episodes IV through VI, all in one film.)

“It’s huge, huge geography,” Chalamet says. “Do you think you could have done this when you were in your 30s?” Chalamet asked Villeneuve on set. “He goes, ‘No way.’ ” The director went on to tell him that he passed on a “huge sci-fi project” earlier in life that he wouldn’t even reveal to Chalamet, but Villeneuve “turned it down precisely because he felt like he didn’t have the tools yet.”

Production designer Patrice Vermette’s life-size sets were so imposing that Chalamet spent time on location in Budapest ahead of the film’s shoot, immersing himself in the palace of Arrakis so that he wouldn’t be distracted by its grandeur when the cameras rolled. “The whole thing is daunting,” Chalamet says. “I didn’t want any part of the day to be lost to ‘Wow, look at what I’m stepping into,’ ” he adds later. Compared to shooting the first two Dune films, he was more or less alone on set. Chalamet remembers it as “a more claustrophobic, isolated experience.” The way Villeneuve puts it: “Timothée created a bubble around himself which allowed him to delve more deeply into the depressive darkness of his character.” He was, after all, preparing to play a murderer.

FIELD OF VISION According to Chalamet, Dune, which is set 20,000 years in a computer-free future, feels “strangely superhuman, strangely very human.” Hoodie and eye cover by Adon; T-shirt by James Perse Los Angeles; necklace by Blackmerle.

Part Three encounters Chalamet’s antihero, Duke Paul Atreides (also known by his Fremen alias Usul, as the religious cult figure Muad’Dib, and the Padishah Emperor of the known universe—you got all that?), at the height of his totalitarianism and the nadir of his soul. Sixty-one billion is the number of deaths attributable to Atreides, who in the Herbert novels compares himself to Adolf Hitler and Genghis Khan. He is a “psychopath,” according to Florence Pugh’s Princess Irulan. Villeneuve tells me there was another detached paranoid figure he compared Atreides to: Howard Hughes.

To get into character, Chalamet studied the personalities of world leaders—“everyone good and bad” and particularly “megalomaniacs across human history.” He notes that “Frank Herbert wrote Messiah to course correct...the first Dune, where Paul is sort of revered as a hero.” He continues: “This is a cautionary tale against cults of personality and figures of charisma.” When I ask if Donald Trump was on his mind, he says “not particularly,” noting that power and its corrosive effects on the soul are “eternally prescient themes.” The film is ultimately a story of atonement—if not redemption—for a fallen messiah.

It was all this research that compelled Chalamet to shave off his globally recognized curly mop. “Decision fatigue is a real thing amongst the world leaders, good and bad, current and past.... The idea of not having to change clothes, not having to sweep the hair out of your face, simple shit like that.” And so Chalamet said goodbye to his Samson-like locks. Did he feel...“like Anne Hathaway in Les Mis?” Exactly. Or Natalie Portman in V for Vendetta, I offer. (He loves V for Vendetta.) Perhaps Demi Moore in G.I. Jane. “We would [shave] it basically every other day. My hair grows quickly, so we would get after it.” Today the curls, as you can see, have returned to their natural state. Power restored.

“Timothée has become much more ambitious as an actor,” Villeneuve tells me when I ask how he’s changed in the decade that they’ve worked together. “He is exploring new artistic paths in a highly exciting way.” Costar Javier Bardem says, “In a way, his growth has been almost chronological with that of his character. In Dune: Part Three, there is a real gravitas to him. He stands firmly in his place, with a confidence and authority that he has earned through his work, his sacrifices, his dedication, and his commitment as an actor and as a professional. You can see it and feel it, and it is incredibly reaffirming to witness.”

Safdie puts it like this: “I believe he’s like hi-fi sound. A good hi-fi system you can listen to in a tiny room and it makes the room feel huge. And he has that ability as an actor...his style of acting is larger-than-life realism.”

“He is always restlessly searching to keep the scene alive,” says Greta Gerwig, who directed Chalamet in Lady Bird and Little Women.“He needs room to scream a scene or whisper it or jump up onto a table or pirouette.”

MAN OF ACTION Chalamet wants his art to speak for itself: “My work is my bones and muscles. I have little interest in putting more of myself out there.” Suit by Gucci; shirt by Harvey Bigg.

When I ask Chalamet if being famous his entire adult life prepared him to play a lonely-at-the-top emperor, he points to the moment in the first Dune when Paul and his mother, Lady Jessica, arrive on Arrakis and are greeted by the entire awe-inspiring army. “There were moments” in his own life, he says, when he realized about his relationship with the public: “Oh, something has shifted.”

Wandering around my apartment, Chalamet is observant and interested. “The picture in your bathroom looks like Greta.” He means Gerwig, though it’s actually Edie Sedgwick balancing on one leg in arabesque, cigarette in hand. (Sedgwick lived in this apartment during her Warhol years, and the picture was taken in the living room where we are sitting.) We look through the 1965 issue of Vogue, in which the picture originally ran.

He points out the French poster for The Graduate in the bedroom, in which a pink Matisse-like cutout of a woman’s elegant leg hovers in a thought bubble above Dustin Hoffman’s head. “I didn’t know it was called that,” he says. “Le Lauréat.” (One journalist recommended that I speak French with Chalamet, as they find him more open when they do. Sadly, I can hardly order dinner in French.)

He loves an Annie Leibovitz picture of Cindy Sherman made up as the sad clown in Edward Hopper’s 1914 Soir Bleu and points out monographs about Ed Ruscha and Harmony Korine on my bookshelf. (“Beast!” he declares about Korine.)

He sweetly asks me about a picture of me officiating my best friends’ wedding.

WORLD VIEWS “I love that being on the edge of a cliff in Iceland, you get the same feeling as being in Grand Central,” says Chalamet, a born and raised New Yorker.

We’re back on the sofa now. I’d asked Chalamet to do a little homework before our meeting: to come prepared to talk about his favorite movie performances. He was a diligent student, but instead came with four films and one play that specifically helped him get ready for his Vanity Fair cover shoot.

“Tree of Life,” he begins, citing Terrence Malick’s impressionistic masterpiece as the “biggest inspiration” for the cover shoot, photographed by Aidan Zamiri over three days in Iceland. “It could have been accomplished over a half day in the studio,” Chalamet says, but they traveled thousands of miles because, as in Tree of Life, “the process is almost as important as the finished product.”

Next up is One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest. “It’s a kick-ass performance, and it’s provocative and heartwarming and full of life and one of the great movie performances of all time.” He cites Cloud Atlas, which the Wachowski sisters made years after The Matrix trilogy, as achieving the kind of scale that inspired the team to trek to the edge of Icelandic cliffs and inside waterfalls. (It’s also one of two films, along with Bruce Robinson’s 1987 Withnail and I, that Christopher Nolan has ever recommended to him.)

Chalamet whips out his orange iPhone—where he has incidentally started a new daily habit of playing chess—to show me the trailer for the Francis Ford Coppola–produced 1982 art house film Koyaanisqatsi, a hypnotic succession of increasingly uneasy urban vignettes, sped up and slowed down. “It’s about the humility you must feel as any person within the scale of the universe,” Chalamet says. “I love that being on the edge of a cliff in Iceland, you get the same feeling as being in Grand Central.” This one was recommended by Safdie and is clearly an inspiration for the relentless, kinetic pacing of his own movies as well. Chalamet is so close to Safdie that even the chess habit is inspired by the match that Safdie and Alfonso Cuarón continue in perpetuity.

“What’s interesting about Timmy is he’s incredibly curious and very sincere, but also has a pretty sharp sense of humor and can be quite jagged,” Safdie himself tells me a week later. “There’s a goofy seriousness to him. He likes to be provoked.”

SMOKE SHOW Next up for Chalamet? A top-secret collaboration with a “phenomenal” filmmaker. “It’s kind of a no-brainer.”

And finally, he gives me Man to Man, Tilda Swinton’s one-woman show currently on at London’s Royal Court Theatre. “It’s about the incredible futility of existence and a person losing their mind,” Chalamet says. “I liked it in this little program I created.”

I’ve never met any actor who prepared for a photo shoot the way he would for a role in a movie. I get the sense that’s just Chalamet’s way: Everything he does in public is considered part of the art. Everything except, perhaps, courtside appearances.

Little provokes Chalamet more than the New York Knicks, and it is the subject about which he gets most animated. “It’s the most quintessential New York team” for many reasons, he says, but chief among them is location, location, location. “It’s not like the Yankees or Mets, Giants, or Jets. It’s in the heart of Manhattan, and it reflected the agony of the New York experience for decades.” Chalamet says he lives two lives: one as himself and one as “fan with a capital F.”

When I ask what his greatest extravagance is, the immediate and definite answer is “sports tickets.” “Those away games weren’t cheap, but...it is the most fun I’ve had in my life as a human.” We know this. Because the best word to describe pictures of Chalamet courtside and in the Knicks locker room is simply ecstatic.

He tells me about traveling through the night from San Antonio back to New York after the Game 5 championship as an all-time life high. “I flew with people that had been working at the Garden for decades,” he says, explaining that Ben Stiller and Fat Joe were along for the ride on an MSG-owned plane. (“I don’t want to sound too out of touch,” he worries. I assure him the reader will understand that commercial airlines aren’t running 2 a.m. departures.) “It was just incredibly raucous, everyone celebrating.”

DISTRESSED OUT Or is he? Chalamet isn’t pressed about trying to emulate his heroes: “It’s less sexy to some degree to wade out in the unknown, but it’s more authentic.”

Chalamet says he will always remember Jalen Brunson’s quiet leadership as the hallmark of the season overall. “It was not the cult of personality” you might expect to lead a championship team, he notes. “It was someone actually quite soft-spoken, reserved, and hardworking, and unassuming.”

On topics other than basketball, he is less enthusiastic. “My work is my bones and muscles. I have little interest in putting more of myself out there,” he says. What’s something that no one asks you that you wish they would? “Nothing. I mean, nothing. I’m not being passive-aggressive about this interview at all, but I think...” he trails off. Chalamet points at the speaker, which is still playing Frank Ocean. “He’s one of the rare people where the vacuum of what’s out there about him helps drive the...” “Curiosity?” I offer. “Beyond curiosity, how brilliant his artistry is. But the economy of movies,” Chalamet says, thinking. “You got to sell a lot of tickets.”

Which is exactly the reason that we’re sitting here together now. Who is his dream collaborator, living or dead? After a long silence, I tell him he can pass. “Okay. Pass.” What does he think of David Ellison’s Skydance taking over Warner Bros., the studio behind Dune? “I’m going to hit a Frank Ocean and be mysterious,” is all he says.

Leonardo DiCaprio once gave him very solid advice. Two rules: no superhero movies, no hard drugs. Would Chalamet have any advice for a 22-year-old getting started? “I think the best thing you can do is encourage people to be confident in what they believe is best for them.” Plus, he adds, “the Kane Parsons of it all brought me tremendous humility,” referencing the 21-year-old YouTuber turned director of the staggeringly successful Backrooms.

He’s vague about future projects. “I got one thing with a phenomenal filmmaker,” he says. “It’s kind of a no-brainer project, and should it get announced, I think you’ll see what I mean.”

Would he ever return to the character of Elio, the protagonist of Call Me by Your Name that gave him his star turn? “A great question. Never say never, but...I’ve grown up with the mindset that you don’t really go near something that is so near and dear to people.” So, that’s a no. “Now, to work with Luca again? In a heartbeat.”

GAME BOY As Chalamet sees it, there are two ways of living his life: one as himself and one as “fan with a capital F.” Jacket by Chrome Hearts; headlamp by Nitecore.

Is there any actor, or artist of any kind, after whose career he would like to model his own? “Who was [Bob] Dylan looking at? Dylan.” He broke the mold, I offer. “He created the mold.” Chalamet wants to be an original too (and perhaps this is what he meant when he declared that he was in “pursuit of greatness” at the 2025 SAG Awards). “It’s less sexy to some degree to wade out in the unknown, but it’s more authentic,” he says. “Especially in the movie industry where people could feel like, Oh, that was the golden age.... You gotta cook it up in a unique way.”

Around 6 p.m., Chalamet gets up off the couch and suits back up in his gorpcore. The Yankees game starts in just a couple of hours, and he has to shower and collect his mom and sister and make his way to the Bronx. I walk him downstairs, amble down the stoop, and almost want to say: Look! We survived!

Fashion Editor: Taylor McNeill. Hair and grooming products by Augustinus Bader. Grooming by Jamie Taylor. Produced on location by Object & Animal and Truenorth. For details, go to VF.com/credits.

#3483. Civilization Dev Lays Off 1/3 Of Staff, New XCOM Game Facing “Development Struggles” – Report

The video game industry's woes continue as Take-Two's 2K division has confirmed that one third of the staff at Civilization and XCOM developer Firaxis Games is being laid off.

Bloomberg confirmed the cuts, which will impact around 60 people. As part of the downsizing, Firaxis studio head Heather Hazen is leaving.

A spokesperson for Firaxis confirmed the restructuring to Bloomberg, saying the cuts are part of an effort to "focus on design, technology, and player experience."

"These decisions are never easy, but they’re essential to build the next chapter of Firaxis," the spokesperson said.

According to Bloomberg's sources, Firaxis is working on a new XCOM game, but it has faced "development struggles" and missed a major milestone this past summer. The game is still going ahead, though the sources said it "may face a shakeup" due to the layoffs.

The latest game from Firaxis, Sid Meier's Civilization VII, was released in February 2025 and had numerous technical issues upon release, though the experience has been improved since then with updates. The entire Civilization series has sold more than 80 million units.

As for the XCOM series, the latest entry from Firaxis was 2020's XCOM: Chimera Squad, and before that was 2016's XCOM 2.

Firaxis was co-founded by Sid Meier in 1996, so 2026 is the studio's 30th anniversary. Take-Two bought the company in 2005 and put the studio and the franchise under the 2K banner.
