#3482. 10 Shows Like 'Cyberpunk: Edgerunners' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Following the dramatic conclusion of Cyberpunk: Edgerunners way back in 2022, the show has returned for a new season set in the megalopolis of Night City with a standalone story and a new cast of characters (by necessity).

Though the aesthetic and themes of cyberpunk have their roots in American science fiction of the 1970s and '80s, anime and manga of the '90s and beyond embraced the form and took it to entirely new places—so much so that a Japanese/Polish co-production of an adaptation of a video game from a Polish designer has taken its cues from a couple of decades' worth of great anime and cerebral sci-fi. Which is to say, if you're looking for more heady sci-fi series, these 10 are a good place to start.

An iconic, effortlessly cool genre classic, Cowboy Bebop is one of the undisputed GOATs of anime, blending western, noir, and crime genres and setting the resultant mash to a killer soundtrack of old-school jazz (which serves much the same purpose as Cyberpunk's propulsive electronic grooves). The title's "cowboys" are bounty hunters in a near-future in which humans have been forced to colonize the solar system after Earth became uninhabitable. Different settings, but both shows offer up ragtag crews with highly dubious fates. Former hitman Spike Spiegel leads his crew on one nearly disastrous mission after another, their standalone adventures all building to a thoroughly memorable climax. Stream Cowboy Bebop on Crunchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

This one's set in 22nd-century Japan, with a slick Blade Runner-esque aesthetic and a setup reminiscent of Minority Report. Here, technology exists to measure intentions, so crimes can be stopped before they’ve occurred, at which point the “criminals” are placed into psychological treatment (à la A Clockwork Orange)—or subject to summary execution because their threat potential is too high. That ability to predict behavior bleeds over into every aspect of life: careers and even relationships are determined in large part by the same systems that sniff out criminal intent. Obviously, this is all perfectly fine, and there’s no potential for abuse or miscalculation whatsoever...though there are a couple of warning signs. The first involves a new Enforcer who becomes a potential murderer himself when he miscalculates the extent of a criminal’s potential to do wrong, and, even more significantly, the existence of a criminal mastermind who is somehow invisible to the tech, even as his criminal actions grow more and more elaborate. Stream Psycho-Pass on Prime Video and Crunchyroll.

Created by Tim Miller and with director David Fincher as an executive producer, this animated anthology series is a grab bag of wildly diverse offerings: Each episode is produced by a different international studio, with the only link between them being one of the three words in the show's title. One episode deals with robotic gladiator fights in dystopian London, another finds us under the threat of sentient yogurt, yet another finds an ambitious cat learning to make use of a family's robot helper. Its format dictates that no two episodes are going to have the same premise, but it shares with Cyberpunk an edgy sensibility and stories set in an apocalyptic future, albeit with a dark sense of humor—its four seasons offer up a mix of tech, sex, violence, and gorgeous animation. Stream Love, Death & Robots on Netflix.

One of several completely standalone spinoffs of the wildly influential 1995 film (itself based on the beloved manga series), Stand Alone Complex requires no prior knowledge. The style is largely the draw, as the series luxuriates in its fictional Nihama City setting, a world unto itself in a future Japan in which cybernetic people hack directly into the internet. Our sympathies are more with the authorities—in this case, Public Security Section 9, a cybercrime and antiterrorism police unit—than the cyber criminals, but the show approaches some of the same themes as Edgerunners with legit punk style. Stream Ghost in the Shell: Stand Alone Complex on Tubi and The Criterion Channel.

In this adaptation of the Richard K. Morgan cyberpunk classic of the same name, Joel Kinnaman and Anthony Mackie (yes, both of them) star as Takeshi "Tak" Kovacs. In this future megacity setting, human consciousness can be transferred between bodies. The tech is widely available, but only the wealthy can afford the backups and protections that make it a form of virtual immortality. Kovacs is a former soldier turned mercenary, revived from a backup after 200 years by Laurens Bancroft (James Purefoy), one of the wealthiest men alive. His motives for bringing the man back are shrouded in mystery, but he's giving Tak a chance to solve a very cold case: his own murder. Stream Altered Carbon on Netflix.

Another popular (and Emmy-winning) game adaptation, Arcane is based on League of Legends, a top-down actioner involving online opponents shooting lasers across a map. It doesn't sound like fodder for a show this impressive, but here we are. The League of Legends lore forms the backdrop for the show, but the pull is in the narrative involving two sisters caught up in the growing conflict between a utopian city and its oppressed underclass, without whom it couldn’t exist. The painted animation style is truly something special—not a stylistic match for Cyberpunk, but the two shows both go far above and beyond to create striking visual worlds. Stream Arcane on Netflix.

Vash the Stampede is a hunted outcast with a dark history that slowly comes to light over the course of the series. He’s got a reputation as a human wrecking ball, bringing destruction wherever he goes, and seemingly just for fun—but in reality he’s far more respectful of life than his pursuers. Still, cities evacuate at the mere possibility of his arrival, and a huge bounty sits on his head (no matter that the bounty hunters do far more damage than Vash). He and his friends—actually a couple of insurance agents—find themselves in a series of misadventures on the planet Gunsmoke, building to a final showdown that caps the series with finality. Visually, it’s probably one of the defining ‘90s shōnen-style action series, with elegantly choreographed gunfights that never get old. Tonally similar, Trigun also shares with Cyberpunk 2 the work of legendary composer Tsuneo Imahori, his music being crucial to both shows. Stream Trigun on Crunchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

Another from animation studio Trigger, Darling in the Franxx leans heavily into the mecha sub-genre, set in a post-apocalypse where children are bred and indoctrinated into piloting the title's massive Franxx to defend the remnants of humanity. Adults are pretty much immortal, so the kids simply don't have any other utility. Two of these teens begin to develop romantic feelings for each other, potentially complicating their usefulness to society and leading to an explosive, bittersweet finale. Stream Darling in the Franxx on Crunchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

What starts out as a relatively straightforward action show about space bounty hunters (the title's “Killjoys”) develops surprising depth over the course of its five seasons. As officially sanctioned Killjoys, the trio at the show’s heart (Hannah John-Kamen, Aaron Ashmore, and Luke Macfarlane) are bound to remain politically neutral at any cost. Initially, that’s a way to get them right into the heat of a fight, but as they develop ties of friendship and family in an exploited community, they come to understand the high cost of unchecked wealth and greed, and the ways in which neutrality always benefits the oppressors. The show’s creators make exceptionally good use of a limited budget and offer up some impressive queer rep along the way, a rarity in pop sci-fi. Stream Killjoys on Tubi or buy it from Prime Video and Apple TV.

Another great cyberpunk metropolis: here it's Kansai, an increasingly lawless city run by elite criminals known as Akudama. #3481. How GTA 6 Is Eligible For The Game Awards This Year

We've known for some time that Grand Theft Auto 6 was likely to be eligible for The Game Awards, and now that 2026's TGA nominees are live, it's official: Not only is GTA eligible, but it actually has the most nominations of any game.

That's somewhat of an unusual situation, given that GTA 6 reviews are not yet live. Regardless, this invites some questions of how or why GTA 6 can be eligible before reviews go out and before the game is available. (Nominations even confirmed a key actor in the game.)

For months, the official website for The Game Awards has listed November 20, 2026 at 9 PM PT as the cutoff date for this year's ceremony, which means that any game that launches before that time can be considered for nomination. As GTA VI is scheduled to launch one day earlier, on November 19, GTA 6 is eligible just like any other game already released this year.

Now, before torches are lit and pitchforks are sharpened, evidence suggests that date was not put in place specifically for GTA to be eligible this year: The Friday before Thanksgiving has routinely been the cutoff for TGA nominations.

Last year, the cutoff was November 21, as referenced in this Polygon article regarding Dispatch's eligibility. In 2024, eligibility was cut off on November 22, as evidenced in this Polygon article exploring the games that missed 2024 and were eligible in 2025.

2018 was the last time a Rockstar project was eligible for most categories at The Game Awards, as Red Dead Redemption II landed 10 nominations and four wins. Notably, one of those wins was not Game of the year, which went to Sony Santa Monica for the God of War reboot.

Grand Theft Auto VI's eligibility for TGA 2026 was never in doubt--well, unless it got delayed again. Now that we're clear of that scenario, it's only a matter of time until we see just how many trophies are headed to Vice City.

#3480. Inside Mormon Wives' Jen Affleck and Zac's Birth, Parenting Plan Amid Split

Pregnant Jen Affleck and estranged husband Zac Affleck are doing their best to be cordial as they prepare to welcome their fourth baby amid their ongoing divorce.

“Zac and Jen are in a good place despite their divorce,” a source exclusively tells Us. “They are coparenting and communication between them has been good.”

Although the Secret Lives of Mormon Wives star, 27, filed for divorce from Zac, 30, earlier this month, the pair “talk every day,” according to the insider.

“Zac and Jen are working on baby names, and are really excited to welcome their baby together,” the source says, noting that Zac “will be in the delivery room with Jen and there every step of the way.”

Jen and Zac will “parent together and are still figuring out the plan” in regards to managing their three, soon-to-be four children, the insider adds.

“Jen has asked Zac to continue living together,” the source tells Us, explaining that while the estranged couple are “currently still living together, Zac is looking for his own place and has told Jen that.”

Us has reached out to reps for Jen and Zac for comment.

Jen and Zac tied the knot in 2019, going on to welcome children Nora, 5, Lucas, 3, and Penny, 16 months, November 2021, July 2023 and June 2025, respectively. Jen announced in June that she is pregnant with baby No. 4.

Fans met Jen and Zac on 2024’s season 1 of SLOMW. Throughout the series, the pair weathered a few storms, and they even briefly separated between seasons 1 and 2 of the show.

The former couple relocated from Utah to California in fall 2025 when Jen was competing on season 34 of Dancing With the Stars. They chose to stay after the show wrapped, but their relationship didn’t improve.

News broke on November 3 that Jen filed for divorce from Zac in Utah, where they got married.

“The same reason why I filed for divorce is the same reason why it was really hard,” Jen exclusively told Us on November 10. “It was this fourth child. I had to ask myself very hard questions like, ‘Is this the type of relationship I want this child to look up to?’”

She confessed, “When I realized it was a no, that’s when I realized that I needed to make a change.”

Fans have gotten even more insight into the pair’s split since Hulu spinoff Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County premiered earlier this month.

During one episode, Jen claimed Zac lost $100,000 gambling which added to their marital issues.

“Someone came to Zac’s parents’ house yesterday and was trying to serve him papers,” Jen told the cameras. “They were looking for him and he was like, ‘Remember we lived in that home in Arizona? I guess I didn’t pay all the extra charges for us to move out.’”

Jen claimed that after feeling uneasy about the situation — and feeling like Zac wasn’t being truthful — she checked their bank and “the money is gone.”

“There was over $100,000 in there. He’s done this before multiple times — whether it was through online poker or it was through investing crypto,” she alleged. “I said, ‘You’re not allowed to do that anymore.’ Because he’s done this multiple times.”

The source exclusively tells Us that Zac allegedly lost only $60,000 from day trading, noting, “Jen and Zac have never been in a position where they have been financially unstable.”

The insider adds, “Zac had been pursuing medical school and stepped back to support Jen’s career” before their breakup.

#3479. This Fighting Game Is Nominated For A TGA Despite Development Shutting Down

Earlier today, Geoff Keighley announced all of the nominees for The Game Awards 2026, the annual celebration of gaming held in Los Angeles. Among expected nominees Grand Theft Auto VI, The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, and Control Resonant was one surprising name: 2XKO has been nominated for Best Fighting Game, despite Riot Games announcing the end of the game's lifecycle earlier this year.

Riot announced that "active development" for the fighting game, featuring characters from League of Legends, would end in December 2026. "Over the last few months, we’ve been monitoring 2XKO’s trajectory closely, and what we’ve seen is painting a clear, consistent picture," Riot said at the time. "While a lot of you jumped in to try the game and there’s an incredible community that plays every day, we haven’t seen enough players stick with the game to get to a path toward sustainability,”

Riot's fighter is joined in the Best Fighting Game category by Invincible Vs., Marvel Tokon: Fighting Souls, Avatar Legends, and My Hero Academia: All's Justice. 2XKO is also not the only game on this list whose future is in jeopardy; soon after it launched in April, Invincible Vs. developer Quarter up laid off reportedly 75% of its staff, while saying that future updates were dependent on the game's overall sales.

Grand Theft Auto VI received the most nominations for a single game at this year's ceremony with eight, including Game of the Year. Control Resonant and Resident Evil Requiem tied for the second-most nominations with six each, while Phantom Blade Zero rounded out the top three with five nominations. Nintendo earned the most nominations for a single publisher, meanwhile, with 12 across the event's 30 awards.

The Game Awards is set to take place December 10 live from the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles, California.

Here's how the icon felt after his fight with the celebrity host.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Amidst all the tributes and wonderful stories about Patrick Stewart that hit the internet after his passing, one other viral video stood out. Stewart's fight with actor and comedian James Corden onstage at the 2011 Glamour Awards was a rare public outburst by the legendary Star Trek actor, and one that he deeply regretted as the years passed.

For those unfamiliar, the video went viral back then when Stewart took the stage and criticized Corden, the host, for looking disinterested between awards. Corden told Stewart to "get on with presenting," which then escalated to Stewart telling the audience he could see Corden's belly sticking out from the back row. Corden jabbed back that he could see Stewart "dying" onstage due to his age, and after one odd joke involving the Jonas Brothers, the moment ended. People have seen that, but fewer might know how Stewart felt afterward.

Stewart later expressed deep regret about the incident while speaking about it to Classic FM (via Glamour). The Star Trek actor admitted he'd been drinking, and it all went off the rails once he took the stage:

My part of the evening came late and it was alcohol (that prompted the remark), I'm afraid. I went too far, I was somewhat out of control. I have nothing but admiration for Mr Corden. I still blush in remembrance of it.

Buzzfeed also reported that Stewart said elsewhere he was upset by a comment Corden made toward another actress earlier in the evening. He began to drink and, unfortunately, made comments that he regretted. Fortunately, he also confirmed that he'd spoken to the Corden since then, and they agreed to bury the hatchet.

The resurfaced viral video was the most I've seen of James Corden since he retired from late-night, and based on how he spoke about the event, I'm sure he wasn't thrilled to see it back in the news either. The comedian later said he had zero problem with Sir Patrick Stewart, and said that despite how it looked at the moment, he was not mad:

I couldn't have less of a problem with him. He just went for it, he was unscripted, and I've no idea where it was going... And I wish I hadn't looked like I was so angry. Because I was just bemused. I'm not entirely sure what he wanted to happen, but I'm sure what happened wasn't what he wanted. But you know, he's Sir Patrick Stewart and he's great. Everyone's allowed a mistake. My hunch is he's a nice guy.

It's important to know the context of how both sides felt after the fact, because unfortunately, I think people unfairly pushed a narrative about the interaction that wasn't true. The implication was that Patrick Stewart hated James Corden, who has been a polarizing figure since stepping into the limelight.

In reality, the moment went down as one of Stewart's biggest embarrassments, and went against many of the other pleasant interactions that the world knew him for. I'm glad that he found the time to reconcile with Corden after what happened all those years ago, but it's sad to see it resurface again after his death.

CinemaBlend continues to pay respects to Patrick Stewart and offers condolences to his friends and family as they mourn his death. I'm sure more stories about the actor will surface ahead of his appearance in Avengers: Doomsday, which is out in theaters on December 18th.

#3477. Court to Hear Christa Pike's Challenge to her 'Indefinite Isolation' in Prison

After Christa Pike’s attorneys challenged her current prison conditions following her failed execution, a federal court is set to hear arguments in the case.

In an emergency motion filed October 30, Pike’s attorneys called on the court to enforce the terms of a 2024 settlement agreement that ended her 28 years in solitary confinement as the only woman on Tennessee’s death row, allowing for her to have group meals, engage in work and other social and recreational activities.

Pike’s attorneys argued in the filing that the Tennessee Department of Correction is wrongly “holding Ms. Pike in indefinite isolation in the prison infirmary,” away from other women in custody, in violation of that agreement.

In a response filed November 4 viewed by Us, Tennessee Attorney General Jonathan Skrmetti argued the court should deny Pike’s emergency motion, writing prison officials have a “constitutional duty to offer medical care to Pike” and “she can be discharged from the infirmary when medically appropriate.”

A judge will hear the opposing arguments from Pike’s legal team and the state on December 1, according to a Friday, November 13, court order.

Pike, 50, who was sentenced to death at the age of 20 after she was convicted of killing her classmate Colleen Slemmer in January 1995, survived two injections of pentobarbital during a botched execution and was taken to a hospital on September 30.

Following her hospital discharge on October 9, her attorneys contend she’s remained wrongly separated from other women receiving medical care at the Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center as she continues to recover.

In a November 6 reply to the state, Pike’s attorneys wrote, “[The Tennessee Department of Correction] cannot botch the execution of Christa Pike and then point to the injuries it caused as the reason Defendants no longer must honor their Settlement Agreement with her.”

“The Agreement guarantees Ms. Pike group meals, work, lobby time, religious services, and recreation. Defendants do not and cannot deny that they have failed to provide these since at least October 9th. The breach is clear, uncontested, and causing daily harm,” the filing continues.

The state contends in its response to Pike’s emergency motion that it’d be premature to transfer Pike to a separate housing area with other inmates in the prison’s infirmary due to her medical needs and designation as a maximum security incident.

In the state’s response, Skrmetti noted Pike once allegedly tried to kill another inmate and faced discipline for an alleged prison escape attempt. He argued that if she were to rejoin others in custody, it could jeopardize other inmates’ safety.

The attorney general wrote that prison officials “have not breached” the 2024 settlement agreement, “and Pike is not entitled to dictate the terms of her medical treatment and housing.”

The order scheduling the December 1 hearing on Pike’s emergency motion doesn’t indicate whether Pike will appear in court.

Pike’s attorneys didn’t immediately respond to an inquiry from Us on Tuesday, November 17.

#3476. BioWare Is Dead, But Mass Effect’s Spiritual Successor Exodus Just Gave Us A Glimpse of A Spicy Romance

For the first time since its announcement during December 2023's The Game Awards, players are getting a look at the female player-character from its upcoming sci-fi RPG Exodus--which was full of Mass Effect DNA back when we previewed it in September.

The default female version of main character Jun Aslan was revealed today via a seven-minute featurette showing off both female-Jun's face and a bit more of the game itself. The trailer also provided a glimpse of a brief romance scene between female-Jun and Suliman, who is one of the game's romanceable NPCs.

When GameSpot previewed the game, only male-Jun was playable, and we didn't get a chance to romance Suliman, but we did manage to earn his approval, suggesting he may be into both masculine and feminine Jun. We also didn't see the character creator, but there certainly appears to be one, as we see Jun sporting a different look during the romantic encounter with Suliman, with voice actress Carina Corti (Mafia: The Old Country, Little Death) providing Jun's voice throughout both scenes.

Jun's male character model recently got a complete makeover after players complained his original look wasn't pleasing to the eye, but up until today, it wasn't clear who was voicing him. Today, Archetype shared that Stephen Oyoung (Marvel's Spider-Man, Marvel's Spider-Man 2) will be voicing the character.

The female-Jun reveal is followed by a featurette called Scrappy Salvager, featuring a behind-the-scenes look at Jun's origins and the way players' decision can impact Jun's trajectory early on in the game.

"We think of players as the co-authors of our story, and that applies to Jun as well," game director Chris King explains in the video. 

Art director Mark Anderson describes Jun as a "little fish in a really big pond," rather than starting off as a typical hero ready to save the world. Additionally, the featurette goes into more detail about Jun's "precognition" ability, which allows them to see glimpses of possible futures. If interpreted correctly, these premonitions may help players make choices that benefit them. But misunderstanding them may lead to consequences that expand far beyond Jun and their friends. Due to the way the game's time dilation mechanic works, player choices can have unexpected effects that impact civilizations for centuries.

After the death of BioWare, it seems the Mass Effect formula will live on in Exodus, with its vast worlds, strange alien races, NPC romances, and narrative choices. It shouldn't come as a surprise, of course--Exodus developer Archetype Entertainment was founded in 2019 by BioWare veterans James Ohlen, Drew Karpshyn, and Chad Robertson.

Exodus launches on April 7, 2027 and is available to wishlist now on the PlayStation Store, Xbox Store, Steam, and the Epic Games Store.

#3474. Five Smartwatch Heart Rate Zone Hacks Every Runner Should Know

If you've spent any time in or around running culture over the last few years, you've undoubtedly encountered someone preaching the gospel of Zone 2 cardio. Legend has it that easy, conversational effort cardio—also known as cardio that takes your heart rate into "Zone 2"—is the secret to unlocking everything from a bigger aerobic engine to faster race times and even a longer life.

To train by heart rate, you aim to keep your heart rate in the "zone" that gives you the desired workout. The catch is that Zone 2 is easy to get wrong, especially since no one can agree on what it actually means.  Your smartwatch can show you your heart rate, but many recreational runners will still drift into a “gray zone” that's too fast to be truly easy, and too slow to give them a real workout. If you're struggling to hit Zone 2 consistently, there are a few smartwatch hacks that can help.

Pace can be a distraction during easy runs, especially considering all the different variables that affect your effort, like hills, humidity, and general fatigue. A 9:30 mile might be Zone 2 on a flat, cool day and Zone 4 on a hot, hilly one.

Dig into your watch's activity settings (on Garmin, it's Activity > Data Screens; on Apple Watch, the Workout app's metrics layout; on Coros, Polar, and Suunto, similar menus) and put live heart rate zone front and center, ideally as a zone number or colored gauge rather than just a raw bpm figure (though this assumes these zones are accurate—more on that below).

Create an alert when your heart rate goes above or below a target range, delivered as a vibration pattern, a beep, or both. Set the alert for the upper boundary of Zone 2, and you've essentially hired a mini coach who taps you on the wrist whenever you get overzealous. Whenever you hear or feel that buzz, you’ll know you need to ease into a slower jog until your heart rate settles.

Instead of free-running and checking your numbers afterward, build structured workouts that carry the targets for you. In Garmin Connect, TrainingPeaks, Apple's Custom Workout feature, Coros Training Hub, or similar platforms, you can create sessions like "10-minute warm-up in Zone 1, 40 minutes in Zone 2, 5-minute cooldown" and sync them straight to your watch.

During the run, your watch displays the current step, the target range, and whether you're above, below, or in the pocket. Many will automatically advance between intervals and alert you when it's time to shift gears.

Heart rate-based intervals, like 4 x 4 minutes in Zone 4 with Zone 1 recovery, where you don't have to do mental math or check the clock.

Progressive long runs that start in Zone 2 and finish in Zone 3.

Hill repeats, where pace is meaningless but effort matters.

Most watches calculate default zones using a generic formula like 220 minus your age, which can be off by 10 to 20 beats for any given individual. If your zones are wrong, your Zone 2 training isn't Zone 2 training.

Here’s how to fix your watch’s heart rate zones:

Find your true max heart rate. The informal way is to just notice what number you see on your watch when you can no longer speak comfortably; the more formal way is this treadmill test. You can also look through your recent hard efforts, like races, hill repeats, or all-out intervals, and see the highest sustained heart rate you've recorded.

Use lactate threshold heart rate instead. Many watches can estimate this automatically after a few hard efforts, and zones built from threshold tend to be more personalized than ones built from max.

Customize the boundaries. Dive into the heart rate zone settings and input your own numbers. Some runners prefer the "MAF" method (180 minus age, with adjustments) for aerobic base building, and most watches let you set that as a custom range.

Recheck every few months. Fitness changes, and so do your zones.

A screen crowded with cadence, vertical oscillation, ground contact time, running power, and lap pace is a recipe for second-guessing.

Create a dedicated Zone 2 data screen with just two or three fields: current heart rate zone, elapsed time, and maybe distance. Turn off auto-scroll so it doesn't flip to a screen full of numbers you don't need. If your watch supports multiple activity profiles, make a separate "Easy Run" profile with this stripped-down layout and keep a different profile for tempo days and races.

A chest strap (or a forearm or upper-arm optical band) is generally more accurate and responsive than the wrist-based sensor on your watch. For heart rate training, where a few beats can mean the difference between Zone 2 and Zone 3, I recommend buying one. This COOSPO heart rate monitor is one of my favorites, and it's only $31.99.

The bottom line: Your smartwatch can make heart rate training far easier, but only if you set it up to support you rather than overwhelm you.

#3473. These Early Black Friday Ring Camera Deals Start at $24.99

If you’re browsing home security options, Ring has one of the best early Black Friday deals that should be on your radar. Right now, you can add an indoor camera and another one at your front door for less than $65. The Ring Indoor Cam 2K is 58% off at $24.99 (originally $59.99), while the Ring Battery Doorbell 2K is 60% off at $39.99 (originally $99.99)—both at their lowest-ever price.

Both offer features like 2K video and two-way talk, but the indoor cam is the simpler purchase if you mainly want to check on a pet or kids and see what’s happening near an entrance. It plugs into an outlet, so there’s no battery to recharge, and its low-light color video helps preserve detail when lights are off or dimmed. However, since it’s a fixed-view camera, keep in mind that you’ll need to position it carefully.

The Battery Doorbell is the better pick if alerting you to visitors, deliveries, and potential intruders is your priority. It has a 140-degree horizontal and vertical field of view that provides head-to-toe framing, plus up to 6x zoom for better detail. You can install it without wiring, though you’ll need to recharge its built-in battery. It also requires a 2.4GHz wifi network.

The main catch with both devices is the ongoing subscription cost: Live viewing, two-way talk, and basic real-time notifications all work without a subscription, but reviewing saved footage requires a paid plan, starting at $4.99 per month or $49.99 annually for one device; coverage for multiple devices at one location starts at $9.99 monthly or $99.99 annually.

At these prices, the Ring Indoor Cam 2K is perfect for occasional live check-ins, while the Ring Battery Doorbell 2K is better suited to monitoring your front entrance. Buying both makes sense if you already have a Ring plan that covers extra devices.

#3472. Kelly Bishop Hints at Tension Between ‘Stars Hollow’ Group on ‘Gilmore Girls’

The unauthorized Gilmore Girls documentary, Drink Coffee, Talk Fast, is here to celebrate more than 25 years of the show’s iconic legacy.

Produced by Ink On Paper Studios and directed by Meghna Balakumar and Kevin Konrad Hanna, the doc features interviews with original cast and crew members, including Kelly Bishop, Scott Patterson, Jared Padalecki, Keiko Agena, Chad Michael Murray and more.

Keep scrolling to see the biggest revelations made in the film:

Diner owner Luke Danes, played by Scott Patterson, was originally intended to be a woman named Daisy. However, the character was ultimately rewritten when The WB requested “more testosterone” in the show to balance out the female characters. Of course, that decision brought fans the beloved romance between Luke and Lorelai Gilmore (Lauren Graham), so we can’t be too upset that Daisy never came to be.

Before Jared Padalecki took on the role of Rory Gilmore’s (Alexis Bledel) first boyfriend, Dean Forrester, two other actors had the role.

“We had to recast the role of Dean,” casting director Jami Rudofsky recalled in the doc.

Casting director Mara Casey added, “There was a Canadian Dean and then there was this other Dean. I think they fired two dudes.”

Padalecki, who was 17 years old when he auditioned for Gilmore Girls, was ready to return home to Texas if he didn’t land the part. Thankfully, Casey, Rudofsky and series creator Amy Sherman-Palladino were all instantly sold on him playing Dean.

Likewise, Lorelai’s best friend, Sookie St. James, was initially played by Alex Borstein in the unaired pilot episode before Melissa McCarthy took on the role. Borstein was unable to play the character due to a scheduling conflict, although she went on to appear in the show as Drella, the harp player, and Miss Celine.

Several actresses auditioned for the role of Lorelai, but one crucial line in the script solidified Graham as the lead.

“In that first scene in Luke’s Diner, there was a reference to Jack Kerouac,” director Lesli Linka Glatter said in the doc, recalling how Graham was the only actress to pronounce the famous novelist’s last name correctly.

“Amy’s writing had so many references to theater and literature and contemporary music,” Glatter recalled. “So we said, ‘You know what? We cannot have someone that doesn’t know who Jack Kerouac is.’”

During the early days of filming Gilmore Girls, The WB frequently called Sherman-Palladino with complaints about the script because the show didn’t fit the network’s target audience. She finally got the calls to stop when she issued an ultimatum: fire her or quit complaining. It worked.

Many of the cast members in the doc recalled having to be “word perfect” when reciting their lines on set. Even replacing “a” with “the” wasn’t allowed. They also had to talk very fast, which is where coffee came in handy.

“We used to have delicious coffee drinks on set,” Rose Abdoo, who played Gypsy, recalled. “We all talked even faster, and I thought, ‘OK, they’re not just trying to treat us. We’re really all jazzed up now.’ … It wasn’t one of those shows where people could improvise… no, every word is there for a reason.”

Murray, who played Chilton student Tristin Dugray, remembered being told by Sherman-Palladino, “Talk faster. I don’t want to cut any pages out of this show.”

Season 3 of Gilmore Girls featured an episode where Jess Mariano (Milo Ventimiglia) traveled to California to get to know his father. The episode doubled as a backdoor pilot for a spinoff called Windward Circle. Though Ventimiglia was on board with the spinoff, the WB ultimately canceled the project after the California episode received poor feedback. It was also reportedly too expensive to film in Venice Beach.

In the doc, Sherilyn Fenn, who played Sasha in the episode and was later recast as Anna Nardini, claimed that The WB thought Ventimiglia couldn’t lead a spinoff.

“The studio was so silly. They said, ‘Oh, Milo’s not strong enough to carry a show,’” she said. (Ventimiglia went on to star as Jack Pearson in the NBC drama This Is Us.)

Gilmore Girls had many cameos from actors who would go on to become famous, including Seth MacFarlane, Jane Lynch, Jon Hamm, Rami Malek and more. Ryan Gosling was almost on that list, too, but he bombed his audition, Rudofsky revealed.

Bledel’s first major role was playing Rory in Gilmore Girls when she was 18 years old. Though she expressed gratitude for the opportunities the show brought her, cast and crew members recalled in the doc that she sometimes struggled with the grueling filming schedule.

“She was just like 18 years old, and ‘I’m here for 60, 70 hours a week. What am I doing with my life?’ And it’s pretty, it’s gruelling,” Mark Strasburg, first assistant camera, said. “It’s something you really had to want to do. There were definitely moments she knew she didn’t want to be there.”

The doc also featured footage of an older interview with Patterson in which he admitted, “Alexis was really overwhelmed by being away from her family, maybe having some second thoughts about what she had gotten herself into. ‘Is this really a way to spend my youth?’ She was terribly homesick. And what was nice to see was the bond that formed off the set between Lauren and Alexis, because Lauren really helped her out.”

While the doc’s participants had mostly fond memories of their time on Gilmore Girls, Kelly Bishop, who played Emily Gilmore, alluded to some behind-the-scenes drama between cast members.

“I loved working with that little nucleus of a family. The Hartford group got along great,” she recalled, referring to herself, the late Ed Herrmann (who played Richard Gilmore), Bledel and Graham. “I guess there was a little bit of problems here and there in Stars Hollow, and I’m not gonna tell you what they were because it’s none of my business, and it was hearsay and I don’t do that.”

While Bishop did not name-drop anyone, others suggested that Graham and Patterson didn’t get along off camera. George Anthony Bell, the show’s dialogue coach, noted that he didn’t think the pair “hung out after the show,” while Strasburg added, “Off screen, I’m not sure if they’re besties, but they don’t really seem to really like each other. But on screen they’re amazing.”

Graham and Patterson previously shut down rumors of a feud. In 2007, Graham told TV Guide that their friendship was a “working relationship like most of them are. But he was so great in that part. I really loved my scenes with him and the chemistry we had. Our banter was among the most fun stuff to do.”

Patterson told 7News in 2023, “I love her, she loves me, we get along very, very well.”

#3471. Who Killed Fashion Founders Bryan Walker and Michelle Min?

Panoramic Hill looms above the UC Berkeley campus, a tree-covered neighborhood cut by steep paths and outdoor staircases. Century-old homes by brand-name architects like Bernard Maybeck and Walter Steilberg dot the incline, which straddles the border of Berkeley and Oakland. Each residence is worth millions; increase the amount for the occasional bit of newer construction. Unlike the busy urban streets below, the area is incredibly quiet. That’s one of the reasons everyone heard the shots.

“I have that stored in my memory, as I will for the rest of my life,” Daniella Salzman tells me, looking out her window at the former home of Michelle Min and her husband, Bryan Walker. The couple, creators of the Bryn Walker clothing brand, were found just outside their residence around 10:45 a.m. on October 2, 2026, shortly after neighbors called 911 to report the sound of gunfire. Initial confusion about jurisdiction sent police from both Berkeley’s and Oakland’s departments to the scene.

By the time paramedics arrived, Walker and Min were dead from what OPD assistant chief Casey Johnson characterized as “apparent gunshots” in a press conference later that day. A firearm, he said, was located at the scene. He declined to offer further details on the case, saying that the department’s homicide division would handle the investigation.

Nearly seven weeks later, we still know next to nothing about how Walker and Min died. While OPD turned down my request to speak with Johnson, it sent me a press release with the same details he laid out on October 2. Follow-up questions were met with: “There are no updates being released other than the information below.”

Bryn Walker store on Vine Street in Berkeley, California.

“I don’t know what has publicly been shared or what privately has been learned about what took place,” Salzman says carefully. Police have been silent since the brief press conference the day the bodies were discovered. But Michelle Min’s brother, Paul Min, hasn’t been quiet.

Within two days after his 63-year-old sister was found dead, Paul spoke with outlets including the LA Times and the California Post, accusing his brother-in-law of killing his wife, then himself, following a series of disastrous financial decisions that led to significant losses and a collapse in his mental state. The interviews, given so soon after the crime, suggest Paul was still in a state of shock over his loss. Walker, who was 61 when he died, was “the most honest, responsible, hardworking guy you have ever known,” Paul told the LA Times. “I loved him like a brother.” Michelle “was utterly devoted to Bryan to the very end,” Paul told the Post, “and he shot her.”

After those interviews, which were published that first weekend in October, Paul fell silent too; I made multiple efforts to arrange an interview but was ultimately unsuccessful. But according to the Post’s interview, Walker “had quietly taken out loans against their properties, and had gambled on risky options and leveraged positions,” with estimated losses of “well over $100 million.” The debt, per the LA Times story, allegedly prompted Walker to suggest that he and the Min siblings “end things”—a proposal that alarmed the Mins, but only because of its implications for Walker’s mental health. Paul didn’t see Walker as a danger: “He said the idea that Walker would or could harm them was absurd to the two of them,” reported the Times.

The Mins came to the US from Korea in 1977, settling first near Kansas City. Michelle met Walker there in the 1980s, and after the Mins’ parents chose to move to California, the siblings, and Walker, followed. In 1992 the couple opened a clothing store in Berkeley that sold goods from other makers. As time went on, they began to manufacture more and more of their own goods.

Eventually, Bryn Walker evolved into a clothing brand known for loose linen looks with an Asian-meets-Swedish flair. “Flowy, a touch eclectic, made for perhaps older women who want to mesh elegant/sophisticated with a bit of boho uniqueness,” a longtime Berkeley resident told me over email. “Women who want to look expensive but with a bit of verve.” When I described the company to one San Francisco resident as “elevated Chico’s,” I got a stern look. “You better not let any of the Bryn Walker moms at Lowell hear you say that,” she said, referencing the city’s hotly competitive public high school. “These are not humorous people.”

Bryn Walker store on Fourth Street in Berkeley, California.

According to the Post piece, Walker “had stepped aside and allowed his designer wife to control their mutual business and his eponymous fashion label,” but it’s not clear when that management change occurred. As the brand grew, it struck a chord with fashion businesses across the country—from luxury boutiques to the family-run department store chain Dillard’s. Bryn Walker also opened its own brick-and-mortar storefronts beyond Berkeley.

Many of those stores are now gone. One Bryn Walker location in Santa Monica closed prior to mid-March of 2021, while a 22-year-old outpost in Palo Alto shuttered in 2020. On the East Coast, a shop in Edgartown, on Martha’s Vineyard, went dark in 2024. A call to its shop in Vineyard Haven was met with a recorded message saying the business would be closed until further notice. That leaves just two company-owned shops, both in Berkeley, where Bryn Walker began.

One of those stores is on Berkeley’s buzzy Fourth Street, a glossy shopping destination lined with outposts of national brands like Apple, Lululemon, and Herman Miller. With items generally priced between $130–$300, it fits right into the overall ethos of that street—and Berkeley—where almost everything is spendy but not flashy; theoretically accessible, though not to those on a budget. During my recent visit to the shop, the sole staffer remained pleasant even after I identified myself as a journalist—but her tone grew firm. “It’s all still too raw,” she said of the tragedy.

I asked if, as he’d said he would in his Post interview, Paul Min had taken over management of the company following its founders’ deaths. “I don’t know about that,” she replied, before declining to speak further. I was told by another local business owner that Bryn Walker employees are actively seeking other employment; it’s unclear what will happen to the label now that its creators are gone. I tried to reach Bryn Walker management by phone and email for this story, but did not receive a response.

Emilie Raguso was one of the first journalists to report on the deaths, for her independent outlet, The Berkeley Scanner. As she began investigating, she “saw that the number of open shops was different based on where you looked,” she says. “I was getting this early inkling of what others later reported as far as the business being in trouble.”

“The writing was on the wall,” she continues, “but there was nothing explicit. It did seem like, Oh, this is not a thriving business.”

Paul’s comments to the media didn’t address the health of the business. Instead, he was focused on Walker and Michelle’s personal finances, which he alleged were laid to waste by Walker’s mismanagement. “Your spouse lied to you and lost over $100 million and you might be out on the streets,” Paul told the Post. “You might go from being one of the wealthiest people in the country to being homeless because your husband lied to you and wagered everything on crazy bets.”

According to Paul, things grew so grim for Walker that the Mins spoke about institutionalizing him. But it’s also unclear how they would have acted on that without Walker’s cooperation. California enacted its CARE Court program in 2023, more easily allowing court-ordered treatment plans for those who might pose a threat to themselves or others. But in practice, courts have been reluctant to take that drastic step, frequently rejecting petitions from those closest to the person in crisis.

Bryn Walker-Pacific Cotton store on Main Street in Vineyard Haven, Massachusetts.

Speaking with the LA Times, Paul said that in Walker and Michelle’s home, he “found a note that lists a couple of [mental health] facilities. I speculate he saw that note or somehow figured out she was going to institutionalize him, but I have no idea.”

Paul’s claim that Walker killed Michelle over snowballing financial fears isn’t out of the realm of possibility, even in a place as wealthy as the Bay Area. One year before Walker and Michelle died, almost to the day, entrepreneur Paula Truong fatally shot her husband, Thomas, and their daughters, Mackenzie and Alexandra, before hanging herself in the garage of their $2.2 million San Francisco home. Reporting found that the family had experienced a string of financial challenges, including several failed business ventures, a home foreclosure, and a number of unpaid debts.

But that was in San Francisco—a sometimes gritty city that people escape with moves to places like Panoramic Hill. “When you get up into the hills, it does feel like a world apart,” Raguso says. “It feels insulated from a lot of the more common disturbances and things that we deal with down on the flatlands.”

Salzman has lived on that hill for more than 20 years, and she’s still struggling with the notion that her neighbor might have killed his wife. “Bryan was very engaged with neighbors who were needing support that were near him,” she says, characterizing him and Michelle as “committed to the community.” But she also believes that the fear of losing wealth can drive people to desperate acts. “We see wealth as being both our greatest need and our greatest opportunity here,” she says, “and we are told that we will be happy when we consume. This is the message that we’re given everywhere we look”—especially in a region with more billionaires than anywhere else in the world.

Raguso isn’t sure why Oakland police are taking so long to announce the results of their investigation. “At some point, there would be a ruling,” she says, citing possible delays with the medical examiner’s office as a reason things haven’t been resolved. According to Salzman, the vacuum of information has inspired her to look at all her neighbors with a little more care. “Part of what I awoke to was how little I know about really what’s going on with people that I’m geographically so close to,” she says.

“I just would have loved for there to have been a way to be a part of showing up for them, even around the little things. The more people that are aware of what is happening, the more people are potentially able to heal.”

#3470. Apple Won't Make a Small Phone so This Company Is Stepping In

Big smartphones have long been the norm. It seems many, if not most, of us prefer our smartphones to be akin to tiny tablets. Even Apple's smallest iPhone isn't that small, with a 6.1-inch display. (Compare that to the 5.4-inch iPhone mini it used to sell.) But just because a lot of us like it that way doesn't mean all of us do.

Despite what companies like Apple would lead you to believe, there are plenty of people out there who want their smartphones to be smaller. For some, the iPhone mini was perfect, featuring a design that most could use comfortably with one hand. While the sales might not have been steady enough for Apple to continue producing the mini line, anecdotally, I know quite a few people who would happily keep using iPhones this small, if only Apple would make more of them. Perhaps you know people like this too; maybe you're one of them.

While the rumor mill does not suggest that Apple plans to make a new iPhone mini, that doesn't mean the dream of the tiny smartphone is dead. Enter "Enough Phone," a new device with a humble goal: to create a "small, modern smartphone that's enough."

Enough Phone really does seem small. The company says its upcoming device is 133mm by 64mm, and less than 12mm thick. That's the equivalent of 5.24 inches by 2.52 inches, and less than 0.47 inches thick. It's remarkably similar to the iPhone 13 mini, at 5.18 by 2.53 inches, and 0.3 inches thick. While the Enough Phone might be a tad larger overall, and perhaps noticeably thicker, it's still reminiscent of that "mini" footprint.

The Enough Phone's 5.3-inch display isn't particularly modern, however. While we don't know the display type, we do know that it has a resolution of 1520 x 720, which may look less sharp to anyone coming from the 2340 x 1080 resolution of the iPhone 13 mini. I'd wager that most people interested in a device like this aren't looking for an ultra-sharp OLED display anyway, but it's worth noting here.

As for the Enough Phone's other specs, the company says it plans to pack in a 2.4GHz MediaTek Dimensity 7500 chip with 8GB of RAM, 128GB of built-in storage, though you can expand that with a microSD card (something you don't see on many smartphones these days). The current plan is to ship with a single 50MP Sony IMX766 rear camera, and a 32MP selfie cam, which would be amongst the highest-resolution front-facing cameras on any smartphone. It supports 5G, Wi-Fi 6, and eSIM, with the option to use a physical SIM as well.

Enough is also aiming to make its smartphone more repairable than the competition. While smartphone OEMs have made slight improvements to repairability in recent years, few phones are made to be opened up by the user, and their components replaced. While Enough Phone isn't fully modular, it is designed with easy-to-open screws, and comes with a fully replaceable 3,500 mAh battery. Combined with promised software support through 2032, Enough says this device "should last you into the next decade."

Now, all of these specs are targets, as the phone is currently in the prototype stage. Enough says that final details may change "slightly" during testing. I would at least hope that the dimensions, particularly the screen size, remain the same by launch. What will likely stay the same, however, are the ringtones: Enough says they hired composer Brian Squillance of LAANDS to produce the jingles for its phone, which is a neat touch.

Unfortunately for Apple fans, however, Enough Phone isn't an iPhone. That said, it doesn't have to be an Android phone, either. While you can buy the phone with Android 17 installed, you can also choose to run OdysseyOS, a minimalist "de-Googled" operating system made by SLEKE. Enough says OdysseyOS is meant for "intentional phone use," which might appeal to anyone looking for a phone that's "dumb" as well as small.

Of course, neither operating system is iOS. Unfortunately for Apple users, the only true iPhone options here are to continue using an old iPhone mini, which Apple does still support, or to opt for an iPhone 17e, the smallest iPhone the company currently makes. It's pretty easy to find a used and refurbished iPhone 13 mini for reasonable price; but while they can still run the latest version of iOS, you won't be able to take advantage of all of Apple's newest features. Plus, while there's no telling how long Apple plans to support the 13 line for, it won't support it forever—by iOS 28 or iOS 29, your phone might lose support entirely.

If the promise of a modern mini smartphone entices you, you can back the Enough Phone on Kickstarter today. While the company's $399 "Super Early Bird" reward is already sold out, as of this article, the "Early Bird" reward is still up. That reward costs $449, and includes a glass screen protector pre-installed, a protective case, a USB-C cable, a USB-C to 3.5mm headphone adapter, a hex screwdriver, and green "Founders' Edition" backplate screws. Enough says that the retail price for its phone will be $599 after the campaign, so you can save $150 by backing the phone today—if you're serious about small phones. The Enough Phone is slated for a May 2027 launch.

There are few things I love more than a reality show, and after years of devouring The Traitors with my Peacock subscription, I was thrilled to hear that the folks behind that Emmy-winning series were creating another. Enter The Mob, another campy competition show that's available in its entirety with a Hulu subscription. The show once again proved that RuPaul's Drag Race alum Willam Belli is a top-tier TV personality, but it turns out that not even the cast knew the rules when cameras went up.

The Mob's jobs feel more urgent than The Traitors' missions, but it took some adjusting to its format. Even the cast had a hard time with this, mostly because they didn't actually know all of the rules of the show they were competing on. During a recent clip from Gayety's Instagram, Willam spoke about her experience shooting the series, saying:

I asked for the rules every episode and I didn't get them until Episode 4, a printed copy. We did not know what was going on and we really wanted to. But information is power, and I understand that you don't want a reality show contestant to have power. So keeping them in dark leads to better stakes for the game and I understand that now.

Well, my mind is blown. It was hard enough to nail down the rules and format of The Mob as a viewer, but the fact that the cast was similarly clueless is truly wild to me. It didn't make the show's first four episodes any less entertaining, even though many of my favorite contestants got whacked way too early. Still, I'd think that the powers that be on production would want the reality TV personalities to at least know everything about the game they were expected to play.

As much as I enjoyed the first season of The Mob, I have to assume that the gameplay might have been even more dynamic if the cast knew the show's rules from the jump. Indeed, the first few eliminations were a little sleepy, such as Dancing with the Stars judge Bruno Tonioli pledging allegiance to Joe Gorga and then immediately getting whacked.

You can see Willam Belli's comments about The Mob and feeling a bit clueless at the start of filming below:

Willam might be the only contestant from RuPaul's Drag Race to get disqualified, but that doesn't mean she went against the rules in every situation. After all, The Mob cast were starting a brand new competition series, and didn't have any previous episodes to use as a reference. The folks who caught on seemed to make it the farthest, but it was curtains for other favorites like Willam, Bruno, and Debi Mazar.

The Mob is streaming in its entirety on Hulu as part of the 2026 TV schedule. We'll just have to see if it gets renewed for a second season, and how the gameplay changes with contestants who know what to expect.

#3468. Teresa Giudice Claims 'Well-Known TV Actress' Was 'So Rude' to Her in New Book

Teresa Giudice might be the self-proclaimed queen of New Jersey, but that hasn’t protected her from being slighted by A-list celebrities from time to time.

Teresa, 54, recalled in her new memoir, The Queen of New Jersey, that unlike meeting the “gracious” Taylor Swift at Coachella Music Festival, “Not every celebrity interaction goes quiet as well.”

She recounted an alleged incident in the book involving an unnamed TV actress that transpired shortly after she rose to fame in 2009 on The Real Housewives of New Jersey.

“[I] was once instructed by my PR team to pose with a well-known TV actress for a photo,” Teresa wrote, noting that the women were both in Los Angeles for an appearance with TV host Mario Lopez. “After we took the photo, I overheard her telling her PR people, ‘Why are you making me take a picture with that woman?’”

The Bravolebrity remembered, “The tone of her voice was so surprising,” writing, “Look, I get if she didn’t know who I was, but to me, that’s just so rude.”

Teresa didn’t identify the actress, but revealed that years later she was back in L.A. having dinner with her husband, Luis “Louie” Ruelas, when a fan came in and asked her for a picture.

“It’s part of this life, and one I happen to enjoy. We took a photo together and chatted for a minute, and then she left us to be seated at her own table,” she shared. “Ten minutes later, who walks in? The actress who had definitely not wanted to take a picture with me all that time ago backstage at Mario Lopez’s show.”

Teresa recalled, “We made brief eye contact — there was definitely no need to say hi — as she was shown to her table.”

The cherry on top for Teresa was when she realized that the actress’ dinner date was the fan who asked her for a photo moments earlier.

“I hope she enjoyed feigning interest as her friend showed her the pictures we’d taken just moments before,” Teresa jokingly wrote.

The reality star added, “I’ll always have respect for a celebrity who doesn’t forget where they came from or who made them. There are a lot of people in this business who can’t stand to stop and pose for a photo or sign something for a fan. Like, really? You think you’re such a big deal that you can’t spare a moment for the very audience whose attention made you who you are?”

The actress in question has not been identified, but there are publicly available photos that show Teresa filming a segment with Lopez, 53, in May 2011 for Extra, which fans speculate could be when the alleged slight took place. No other famous individuals are visible in the pictures.

In addition to juicy tales of celebrity run-ins, Teresa’s new book promises to tell-all — including the highs and lows of her RHONJ break, her first husband Joe Giudice’s deportation and her road to a second love. (Teresa will be back for season 15 of RHONJ, premiering in January, following the show’s hiatus.)

“Only a true queen can rise and fall and rise again, sweetheart. Take notes,” the book tease reads.

The memoir will reflect on Teresa’s “two tumultuous decades in the public eye,” as well as her “biggest triumphs, heartbreaks, feuds, and controversies of her life with newfound perspective,” according to the brief synopsis.

“Raw, funny, emotional, and unapologetic, The Queen of New Jersey is the story of a woman who has been cast as everything from villain to victim — but refuses to let anyone else write her legacy,” the publisher adds. “After all, if the crown fits, wear it.”

The Queen of New Jersey is now available for purchase.

#3466. Atlas Atelier Is Making Makeup for People Who Want to Be Remembered

You know how everyone is debating whether smoking is back? Atlas Atelier is like the subject of the makeup version of that conversation, in both its long, skinny lipsticks that evoke a cheeky cigarette and its past-bedtime, maybe something a little naughty is happening vibe. The Paris-based brand makes just lipstick, blush, and a black liquid eyeliner, all engineered to be best shown off at night, maybe under the light of candles, or as you sip a cocktail or wear a jacket with strong shoulders. It’s makeup that is supposed to look like makeup. Severe is not too strong a word to use.

The brand’s late-30s founder, Michelle Duncan, doesn’t smoke herself and doesn’t do barely there makeup along the lines of Rhode, Rare Beauty, or Glossier. “I am a New Yorker, and I’ve been living in Paris primarily for the last four or five years. When I arrived in Paris, everyone was so well-heeled that you would never see somebody wearing a gym look to go to dinner. This resonated with me about this idea of dressing up to go out no matter what you were doing, even if it’s going to a café. That was a huge inspiration for me,” she says.

Duncan knew the industry she was getting into. She’s a veteran of brands owned by Estée Lauder, including both MAC and Tom Ford Beauty, and she also worked for Cartier. Atlas Atelier—the “atlas” is in homage to Ayn Rand’s Atlas Shrugged—just came out this fall in the US (now available at Violet Grey and Bergdorf Goodman). Vanity Fair spoke to Duncan about Paris expat life, rejecting celebrity brands, and what happens to makeup in unstable times.

The interview that follows has been condensed for length and clarity.

Vanity Fair: You know the challenges of the beauty industry. You’re not an influencer; you didn’t pick a celebrity to be the face of the brand or to partner with. Why not make it easier on yourself?

Michelle Duncan: Friends will ask, “Didn’t you want to do this with a celeb?” I wouldn’t want to. Culture and society is so focused on a quick buck right this second, which I’m totally into. I love making money very fast. This is so much about the world of Atlas, with the packaging and with the storytelling. The brand ethos of Atlas is about the night, about this seductive environment that, to me, will actually cut through the clutter in a long-term way. When a high-profile person launches a brand, the bet that they’re taking is on who they are as a person. For me, the bet is, do you buy into Atlas’s story?

Makeup has gotten very big and plastic and in some ways looks like toys. That was sort of my first remit on it. The whole brief was: We want to create something that looks like an object that you want to be able to keep. My inspirations really are the 1930s, the Art Deco, Paris moment, and how do we make it leap into the ’80s in some ways because that’s obviously also just a second extension of the ’30s?

The 1980s version of Art Deco is so good. All that lacquer and glass blocks and chrome lamps.

It felt like something that was radically different from what’s going on in the world right now, at least in beauty land. We’re exiting this no-makeup era, or hopefully exiting this quiet-luxury era. Those things were very pared back. Maybe focusing more internally about wellness and things like that. I understood that this was missing and that it was going to come back.

The idea of self-expression in a sort of glamorous way. In the 1930s, it was not a great time in the world. And if we remember, the 1980s in New York City was decadent and over the top and seemed very fun, but as a reaction to what was going on. I would argue that we are kind of in that place right now. We don’t really need to go into politics, but it is chaos right now. And so the answer to that is always this other form of self-expression.

The name of the brand is a reference to Atlas Shrugged. Are you a big fan of Ayn Rand?

I’ve always admired and been inspired by Dagny Taggart, one of the most iconic characters in 20th-century literature. She’s written as a fiercely independent entrepreneur in a male-dominated world, who is in control of her own life and embracing its complexity. When creating my business, I was trying to channel that vision of what a woman can be: intellectually formidable, professionally ambitious, and comfortable with her sensuality. I was especially struck by one moment in the novel, when Dagny draws on a statue using her lipstick, reminding us that makeup isn’t just to change our appearance—it can be a tool for women to own their own power. I wanted to create a makeup line that gave women that same feeling of confidence, ambition, and sensuality through tools like lipstick, blush, and eyeliner.

Yes. I have been wearing this winged-eyeliner situation for a very long time. Actually, since I was a teenager. If I don’t have my eyeliner on, I feel naked and I don’t feel like I have everything with me.

So you’re wearing eyeliner at home. What about the people who are reading this who may be thinking, I never go out, or I have kids, or I’m tired, or I work a lot, or all of those things? Do you want people to go out a lot? Do you go out a lot? Is it more just the mindset of going out at nighttime?

The idea of my brand is it should be a pleasure to put on makeup, and I want people to experience pleasure again and just forget about all of the things that are happening, like picking up the kids, or going to the grocery store, or getting the dry cleaning, or whatever it is. Just remembering what it means to have a nice time and be inspired by the night. I, on purpose and by design, did not launch foundations or these technical components of makeup, because that’s just not really what it’s about.

How is expat life? I know so many people who have moved to France, or they would love to move to France. What do you think that’s about?

In my social circle, it tends to consist of either people somehow in the fashion industry, the music industry, or the arts communities. A lot of those industries have just become quite commercial in America, as an example. And I haven’t lived in a lot of other countries, so I don’t really know expat life so well. But the amount of Italians that are here, the Spanish, the Germans, the Americans, and everyone just has this chaotic, frenetic energy of being around each other and doing things together. It’s pretty remarkable.

I know you’re not doing celebrity spokespeople, but who would you want if you didn’t have to think about money or access or if they already had a beauty contract?

Somebody like [the artist] Nadia Lee Cohen. She’s super glamorous. She’s quite creative. She’s a genius in a lot of ways, and she actually uses makeup as art. And then somebody like Dakota Johnson. I think she’s so chic now. Dua Lipa. I love her. She’s got the perfect energy for this. She’s there, she’s having a good time, and she’s powerful.

Do you want to expand into other products ? It feels like you could do a fragrance. Or maybe a very chic makeup remover?

I can’t wait for the day that we are able to launch a fragrance because that is one of those things you remember, along with lip color. You remember what they smell like, and when they leave the room, and so that’s the impression that Atlas is supposed to be giving—you’re remembered when you left the room.

#3464. Three Ways to Avoid CAPTCHA Prompts When Using a VPN

VPNs make it harder to track your online activity across websites, but it also makes them suspicious about your origins. When you borrow an IP address that hundreds of other people are also using for any number of reasons, you’re much more likely to get repeat verification requests from online firewalls.

CAPTCHAs are simple puzzles that websites use to filter out bots and spam. They’re supposed to be easy for people but hard for robots, such as simple object recognition tasks or audio-visual challenges. However, they can still disrupt your browsing experience if they happen too frequently.

Most modern CAPTCHA providers, like Google's reCAPTCHA v3 or Cloudflare Turnstile, start working long before they give you a puzzle to solve. It usually starts with a risk score that studies your IP address, browser and device signals, or recent online activity.

If the CAPTCHA provider can’t confidently identify your request as human based on those signals, it requests that you complete a puzzle before deciding if the request should be blocked. That means when you get repeat CAPTCHA requests, there’s something affecting your browser’s risk score. For example, popular VPN servers spread the same IP address across any number of users, which can easily make a website mistake you for a bot farm. If you change your IP address frequently by switching servers often, that might look suspicious too.

Luckily, there are ways to deal with frequent CAPTCHA requests using tools and services available with your browser and VPN. Cloudflare has already cut its CAPTCHA requests by 91% using its Managed Challenge platform. Apple has also been shipping token-based verification on devices since iOS 16 and macOS Ventura. In June 2026, Cloudflare even announced a joint effort called the Private Access Control Tokens (PACT) standard with Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Shopify.

While there’s no direct off switch for CAPTCHAs, you can use different fixes to improve your browser’s trust signals when using the internet. That way, you’re less likely to be hounded by verification requests.

The easiest fix for repeat CAPTCHAs is to stop connecting to whichever server your VPN app picks automatically. Proton recommends choosing servers with lower traffic load. In fact, its apps display load as a percentage to help you avoid the most crowded options. I'd also skip big traffic hubs like New York or London, since that's where most traffic originates from. Servers in smaller cities located nearby are often just as fast but never as populated.

You should also avoid changing IP addresses too frequently, which can look suspicious on its own. Pick a server that seems to behave well, then continue using it for at least one session. Also remember you’re more likely to get premium server options if you’re on a paid VPN plan. Major platforms like ExpressVPN, Surfshark, Proton, and Nord are particularly likely to have a larger server collection to pick from.

Costs nothing more than your current subscription

Hopping between servers often can backfire

Private Access Tokens (PAT) let you verify the authenticity of your request using your device rather than an IP address. Apple calls it Automatic Verification, where an Apple server validates your device and Apple Account to assign you an anonymous token.

To enable Automatic Verification on an iPhone or iPad, go to Settings > [your name] > Sign-In & Security > Automatic Verification. On a Mac, open System Settings > [your name] > Sign-In & Security > Automatic Verification.

Unfortunately, there’s no equivalent feature for Windows, Android, and Linux users. That said, Cloudflare offers the Silk extension for Chrome, Firefox, and Edge that serves a similar function. A quick look at the ratings will tell you it’s not as effective, but Cloudflare’s upcoming cross-browser standard called PACT seems promising once it is released.

Doesn’t share personal details with websites

Chrome and Firefox extensions can be unreliable

If you pay a bit extra for a dedicated IP add-on, VPN providers can assign you a unique IP address that isn’t shared with anyone else. For example, NordVPN offers dedicated IPs in 30 countries for $2-5 a month and Surfshark charges $3.75 a month for it.

There are also dedicated providers like Private Internet Access, which charges $3.99 per month for a zero-trust setup so not even their employees know which IP address is assigned to you. On the other hand, Proton VPN offers dedicated IPs only to business plan users, so you’ll need to be on the Workspace Standard, Premium, or Enterprise plans to get one.

That said, there is a trade-off here too. NordVPN itself admits that a dedicated IP makes it easier to link online activity back to a single user. Also, many websites can still tell that the IP address originated from a VPN data center rather than a consumer’s device.

Get unique IP addresses with pristine reputation

Works across desktop, mobile, and even smart TVs

Also functions as an allowlisted address for work

#3463. Vanity Fair Announces New Hires and Promotions Across Departments

Vanity Fair Global Editorial Director Mark Guiducci today announced 11 new hires and appointments to the magazine’s masthead, deepening the magazine’s coverage across technology and politics, while adding talent to its operations and creative teams.

Vanity Fair’s new hires bring fresh perspectives to the magazine’s reporting on power and influence, alongside new creative voices to help shape its visual storytelling.

Maggie Coughlan is promoted to global managing editor. Since joining the team in 2021, she has held several positions at Vanity Fair, most recently as executive editor. She previously held editorial roles at the New York Post and People.com. She holds a master’s degree in digital publishing from NYU.

Emily Shugerman joins Vanity Fair as a senior staff writer reporting on wealth and politics on the West Coast. Emily comes from The San Francisco Standard, where she covered the shifting political allegiances of Silicon Valley’s richest, the fight over California’s proposed billionaire tax, and the growing power of AI lab workers. Before that, she was a reporter at The Daily Beast, where her investigations spurred leadership changes at national nonprofits and policy shifts at major corporations. Her work has also appeared in The Cut and The Guardian. She lives in San Francisco.

Jack Holmes joins as a senior editor for Vanity Fair, where he’s been editing features and political coverage since January. He will continue that work and expand into society and technology. Previously he was a senior staff writer and political editor for Esquire. He’s also the founder and publisher of The Football Weekend, a publication covering world soccer. Jack graduated from Vanderbilt University with a degree in philosophy and political science.

Nina Joyce is vice president of communications, based in New York, leading Vanity Fair’s communications globally. With 17 years of experience, she previously oversaw media relations for Condé Nast’s UK business and portfolio of brands, managing corporate reputation, brand strategy and major cultural events. Prior to joining Condé Nast, Nina spent a decade at Vice Media Group, holding senior roles across VICE, Refinery29, and i-D, and ultimately leading corporate PR across EMEA.

Roxanne Doucet joins as global visuals director. She has worked across New York and Paris, and collaborated with renowned artists and luxury houses including Dior, Loewe, and Balenciaga, building a practice rooted in fine art, documentary photography, and editorial storytelling. She was previously visual director at Vogue US and has consulted for Vogue France.

Dondre Stuetley joins Vanity Fair as senior visuals editor. Previously he was the photo editor at WSJ Magazine, commissioning stories on art, fashion, entertainment, design, food, and architecture.

Sameet Sharma joins as senior visuals editor. He was most recently the visuals director at V Magazine, and prior to V, he oversaw visual production at G-III, working on brands such as DKNY and Karl Lagerfeld. He also brings experience from Hearst magazines, where he worked on the photo teams at ELLE, Marie Claire, and Esquire.

Christian Zelaya joins as a senior designer. He brings more than five years of experience shaping editorial reporting into creative and clever visual stories for digital and social platforms and attracting readers for global brands like NBC, Forbes, and Scholastic.

Michael Kanyongolo joins Vanity Fair as audience development manager. He was most recently the news producer for Quanta Magazine, where he carried out web development, visual design, and production. He previously worked on web production at the New York Post and has a background in media and psychology.

Nazanin Hakim joins Vanity Fair as a creative producer on the video team. She brings a background in documentary filmmaking, having worked on a range of projects exploring politics, culture, and technology, including the Emmy-nominated series Turning Point: 9/11 and the War on Terror and What’s Next? The Future With Bill Gates.

Chris Black joins Vanity Fair as a contributing editor. He is a writer, photographer, and cohost of How Long Gone. He lives in New York and Los Angeles.
