It's a wild time for the superhero genre, specifically on the DC side of things. James Gunn's departure as co-CEO of the studio broke the internet, and fans who spent years watching the DC movies in order have countless questions about what comes next. I've been especially curious about the future of The Penguin (which is streaming with a HBO Max subscription), and now we have an idea about what's going on behind the scenes.

The Penguin is a spinoff of The Batman, and became an Emmy-winning hit after it arrived on HBO. The TV series made me way more invested in Matt Reeves' franchise, and I desperately want a sophomore season to be green lit. During Deadline's recent report about where things stand at DC, it claims that The Penguin showrunner Lauren LeFranc is "in talks" to produce a Poison Ivy series. Unfortunately, the studio is focused on The Batman: Part II before it can plan any potential return to The Penguin.

The Batman: Part II is in the midst of filming, following delays and Matt Reeves' departure due to a family issue. Amidst leadership shakeups, the studio is seemingly focused on getting that title in the can. Fingers crossed that we we get more of The Penguin whenever that movie is finally completed.

The idea of Lauren LeFranc producing a Poison Ivy TV series is a thrilling one, although that developing project isn't set within the Matt Reeves Batman universe. I'll be sat if/when that show comes to life, but I also really need to see more of The Penguin, particularly Cristin Milioti's Sofia Falcone/ The Hangman.

Sofia was one of the main protagonists of The Penguin, and the actress' performance was incredible and earned her an Emmy Award. Unfortunately, Milioti won't be part of The Batman: Part II, despite her popularity among fans. What's more, Colin Farrell claimed he's only in two scenes of the forthcoming sequel. So why not put Cobblepot and Falcone center stage for a second installment of the acclaimed HBO series?

Right now there are countless questions about upcoming DC movies, and what's coming next for the burgeoning DC Universe. We're currently only a few installments into the original plans for Gunn's first slate of projects, titled Gods and Monsters. His replacement Jeremy Latcham is expected to start his run as the new CEO of the studio on December 1st, so maybe we'll get more information then.

As of now, The Batman: Part II is expected to arrive in theaters on February 18th, 2028. If we have to wait that long before getting more news about The Penguin's future, fans like me are going to have to continue practicing patience. Give us more of Sofia Falcone, you cowards!

#3460. Nvidia’s Jensen Huang May Just Survive His Scandal

Read A Billion to One: From the mad scientists to the megadonors, a dispatch on the money, power, and influence of technology.

Exactly three years ago today, the tech world found itself in an all-too-familiar crisis. On an otherwise ordinary Friday afternoon, the board of OpenAI abruptly fired Sam Altman, following a secretive deliberation about what was believed to be a pattern of deceptive behavior by the CEO. A shock wave of panic rippled through the industry: Employees rallied around Altman, who set up a makeshift war room in his Russian Hill home; investors made furious calls to the board to demand a reversal; and Satya Nadella offered to create the conditions within Microsoft for Altman and his loyalists to rebuild OpenAI from the ground up.

As the members of OpenAI’s board racked their brains for who might make a worthy replacement, the extent of their miscalculation quickly dawned on them. OpenAI could not survive without Altman, and the tech industry might not survive without OpenAI. Within four days of Altman’s firing (an event so fleeting that it came to be known as “the blip”), he was reinstated as CEO, and the board coup that failed to kill him only made him stronger.

Three years later, the foibles of a different man at a different AI company—Jensen Huang, who resigned from his post as CEO of Nvidia last week after the revelation of several compromising affairs—have thrown the industry and the stock market into tumult.

Not one to go down without a fight, Huang has reportedly hunkered down with his inner circle to plot his own comeback. Meanwhile, a petition to reinstate him, pending an independent investigation not unlike the one that exonerated Altman, has garnered nearly 200,000 signatures, including from the likes of Elon Musk, Travis Kalanick, and Garry Tan. Even President Trump has weighed in, noting that he “would certainly not mind” if Huang were reinstated. The news from today’s earnings report that the company had brought in a record-breaking $100 billion+ in sales last quarter under Huang’s leadership will only help their cause.

While an inside source told CNBC yesterday that Nvidia’s board is not considering reinstating Huang, the former executive is continuing to court public opinion independently. “I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said in a public statement Tuesday. “If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”

It would be difficult to overstate Huang’s influence on the AI industry and US tech policy at large.

This entire mess has felt uncannily validating of the thesis behind Vanity Fair’s New Establishment list this fall, for which I wrote, “Never in the list’s history have the scale and the stakes of individual influence felt so high,” noting the “Ouroboros of investments and insular networks that make you realize how small and self-serving circles of power can be—and how quickly they could come tumbling down.”

We’ve officially entered the age of the too-big-to-fail CEO, in which our economy increasingly hinges on—and endlessly forgives—the moods and misdeeds of a handful of powerful men with few accountability structures. It’s not just the companies they founded that have become entwined with these founders. “The whole economy has basically been financed by Nvidia and in turn by Jensen’s ability to raise money,” says Yoni Rechtman, a partner at Slow Ventures.

Huang deserves a great deal of credit for having built his company from the ground up. But his trespasses—namely, becoming romantically involved with someone the State Department has linked to Chinese intelligence, and who has undeniably helped get America’s high-performance chips into the hands of our adversaries—are more than worthy of the scrutiny they’ve received.

Like a person who’s sick with a life-threatening illness but refuses to make a will, Huang demonstrated a staggeringly hubristic leadership. He had no real succession plan, installed a board and executive staff of yes-men and women, and created a “culture of omertà,” as his biographer, Stephen Witt, put it, that allowed his affairs to become an open secret within the company. Nvidia didn’t even protect itself with basic D&O insurance, which would have shielded it from the kinds of shareholder lawsuits it could now face. The Dow, S&P 500, and Nasdaq have all continued their precipitous decline since the news of his departure was announced last week.

As a result, how many of us have found ourselves asking, Why should the fate of my 401(k) have anything to do with one man’s sex life?

If you need another example, consider Musk, who has gained almost single-handed control over our space and satellite infrastructure. At SpaceX, he’s also become a master of the newly popular dual-class voting structures that have allowed founders like himself and Mark Zuckerberg to consolidate control of their companies. On more than one occasion, his erratic whims have left our geopolitical fate hanging in the balance.

Perhaps start-ups do need these larger-than-life characters to get off the ground. As Rechtman puts it to me, “Great businesses don’t get built by committee. They get built by small groups of people and singular leaders. And necessarily, in the pursuit of some huge and lofty project, a person becomes elevated to the status of ‘great.’”

But as companies mature—and especially as they go public—they owe it to themselves and to investors to outgrow their founders. Plenty of the companies keeping our economy afloat, like Apple, Amazon, Microsoft, and Netflix, have indeed survived the parting of their founders.

Unfortunately, public markets are now falling victim to the same hype frenzy as VCs. AI-linked stocks now account for nearly half of the S&P 500, and 47 of those stocks made up three quarters of the index’s gains in the first half of this year. Nvidia, in one way or another, is connected to just about all of those companies through an intricate web of loans, partnerships, and investments.

So how do we deal with tech’s “great man” problem? This extreme concentration of power has helped foster a startling lack of resilience in our geopolitical and economic systems. But ask any antitrust expert, and they’ll remind you that it can also erode product quality, endanger consumer protections, and raise prices.

The answer cannot simply be for these men to improve their moral character, and it cannot be for us to become more forgiving. After all, any one of them could drop dead of a heart attack and leave us in the same predicament.

Walter Isaacson, the Silicon Valley biographer who is now interviewing many of the field’s “great men” on his new podcast, The Builders, believes the only possible answer “is to have more entrepreneurs who can build competing products, who can shoot off rockets and get them into orbit and create satellites and create chips and build fabrication plants.”

Rumors are already circulating that if he does not return to Nvidia, Huang may start his own competitive chip manufacturer, which helps explain why VCs are lining up to demonstrate their goodwill.

In the meantime, as we prepare for more mega IPOs, we would be wise to examine the structure of these deals to see what checks on power exist within these companies, from strong succession plans to empowered boards. Unfortunately, Anthropic is preparing super-voting shares for founders, which will give them decisive control over the company following its $1.4 trillion IPO. But hey, at least there are seven of them.

#3458. Apple, Chase, United Outages: What’s Going On?

Read A Billion to One: From the mad scientists to the megadonors, a dispatch on the money, power, and influence of technology.

Every time I see a new headline about yet another system outage this week, the beat of “We Didn’t Start the Fire” starts playing in my head: “Microsoft, NSA, grounded planes from FAA / United Airlines, Chase Bank, can’t send funds on Apple Pay…”

It feels like I could write a parody verse a day at the rate our infrastructure is faltering. A few weeks ago I wrote about the spate of cybersecurity incidents that led the industry to label last month “Black October.” Now my phone is blowing up, with everyone from colleagues to high school friends asking, what the hell is going on out there?

Are we under attack by a rogue nation? Are outdated software systems suddenly all throwing in the towel? Is this all just cyber-business as usual, with an unusually on-edge public?

I’m inclined to believe it’s some combination of all of the above. The FBI issued an urgent warning today that bad actors have been using ARTEX, the open-source AI penetration testing platform, to attempt widespread attacks. A source at a financial services company tells me, “It’s been a miserable month…. Just constant probing and hacking attempts.” Companies—and especially government agencies—with outdated software systems are scrambling to patch these vulnerabilities, and are often unable to do so securely without taking their systems entirely offline.

“What used to take a skilled operator days or weeks of chaining is now happening in hours,” says Snehal Antani, cofounder and CEO of the cybersecurity firm Horizon3. In other words: With AI, bad actors can pretty easily jiggle every doorknob around the globe to see who’s left their doors unlocked.

Meanwhile, the total lack of clarity from the Trump administration hasn’t exactly been reassuring. Even one administration-aligned VC partner I spoke with this morning called the joint presser between Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin a “clown show.”

For now, I’d urge you to heed the same advice I gave last time I wrote about this: Make sure those passwords are airtight and that multifactor authentication is activated. And maybe, just maybe, stock up on some light supplies you’d like to have around if 21st-century services stop working the way they’re supposed to.

“Going forward, expect this to become normal rather than exceptional,” Antani tells me. “We should expect persistent disruption of digital services—travel, banking, commerce, etc.—in the coming months as these organizations scramble to quickly improve their cyber resilience.”

$7 billion: That’s how much Sound Ventures, the firm founded by actor turned VC Ashton Kutcher and former music manager Guy Oseary, stands to profit from its 0.5% stake in Anthropic after the IPO this week.

#3457. I Played Wendy's RPG, and It's Actually Worth It for the Free Food

November is a huge month for video games. Nintendo dropped its remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the Switch 2 last week, and the long-awaited Grand Theft Auto VI is right around the corner. But the game we've been waiting for most of all also launched this month: WendyQuest, the free RPG from Wendy's. (No, this is not a joke.)

Despite the absurdity of a hamburger chain making a full video game (complete with Wendy's-themed puns), the thing is, this game is pretty solid—even if it is a promotion at the end of the day. WendyQuest's main purpose is to offer customers coupons they can use toward purchases in real life, though it's a bit of a commitment. It took me just under an hour of gameplay before I earned my first coupon, and Wendy's says it takes roughly 15 hours to beat. All that to say, this is a pretty unique marketing campaign.

I was surprised booting up WendyQuest on my iPhone. This doesn't necessarily feel like a thrown-together product. On the flip side, the production quality is quite high. The music is solid and very much traditionally RPG; there are even three save slots, in case you plan to return to this RPG again and again.

There's even a story, albeit cheesy (no pun intended): As the game explains, the "Four Great Spirits of Flavor" created Savoria, "a food-rich paradise." All was well until Mech Corp, led by the evil Dr. MechBorg, built robots to take over Savoria. The plot is far from compelling, and the writing can be a little over the top, but hey, I'll give them credit: They thought through a full story here.

You play as Wendy, the "representation of true culinary excellence and taste as dictated by the four ancient spirits of flavor." Wendy (or The Wendy, as some call her) is tasked with saving the world, traveling between villages and picking up new characters along the way. The game world even has "real" Wendy's locations you can visit. These act like inns and shops in other RPGs, giving you a chance to heal while also buying equipment.

Like other RPGs, WendyQuest uses turn-based combat. You have to charge up your attacks, but stop before they hit 100%, or you'll miss. (It took me a while to master the timing.) I'm pretty impressed with how challenging some of these battles can be, though you are quickly given the option of an amulet that gives you a huge leg-up in combat. You don't have to take it, but it makes fights easier if you're only in it for the coupons. That, combined with the spatulas the game encourages you to buy, lets you mow down enemies. You can also utilize your companions here: "Frygor," for example, can either attack enemies with a barrage of fries, or use those fries to build a shield to protect you.

While there are tons of enemies to fight, the key baddies are the "mechs." There are five in total, and after you defeat each, you get a coupon. Spoiler alert: The first mech drops the "Fry Stone," which nets you a coupon for a free order of medium fries—though you need to buy something in tandem, as well as use the Wendy's app. While I stopped my gaming here for this article, the other four coupons are:

Free biscuit or croissant (I didn't even know Wendy's sold biscuits and croissants)

Again, it's wild that WendyQuest has a 10+ hour campaign, with over 1,000 lines of dialogue to boot. I'm not sure this is a game I'm going to see through to the end, but I'll admit, it's a fun marketing approach from Wendy's. Sure, they could have run a promotion in the Wendy's app to give people coupons, but instead, they built an entire RPG. I respect it. You can download the game for iOS, Android, or Steam.

#3456. The Mighty Nein Season 2 Officially Has Fans Worried About One Major Plot Change

Prime Video teases a pirate-soaked second season, but will some major developments be left behind?

The Mighty Nein season 2 is officially set to return to our TV screens in March 2027. And while Critical Role fans may be a little put out by Amazon's new episode schedule, the season’s content has Critters excited for what’s to come from our band of lovable misfits.

However, there does seem to be a significant catch: Season 2 may be widening the gap between the show and the original Dungeons & Dragons campaign even further than season 1 did. While the first season already moved away from the source campaign in several ways, the second season could be taking those departures even further.

[Ed. note: This article contains spoilers for the tabletop campaign of The Mighty Nein.]

Prime Video’s announcement for season 2 of The Mighty Nein gave Critters a glimpse of what to expect. You can read the summary below.

“In Season Two, The Mighty Nein set off on a pirate adventure across the high seas as they face their complicated pasts and hurtle toward a treacherous future. While Fjord’s burgeoning powers tempt him down a dark path, the Beacon reveals its own enticing possibilities, and the group must choose between newfound magic and their friendship.”

On the surface, it looks like business as usual for the Mighty Nein (there are only seven of them, but we digress). However, some eagle-eyed Critters who have watched the original 141 episodes of the tabletop campaign have started to speculate what this new plot summary could mean for The Mighty Nein season 2’s story.

Last time, Critters left off with the Mighty Nein encountering the aasimar barbarian Yasha in the Zadash sewers after stealing the Luxon Beacon. Briefly free from the mind-control of Obann, a cambion, Yasha pleaded with the group to help her.

Though season 1 has already introduced several differences — for example, Yasha wasn’t introduced alongside Mollymauk as part of the Fletching and Moondrop Traveling Carnival of Curiosities troupe — the new season’s summary, combined with season 1’s ending, has fans speculating that the Iron Shepherds arc may be skipped entirely in favor of jumping straight to the Mighty Nein’s pirate arc.

The Iron Shepherds arc is a formative experience for the group, as it comes shortly after the Mighty Nein are given a task by the Gentleman (a crime boss in the city of Zadash) to head to Shadycreek Run and retrieve an ally of his. However, on the way there, the group is ambushed in the middle of the night, resulting in the capture of Fjord, Jester, and Yasha by a group of slavers known as The Iron Shepherds. When the rest of the group tries to deal with the slavers, they find themselves overwhelmed, with Mollymauk dying in the process.

The plot summary of Season 2, however, suggests nothing of the sort; its main focus is the pirate arc that comes afterward. Now, this could be Critical Role and Prime Video choosing to obscure the Iron Shepherds arc entirely to surprise new fans with what’s to come. That said, given how many changes Critical Role has already made to the campaign — and for what it’s worth, we think they are for the better — there’s also a chance the Iron Shepherds' encounter will be woven into the pirate arc. After all, the Mighty Nein make plenty of enemies during that arc, too, including Captain Avantika, who plays a major role in Fjord’s storyline. Could she be the one who ends up slaughtering Mollymauk?

It’s hard to predict what changes are coming to The Mighty Nein season 2, but given how much the first season changed from the original campaign, Critters should brace for even more in March 2027.

The Mighty Nein airs exclusively on Prime Video. Season 1 is available to watch now, with season 2 set to debut on March 24, 2027.

Yellowjackets is arguably one of the best Paramount+ shows, although it required fans to get a Paramount+ subscription including Showtime. I'm personally a hardcore fan who is hyped about the fourth and final season's premiere this month. Folks are hoping to have Yellowjackets' biggest mysteries solved before it ends its run, and hopefully joins the ranks of TV shows that actually ended well. We know that the series guards it secrets from the public, but it turns out that even the cast is left in the dark about spoilers.

Yellowjackets' cast is an incredible multi-generational ensemble who tell the story across two timelines. The pressure is on for the Emmy-nominated series to stick the landing, and provide answers about various long-standing mysteries. In a recent interview with ScreenRant, Teen Shauna actress Sophie Nélisse was asked if she knew her character's fate ahead of time, to which she said:

No, we actually don't get the scripts more than like a week in advance, which is kind of fun because on set we're all sort of plotting and trying to reflect on what we have. We were coming up with our own theories of what the finale was going to look like, but we had no idea how they were going to get rescued, how their time in the wilderness would end. I obviously knew that Shauna was going to get married because we saw that.

Well, my mind is blown. While Yellowjackets fans are being kept away from spoilers, I had no idea how tight the security was for even the cast. They only got each new script a week in advance, so Nélisse and her costars weren't able to use the full arc of their character to inform each performance. Instead they had to take things episode by episode and play each moment with honesty without looking ahead.

Fans have lingering questions about the No Eyed Man as well as the mystery involving Crystal's dead body. While we're still in the dark for now, so was the cast. The Heated Rivalry actress went on to say:

We just kind of went day by day with it. We were just always so excited when we got a new script because, as the audience feels when they finish an episode, it always kind of leaves us on a cliffhanger. That's how, whenever we read a script, we'd all message in the group chat, being like, ‘Oh, this one is so good! I love this bit, and I love that bit.’

Celebrities: sometimes they really are just like us. Despite being the actors bringing Yellowjackets to life, they were left with episode cliffhangers in the midst of shooting Season 4. I have to wonder if Sophie Nélisse and her co-stars even know all the twists that are coming with the show's final season on the air.

Yellowjackets Season 4 will premiere on November 20th as part of the 2026 TV schedule. The pressure is on for the drama series to stick the landing, but it looks like we'll get plenty of surprises in the final set of episodes.

If you've never owned an OLED before, there are some things you need to know to make sure it's a good fit for you. Perhaps most important is that they don't get as bright as QLEDs or LED TVs. There is also no Dolby Vision support (though there is support for HDR10+, HDR10, and HLG). But that is where the cons stop.

The S84H offers the near-perfect black levels you can expect from any OLED TV, making the contrast look incredible. OLED TVs are not normally priced under $1,000, especially newer models like this one. It's an incredible value for the money. #3452. 8 Biggest Snubs in the 2026 Game Awards Nominations

The Game Awards has announced its official list of nominees for this year’s prizes. Among the nominees are plenty of obvious contenders, such as Grand Theft Auto 6, Resident Evil Requiem, and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. There was stiff competition across several categories, meaning that some worthy games — and Polygon favorites — didn’t make the shortlist for certain prizes. These are the biggest TGA nomination snubs of 2026.

As one eagle-eyed Resetera user pointed out, Sony just broke a streak that dates all the way back to 2015. This marks the first time in 11 years that a first-party PlayStation release hasn't received a Game of the Year nomination. During that 11-year streak, Sony took home three GOTY trophies: God of War (2018), The Last of Us Part 2 (2020), and Astro Bot (2024). This year's big first-party game from PlayStation was Marvel's Wolverine, which is currently sitting at a 75 on Metacritic and incited a whole lot of debate about difficulty and UI design. The game was nominated in two categories: Best Performance for Liam McIntyre and Innovation in Accessibility.

This outcome won't come as a surprise to Polygon's Oli Welsh, who predicted Marvel's Wolverine missing out on a GOTY nomination and snapping Sony's impressive streak all the way back in September.

There were a ton of fantastic video game performances this year, and somebody’s favorite was bound to get left out. Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave fan favorite Jimmie Yamaguchi gave an outstanding performance as the oddball scholar Fabio, and by every measure, it deserved a nomination. In less capable hands, Fabio’s starry-eyed devotion to Fortune’s Weave co-protagonist Dietrich could have been played for laughs, but Yamaguchi makes the budding romance between these men believable and heartfelt.

Manni L. Perez was nominated for GTA 6, presumably for portraying Lucia Caminos. (Funnily enough, developer Rockstar Games has not yet officially confirmed Perez is actually playing Lucia, despite longstanding online rumors.) Apparently, the actor who played co-lead Jason Duval didn’t make enough of an impact with players to score a nomination.

Blizzard’s World of Warcraft has had a massive year, with the launch of its reimagined Classic experience, World of Warcraft: Forever. The team also released major updates for the modern version of the beloved MMORPG, like March’s Midnight expansion. Those changes weren’t enough to move the needle with voters, and WoW was also left out of the Best Community Support category.

The popular farming sim, which entered early access in 2024 before its full release this year, may have more than 26,000 “overwhelmingly positive” reviews on Steam, but that wasn’t enough for it to snag a nomination in any category. Best Debut Indie might have been Fields of Mistria’s best shot at a prize, but it wouldn’t have been out of place in Best Sim/Strategy or the broader Best Indie category, either.

Despite a wobbly third act, Fortune’s Weave is one of our favorite games of 2026, one of the best games available for the Nintendo Switch 2, and one of the best-reviewed games of the year. Surprisingly, developer Intelligent Systems’ epic strategy RPG only managed to pick up one nomination, for Best Role-Playing Game. It stands a decent chance of taking this one home: other nominees include Final Fantasy Resonance, Monster Hunter Stories 3, The Blood of Dawnwalker, and Trails in the Sky 2nd Chapter.

Pearl Abyss’s open-world adventure game was an early-year frontrunner for a GOTY nom, even after middling reviews and a rocky launch. While it wasn’t a critical darling, it did have a pretty massive online following that made the prospect of several nominations seem likely. Surprisingly, Crimson Desert will compete in just one category: Best Community Support.

Bungie’s extraction shooter managed to snag a nomination for Best Multiplayer Game, which it frankly stands little chance of winning against a field that includes two indie chart-toppers and a well-regarded Call of Duty. However, the stylish game was overlooked in the Best Art Direction category, perhaps partly due to the shadow cast by a 2025 plagiarism scandal where Bungie admitted to using an artist’s designs without proper credit. (Bungie later credited her as a Visual Design Consultant.) Marathon’s retro-future meets Y2K cyberpunk aesthetic truly stands out in a sea of Unreal Engine 5 homogeneity, and it’s a shame to see it overlooked here.

Both the Best Indie and Best Debut Indie categories have some stiff competition this year. However, no independent game managed to get a nomination for Game of the Year in 2026. While there weren’t a ton of indie contenders for the top category this year, Polygon’s Oli Welsh had the co-op adventure Big Walk pegged as a dark horse, though developer House House’s recent AI controversy likely didn’t help matters.

The lack of an indie GOTY nominee represents a pretty massive shift from the 2025 crop, which included a record-setting three games developed by independent studios: Hades 2, Hollow Knight: Silksong, and Clair Obscur: Expedition 33. Sandfall Interactive’s much-loved RPG managed to take home the top prize and a total of nine Game Awards, the most wins by a single game. 2024 also saw one indie crack the category, Balatro, though the top honors went to Astro Bot.

The Game Awards 2026 will stream live on Disney+, YouTube, and Twitch, on Thursday, Dec. 10, starting at 7:30 p.m. EST / 4:30 p.m. PST.

#3451. Jennifer Connelly's Forgotten '90s Disney Superhero Movie Deserved Its Own Franchise

After Tim Burton's "Batman" film became an inescapably huge success in the summer of 1989 and set off to expand into its weirdly experimental sequel in 1992, there was a mad rush by other studios to hop a trend and get their own piece of that lucrative superhero pie — sort of. Studio executives of the early '90s seem to have been drawn more to Burton's retro aesthetics than the actual idea of a superhero, so rather than expanding into bringing other iconic DC characters like Wonder Woman to the big screen, or heading across the street to give the Marvel universe a shot at cinematic glory, we got a rush of big-screen revivals of other throwback comic strip heroes. The results were, well, let's just put it nicely and say they were pretty mixed in terms of quality.

While they undoubtedly have their fans out there, pulp hero movies like 1990's "Dick Tracy," 1994's "The Shadow," and 1996's "The Phantom" simply were not able to reach the same levels of success. It may have been that audiences just liked Batman way more than they liked characters who had never been as popular as the Caped Crusader, or that these movies just weren't very good. Maybe people were just simply not prepared to slam evil. Whatever it was, none of those movies managed to launch their heroes into a franchise.

There is, however, one member of that crowd that absolutely deserved better: 1991's "The Rocketeer," in which Jennifer Connelly, Billy Campbell, and a rocket-powered jetpack faced off against Nazis in Los Angeles circa 1938.

One big difference that set "The Rocketeer" apart from the surrounding crop of pulp hero flicks was that its source material was actually pretty contemporary. Cliff Secord and his supporting cast were created in 1982 by the legendary comics creator Dave Stevens, and had been an indie favorite since its introduction. All things considered, Stevens produced a relatively small number of comics about the Rocketeer — his entire run with the character fits into a single 120-page hardcover — but his lavish, gorgeous art and incredible storytelling make it a timeless classic even today. Sadly, Stevens passed away in 2008 after a long battle with leukemia, which had long affected his output.

Looking back, it's easy to see why Disney jumped on "The Rocketeer." Since it was a throwback to the adventure serials and comic strip heroes of the '30s and '40s, Stevens' work already had the modern spin on the kind of pulpy action that movies like "Dick Tracy" and "The Shadow" struggled with, and incorporated a lot of the same elements. In fact, the "Rocketeer" comics even included thinly veiled versions of pulp heroes like The Shadow and Doc Savage in supporting roles, with just enough of their serial numbers filed off to avoid a copyright lawsuit. (Needless to say, those characters didn't make it into the film version.)

There were real-life influences, too; in the film, the jetpack was created by Howard Hughes, and Timothy Dalton's villainous Neville Sinclair was based on actor (and real-life villain) Errol Flynn. Connelly's character, appropriately renamed Jenny, was based on Cliff's comics girlfriend Betty, who was in turn inspired by pin-up icon Bettie Page, of whom Stevens was a dedicated and unabashed fan.

As for the film, while it lacks the lushness of Stevens' comics art, it told the classic story of "boy loves girl, boy finds rocket pack, boy has to rescue girl from an evil Nazi actor played by one of the lesser James Bonds" in a fun, engaging way that made it a cult classic. It also has a connection to the modern Marvel Cinematic Universe. Two decades after "The Rocketeer," its director, Joe Johnston, would direct another, more successful retro-inspired superhero movie, 2011's "Captain America: The First Avenger."

According to an interview with Stevens, the original plan for "The Rocketeer" had been to make a trilogy that would've skewed slightly more adult:

"So, we had a lot of interesting meetings with executives who passed on it but gave us some good criticisms. The last studio on the list was Disney. They took one look at it, and said 'toys!' So ... that's where we eventually made the deal. We originally signed on as a trilogy at Touchstone, the division of Disney doing more adult-themed films. [...] As soon as we all signed on, [Disney executive Jeffrey] Katzenberg pulled a switch and said, 'Nope, it's going to be a Disney release, because Disney needs a live-action hit.' So immediately, Betty and anything else "adult" went right out with the bathwater."

We'll never know if a more adult-oriented version of "The Rocketeer" that kept elements like Betty's glamour modeling day job intact would've been successful enough to get us that trilogy, but the movie we got is well worth revisiting, even though it was crushed by "Robin Hood: Prince of Thieves" and "Terminator 2" at the box office.

#3448. Netflix Adds The 2026 Horror Movie That Made Over 500x Its Budget At The Box Office

"Obsession" passed a box office milestone only five other horror films ever have when it crossed the $500 million mark. That would be an achievement regardless of its budget, but this movie only cost $600,000 to $750,000 to make. That means that when "Obsession" brought in $524.4 million by the end of its unprecedented box office run, it had made more than 500 times its budget.

For a while, that made "Obsession" the most profitable movie ever at the box office, until it was technically dethroned by the low-budget Chinese movie "Niu Lai." Still, it remains one of the most stunning horror success stories of recent years, which is especially impressive considering we've seen multiple low-budget horror movies become hits of late. But if you somehow managed to miss out on all of this, or just want to revisit one of the best horror movies of 2026, Netflix has you covered.

"Obsession" has a relatively simple premise, yet its execution and the lead performances elevate it beyond your typical low-budget horror fare. The film stars Michael Johnston as Baron "Bear" Bailey, a luckless music store worker who has a major crush on his friend/co-worker Nikki Freeman (Inde Navarrette). After buying a One Wish Willow toy, he wishes that Nikki loved him more than anyone in the world and gets everything he asked for and more. The only problem is, Nikki becomes absolutely obsessed with him, to the extent she's willing to hurt anyone who gets in her way.

It's well worth doing so. "Obsession" is a confident crowd-pleaser with a killer lead performance from Navarette. In fact the actor's portrayal of Nikki proved to be her breakout turn, landing Navarrette a role as Rogue in the Marvel Cinematic Universe's upcoming "X-Men" movie reboot. No doubt, more high-profile roles await. As such, even if you're not too intrigued by the prospect of a twisted girlfriend causing violent chaos, you should at least check out "Obsession" to see one of the best performances of 2026 and the beginning of a star's ascendence. The film is streaming on Netflix as of November 17, 2026.

#3447. Update Your iPhone to Prevent People From Seeing iMessages They Shouldn't

Has this ever happened to you? You add someone new to an iMessage group chat, and wonder, "Huh, can they see any of the messages from before they were added?" The answer to that question is supposed to be "no." By design, new iMessage group chat members are only privy to texts that arrive after they were added. When they join, it's essentially a blank slate, as if you just created the group for the first time. At least, that's how it's intended to work.

As it turns out, there's a bug with iMessage that may allow new group chat members to see texts from before they were added to the chat. That's a problem, and not just for the iPhone users out there talking smack about people before inviting them to join the group chat. It means iMessage, and Apple's platforms in general, aren't working like they're supposed to be. You don't have to be talking behind people's backs to not want new members seeing existing chats. Maybe you're planning a surprise party for someone, and add them to the group once everyone's in on the plan; maybe the texts in the chat aren't relevant to the current group, and the person joining simply does not need to access them.

That's not all: There exists another security flaw that could allow remote hackers to join an iMessage group and receive new messages. You might add a new user to a group chat and inadvertently invite them to read all existing messages, while at the same time being attacked by a bad actor who can then intercept all future messages. Not good.

Luckily, there's currently a fix for these problems. Apple patched (and revealed) the bugs, along with seven other security flaws, with a series of software updates on Monday for iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Watch, and Vision Pro. Not all of the updates include patches for these two iMessage flaws—specifically, some of the updates for older Apple devices. But the rest, including iOS 27.2.1, macOS 27.2.1, macOS 26.7.3, macOS 15.8.3, watchOS 27.2.1, and visionOS 27.2.1, include the iMessage patches.

Each update includes its own list of patches, but, for this article, I'll take a look at the nine patches in iOS 27.2.1. You'll find the two iMessage bugs, plus seven other patches, in the list below:

AirPlay: Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to bypass the rate limit on pairing code attempts. Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113968: Apple

App Intents: Impact: An app may be able to access sensitive user data. Description: An authorization issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113963: László Várady

Bluetooth: Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to corrupt process memory. Description: A use-after-free issue was addressed with improved memory management. CVE-2026-113970: Apple

brotli: Impact: Processing maliciously crafted input may lead to memory corruption. Description: An out-of-bounds write issue was addressed with improved input validation. CVE-2026-111497

CoreUtils: Impact: A malicious Bluetooth device may be able to establish a pairing without user interaction. Description: This issue was addressed with improved checks. CVE-2026-113965: Apple

CoreUtils: Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to bypass the rate limit on pairing code attempts and pair with a device without user interaction. Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113964: an anonymous researcher

Messages: Impact: A remote attacker may be able to join an iMessage group chat and receive its messages. Description: An authorization issue was addressed with improved validation. CVE-2026-113961: an anonymous researcher

Messages: Impact: A user added to an iMessage group may be able to access messages sent before they joined. Description: This issue was addressed by removing the vulnerable code. CVE-2026-113960: an anonymous researcher

Rapportd: Impact: An attacker on the same network may be able to bypass the rate limit on AirPlay pairing code attempts. Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113969: Apple

For a full accounting of the patches included in the other security updates, check out Apple's official security releases site.

To install Apple's latest security updates, you'll simply need to update your device as you usually do. On iPhone, iPad, Apple Watch, and Vision Pro, head to Settings > General > Software Update; on Mac, go to System Settings > General > Software Update. Here, follow the on-screen instructions to download and install the latest version of your device's software.

#3446. 5 Reasons Why Robert Pattinson Could Be The Best James Bond Yet

Robert Pattinson has officially been cast as James Bond, beating out several promising contenders to take the coveted role. Denis Villeneuve will oversee the upcoming 26th Bond installment, and he couldn't have chosen a more dynamic and interesting leading man.

Thus far, Bond fans have reacted to Pattinson's casting with both excitement and wariness — which is to be expected. After all, the British actor is one of the biggest stars in Hollywood and is therefore unlike any actor to be cast in the role throughout the franchise's more than 60-year history. But clearly Villeneuve and new Bond custodians Amazon MGM have been impressed by the actor, and frankly it's not hard to see why.

The "Primetime" star has been delivering consistently compelling performances for years now, and if nothing else it will be fascinating to see what he does to make England's greatest spy his own. Sure, on the surface he seems like a safe choice — A-lister white guy with a string of hits to his name. But part of what makes Pattinson so exciting as an actor is his unpredictability. Beyond that, there are myriad reasons why he could not only make a great 007, but might just give us the best Bond yet. Here are five of them.

Robert Pattinson is a big star with the kind of look you'd associate with James Bond. But he's made no secret of the fact he's also a bit of a weirdo underneath it all, and in that sense he shares something in common with Bond.

007 is a similarly deceptive character. Like Pattinson, he's a refined, handsome white guy with an urbane manner. But in the first Bond book, "Casino Royale," author Ian Fleming described him as a "blunt instrument." That element has been integral to the character since his inception. That is to say, Bond is much more than a posh boy with a licence to kill. He's damaged, troubled, maybe a little rough around the edges. Sure, his cinematic history has proved the character lends himself to interpretation, but the best Bond performances have integrated that dark side to some extent.

Pattinson could give us the best version of that to date. Remember that short film he made for GQ about his mounting anxiety over leaving his hotel room to get a hotdog? Something's up with this guy in the best way possible, and every role he's taken since then has been testament to that fact. From his lecherous, questionably-accented preacher in "The Devil all the Time" to his delightfully unhinged nineteenth-Century lighthouse keeper in "The Lighthouse," Pattinson has clearly been having a ball playing crazy (and that's not to mention some of his most Pattinsoniest performances in films such as "Good Time" and "The King"). He'll have to keep it under control for Bond, but 007 needs an edge to be interesting, and Pattinson has a wild unpredictability could be the best thing to ever happen to the character.

Robert Pattinson's casting as James Bond breaks a 60-year tradition of unknown actors being given the role. For Bond purists, such a thing is basically sacrilegious. For everyone else, it might just be the most exciting thing to happen to Bond since 1962's "Dr. No" kicked off cinema's most enduring franchise.

Look, there's a chance Pattinson could be distracting as 007. Bond is a male fantasy come to life, and part of the series' success could well be attributed to the fact it's easier for audiences to project themselves onto relative unknowns. On the other hand, it only takes one Bond movie for an actor to become a major star, so there'll always be diminishing returns in that respect. What's more, I think it's fair to say we need big changes after the multiple duds that characterized Daniel Craig's last few years as Bond. The franchise was in danger of becoming less relevant than it once was, and casting a star of Pattinson's standing, in a movie directed by the similarly esteemed Denis Villeneuve is a way to remind people of the saga's blue chip status.

What's more, we're not talking about any A-lister here. Pattinson has proved time and again he has the ability to completely disappear into a role. So, what we're actually getting is an actor with the gravitas and appeal of a megastar who is simultaneously able to become a cinematic cipher onto which we can all project our fantasies of becoming the most lethal instrument the Secret Intelligence Service has at its disposal. As the first millennial Bond, and the first major star to take on the role, Pattinson could prove to be a master stroke of casting on Villeneuve's part.

There was a major turning point in Robert Pattinson's career whereby he seemed to throw caution to the wind and embrace the most challenging, unusual, and downright insane roles he could. In 2017, the year "Good Time" debuted, GQ exclaimed that "the new Rob Pattinson is defined by his willingness to go berserk or go home." Ever since then he has delivered back to back unforgettable performances that have seen the middle class London boy disappear into some of the most unique characters to appear on-screen in the last decade.

Part of it was an attempt to escape the shadow of the "Twilight" saga, with which he'd made his name. But his portrayals of these more off-kilter characters that came in the wake of his decision to recalibrate felt so natural and honest that it was like he was finally able to be himself, paradoxically by playing people so completely unlike himself.

What's even more impressive is that he hasn't slowed down since deciding to "go berserk." 2026 saw him deliver yet another electric performance in the dark, unsettling media satire thriller "Primetime," in which he completely disappeared behind the mask of "To Catch a Predator" host Chris Hanson. Pattinson just can't seem to deliver a bad performance. Wild, sure. Unpredictable? Absolutely. But he's never been anything less than magnetic and seems incapable of being boring. That should be hugely exciting for James Bond fans.

"Tenet" was full of confusing moments but Robert Pattinson's ability to portray a debonair spy with a quietly simmering intensity was not in question. The actor played Neil in Christopher Nolan's thriller. A mysterious operative who helps John David Washington's Protagonist throughout the film, Neil possesses all the charisma of James Bond and even seems to have a bit of a dark side.

All you need to see to be convinced Pattinson has what it takes to play Bond is the scene in which Neil scopes out the freeport where he plans to steal a priceless art piece. As he's shown around the facility, Pattinson's agent simultaneously exudes a polite charm and a kind of palpable ruthlessness, smiling at his tour guide before staring intently at possible escape routes and security measures. You can feel the cogs turning as he looks around, with Pattinson managing to convey a real sense of Neil's thought processes. When he's told about the freeport's security system, which sucks the air out of a room within 10 seconds, he simply says "Blimey," an ironic understatement accompanied by a wry smile more than worthy of 007.

Surely nobody ever doubted Pattinson could play an urbane sleuth who looks remarkably sharp in a suit. But his "Tenet" performance hints at something more interesting. The brief moments when Pattinson's agent drops the charming facade and focuses his attention on various parts of the building's design convey a cold, calculating intensity that bodes well for a Bond with a truly dark side. Nolan's confounding thriller is an exciting proof of concept for Pattinson's Bond and his ability to exude both charisma and a striking cold-bloodedness unlike any 007 yet seen on-screen.

If you were told Robert Pattinson went to Eton and Oxford you probably wouldn't have a hard time believing it. He didn't, but it feels like he'd be very much at home in the public school boy milieu. That's interesting because while previous James Bond actors have managed to affect that kind of high-born aura, Pattinson is the first to just sort of have it from the get go.

He's an upper-middle class white Londoner with a Received Pronunciation accent and an urbane, sophisticated manner. Sure, he's also the guy who can't stop nervously laughing in interviews and who seems to run on pure anxiety most of the time. But there's no denying he has the sort of heritage you'd associate with Bond.

Roger Moore — the only other London-born actor to play Bond — had something similar, but undercut it with his famously tongue-in-cheek portrayal. Sean Connery was, of course, Scottish, Timothy Dalton was born in Wales, Pierce Brosnan is Irish, and Daniel Craig is from Chester in North England. Each of them brought something unique to the role, but of all the James Bond actors Pattinson seems like the first who won't have to work too hard at exuding the kind of aura we've come to expect from a character Idles frontman Joe Talbot described as a "murderous toff."

#3445. Dune Magic: The Gathering Crossover Officially Confirmed After Major Leak

Arrakis, its noble houses, and its legendary sandworms are getting the Magic card treatment

The spice must flow, and so must the Secret Lair drops. After several days of leaks circulating online, Dune is officially crossing over with Magic: The Gathering, with Wizards of the Coast teasing the collaboration through the official MTG Secret Lair account.

The announcement follows a series of leaked promotional images that surfaced on Reddit and Discord on Nov. 12, giving players an early look at what appeared to be three Dune-themed Secret Lair collections. The official teaser now confirms that the collaboration is real.

The superdrop is expected to arrive on the Secret Lair website on Nov. 30, giving fans a little time to prepare their spice reserves.

According to the leaked images, the collection features three separate drops. The first introduces eight mechanically unique legendary creatures based on characters from the franchise, including Paul Atreides, Chani, Baron Vladimir Harkonnen, Princess Irulan, and Reverend Mother Jessica.

The second collection focuses on Arrakis and its enormous sandworms, introducing Shai-Hulud as a new Magic card alongside Dune-inspired reprints. The third, titled Spice Harvest, features familiar cards reimagined as items and technology from the franchise. Among the leaked reprints are Darksteel Forge, Revel in Riches, and Halo Fountain.

The leaks have generated plenty of excitement among Magic players, with some already discussing potential Commander decks built around the new characters. Others were less enthusiastic about the use of movie actors' likenesses instead of original character artwork, while several fans were quick to ask whether Duncan Idaho would make the cut.

The timing also makes sense for the crossover. Dune: Part Three is scheduled to hit theaters on Dec. 18, 2026, just weeks after the Secret Lair collection arrives. For now, players won't have to wait much longer to see how much of Arrakis makes its way into their Magic collections.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The last time I saw Jared Padalecki, he was – here come some The Boys spoilers – brutally running through and killing people as Mister Marathon. The next time I saw him, he was playing an actor in a wholesome Netflix rom-com on the 2026 Christmas movie schedule. Talk about range. Seriously, I don’t think you can get something more different from a holiday romance than The Boys. So, when I spoke to Padalecki about his new rom-com, Guarding Stars, I asked what it was like jumping between the two projects.

When I was chatting with Padalecki about his book-to-screen adaptation of Katherine Center’s rom-com The Bodyguard, I also mentioned that the last time I saw him was for the Supernatural reunion on The Boys. He immediately cut in to say that the two projects are “very different,” and when I asked him what it was like to jump from one to the other, he explained:

That is weird. It was weird. It was also weird jumping into The Boys in the first place. You know, I'd seen every episode of the show that was out, but I knew I'd be there with [Eric] Kripke and Phil Sgriccia and [Jensen] Ackles and Misha [Collins]. So that was fun.

What’s funny is Jensen Ackles also described this reunion as “weird.” Anyway, getting to Padalecki’s comments, he told me that when it came to The Boys, he wasn’t exactly telling his parents or children to use their Amazon Prime subscription to see it. It was gory and wild, so yeah, that left him saying:

It was one of those things also where I was like telling my mom and dad like, ‘Maybe don't watch this yet’ or like ‘Maybe don't watch it with any people under the age of 21 or 18 or whatever.’ But it was fun.

Well, considering this reunion was called “one of the most fun and bloodiest hours in all of 2026 TV,” I can see why Padalecki wasn’t exactly recommending it to children. However, he had a blast, and when it came time to flip the switch from blood, gore and grossness to wholesome Christmas and romance, it wasn’t a problem. He might have Supernatural to thank for that, as the actor explained:

Every character is, for me, its own kind of entity. You know, I mean, even on Supernatural, I played 20 different versions of Sam, including playing Jared Paddleleki, you know? So I had some experience bouncing around between different versions of whatever my face looks like. But I enjoyed it, actually.

I would imagine that going from playing a wild superhero in maybe the crudest show on TV to working on a Christmas movie that’s made for families would be very fun. You’d get the best of both worlds in a lot of ways, and while whiplash may have been involved, jumping from one production to the other was great for Padalecki.

He also told me that Guarding Stars, which is a project on the 2026 movie schedule that sees him play an actor opposite Leighton Meester’s bodyguard as they decide they need to fake date, served as a nice palate cleanser, or shower, if you will:

After finishing an episode of The Boys, you really want to take a shower and, like, get rid of it, especially the way you know my character ended in The Boys, literally. But this movie was feel-good. You went there, and you're like, ‘I'm gonna watch this with my kids and grandparents or whatever.’

I mean, Jared Padalecki did, as he said, literally have to take a shower after The Boys; he was covered in so much blood after all was said and done. Going to do a Christmas movie afterward helped metaphorically cleanse him too.

As I mentioned, in Guarding Stars, Padalecki plays an actor, Jack, who has to work with a bodyguard, who is played by Leighton Meester. They decide to fake date in an effort to keep her cover, and obviously, as these rom-coms go, cute shenanigans ensue, wholesome family moments happen, and real romantic feelings develop. It’s adorable!

Now, "adorable" is not an adjective you’d use to describe The Boys, so I can see why Jared Padalecki thought it was “weird” to jump between the two projects.

Now, if you’d like to see him drenched in blood, you can stream The Boys on Amazon Prime. If you want to see him falling head over heels for his bodyguard, you can catch Guarding Stars on Netflix starting November 18.

#3443. This AirPods Feature Fixed My Biggest Problem With Listening to Podcasts to Fall Asleep

We're highlighting the small changes—from useful new gadgets, to fresh productivity techniques, to efficient hacks—that are improving our lives on a weekly basis.

There's lots to recommend about podcasts (and lots of podcasts to recommend), but one of their biggest benefits—for me, anyway—has little to do with what a particular show is about or even who hosts it: They're great for dissociating. I often have a podcast playing to distract my anxious brain from whatever I'm worried about (which, in 2026, is usually slightly less than everything).

Any time I don't want to be alone with my thoughts (say, when commuting or doing mindless chores), I can put on a podcast and be entertained by a couple of goobers talking about movies rather than spinning my wheels about my son's middle school applications. And there's no time I want to disassociate from reality more than bedtime.

For years I've used podcasts as a non-pharmaceutical sleep aid, and few things are more effective at helping me drop off quickly. Unfortunately, for years this also meant that once I fell asleep, the podcast kept playing. I have my podcast app set to delete episodes once finished, so if it was a show I cared about, I'd need to do a lot of redownloading and scrubbing through to find where I left off—that is, until I upgraded my earbuds to the AirPods Pro 3.

The AirPods Pro 3 launched alongside iOS 26 in the fall of 2025 with flashy features like vastly improved noise cancellation, Live Translation, Heart Rate Sensing, and hearing health settings, all of them quite welcome on a set of $250 premium earbuds. But the best new AirPods feature was one I didn't even know about when I decided to upgrade my four-year-old Beats Fit Pro.

In the AirPods settings (accessible via your iPhone's Settings app), if you tap Audio & Routing and scroll down, you'll see an option to turn on a setting called Pause Media When Falling Asleep. I don't think I need to tell you what this setting does. I can tell you that it works great.

According to Apple, the feature works by sensing when you're drifting off using the earbuds' built-in accelerometer to track your movement (or lack thereof). Once your earbuds have determined that you're falling asleep, they will pause your audio for you. And it isn't just the 2025 AirPods Pro 3 that support it—it also works on the second-generation AirPods Pro as well as the AirPods 4 and the AirPods 5.

I'll admit that I don't really understand how the AirPods Pro 3 can tell I'm falling asleep versus just lying very still, but I've never had them pause accidentally during active listening. Conversely, whenever I go back to the podcast I was listening to the night before, I'll find that the audio paused within a minute or two of the last part I remember hearing.

The AirPods Pro 3 aren't the only earbuds with a feature like this, but you'll most often only find it in dedicated "sleep earbuds" designed specifically for the purpose. While many of those offer extra health features like the ability to track your sleep cycles, I'm not really interested in that (my Apple Watch does most of it, and I don't look at that data anyway). Pausing my audio when I'm asleep is really all I need, and the AirPods Pro 3 do it well enough that I don't need to bother with a pair of dedicated bedtime buds.

#3442. The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping Review: Haymitch's Prequel Delivers

Suzanne Collins, the woman behind the young adult dystopian phenomenon known as the Hunger Games franchise, seems like she's pretty calculated with her prequels. I mean this as a good thing. Instead of pumping out endless content and prequels that don't really serve the original narrative (ahem, the apparently permanently unfinished Fantastic Beasts franchise), Collins sticks to stories that help us understand key characters and stories from the first three novels ("The Hunger Games" and its sequels "Catching Fire" and "Mockingjay").

This was true of the 2023 big-screen prequel "The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes," which casts Tom Blyth as future Panem president Coriolanus Snow and explains how and why he grew into the villain faced by Jennifer Lawrence's Katniss in the original films (where he's played by Donald Sutherland). This is, thankfully, also true of the Haymitch Abernathy prequel "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping," based on the 2025 novel "Sunrise on the Reaping."

Haymitch — a role originated by Woody Harrelson and played spectacularly by "We Were Liars" and "East of Eden" alum Joseph Zada in this new film — is sixteen during the Second Quarter Quell, a sort of demented "special edition" of the titular Games that take place every 25 years. For the 50th Games, the all-powerful Capitol in charge of Panem reaps double the number of tributes from each of the totalitarian nation's 12 districts, meaning that 48 kids will enter the arena and only one will survive. Frankly, this premise is immediately intriguing, but director Francis Lawrence and screenwriters Billy Ray and Michael Lesslie ensure that, beyond the shock value, this story remains human, emotional, and gripping from beginning to end. Much of that is also thanks to Zada, who delivers an unforgettable performance.

Playing an established franchise character — especially one originated by an incredibly famous and acclaimed actor — must be a tough undertaking, and I'll get back to the highlights and lowlights of that exact situation before long. First, though, I want to soundly and unrestrainedly praise Joseph Zada, an actor with a massive responsibility in this film. Without a good Haymitch, "Sunrise on the Reaping" fails.

Thankfully, Zada is more than up to the task, and the movie's extremely speedy — but not overly so — pacing means that he has to go through a massive emotional journey in a relatively short amount of time. Zada sells every second as Haymitch, whether he's promising his District 12 girlfriend Lenore Dove Baird (Whitney Peak) that he'll see her after the reaping to breaking down crying just before he enters an arena filled with, presumably, 47 kids who hope to kill him.

Zada is great, but much like Haymitch, he doesn't do it alone. Because, again, "Sunrise on the Reaping" moves at such a quick clip — to be fair, it packs 400 pages into about 2 hours and 40 minutes — he's the character we bond with the most, and the character Haymitch himself bonds with the most is arguably Maysilee Donner, his fellow District 12 tribute played by Mckenna Grace. Despite being enemies back home, where Maysilee is a sort of petty schoolyard bully, the two become unlikely allies who end up making it to the end of the Games together, and Grace brings a steeliness to her role that eventually falls away to reveal an understandably scared young girl. It certainly helps that Francis Lawrence and his team built an astounding world for his performers.

Joseph Zada and Mckenna Grace, the standouts among the tributes — with respect to Ben Wang, Molly McCann, and Iona Bell, the first of whom plays District 12 tribute Wyatt Callow and the rest of whom play Louella and "Lou Lou" McCoy, they, uh, aren't in the movie as much for reasons you can probably ascertain — deliver exceptional performances, but respect must be paid to Francis Lawrence's overall vision and the stunning world-building that he and his creative team deliver in "Sunrise on the Reaping."

When I spoke to Lawrence about the film and other dystopian teen movies he's directed (or is set to direct), he said, "I think the dystopian aspect of these worlds, a lot of it, for me, is about the world-building." This love of the game is evident, because "Sunrise on the Reaping" looks and feels phenomenal.

If you're familiar with the Hunger Games franchise, you know that we've gotten to see two very different eras of Panem, which come with understandably different technical developments. In "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes," everything is relatively primitive; beginning in "The Hunger Games," the tech is much more advanced after several decades. "Sunrise on the Reaping" falling pretty squarely in the middle here is particularly cool because of the small details of the world; one such example that I really appreciated is the tributes being lifted into the arena on small platforms as opposed to the tubes we see Katniss and other tributes enter years later. Without spoilers, the technical logistics of the arena play an outsized role in "Sunrise on the Reaping," and the world feels rich, full, and disturbingly real in the best way.

"The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" is chock-a-block full of characters you'll remember from previous installments like "The Hunger Games: Catching Fire" and both parts of "The Hunger Games: Mockingjay," and the results are ... a bit mixed. (It was confirmed, long before the film's release, that Jennifer Lawrence and Josh Hutcherson would reprise their roles as Katniss Everdeen and Peeta Mellark; how exactly that transpires will remain a secret until you sit down and see the movie.) I'm going to mention the breakneck pacing again here, and it's not a bad thing, but it does mean that a lot of characters are introduced and summarily disappear; this is also true of Billy Porter's larger-than-life Capitol stylist Magno Stift, though his legal wife and nemesis Drusilla Sickle, a plastic surgery nightmare gamely played by a vamping Glenn Close, gets much more play.

I wish we'd seen more of Elle Fanning's take on Effie Trinket, a character originally played by Elizabeth Banks, but she's reliably great in her scenes; Kieran Culkin plays a pre-Stanley Tucci version of Caesar Flickerman and is bombastic, over-the-top, and undeniably sharp and dynamic. Jesse Plemons does great work, as always, stepping into Philip Seymour Hoffman's shoes as the taciturn turncoat Plutarch Heavensbee, echoing Hoffman's performance while making it his own.

The best and worst performers behind recurring characters, though, are Ralph Fiennes and Kelvin Harrison Jr. Fiennes manages to bridge the gap between Tom Blyth and Donald Sutherland as Panem's president Coriolanus Snow, but Harrison Jr. is, I am sorry to say, doing a sort of "Saturday Night Live" impression of his predecessor Jeffrey Wright. I appreciate the ask here is big, but sadly, not every actor rises fully to the challenge.

If I have one big "nit to pick" in "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping," it's a problem that affects a lot of adaptations: it over-explains a lot. Because the book is told from Haymitch's point of view, we learn a lot as he infers and gleans; the movie has to painstakingly say all of that. Still, it's a minor quibble.

Before the release of "Sunrise on the Reaping," I saw and heard chatter, anecdotally, that this movie would surpass "The Hunger Games: Catching Fire" in sheer quality. Respectfully, I have to disagree. Not only is "Catching Fire" the best Hunger Games movie by a long shot and just a really great and well-made movie in its own right — Francis Lawrence, thank you again for that incredible aspect ratio change as we enter the arena, and thanks to your cinematographer Jo Willems as well — but "Catching Fire" doesn't have to explain its narrative as intensely as "Sunrise on the Reaping" does. Still, this is simply a quirk of adaptation, and "Catching Fire" being able to narratively coast off of its predecessor is an unfair advantage.

"Sunrise on the Reaping" might not beat "Catching Fire," but it is a truly excellent addition to the Hunger Games film franchise — and it's one of the most thrilling action movies of the year. As this universe continues to expand (that is, if Suzanne Collins decides to write future books), if we keep Lawrence at the helm and keep casting top-notch actors, Hunger Games fans will remain in excellent hands.

"The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" opens in theaters on November 20, 2026.

Chase bank appears to be suffering an online banking outage. On the outage tracking site, Down Detector, reports slowly starting rolling in this morning before suddenly spiking around 10 am Pacific.

Chase released a pair of statements throughout the nearly eight hour outage. The bank claimed that a technical issue brought its services down and was clear that it did not consider the issues a cyberattack.

Tom's Guide tried to confirm with the company but customers claimed that tellers at Chase locations couldn't operate their systems either. At least one support tweet on X seemed to confirm this.

Chase never said if its non-digital locations were compromised.

Here's what we learned throughout the day.

@veeramarni We saw your post and want to reach out. I do apologize, it appears that we are currently working to resolve an issue with online banking. Please try again at a later time. We're sorry for any inconvenience, and appreciate your patience. ^RRNovember 16, 2026

So far, I haven't seen Chase say anything on any official channels as a formal post.

The best I've come across is from Chase Support on X where the company said that it is "working to resolve an issue with online banking."

Over on Down Detector reports started rolling in around 6:30 am Pacific/9:30 am ET but didn't really start spiking until 9:00 am PT. As of this posting there are more than 4,000 reports on the site.

I am seeing hundreds of reports for Bank of America, JP Morgan, Wells Fargo and Zelle, but based on the amounts and the ability to log in to accounts with those banks, I currently believe this incident is isolated to Chase.

However, if you're trying to send or receive money from or to a Chase account, you will likely have problems.

According to posters on Reddit, people have said that after attempting online transactions they ended up going to their location branch.

Multiple people said that the Chase tellers told them all their systems were down and they couldn't do anything.

"Then went to branch to ask about it they said they can’t do anything because their system is down smh," said one representative poster.

Tom's Guide has reached out to Chase for comment.

I'm seeing reports and comments that people are having trouble logging into other banks including Bank of America and Wells Fargo.

I've been able to login into Wells, but that may not be universal.

Lets u know, are you having problems with your bank?

Chase has not responded to Tom's Guide as of this posting; however, a spokesperson did give a statement to the San Francisco Chronicle.

“Due to a technical issue, some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete, but customers still have access to their accounts and funds,” a Chase spokesperson told the paper. “We are working to resolve this as quickly as possible.”

This does seem to contradict users on social media claiming they can't log in.

Analyst Bruce Schneier (Security Technologist; Fellow at Harvard Kennedy School) is an internationally renowned security technologist.

We asked him why companies don't have redundancies to prevent outages:

"Redundancies reduce profitability, and it is the goal of shareholders these days to wring all excess profits out of any and every company. Thatreduces resilience in general, and redundancy in particular.”

With the Outlook outage last week, and more every day, Schneier expects more will come.

"I guess I’m not surprised. Our systems are very fragile these days. Fragile systems are the most profitable in the near term. And there is no incentive to focus on the long term.”

Reports are starting to go Down Detector, though as of this posting they are still around 4,000 after a peak of 5,000 reports about 30 minutes ago.

A Chase spokesperson has responded to our inquiries with a similar statement as the one received by the San Francisco Chronicle.

“Due to a technical issue, some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete but customers still have access to their accounts and funds. We are working to resolve this as quickly as possible."

However, our statement had one extra line saying that the issue was not cyber-related, meaning it is something in the Chase systems and not a malicious attack.

"This is a technical issue, not cyber related.”

The spokesperson did not indicate how long it would take to resolve the issue or any potential causes.

Yahoo! Finance is tracking statements from different banks. Wells Fargo and Bank of America have received some outage reports, but not as many as Chase, which again suggests that it's an issue between Chase and other banks.

"You can still access your accounts through our ATMs, banking locations, and customer service," the Wells Fargo website reportedly reads.

I have a Wells Fargo account and could not find that statement, but I've also had no issues logging in or using my accounts online, so my experience may not be the same.

Bank of America has not released a statement.

After an initial decline, reports on Down Detector hit a momentary plateau. For the last half an hour, they've started a slow but steady decline.

Let me know if you're able to access your Chase account since reports started going down.

As of this writing, reports are under 3,200 for the first time since 10 am PT, about 3 hours ago.

Chase has been suffering a technical outage for more than 4 and a half hours.

Again, we saw an initial stream of reports around 7 am PT/10 am ET, with the real spike hitting two hours later.

Chase has said in statements that the problem is a technical one, not an attack. It's not clear what the issue is and it appears to affect both online banking and in-person transactions at their banks.

Reports have declined but not enough to declare the outage over. People are still reporting that they can't access their accounts.

We have asked Chase for clarification but haven't received any updates since the first statement.

I just received an update from Chase. Here's what the bank is saying now.

Per the bank's spokesperson, JPMorganChase apparently experienced a software bug in "on-premise hardware system", which the spokesperson reiterated there is "no evidence this is cyber-related."

The statement claims that customers still have access to their accounts and funds. They did not respond to questions about issues affecting brick-and-mortar banks.

"We’re working diligently to resolve this by the end of the day today." It's unclear which timezone that end of day actually refers to.

Reports on Down Detector have halved in the last hour dropped from about 3,800 to 1,780.

Its been a slow decline but it appears things are coming back online for people.

People who've regained access have said they've been able to use Zelle, withdraw money and successfully login to the app or the browser.

I am seeing mixed comments from people saying they have access, while others say they still can't login to the app.

From what I can tell, the Chase outage finally appears to be over. Reports are still over 500 but most comments and social posts are indicating that people have access to their accounts again.

I have not a seen a "We're back" post from Chase or JPMorgan.

#3439. Does The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping Have A Post-Credits Scene? A Spoiler-Free Guide

Get ready for the 50th Hunger Games. "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" is the sixth big screen entry in the dystopian YA franchise and another prequel film set before the events of the 2012 "Hunger Games" movie that started it all. This time, it's all about Haymitch Abernathy and the games that turned him into a champion. But is this the last ride for the property? Or might there be more to come?

"Sunrise on the Reaping" offers a thrilling new look at beloved "Hunger Games" characters, but it is a prequel. Much like "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes" before it, it's filling in gaps in the timeline of this universe. So, it's not directly setting up sequels like the original run of "Hunger Games" movies. That said, Lionsgate may yet want to lay some seeds for future installments, and in the realm of franchise filmmaking, credits scenes are the best way to do that.

Credit scenes have become expected fare in so many properties. Add that to the fact that Jennifer Lawrence's Katniss and Josh Hutcherson's Peeta are returning in this new "Hunger Games" prequel, and there's even more reason for fans to think there could be something extra during the end credits. So, we're here to offer a spoiler-free guide to the movie's credits scene situation. Seriously, we will not spoil anything meaningful whatsoever. This is merely about giving viewers information to enhance the experience. With that out of the way, let's get to the matter at hand.

No, "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" doesn't have any credits scenes of any kind to speak of. No post-credits scene, no mid-credits scene, nothing at all. Once the credits roll, the movie is over. At which time, viewers can safely make a break for the lobby or the bathroom without fear of missing out on anything else.

Joseph Zada ("East of Eden") leads the cast of this new "Hunger Games" prequel as a young Haymitch Abernathy, with modern villain expert Ralph Fiennes co-starring as President Snow. As for what folks can expect from this much-anticipated installment? The synopsis for the movie reads as follows:

"The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" revisits the world of Panem and follows young Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada) 24 years before the events of "The Hunger Games," starting on the morning of the reaping of the 50th Hunger Games, also known as the Second Quarter Quell.

The cast also includes Jesse Plemons (Plutarch Heavensbee), Glenn Close (Drusilla Sickle), Kieran Culkin (Caesar Flickerman), Elle Fanning (Effie Trinket), Mckenna Grace (Maysilee Donner), Maya Hawke (Wiress), Whitney Peak (Lenore Dove Baird), and Kelvin Harrison Jr. (Beetee Latier). Francis Lawrence, who directed the emotionally obliterating all-time great Stephen King adaptation "The Long Walk" in addition to several prior entries in this franchise, has returned to the director's chair once more.

"The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" hits theaters on November 20, 2026.
