When it comes to celebrity nicknames, is there any better than “JLo”? Jennifer Lopez’s moniker has been synonymous with her storied career for years. It’s been used in her music, it's her social media handle and has been used to name her fashion, fragrance and skincare lines. Although I just found out about how it started. Honestly, I’m so surprised this wasn’t common knowledge to me until today.

JLo has been JLo for over two decades. When the pop star, actress and businesswoman was recently asked about how she got it, here’s what she said:

Heavy D… Sony had Sony Studios down in Manhattan and everybody used to record in there. You could see all the Sony artists in there. And, Heavy would be in there, and he came by one day and I was recording, and I think I was recording my second album, the JLo album. And, I hadn’t named it the JLo album yet. And he came in and he was like, ‘What’s up Jenny Lo? JLo’s in the house.’ He just started calling me that, and I was like, ‘I think I’m gonna name my album JLo’.

Heavy D was a Jamaican-American rapper who had hits such as “Now That We Found Love”, “Got Me Waiting” and “We Got Our Own Thang” in the late 1980s and early 1990s. The rapper tragically died at the age of 44 of a pulmonary embolism back in 2011. As JLo recalled, Heavy D wasn’t only the first person to give her the nickname, it also inspired her to name her second album, J.Lo. When talking about the origin of the name, she also added this:

I never expected it to stick the way it did. I just thought I was going to name the album JLo. And also, [rappers] started putting me in songs as Jennifer Lo, JLo, Jenny Lo. Like, it was a thing. I was already an actress, and I had already made my first record and that had hit, so now they knew who I was, and relationships that were kind of high profile, and they would write about us.

The JLo album came out back in 2001, and the rest is history; she’s been JLo ever since. Along with the album title itself, Lopez noted that she also started being called the nickname in rap songs like Pitbull’s “Culo,” Jay-Z’s “Lost One”.

As she also mentioned, the nickname also got picked up when it came to tabloids writing about her famed relationships – like being one half of Bennifer of course. When JLo was married to Ben Affleck, she officially took his last name for a time, but she never stopped being JLo. And I can’t imagine the nickname ever going away for the superstar.

The origins of JLo came up when she was on the Friends Keep Secrets podcast. Lopez is currently promoting her concert special, The JLo Show. The two-hour affair showcases JLo’s final performance at her Las Vegas residency at The Colosseum at Caesars Palace, which happened in March of this year. It's set to premiere on the 2026 TV schedule on November 26 at 8 p.m. on CBS and with a Paramount+ subscription.

The story of JLo's nickname is so random, but that’s why it’s such a good story. Sometimes you never know how one decision might change your whole career, which was the case with Jennifer Lopez and her JLo album.

#3436. First Reactions To Brad Pitt's Cliff Booth Movie Have Critics United

It's not every day that we get a continuation of one of Quentin Tarantino's most acclaimed movies. Heck, it's not every day we even get a new script at all from the movie-loving auteur. Ever since he debuted "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood" in 2019, Tarantino hasn't directed a single feature film — likely a consequence of his self-imposed (and rather silly) rule to limit himself to only directing 10 total movies. But whatever the case may be, he was clearly interested in diving deeper into this alternate-history world with "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth," only this time, he handed over the reins of his script to David Fincher.

Could this unlikely collaboration between Fincher and Tarantino, two very different artists, yield fruit? It sure seems like it has, based on early reactions from the film's Los Angeles premiere. It seems like the entire movie industry has been waiting for this moment, despite the unusual nature of this sequel. Set in 1977, eight years after the events of "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood," the sequel focuses solely on Brad Pitt's past-his-prime stuntman Cliff Booth long after his harrowing encounter with the Manson family. Gone are his free-wheeling days playing backup to Leonardo DiCaprio's Rick Dalton, replaced by the reality of having to find a new way forward in a much different world. As the film's colorful synopsis puts it, "the fairytale is over."

But not for us! "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" held its premiere screening last night, and social media is positively abuzz with hype from those in attendance. For those looking for a handy roundup of all the first reactions, you've come to the right place.

Is it really possible that we have yet another "Best movie of 2026" contender on our hands this late in the year? If anyone could pull that off, well, we suppose it'd be the dream team of David Fincher and Quentin Tarantino. Starring Brad Pitt, Elizabeth Debicki, Scott Caan, Yahya Abdul-Mateen II, Carla Gugino, Matt Groove, JB Tadena, the great Peter Weller, and many more, "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" has plenty of star power going for it. But dare we even hope that Tarantino managed to make lightning strike twice, revisiting this deeply nostalgic world for a second time and somehow living up to the hype?

That seems to be the main takeaway from the critics, journalists, and other lucky fans at the Los Angeles premiere. We'll start with Variety awards pundit Clayton Davis, who described the picture as "a wild, hilarious hangout movie" featuring Pitt's "best performance" since his last time in the role as Cliff Booth. He added, "The cinematography is gorgeous. If the 2019 film was a love letter to L.A., this one is a full-on sonnet [..] Fincher and Tarantino haven't been this much fun in years."

As if that wasn't high praise enough, critic Courtney Howard echoed those sentiments and called the sequel "a pure riot. David Fincher's play at a nostalgic bygone era Quentin Tarantino loves works like gangbusters. Takes time to form, but plays like a LA film noir hangout picture." Meanwhile, Germain Lussier of io9 came out swinging and proclaimed this "my favorite movie of the year and it's not even close. Hilarious, exciting, romantic, you'll never guess what happens next and probably not believe it then anyway. Couldn't love it more if I tried."

Of course, as with any significant Hollywood premiere, some of the more interesting reactions are the ones that go against the grain. While most responses are united in singing the praises of "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth," a select handful note that they may need some time with this movie to fully soak it in. In a world of extremes, reactions that run towards the middle ground are certainly refreshing, at least.

Longtime critic and entertainment journalist Todd Gilchrist suggested that he was still undecided on whether David Fincher and Quentin Tarantino's unique sensibilities are fully a match made in heaven. "I quite liked 'The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,' but as with all Tarantino projects, I need to see it (at least) twice to properly digest it. I'm not yet convinced QT's shambling, novelistic approach and Fincher's precision are exactly compatible." Erik Anderson of Awards Watch went even further, highlighting that, "Despite some fun and energetic sequences, I found 'The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth' to be tonally a bit messy [...] It seemed to want a 70s noir style but should have leaned in more."

As always, each viewer's mileage may vary. Luckily, fans won't have to wait much longer. "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" will receive an exclusive two-week window in IMAX theaters starting on November 25, 2026. It will then come to Netflix on December 23, 2026.

#3432. 5 Actresses Who Would Be Perfect James Bond Girls Opposite Robert Pattinson

Who should play the next Bond Girl? We have a few ideas.

It's finally been confirmed that Robert Pattinson will be playing James Bond in the next canonical feature film about Ian Fleming's stalwart British spy. Back in February 2025, Amazon gained creative control of the character, and while we expressed some consternation over the deal, that didn't stop film fans everywhere from speculating what a James Bond movie might look like in the 2020s. Fast-forward to 2026, and there were several finalists for the role of the new Bond himself, among them Nicholas Hoult, Callum Turner, Jack Lowden, Josh O'Connor, and the ultimate winner, i.e. Pattinson.

Now, of course, we can play further speculation games. With 007 in place, fans will now have a marvelous time pondering who might be playing other notable James Bond supporting figures like Ms. Moneypenny, M, Q, Blofeld, Felix Leiter, etc.

And, as is a long (and perhaps sexist) tradition in James Bond lore, he must always be paired with a "Bond Girl" or two in every movie. Bond will inevitably meet and seduce an attractive woman, and the woman will typically prove to be an invaluable ally, a secret enemy, or a doomed innocent who is killed to move the action forward. Some models and actors have even elevated their "Bond Girl" roles into fascinating new characters.

I'd have loved to see O'Connor play a gender-flipped version of a Bond Girl, as we haven't yet had any "Bond Boys," and their time has definitely come. Pattinson could easily seduce men and women equally, and depicting O'Connor in bed with Pattinson would be a fantastic "second place" prize for the actor.

Who should play a Bond Girl opposite Pattinson? We think the following performers would do well.

Florence Pugh may be the most obvious choice for the next James Bond movie. Pugh already has spy-movie-adjacent experience playing Black Widow Yelena in several films and TV shows in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, including 2026's ultra-hit "Spider-Man: Brand New Day," so she could likely slip into the role of a slinky espionage expert with ease. Indeed, she kind of played a Bond Girl-like role in "Brand New Day," anyway, appearing nude in a hot tub as Yelena and offering some vital exposition to the movie's hero. But it doesn't take too much imagination to envision Pugh slithering through a casino or fancy-dress ball, wearing an expensive, Met Gala-worthy gown, snarling at Bond and talking to him with power and confidence.

Pugh is a forceful and talented actor, and it seems to me that she would be able to bite into a Bond Girl role with enthusiasm. Robert Pattinson is also quite versatile and, in the right roles, intense and zany. I suspect that Pugh would be able to match Pattinson's hidden livewire energy, allowing the two to crackle. Additionally, Pugh has previously worked with Denis Villeneuve, the director of the next Bond flick, having played Princess Irulan in Villeneuve's "Dune: Part Two" and the upcoming "Dune: Part Three."

So, the question now arises: would Pugh's Bond Girl be a helpful ally, a doomed innocent, or a secret enemy? Every instinct in my body dictates that she'd end up being the third type, holding a gun on 007 while they both wear nothing but a bedsheet.

Katy O'Brian's breakout role was playing the itinerant queer bodybuilder Jackie in Rose Glass' amazing 2024 crime flick "Love Lies Bleeding," which I thought was one of the best movies of its year. What's more, it's clear from her performance in that film that O'Brian is destined to be a star. She possesses a forceful energy and a lot of screen presence, able to balance the intensity from her co-star, Kristen Stewart.

Some might also recognize O'Brian for her supporting role as Jentorra in 2023's overpriced Marvel actioner "Ant-Man and the Wasp: Quantumania." The actor has since appeared in the blockbuster films "Twisters" and "Mission: Impossible — The Final Reckoning" and had a supporting role on the "Star Wars" TV series "The Mandalorian," so she's clearly comfortable with giant productions and would not feel out-of-place in a James Bond movie.

O'Brian has experience in a wide variety of other films, too, having played the lead in the drag queen-themed 2025 zombie movie "Queens of the Dead" and appeared in the biopic "Christy" opposite Sydney Sweeney. Most recently, she appeared in Edgar Wright's "The Running Man" adaptation.

I can picture a scene wherein 007 travels to a bar somewhere and trades barbs with O'Brian, whose biceps are bigger than his. They can then admire the other women in the joint together, sharing a drink and a seeming flirtation, along with some secret information. Then, once something goes wrong and bad guys begin extracting weapons, Pattinson and O'Brian could stand back-to-back and kick a little butt. She has a black belt in hapkido, after all.

Danai Gurira's first major screen credit came in 2004 when she appeared in an episode of "Law & Order: Criminal Intent." From there, she continued to plug away at her career, appearing in episodes of shows like "Life on Mars," "Lie to Me," and "Treme." However, her real big break came when she began appearing on the hit zombie series "The Walking Dead" as Michonne, a character who's become so recognizable that her likeness has shown up in non-"Walking Dead" video games like 2026's "World War Z."

Her career only continued to swing upward when she co-starred in the 2018 MCU blockbuster "Black Panther" as Okoye, the leader of the Wakandan royal guard. And none of this even scrapes her amazing theater career, with Gurira having authored several plays and scored a Pulitzer nomination for her play "In the Continuum."

When James Bond steps into a room, he usually fills it with his charisma and poise. The women he meets, then, should be able to match one of those qualities, and Gurira could do that in abundance. And here's the thing: She's capable of playing either a poised spy contact in a gown or a rough-and-tumble underground figure with equal skill. No doubt, she could swish across a ballroom, dancing with 007 as Strauss plays on the soundtrack, or she could welcome 007 into a dingy basement to flirt while she smokes a cigarette, only to start swinging her baseball bat at the rival spies who would inevitably infiltrate the area.

Most folks wouldn't recognize Arden Cho's face, but they would definitely recognize her voice, as she played the lead character Rumi in Netflix's super-hit animated film "KPop Demon Hunters." But even if that movie somehow passed you by, Cho has been racking up screen credits for decades, appearing in TV shows like "CSI: NY" and in low-rent movies like "Mega Python vs. Gatoroid." Her most prominent live-action TV roles include her turns as Kira on the "Teen Wolf" series, Emily on "Chicago Med," and Ingrid in "Partner Track."

Cho is also a pop star in her own right, having released her first single back in 2011, a song titled "I'm Just a Girl." (A quick note: Despite the actor being a fantastic singer, Rumi's singing voice in "KPop Demon Hunters" was provided by singer EJAE.) Cho is a professional model as well, having worked on campaigns for Nike and Apple, so she would be wholly comfortable in dazzling gowns and sporting high-end makeup. Her profile is certainly rising thanks to the popularity of "KPop Demon Hunters," and she is slated to appear in the upcoming K-Pop-themed feature film "Perfect Girl."

It's hard to say what kind of chemistry Cho would have with Robert Pattinson, although she certainly seems more down-to-earth and relatable. Pattinson, meanwhile, comes across as relatively aloof. As such, one can envision Cho playing a smoky, clever figure who's able to crack wise with 007 without him being quick enough to notice.

Hunter Schafer's filmography isn't terribly large, but her profile in popular culture is enormous. She rose to fame playing the role of Jules in the HBO series "Euphoria," and her movies and TV shows since have all been either fascinating art pictures or high-profile franchise entertainments. Case in point: Schafer appeared as Tigris in "The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes" in 2023 and played the lead role in the zany Dan Stevens horror film "Cuckoo" in 2024. That same year, she also had a small role in Yorgos Lanthimos' "Kinds of Kindness," which is maybe the most Yorgos Lanthimos movie that ever Lanthimosed. Then, in 2026, she briefly appeared in David Lowery's sapphic pop diva drama "Mother Mary" and will soon appear in the sci-fi series "Blade Runner 2099."

Schafer is dazzling on screen, bringing both sophistication and naivete to her roles, often simultaneously. She looks like an elven princess, and it's almost a pity she was not cast as Princess Zelda in the upcoming "The Legend of Zelda" movie (with the role instead going to Bo Bragason).

I don't know if Schafer has any fight or stunt training, but one can easily imagine her in a lovely dress dancing with, and kissing, James Bond. No doubt, she could serve as a gentle counterpoint to a relatively gruff Bond, and she would only be the second trans actor to appear in a James Bond movie after Caroline Cossey in "For Your Eyes Only." Schafer, however, could — and should — play a much larger role. I can see her kicking glutes and smirking while doing it.

#3431. 10 Hacks Every Waze User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Waze is a crowdsourced navigation app designed to help you get where you're going as quickly and with as much information about your route as possible. Where Google Maps and Apple Maps offer relatively straightforward directions, Waze tries to outsmart these alternatives by integrating real-time community feedback about hazards, speed traps, road closures, and more. If you are switching to Waze or using it alongside your other navigation tools, these are the hacks to help you maximize everything the app has to offer.

If you find yourself losing track of time or running late for events, Waze can notify you when it's time to leave—based on your current location and live traffic—so you arrive on schedule. You can set up "Time to leave" reminders in advance for individual planned drives, or you can sync your calendar to receive notifications for scheduled events. Calendar sync connects to your device's default calendar app, but you can change this to a third-party alternative if you prefer. Calendar events must include a navigable address to trigger reminders, and you must select Plan a drive in Waze for the event.

Waze has a feature called "child reminders," which are notifications to check for children before you get out of the car. This is clearly an incredibly important use case, but you can also use these alerts for custom messages, like "Don't forget the groceries!" In Waze, tap the menu button > Settings > Reminders > Child reminder and select Custom message.

Variable speed limits, especially on unfamiliar routes, can result in you speeding when you don't mean to. But Waze can alert you if you exceed a customized speed threshold so you aren't caught by surprise or at higher risk of being ticketed. From the menu, go to Settings > Speedometer and turn on Show speedometer. Tap Speeding threshold to select what limit you want to trigger alerts, and turn on Alert at threshold if you want Waze to play a sound.

Waze offers a wealth of information on routes to help drivers navigate obstacles and hazards, but this can clutter your map and distract you from the most critical information, especially in congested, high-traffic areas. Waze says it limits and prioritizes alerts automatically, but you can actually customize which alerts you see based on what's most important to you. From the menu, go to Settings > Alerts and reports > Reports and select the relevant alerts.

In the same Alerts and reports menu, you can enable Alert while driving, which will give you an audio warning and an onscreen pop-up about your selected hazards. This allows you to run navigation via a different map app (like Google Maps or Apple Maps) in the foreground while still getting Waze data in the background.

Waze integrates with toll road and HOV lane passes, so if you have an express or fast lane subscription, your route will optimize for it. If you don't, Waze can still account for HOV lane eligibility if you tell it how many passengers are in your car. From the menu, go to Settings > Toll and HOV passes and tap the plus icon to add your pass(es) from the list. If you need to add your passenger count instead, you can do so from View routes and enable the HOV option.

If you're driving through an unfamiliar, highly congested, or poorly designed area, you can ask Waze to help you avoid tricky maneuvers, such as crossing multiple lanes of traffic or turning left at intersections without lights. This prioritizes ease over speed using protected green arrows, roundabouts, and right turns. From the menu, go to Settings > Navigation, Avoid difficult intersections and select Always. You can also ask Waze to avoid toll roads, ferries, freeways, and unpaved roads.

Waze has a built-in audio player that syncs with your preferred listening platform—such as Spotify, YouTube Music, and Pandora—so you can control your music without having to navigate between apps. (As Waze is a Google product, Apple Music isn't included.) Simply tap the music icon on the map to select your audio player and hit Accept. If you don't see the icon, go to Settings > Audio player and turn on Show on the map.

If you want to make audio directions more interesting, you can select a celebrity or character voice to help you navigate. Recent appearances include Bill Hader's Cat in the Hat and Ziggy Marley. Tap the speaker icon > Current voice to search for the voice or language you want to use. You can also record directions in your own voice.

#3430. Robert Pattinson Wasn't The First Choice For James Bond — But The Original Favorite Dropped Out

Not to give Amazon any free ideas, but the behind-the-scenes drama swirling around the biggest casting call of the year sounds like it could've been a reality TV series in its own right. The fateful search for who would don their most finely-tailored suit and their trusty Walther PPK came to an abrupt end this week, as Robert Pattinson was officially announced as our newest James Bond. But amid all the hoopla and hype, details have already begun trickling in concerning how this high-stakes round of musical chairs came to a close.

As it turns out, Pattinson may have won the highly-coveted role ... but he wasn't the first choice. To be fair, that seems evident enough from the fact that neither his name nor Nicholas Hoult's appeared in most reports identifying the finalists until late in this lengthy process. The intrigue goes much deeper than that, however.

There's a lot more that goes into casting decisions for James Bond than simply who looks best in a suit. The role is notorious for singlehandedly changing the lives of each and every performer practically overnight, especially in light of the usual Bond tradition of picking (relative) unknowns for the title role. There's life before Bond and life after Bond — and not everybody is cut out for all the fame and pressure and (occasionally) backlash that inevitably come with it.

It'll always be to Josh O'Connor's enduring credit that, according to this Puck report, he recognized these factors ahead of time and decided that it simply wasn't worth it for him. For the rest of us mere mortals, it may be tempting to look at nothing but the popularity and wealth and prestige associated with playing England's most defining fictional spy. If so, well, look no further than the toll this clearly took on our previous Bond. Not only did Daniel Craig have to overcome some seriously nasty comments about his physical appearance in the early going, but certain provocative comments late in his run also revealed the arduous nature of these big-budget productions and the many, many off-screen responsibilities associated with it.

Still, as excited as we are to see Robert Pattinson as Bond (and as someone who survived the "Twilight" phenomenon, he may be uniquely prepared for this in a way nobody else ever has), we'll always wonder what O'Connor could've done with the part. Villeneuve obviously saw that potential himself, and the "Dune" filmmaker is certainly no slouch when it comes to casting. Whatever comes next, we'll be seated for O'Connor's next big performance.

She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

Amazon is offering early Black Friday discounts on like-new versions of its 2024 Kindles, with prices starting at $152.99 for the Paperwhite and savings of $27 to $75 across five models that include the color-screen Colorsoft and the pen-equipped Kindle Scribe. All five are a generation behind Amazon's current lineup: The company introduced redesigned Paperwhite and Colorsoft models (plus accessories) in October, with the new Paperwhite now starting at $199.99, and replaced the 2024 Scribe with a third-generation model in December 2025. As for its “like-new” label, it means these are pre-owned devices that Amazon has tested and certified to look and work like new.

The Like-New Kindle Paperwhite (16GB) is down to $152.99 from $179.99 and covers just about everything most people need for everyday reading, including enough storage for thousands of ebooks. Its seven-inch, 300ppi glare-free display is larger than the previous generation’s 6.8-inch screen, with faster page turns, an adjustable warm light, IPX8 water resistance, and up to 12 weeks of battery life. As PCMag notes in its review, it's a great option for readers who don't need color or handwriting features.

The Like-New Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition (32GB) is down to $190.99 from $224.99, making it just $38 more than the like-new Paperwhite (16GB). For that relatively small difference, you're doubling the storage to 32GB and getting wireless charging, an ad-free lock screen, and a front light that automatically adjusts to your surroundings—on top of the same sharp seven-inch display, IPX8 water resistance, and up to 12 weeks of battery life as the standard Paperwhite, as noted by this PCMag review.

The Like-New Kindle Colorsoft (16GB) is down to $220.99 from $260.99 and offers something the Paperwhite models can’t: a color E-Ink display, which makes it well suited to comics, graphic novels, illustrated books, and travel guides. Its seven-inch screen shows that color content at 150ppi while keeping text at a sharp 300ppi, and you can mark passages in multiple highlight colors to keep your notes organized. That said, colors are noticeably more muted than on a conventional tablet, and battery life tops out at eight weeks, compared with 12 weeks on the Paperwhite.

The Like-New Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition (32GB) is down to $243.99 from $287.99, making it just $23 more than the standard like-new Colorsoft. For that modest increase, you're getting twice the storage at 32GB, which is particularly useful for comics, manga, and graphic novels that take up more space than regular ebooks, along with wireless charging, an automatically adjusting front light, and an ad-free lock screen. However, as PCMag notes in its review, the color display produces more subdued tones than a conventional tablet, so the Paperwhite remains the more economical choice if you primarily read novels.

The Like-New Kindle Scribe (16GB) is down to $284.99 from $359.99, the biggest dollar discount in this roundup. Unlike the other Kindles here, it's built for reading and writing, with a 10.2-inch, 300ppi glare-free display and a Premium Pen with an eraser and shortcut button—making it the most versatile option for readers who want an e-reader that doubles as a digital notebook.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.

Yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, and we vet our deals to make sure they’re the best ones. You can also refer to guides like our live blog that have already done all of the vetting for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

#3428. GTA 6's Game Awards Nominations Are Exactly What Everyone Predicted

Going into Tuesday’s reveal of the 2026 Game Awards nominees, the question wasn’t whether or not Grand Theft Auto 6 would pick up any nominations. It was more about how many nominations it would get. And now that the dust has cleared, GTA 6’s Game Awards nominations rolled out pretty much…exactly as expected.

But it’s nevertheless an unconventional situation. The game isn’t out yet. Reviews haven’t been published. Still, GTA 6 ultimately picked up eight nominations — the most of any game in 2026, immediately cementing it as a frontrunner for the GOTY race. It was nominated in the following categories:

This falls short of records set by Sandfall Interactive’s beloved parry simulator Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, which Polygon’s Oli Welsh predicted was an impossible gambit for GTA 6 anyway.

In 2025, Clair Obscur was nominated for 13 categories and won nine awards. That means GTA 6 could win every category it’s nominated in and still fall short of Clair Obscur’s record. At best, it could tie, depending on how the Player’s Voice category — which is voted on entirely by the public — plays out. As far as sheer number of nominations, purely on grounds of eligibility, it was never going to set the bar. Clair Obscur was up for two categories GTA 6 would never be eligible for (Best Indie Game and Best Debut Indie Game), and its ensemble cast carried it to three Best Performance nominations (Ben Starr, Charlie Cox, and Jennifer English, the latter of whom won).

Whatever happens, GTA 6’s raft of nominations reveals details about a wildly anticipated game that, to date, has only been seen through selected marketing materials and curated media coverage. A Best Score and Music nomination suggests Grand Theft Auto’s pedigree of killer soundtracks remains unshaken. A Best Game Direction nomination reaffirms Rockstar’s pedigree of immaculately conceived game design. Snagging a Best Narrative nomination — in a year full of narratively rich games that nevertheless excluded the sprawling, ambitious, deliciously messy Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave from the field — suggests GTA 6 might be something more nuanced than a mayhem-packed sandbox.

But perhaps the biggest reveal is in Perez’s nomination for Best Performance. The Game Awards did not officially say what role she plays in GTA 6, but these things tend to go to lead characters, which aligns with a long-standing rumor among fans that Perez portrays Lucia, one of the game’s protagonists. That GTA 6 only nabbed one Best Performance nomination additionally suggests one of two things: that she’s the only good performance in GTA 6, or that her performance is miles above and beyond everyone else in the game (which includes recent Emmy winner Stephen Root among its officially revealed cast).

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

All told, GTA 6 ended up nominated in basically every category it conceivably could’ve been nominated in: the top category, the top of one genre category (games are only allowed to compete in one of those), all three technical categories, and all three general artistic categories.

At the top of 2026, much ado was made about the shadow cast by GTA 6 over this year’s GOTY race — if the game was released in time, of course. For a large part of the year, particularly when it was still hard to believe that this thing was actually coming out, when it still felt like it might’ve been delayed, there were hints that this year would fold out in interesting, unexpected ways. On a podium left empty, who clambers to the top? A licensed Star Wars game? A 120-hour tactical soap opera? Another indie darling? None of those ended up nominated for the evening’s top prize. Now that we’re fast approaching the finish line, the race is playing out precisely as many expected a year ago.

#3427. 20 Years Ago Today: The Best James Bond Movie Ever Made Was Released In Theaters

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

There are very few franchises in cinema history that can compete with James Bond in terms of sheer viability across multiple decades. From "Dr. No," which kicked off cinema's most enduring franchise, to Daniel Craig's swan song "No Time to Die," 007 has endured. But 20 years ago, Bond reached his full potential as an icon of the silver screen.

20 years ago today, director Martin Campbell's "Casino Royale" first hit theaters. At the time, Craig was an up-and-coming star who wasn't a popular choice to take over as author Ian Fleming's beloved British creation. He was taking over for Pierce Brosnan, who had an uneven four film run that ended with arguably the worst James Bond movie of all time, "Die Another Day." To put it lightly, the pressure was on, but Campbell and Craig delivered in a huge way. "Casino Royale" is an undeniable masterwork of blockbuster filmmaking.

In stark contrast to "Die Another Day," which came out just four years earlier, "Casino Royale" was gritty, grounded, and opened up Bond to a new generation, while also serving as a welcome surprise to those who'd loved 007 for years. Opinions vary as they always do, but two decades removed, this pitch perfect piece of franchise filmmaking stands head and shoulders above everything that's come before or since. At the very least, it sits firmly in the top three with some room for debate.

What wasn't up for debate? Bond, James Bond was back, baby. Be it someone's first "Bond" movie or their 20th, this worked like gangbusters. It's the kind of movie that can make someone a fan of a franchise for life.

Just to show my hand, I've been watching "James Bond" for over 30 years and "Skyfall" was the movie that made me a lifelong fan. That said, I can admit that "Casino Royale" is very arguably the "better" movie, even if I personally enjoy "Skyfall" more. Every single time I watch it, I marvel at how perfect it is.

It certainly doesn't hurt that Martin Campbell has a real eye for 007. "GoldenEye" was the most important box office hit in "James Bond" history, as it had to relaunch the franchise following a six-year gap. Campbell is the man who knew how to bring Bond into the '90s with a fresh take. Similarly, when it was time to bring Bond into the 21st century, Campbell was called upon to work his magic. What's fascinating, though, is that "GoldenEye" and "Casino Royale" couldn't be more different.

"GoldenEye" was something of a grab bag, mixing some of the best elements of the Sean Connery and Roger Moore eras into one. "Casino Royale," on the other hand, was a full-blown origin story, adapting Ian Fleming's very first "Bond" novel. It was also very modern, totally willing to embrace the future and move away from the past. But that doesn't mean it forgot what Bond can and should be.

Campbell managed to get the most out of Craig's performance, turning him into both a handsome, charming devil of a man, as well as a ruthless killer. It's fun. It's glamorous. It's hair-raising. It's sexy. It's not so serious that it loses the fun along the way. It's truly the platonic ideal of what a "James Bond" movie should be, and the culmination of more than four decades of filmmaking up to that point.

"Casino Royale" has something for every fan. There are people who grew up with movies like "Goldfinger" who will always love that as the quintessential "Bond" movie, but those classics don't resonate with some modern viewers. There are those who relish the camp and deeply British sensibilities of something like "The Spy Who Loved Me," but that may not work for a younger viewer who is trying to understand who this 007 fellow is.

This movie encapsulates the Bond-ness of it all in a way that everyone can enjoy. It certainly doesn't hurt that Mads Mikkelsen's Le Chiffre is one of the greatest James Bond villains ever. Or that the big climax at the center of the film is at a poker table, rather than some giant action sequence. Don't get me wrong, we get plenty of action, but the poker game is a subversion of expectations and embraces a big part of Bond's history.

Then there's Vesper Lynd. Vesper Lynd in "Casino Royale" was the most difficult Bond girl to cast, but Eva Green ate the role up and gave an emotional core to the movie. A meaningful love interest is something that so many of the Bond films are missing, as he tends to think of women as "disposable pleasures," to quote Lynd. The relationship here raises the stakes, and the chemistry between Green and Craig is off the charts.

2012's "Skyfall" became the biggest Bond movie ever, but there's no way that would have happened if "Casino Royale" didn't tee up the ball so beautifully. This is the movie that this franchise is going to have to measure up to from now until the end of time. This set a new high-water mark for one of cinema's most long-lasting icons.

You can grab "Casino Royale" on Blu-ray from Amazon.

#3426. Ring's New $250 Indoor Camera Drone Sounds Terrifying

Ring made its name with its smart doorbells with built-in cameras, and now sells more indoor cameras than any other company, capturing more than 40% of the market. When you've already moved tens of millions of devices (enough to raise serious concerns about their use as part of the surveillance state), you always need to keep innovating, and today, the company announced a product it has been working on for a decade: an indoor camera drone powered by artificial intelligence. I got a chance to check it out during a media event yesterday, and I can report that, as harbingers of our dystopian future go, it is only mildly terrifying.

The drone camera is one of two products in the company's new Ring Robotics line, alongside a "rover cam" that looks kind of like the canister of a vacuum cleaner attached to an iPad. While the Ring Rover Cam is priced at $999.99 and targeted at businesses, the Ring Drone Cam is a much more affordable $249.99, reasonable enough that it will appeal to consumers looking for another way to keep (robot) eyes on their stuff.

The drone camera records 2K video and has a 148-degree field of view and the ability to rotate 360 degrees. It works with existing Ring cameras, doorbells, sensors, and alarms, as well as the Alexa Home Map. It has a flight time of eight minutes, and once it returns to its base station, it takes around an hour to fully recharge (eight minutes on the dock will give it one minute in the air).

As Ring founder Jamie Siminoff explained during the preview event, the company has been trying to build a workable camera drone for around a decade, but couldn't overcome certain design challenges until the advancement of AI models that allow the device to handle most of the computing—from route programming to threat detection—via the cloud, so the drones can be smaller and lighter.

According to Ring, when setting up the Ring Drone Cam, you carry it around your house, allowing it to map the interior. It will "intelligently identify rooms and suggest patrol points: spots worth extra attention." When sent out on "patrol," the drone's AI pilot will travel between hotspots, sensing and avoiding furniture and other obstacles along the way.The Ring Drone Cam works with other Ring cameras, so if an alert is triggered somewhere in your home—say, a window opening unexpectedly—the drone will take off to investigate. It has a built-in security light that will make its presence known, so it can also act as a deterrent, though the screaming sound of its spinning propellers will accomplish that just as well.

According to Ring, the drone camera can deliver peace of mind whether you're home or away, and admittedly I do like the idea of being able to check on my pets or make sure no pipes have burst while I'm at work or on vacation (though admittedly you can get the same sort of monitoring without involving an AI device that looks like a mini version of the flying robots from The Terminator).

I admit that the Ring Drone Cam seems pretty cool, provided I don't think about it too much. I don't know that I really feel the need to have every inch of my home covered in security cameras, but I do like the idea that the drone could, for example, go to check out what's going on if one of my smoke alarms' temperature sensors reports that one spot in the house is all of a sudden hotter than it should be.

If you're ready to enter this brave new world of security, you'll have to wait a bit longer: The Ring Drone Camera isn't expected to ship until January 2027, but you can sign up to be alerted when it is available for preorder now.

#3425. Magic: The Gathering Boss Reveals the Next Marvel Set’s Surprising Origin Story

Aaron Forsythe said Magic’s original narrative got ‘total buy-in’ from Marvel

Aaron Forsythe said Magic’s original narrative got ‘total buy-in’ from Marvel

Magic: The Gathering has already released two Universes Beyond sets based on Marvel Comics, with Marvel’s Spider-Man in 2025 and Marvel Super Heroes in 2026. The game’s designers are taking a very different approach to their third tie-in set, Darkhold Destiny, which will launch in 2027. Rather than simply making cards based on iconic characters and comic book arcs, Wizards of the Coast designers worked with Marvel to create an entirely new storyline designed with the game’s mechanics in mind. Magic’s vice president of design Aaron Forsythe told Polygon at MagicCon Atlanta that the inspiration for the new approach came from an unlikely source.

“My daughter was actually playing the Guardians of the Galaxy game on Xbox, which has a cool story,” Forsythe says. “It’s not from a comic, it’s not from a movie. They just let the game studio make their own story that fit the medium they were trying to use. It seems like they should let us do that.”

Forsythe says he received “total buy-in” from Marvel as soon as he brought up the idea.

“I think a lot of that was the trust we had built up working on the first two sets and the Secret Lair,” he said. “They saw that we aren't just a licensing team that wants to put the Hulk on a T-shirt. We create our own worlds and stories, and as creators, they could really appreciate the work we did and gave us the green light right away.”

Development on Darkhold Destiny actually began before Marvel’s Spider-Man launched — Forsythe said all Universes Beyond sets take four years to develop, as opposed to the typical three-year timeline for in-universe sets, because they need to get so much feedback from licensing partners. But even without player feedback, Forsythe says he realized something was missing from Spider-Man and Marvel Super Heroes that hadn’t been a problem in other Universes Beyond sets.

“The Marvel sets in particular are not driven by any real narrative,” he says. “We have some saga cards that talk about the death of Gwen Stacy, which we know people know. The Lord of the Rings has a linear story. Everybody knows how that story plays out. In Final Fantasy, there were 16 mostly linear stories woven together in a way that everyone who's touched those games has experienced. Marvel, with 60 years of stuff and us not using the movies — which are the stories people mostly know nowadays — we’re just picking moments in time, characters, and different sagas and whatnot. As a whole, it did not feel like it was telling much of a story.”

Magic’s designers created an original character, Fraxi, Scion of Yggdrasil, who will appear in Darkhold Destiny and a tie-in comic alongside Marvel favorites like Thor and Doctor Strange. The goal is to satisfy Magic players who want a story while still bringing in Marvel fans who will become committed players.

“I'm not going to say there aren't any tourist fans that just want buy their Spider-Man cards and go home,” Forsythe says. “But mostly once you dip your toes in, once you start building a deck, once you see your friend's Commander deck, once you go online and start reading about all the stuff that's out there, once you go to a store or a tournament or a convention, sure Spider-Man brought you in, but this aperture opens up into this vast, incredible world.”

Forsythe says Darkhold Destiny and the two other still unannounced Universes Beyond sets releasing next year will incorporate feedback they’ve been getting from players about the game’s various crossovers. He hopes these improvements will encourage even the most skeptical Magic players to give Universes Beyond a chance as the licensed sets have also helped bring lapsed players back to the hobby.

“There are some parts of the audience that are doubling down on the Magic IP stuff, being holdouts against UB like, ‘We'll show them! We'll all buy Reality Fracture!’” Forsythe says. “I would just say that UB is both getting new fans, and it's reactivated a lot of people too. I've heard 25 times in the last two days of some IP reactivating somebody like, ‘I'd forgotten about Magic, but it was fun and this thing you did got me back in. And now I'm here.'”

#3424. Robert Pattinson Escaped The Batman 3 Contract Ahead Of James Bond Casting (Report)

The search is over, Robert Pattinson is officially our newest James Bond, and director Denis Villeneuve can now look forward to filling all the various supporting roles surrounding the title character for the upcoming "Bond 26" ... but there's plenty of uncertainty to go around. We'll likely be dissecting this casting choice in all of its infinite implications for weeks and months and even years to come. For now, though, more details continue to be revealed as we attempt to wrap our minds around what Pattinson's newest role will mean for his other high-profile franchise.

That's the Batman-sized question of the day. There has been no official word on the status of Matt Reeves' "The Batman" movies going forward. As fans know, the director stepped away from filming "Part II" due to personal reasons and welcomed Steven Soderbergh to carry the production across the finish line. On top of that, the recent turnover at DC Studios further has thrown the future of the DC Universe and all of its various offshoots into flux. Rest assured, nothing short of an act of the movie gods will prevent "The Batman Part II" from eventually releasing — but what comes after that?

A new report is finally beginning to provide answers. According to The Wrap, all the fevered debate over whether the same film star should be playing both Batman and Bond might be for naught. Journalist Drew Taylor suggests that the recent turmoil with "The Batman Part II" has given Pattinson an out from his deal, which originally included a third trilogy-capping movie. Instead, the outlet cites an anonymous source who indicates that the "protracted production" of the long-delayed sequel "has allowed Pattinson to slip out from under his contract."

In short, this could be what freed up Pattinson to pursue Bond.

The many complicating factors going into Robert Pattinson's casting as James Bond are starting to come into focus. We only just found out that the "Primetime" star and "The Odyssey" scene-stealer wasn't initially the first choice for Bond – Josh O'Connor was, until he reportedly dropped out. Now, it seems that Pattinson's days in the cape and cowl are numbered, which we speculated about soon after the Bond news first broke. We certainly hate being the bearers of bad news, as most fans would've loved to see Matt Reeves and Pattinson complete a full-fledged trilogy of "The Batman" films. Unfortunately, this may be the closest we get to confirmation that this simply isn't to be.

While nobody from Skydance or Pattinson's camp have commented on the situation, The Wrap does suggest a way for Pattinson to balance his roles as both Batman and Bond, should the need arise. (As we know, things in Hollywood can always change on a dime and, theoretically, nothing is preventing Pattinson, Reeves, and Skydance from coming together to hammer out terms for a third film together.) While both tend to require lengthy productions, it's possible neither franchise may even overlap much, allowing Pattinson to work out his schedule so that he can spend time at MI6 and Gotham City.

This added responsibility as Bond will only make Pattinson even busier than he already is, but he knew what he was signing up for with this role. On the face of it, we're erring on the side of "The Batman Part II" marking the end of his tenure with DC. If so, a series of movies with Pattinson as the world's most famous super-spy isn't anything to sneeze at, either.

Home security cameras have become ordinary household hardware. SafeHome.org’s 2026 survey of 2,435 US adults found that 61% of households have at least one, up from 52% in 2024 and 42% in 2023, while video doorbells have reached 48% of households. Renters drove much of that growth. Their adoption rate jumped from 42% to 54% between 2024 and 2026, which makes sense given how many battery-powered cameras can be mounted without drilling and moved at the end of a lease.

In other words, when looking for one of the best home security cameras, it makes more sense to start with the features and subscription, rather than the headline numbers on the spec sheet. That, of course, can make finding the right one even harder. Here are some things to keep in mind when looking for a home security camera.

Arlo's Essential Wireless Security Camera helps you keep an eye on all the places that matter most. With Smart Detection for people, pets and packages, along with real-time alerts and color night vision, this high-quality security camera will give you peace of mind. Get two wire-free, rechargeable cameras this Black Friday, and with easy installation, they'll be up and running for the holidays.

The best way to figure out what security camera is right for you is to start with thinking about what you actually need a camera for.

A video doorbell suits packages and callers because its head-to-toe view and two-way talk are built around a front door. A driveway or yard needs a weatherproof outdoor camera, while a floodlight camera covers a broader area and adds deterrence. As a rule, cover each entry point instead of asking one camera to watch the entire property.

Prices generally fall into three useful bands. Budget models can be found for as little as $29, but you can still find features like 2K video and a pan-and-tilt designs that physically turn to cover a room. Mid-range models (around $100) offer good value, with additional features or better designs. Premium hardware reaches the $249 level and beyond, where you'll find such things as 4K video.

The number of megapixels figure on the box matters less than how many pixels land on a face. A 4-megapixel camera with a 2,560-pixel-wide image and an 80-degree lens can, under the older IEC 62676-4 identification guideline, identify someone at roughly 20 feet. A 4K camera captures 3,840 pixels across, but pair it with a wider 100-degree lens and that estimate rises only to about 21 feet. The extra pixels have been spent on width, so with the same lens, 4K gives you roughly twice the identification distance of 1080p, not four times.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Treat these numbers as geometry rather than guarantees, especially since the IEC standard for measuring detail at distance was revised in 2025. It uses 500 pixels per meter of scene width for validating a known person and 1,500 for high-certainty identification, while many spec sheets still rely on the older 250-pixel guideline. For a doorbell, 1080p is generally enough because visitors are close. For outdoor cameras, 2K, usually around 2,560 pixels across, is the sensible default. Pay for 4K when you need more detail at distance rather than simply a wider view, and check that your storage and Wi-Fi can handle it.

That said, two ordinary cameras in the right places will often beat one expensive 4K model covering everything badly.

“Spend less time chasing the highest resolution number in isolation. More detail can be useful, but placement, nighttime visibility, and useful notifications deserve just as much attention,” says Lars Felber, director of PR at Eve Systems. “A camera pointed at the wrong part of the porch can miss what matters regardless of its resolution.”

Judge a camera on its night footage, too. Infrared night vision uses light outside the visible spectrum to produce a black-and-white image in darkness, so it can show details relatively cleanly, but not with any color. Color night vision needs ambient light from a streetlamp or porch, or a built-in light — though often color night vision is a little less detailed, and usually can't see as far.

Watch for smeared movement too, since some battery cameras reduce their frame rate at night. Keep the lens away from glass and nearby eaves, which can bounce infrared light back into it.

Power decides where a camera can go and whether it can record continuously. Battery models are the easiest to install and the most renter-friendly, but they sleep until motion wakes them, so you get event clips rather than a full timeline and may lose the moments just before a trigger. Plug-in models remove charging breaks but leave you with a cable to route. Hardwired doorbells and floodlights can support 24/7 recording.

Power over Ethernet, usually shortened to PoE, carries power and data down one network cable for a more dependable connection. PoE requires cabling and a compatible switch or recorder, which is more work than most people want for a single doorbell. Solar models are the compromise. Solar models still have a battery, but solar panels keep the battery topped up so you don't need to worry about manual charging.

A solar panel is often the more practical upgrade for an awkward outdoor mount. Just about every company that makes one of the best outdoor security cameras offers a compatible panel. You’ll need a position with dependable sun, and short winter days can still leave the camera reliant on its battery, though it still beats climbing a ladder every few weeks.

Outdoor hardware also needs a weather rating. IP65, which means dust-tight and protected against low-pressure water jets, is a common floor for outdoor cameras and suits eave-mounted units, while IP66 is the better target for fully exposed walls. Check the stated operating temperature too. Arlo rates the Pro 6 down to −4°F, while cheaper models don’t always cope as well with freezing conditions. If you live somewhere that gets truly cold, like Canada, many models may not work for you.

Before drilling, test Wi-Fi at the exact mount point with your phone. Exterior walls and foil-backed insulation can badly weaken 5GHz Wi-Fi, which is fast but relatively short-ranged. Many budget cameras use only 2.4GHz, which reaches farther but contends with more household congestion.

Finally, check your upload speed if you plan to run several cloud cameras. Local recording to a memory card or hub doesn’t use that upload link, but continuous cloud video can saturate it surprisingly quickly.

Often, the price you pay for the camera itself is just a starting point. You still have to store video — and unless you can do so locally, you may have to pay for a subscription.

A local hub splits the difference. These live in your house, but are connected to your cameras wirelessly, so footage can survive both a damaged camera and an internet outage. A hybrid setup is generally the better choice, with local recording for continuity and cloud copies for important events.

“One of the most important things to look for in a home security camera is if a subscription is required to set up and use the device,” says Carney. “Going into the purchasing process, consumers should be aware that some security companies tack on a required subscription as a hidden cost without being transparent about it at purchase.”

Without a plan, some company's cameras will only let you view live events, and not save recordings, or access all of a camera's features. Be sure to look at the price of the subscription, and see if what's being offered is worth the long-term investment.

Once footage is being recorded, the next problem is getting alerted only when it matters. A camera that pings every time a car passes will eventually be ignored. Custom motion zones, sensible sensitivity controls and reliable person, vehicle and package detection do more for daily use than another AI label. At a door, two-way audio is worth having too, so you can speak to a courier without opening it.

“A camera can be very advanced and still fail at its only job if notifications are delayed,” says Rod Sides, founder of Loxx Boxx. “Worse, if it displays too many notifications in a way that you haven’t customized, you’re more likely to overlook the one important notification that may pop up.”

And don’t forget the microphone, since many cameras record audio by default. Recording a private conversation without everyone’s consent can break the law in all-party consent states such as California. If you don’t need sound or two-way talk, switching it off is the safer default.

“What consumers can spend less time worrying about is having the highest resolution or every bell and whistle on the market,” says Zavin. “Instead, focus on what the camera can actually do when a potential threat arises.”

For most homes, a well-placed 2K camera with accurate detection and a local fallback is the better buy. Step up to 4K or paid AI search if you have a specific use for them, not just because they're available.

#3422. 10 Shows Like 'Minimum Wage' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Spinning off of a popular web series, Netflix's Minimum Wage is currently in the middle of a 28-episode first-season run. If that sounds like a lot of episodes for a show in 2026, keep in mind that they're generally less than 15 minutes each, which is perfect for your overloaded to-watch list—especially when they go down so easily. This cringe workplace mockumentary follows the crew of teenagers running a failing pizza place and making (you guessed it) minimum wage; they're under enormous pressure from their boss (Randall Park) to save the business and their one dumb source of income.

The punchy episodes will leave you plenty of time to explore other streaming shows dealing with the utter ridiculousness of the modern workplace. Here are 10 to get you started.

Workplace comedies usually revolve around white-collar office environments (The Mary Tyler Moore Show, 30 Rock, Parks and Recreation, etc.). Like Minimum Wage, Superstore instead follows the staff of Cloud 9, a generic big-box retailer. The show’s deep bench and diverse cast are largely focused on the jokes, but much of that comedy involves the relatable situation of working a job that demands commitment and a smiley attitude in the face of both entitled customers and obnoxious bosses. It's a different venue and age bracket, but a nutty workplace is a nutty workplace. Stream Superstore on Hulu and Peacock.

We're moving away from the workplace and aging things up a bit, but no worries: the name is a little ironic given that the codependent, co-habitating twenty-somethings of the title are hardly mature. Five friends are cohabiting in the childhood home of Samir (Malik Elassal), and dealing with the uniquely Gen-Z humiliations around dating, work, and even health insurance. Only one member of the group has an actual reasonably good job, while career paths for the others include being a temp, waiter, and a part-time ballet instructor. Stream Adults on Hulu.

This offbeat workplace comedy kicks off with a fabulous premise: Jeong Bok-dong (Kim Byung-chul) was a high-level director in a major corporation until one bad meeting saw him demoted. To president! ...of the company's failing Pegasus Mart offshoot. Bok-dong makes it his mission to get revenge by bankrupting the store, hiring eccentrics to execute eccentric, entirely whackadoo plans and accidentally getting Pegasus noticed by customers, who quickly make it more popular than ever. Think The Producers, but in retail. Stream Pegasus Market on Tubi.

It might sound a little (or a lot) niche, but we’ve seen enough headlines about the working conditions at many video game production houses to understand why a workplace comedy set against such a backdrop would make for a dark and juicy comedy. Charlotte Nicdao and Rob McElhenney are the leads, playing a brilliant workaholic and an unsociable egomaniac, respectively, and the chemistry between them gives the show more than enough spark. There's also a four-episode spin-off called Side Quest. Stream Mythic Quest.

A half-hour comedy-drama with an emphasis on the comedy, Gentefied follows three Mexican-American cousins who have built lives in Los Angeles, only to be faced with a new challenge: the looming gentrification of the neighborhood they helped to build via their family's taco shop. Gentefied has a baked-in sense of place and culture and a lot of heart; the second season is even better than the first. Stream Gentefied on Netflix.

Perhaps there's a bit of counter-programming in this dramedy about a couple of scrappy New York City outsiders, but there's a fundamental goofiness to this show about a couple of nice guys who are great at getting themselves into trouble, and equally good at talking themselves out of it. Bryan Greenberg plays Ben Epstein, a quiet guy with any number of big ideas, while Victor Rasuk plays the outgoing, often shameless Cam Calderon; together they manage a startup clothing business with the benefits of neither money nor experience, amiably hustling their way to success, maybe. Stream How to Make It in America on HBO Max and Netflix.

Debuting at the beginning of the Obama administration before getting a surprise revival just a couple of years ago, Party Down is an acclaimed cult sitcom for the ages—lots of laughs, low ratings, and always worth rediscovering. A group of six (or so) struggling LA actors and writers work as cater waiters for a fancy company, with every episode into a new and wildly absurd situation, even as their aspirations far outstrip their actual lives. Stream Party Down on Prime Video and Netflix.

A legitimate sitcom that just happens to be set in Northern Ireland during the violent Troubles of the 1990s, when clashes between nationalists and unionists frequently resulted in violence. It’s a fascinating contrast, brought to life by a writer and creator (Lisa McGee) who lived it. It’s also laugh-out-loud funny—though it doesn’t make any allowances for audiences unaccustomed to Irish accents, so don’t feel bad if you need subtitles until you get the hang of it. Erin, Orla, Clare, and Michelle are joined by James, the only male student at their Catholic girls' school, dealing with normal growing-up stuff in absurd times. This world is a far cry from that of Minimum Wage, but Lisa McGee's sense of the absurd connects both shows—if the setting is a bit more dramatic, the comedy is just as wonderfully silly. Stream Derry Girls on Netflix.

Not a comedy! But about as good an indication of where we are in the modern global workplace as you're likely to find. Hyuk‑jun is a young guy saddled with debt who signs on for some part-time work at a job agency...at 50x the going rate, no less (should've been a red flag). Each new assignment places him in new and increasingly horrific situations, with increasingly arbitrary-seeming rules. But, hey, in 2026, it's a living. Stream Dead-End Job on Netflix.

It's an office (obviously) and not a pizza joint, but the point here is kinda that white-collar jobs in the 21st century can be at least as soul-killing as working customer service. The Office inherited some of the finer tropes of the workplace comedy (mostly involving tossing together a group of weirdos overly invested in their jobs) while also launching a million mockumentary-style shows, running for nine seasons, and becoming one of the most popular shows of its era. Stream The Office on Peacock.

#3421. Constantine Sequel With Keanu Reeves Gets Update After James Gunn's DC Universe Exit

The entertainment world is still reeling from the recent shake-up at DC Studios. James Gunn and Peter Safran have departed their posts as heads of the studio, meaning the DC Universe is in for some big changes. In fact, Gunn's DCU is reportedly being dismantled as DC Studios prepares for another reset. Whether that's good or bad remains to be seen and will be a matter of personal opinion. However, it could be good for the long-awaited sequel "Constantine 2."

In an interview with Collider, director Francis Lawrence addressed the status of the proposed follow-up to his 2005 DC Comics adaptation starring Keanu Reeves. The "Constantine" sequel was said to be officially happening with Lawrence returning back in 2022, but updates have been few and far between ever since. And while Lawrence clarified that he doesn't "want anybody to lose their jobs," he said the latest happenings at DC Studios are ultimately beneficial to his "Constantine" follow-up. As he put it:

"We have an idea, and we have a script, and we've been wanting to make it, and the people that were at DC were an impediment to us making it. So, we are now more hopeful as of yesterday's news that maybe now there will be another opportunity. But again, we've been trying to make this for 20-something years, and there's always been obstacles in the road to making it, and it's not me, it's not Keanu, it's not [producer] Akiva [Goldsman]. J.J. [Abrams] is on it as well. We all want to do it.

"It's really going to be people at Paramount, Warner, whoever's running DC now, getting everybody on board to say, like, 'Hey, we can do a sequel of our version of 'Constantine,?" Lawrence added.

Setting aside one's personal feelings about James Gunn and Peter Safran no longer being at DC Studios, this is a movie that all involved have wanted to make for a long time. Keanu Reeves kept pestering Warner Bros. about "Constantine 2" until it said yes, but that happened before Gunn and Safran were installed to launch their DC Universe. That complicated matters. Now, the situation is complicated once again, only this time in a way that could benefit Francis Lawrence and Reeves.

We only just got word that DC Studios is developing a new John Constantine movie, but that was also before the announcement about Gunn and Safran leaving broke. Even so, Lawrence addressed that as well, suggesting that both projects could co-exist:

"Personally, I don't even care if somebody has a plan for some sort of shared universe, and they want to do another version of Constantine. If they just let us do the sequel to our version, they can coexist. So, I have renewed hope as of yesterday that there might be some possibility for forward movement there."

2005's "Constantine" wasn't an out-and-out hit at the time of its release, but it's become something of a fan favorite over time. I previously noted that a "Constantine" legacy sequel would have mixed box office prospects, yet it might just work at the right price. It's simply a matter of whether or not the regime at Skydance, Warner Bros.' new parent company, sees this as a prudent investment. Reeves is currently a bigger star than he's ever been, while Lawrence, who has shepherded the "Hunger Games" movies for years, knows how to make a hit. We'll see how things shake out.

"Constantine 2" doesn't have a release date yet, but stay tuned.

#3420. There’s a Good Reason the NYC Marathon Winners Wore These Watches

Over 60,000 runners crossed the finish line at the New York City Marathon last week. When you think of the elites fighting for a spot on the podium, you might expect to see only the priciest, most feature-packed GPS watches money can buy—historically, this meant the most premium Garmin Forerunners. Looking at the wrists of this year's New York City Marathon podium finishers, though,  you’ll see that Garmin—the name most recreational runners reach for by default—was far from the only brand on the course.

Here are the watches I’ve been able to confirm among the top NYC Marathon finishers:

Men's winner, Andreas Almgren: Coros Pace 4 Pro (sponsored)

Men's runner-up, Yemaneberhan Crippa: Amazfit Cheetah 2 Pro (sponsored)

Women's runner-up, Jessica McClain: Garmin Forerunner 570 (sponsored)

Women's third place, Hellen Obiri: Coros Pace 4 (sponsored)

Nonbinary winner, Ryan Montgomery: Suunto Race 3S (almost certainly sponsored, since this watch was released last month)

An important disclaimer: I haven't spoken with any of these athletes. What follows is my opinion, based on what I know running watches offer the people who wear them.

"Garmin" has long been the default answer to "what running watch should I buy?" It earned that spot with reliable GPS, excellent software, and a huge ecosystem. And on this podium, it's represented by a Forerunner 570—a great watch, but at a price tag most runners would struggle to justify.

Of course, sponsorships muddy the water, since athletes wear what their sponsors put on their wrists. But that's exactly the point: Other brands are investing in elite runners because they believe their products can stand next to Garmin's, and it looks like they’re making the right bet.

It's fair to ask whether Garmin's grip is loosening. The company has increasingly pushed toward the fanciest watches with the most features at higher and higher price points. The Forerunner 570 starts north of $500. Meanwhile, COROS, Amazfit, and others are proving that a perfectly solid, competitive watch doesn't need to cost that much. Is Garmin still the best running watch overall? For ecosystem, polish, and depth of features, it's still a strong contender. But "best" no longer means "the only serious option," and the gap between Garmin and the field is narrower than it has been in years. Sponsored or not, seeing two Coros Pace 4s and an Amazfit Cheetah 2 Pro among the top finishers is worth noting.

You don’t need an expensive watch to be elite—just look at the cheap running watches worn by the men who broke the sub-two-hour barrier at the London Marathon this past spring. Training load scores, recovery metrics, maps, music, and smart notifications are nice, but they're extras. If you're shopping for a watch, spend your money on the basics being done right, and don't feel pressured to pay for features you'll never use. Everything besides your time and pace is icing on the cake.

Whichever brand you choose, focus on these basics in your running watch:

The New York City Marathon podium shows a running-watch market that's a bit more competitive and intriguing than the era of "just buy a Garmin" suggests. Garmin is still excellent, but now we’re seeing proof that Coros, Amazfit, and Suunto are all making watches good enough for the fastest humans on the planet. If they can trust those watches on their biggest days, the rest of us can probably trust them with our Saturday long runs.

#3419. Christian Bale Pushed To Play Batman Before Christopher Nolan's Reboot Was Announced

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

The Tim Burton "Batman" films introduced the wider public to a more gothic Batman, but they only scratch the surface of Batman's (Michael Keaton) own character. Conversely, the Joel Schumacher movies drowned in their attempts to recreate the campy 1960s "Batman" show, but both "Batman Forever" and "Batman and Robin" at least try to understand Bruce Wayne (Val Kilmer then George Clooney).

Christopher Nolan's still-beloved "Batman Begins" finally struck the balance, putting Batman (Christian Bale) in a darker movie and also creating a believable and compelling lead out of Bruce Wayne. In effect, "Batman Begins" perfects what "Batman Forever" tried. Since he starred in the most consistently good "Batman" movies, it's also little surprise Christian Bale is still considered one of the best Batman actors.

In 2005, during the "Batman Begins" press cycle, in an interview with Blackfilm, Bale said he had wanted to play Batman for a while. He'd claimed he even asked his agent to "keep [their] eyes out" for a Batman movie before it was announced Nolan was doing "Batman Begins." Bale continued:

"By the time I actually came to be cast I [had] kind of gotten so obsessed about it that, I kind of viewed it as it being mine already. It would've been more like...if they had told me like 'No, it's not yours,' I would've been like 'No way that's not working out, that's not going to happen.'"

Indeed, Bale wasn't Nolan's only choice for the role. Josh Hartnett turned it down, while Cillian Murphy's screen test got him cast as the Scarecrow instead. But considering Bale's determination, and talent (he'd recently cast off his child actor image with "American Psycho"), it's little surprise he got the part. What quality is more like Batman than refusing to accept defeat?

In the aforementioned Blackfilm interview, Bale claims he wasn't a Batman fan from childhood, but reading some comics won him over. He specifically listed Grant Morrison and Dave McKean's "Arkham Asylum," Frank Miller and David Mazzucchelli's "Batman: Year One," and Jeph Loeb and Tim Sale's "The Long Halloween" and "Dark Victory." He named those same four in a 2005 interview with Wizard Magazine, as well as Alex Ross' "War on Crime."

"I realized that [Batman] was a really great character, a dark severe character unlike anything that I had realized he [could] be before," Bale said to Blackfilm. Now, keep in mind, every actor who appears in a superhero movie says during the press cycle they read the comics and fell in love with the character. And, every time, I'm skeptical that it's more than just PR talking points (unless the actor's name is "Nicolas Cage" or "Iman Vellani").

The comics Bale named are all from the late 1980s through the 1990s, when "dark Batman" was becoming the norm and comic writers/artists were now considering the character a prestige assignment. To this day, those books remain some of the essential Batman stories recommended to new readers, in part because they can make you take Batman seriously.

Part of the sales pitch for "Batman Begins" was, coming off of the disastrous "Batman and Robin," that this Batman would be different. Naming comics the fans love as influences is a great way to get them on your side. Bale claiming he wasn't a Batman fan until reading those comics showed him the darker side of Batman, with the implicit promise "Batman Begins" would do the same for the moviegoing public, is even a compelling fan-friendly meta-narrative.

Where Christian Bale's claims about his comic reading have some substance is that those books do influence "Batman Begins." As an origin story, the movie takes the most from "Year One." Like in that comic, "Batman Begins" features Bruce learning to be Batman through trial and error, as well as forming an alliance with Detective Jim Gordon (Gary Oldman). "Begins" also includes mob boss Carmine Falcone (Tom Wilkinson), who was introduced in "Year One."

"Batman Begins" isn't outright horror like "Arkham Asylum" is, but many scenes do have a genuinely scary and intense atmosphere because of the League of Shadows' fear toxin. In turn, "The Dark Knight" takes after "The Long Halloween," having Batman, Gordon, and District Attorney Harvey Dent (Aaron Eckhart) form a triumvirate to take down the Gotham mob.

Christopher Nolan, for his part, cited 1989 comic "The Man Who Falls" by Dennis O'Neil and Dick Giordano, which tells Bruce Wayne's life from childhood to crime fighting. "Batman Begins" has a similar scope of time. During the 1970s, O'Neil (who wrote novelizations of both "Batman Begins" and "The Dark Knight") had pushed Batman in a darker direction alongside artist Neal Adams. The pair notably created the villain Ra's al Ghul, who appears in "Batman Begins" (played by Liam Neeson) as Bruce's mentor and the twist villain. A scene of Bruce and Ra's sword-fighting mirrors their duel in O'Neil and Adams' "Batman" #244.

The O'Neil/Adams Batman stories were also a stylistic influence on "Batman: The Animated Series." In turn, "Batman Begins" lifted one of its plot points from that show's episode "Dreams in Darkness," where the Scarecrow tries to poison Gotham's water supply. The people who made "Batman Begins" respected the character and that respect shows onscreen.
