#3401. Hackers Now Want Your Browser Sessions More Than Your Passwords, but You Can Stop Them

There’s a very organized dark web supply chain that attackers use to trade in stealer logs. Russian Market has effectively replaced Genesis Market as the new storefront for black hat cybercriminals, although much of the market has also shifted to private channels on Telegram.

According to threat analysts at DarkOwl, approximately 180,000 stealer logs were sold on Russian Market in just the first half of 2025. What's more, Russian Market is a well-designed storefront that users can access even without Onion links or the Tor browser. That means anyone could go there and buy a bunch of stealer logs to start attempting account takeovers at scale.

Meanwhile, Flare Research estimates that this isn’t even close to the actual scale of the threat, because 90% of stealer logs now surface privately on Telegram. There, automated chatbots let scammers shop for stealer logs like it’s Amazon, with options to filter by country, app, and account privilege. Logs sell for anywhere between $5 and $500 a piece, depending on the estimated value of the target accounts.

The easiest way to go about this is to take a look through all your active devices and their locations in your account settings on most websites. If you see a device or location you don’t recognize, you are likely the subject of an ongoing breach. However, keep in mind that this may not always be a reliable method if you use iCloud Private Relay or a VPN. Still, it's generally best practice to log out of all active sessions every once in a while and perform a fresh login to invalidate any unauthorized sessions.

Reset the passwords on your email account, enable two-factor authentication for added protection, and sign out of all sessions before doing a fresh login. Your email inbox is the single point of entry for most attacks because that’s where most websites send their verification codes or magic links.

Sign out of all active sessions on every account that you suspect is compromised. This will log out any attackers who are currently on a hijacked browsing session.

Change your passwords on every platform in order of priority. Start with banking websites, cloud storage providers, and password managers first.

Look through each compromised account’s third-party integrations and app permissions. Revoke access if you can’t recognize an app, or it looks suspicious. Also make sure to rotate any API keys that you’re currently using, since those may have been compromised as well.

But while the initiative has already been open-sourced, no other major online provider has begun offering native support for it as of this article. That means DBSC’s security benefits are limited to Google services like Gmail and Docs, Chrome for Windows, and third-party websites that offer single sign-on (SSO) options for your Google account. We might see a wider rollout in the near future, though.

#3400. Project Hail Mary's Animation Supervisor Explains The Huge Impact Of Rocky's Tiny Movements

It's been a great year for films, but few of them came close to captivating our hearts quite like "Project Hail Mary," one of the best movies of 2026. It's the rare movie that actually lives up to all its hype and warrants the superlatives. That's because the films delivers a rousing, thrilling, moving sci-fi story that's a celebration of the human spirit, friendship, science, and even the language of cinema as it transports us to unique worlds and introduces memorable creatures.

Indeed, few characters have captured the collective hearts of moviegoers this year quite like Rocky the alien, the surprisingly practical animatronic rock spider thing that's the best friend you could ever have. Rocky is adorable and funny, yet he's also very thoughtful and eats in a hilariously gross manner. And while Ryan Gosling is a great comedic actor on his own, pairing him as the space explorer Ryland Grace with Rocky results in pure comedy gold that simultaneously tugs at the heartstrings.

But it's not just Rocky's voice and dialogue that make the character so impactful. As Senior Animation Supervisor Arslan Elver told Art of VFX, it's Rocky's tinier movements that had the biggest effect on his ability to express emotions and thoughts.

"Because we are animating in CG, that gave us really subtle control like no other to move him around, sometimes very, very little," Elver explained. "In the scene where Rocky realizes Grace is on a one-way trip and Rocky eventually offers his fuel, this scene was a great testament to fine detail and how little movement can be so effective. A little look down or pull back of his carapace was telling a lot on a big screen when Rocky was acting."

As much as movie fans love to praise Andy Serkis' various motion-capture performances (which, don't get me wrong, they're fantastic), it's also worth remembering that it took many, many digital artists to turn his expressions and movements into actual CGI characters. After all, CGI is still art, and it not only has to look good but act as well.

In keeping with this, Arslan Elver told Art of VFX that a lot of visual effects work went into Rocky's performance in general, much of it taking direct inspiration from the original "Project Hail Mary" book by Andy Weir. "The famous word from the book, 'Question,' was another idiosyncrasy we brought on to his performance," Elver recalled. "Tapping with one leg was something we utilized across the show; even when he is hanging in the habitrail, that was his signature movement."

On top of making Rocky feel as alive as Grace, these moments speak to his arc in "Project Hail Mary." Earlier on in the film, for example, Rocky is weary of Grace. However, he quickly starts mocking the human and acting reckless, right up until he learns to trust Grace and care about him. In the end, the way Rocky reacts to things around him, be they new alien technology or concepts, helps to give the movie its heart and soul.

Likewise, Rocky's voice is the result of small but important choices, like puppeteer and voice actor James Ortiz deciding to replicate the imperfection in Rocky's hastily-built translation system in his performance. It's a small detail that's easy to miss, but knowing it was a conscious choice to have Rocky's voice sound kind of glitchy only makes him feel that much more real.

#3399. Desire, Death, and a Breakthrough Year for Queer Cinema

A willingness to die for sex is a familiar bargain for queer people. Born in the twentieth century at the wrong place and time? Beware of Nazis, AIDS, and other mortal dangers. Hollywood has at times depicted these threats in ways that emphasize the humanity of LGBTQ+ people, as when Tom Hanks played a lawyer dying of AIDS in “Philadelphia,” during the height of the epidemic in 1993. The industry also has a history of finding ever more creative ways to kill off and scapegoat queer characters, a trope that as recently as 10 years ago seemed to be running amok.

But a more twisted and nervy dance between desire and death has unfolded in this year’s spate of particularly macabre queer films. After years of what felt like permanent advances in rights and representation, LGBTQ+ people have been stung by backlash, including attacks on gender-affirming care, legal threats to marriage equality, and cuts to suicide prevention. Amid a reduced perception of safety, anxieties about the possibilities and consequences of nonnormative desire are spilling out onscreen like so much fake blood. Even so, their formulation is evidence of social and creative progress. Related Stories ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Review: They Shoot Franchises, Don’t They? ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ First Reactions: Quentin Tarantino and David Fincher Deliver a ‘Pure Riot’ of a Hangout Movie

This alarm has played out, perhaps most obviously, in horror films. In Adrian Chiarella’s “Leviticus” and Jane Schoenbrun’s “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma,” same-sex attraction engenders extreme and potentially deadly terror, be it from detractors or the people it consumes. Both films explore not the evils of queerness — an argument that belongs to the tradition of queer-coded villains — but the horrors of having one’s desires villainized.

The year’s queer history films also subvert conventional narratives around sexuality and deadly fates. In Andrew Scott’s awards-season vehicle “Elsinore,” Ian Charleson’s dying wish to play Hamlet is one many actors would share; the film doesn’t focus on how or why he has AIDS, but what he wants to do before it kills him. The Spanish epic “La Bola Negra” depicts forbidden romance, but desire isn’t what dooms its multiple generations of queer men. The fact that they’re swept up in the currents of history, just like everyone else, is part of the film’s revolutionary power.

The era for combatting the notion that being gay is a no good, very bad thing in a straightforward way finally seems to have passed. Usually such sermons were preaching to the choir anyway. Gone is the teary earnestness of a conversion therapy drama like “Boy Erased,” from 2018, in which much of the trauma wrought on Lucas Hedges’ character derives from the church but is carried out by earthly messengers. In “Leviticus,” when a healer tries to pray the gay away from a pair of lovesick adolescents, he conjures supernatural and murderous doppelgangers.

After rituals of deliverance are performed over the convulsing bodies of a pair of schoolmates (played by Joe Bird and Stacy Clausen), each one is haunted by an illusion of the other that tries to kill them. The concept of “Leviticus,” named for the Old Testament book that forbids man to lie with man, partly functions as a wry play on the idea that you never get over your first crush. It also takes the fear that so many queer people know well — that what you desire most will be your downfall — to literal and horrifying extremes. Imagining the bigotry of organized religion as a senselessly violent supernatural force is a radical reversal. The boys aren’t the problem; the boogeymen that torment them spring from the so-called good book.

Schoenbrun’s meta queer fantasia “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma” likewise performs a canonical revision. The nonbinary killer in the campy franchise within the film were themselves killed and sunk to the bottom of a lake by their comically gender-panicked peers. A victim seeking revenge, the TV-headed slasher is called Little Death, a nod to a French term for orgasm, la petite mort. Hannah Einbinder’s millennial filmmaker is on a quest to reboot the franchise, but more significantly, to achieve her own “little death.” In order to grow more comfortable with sex, and give into her own desires, her fear of intimacy — one that, again, many queer people know well — needs to be killed.

The movie ultimately intertwines fear of death with the fear of intimacy in a way that demonstrates the stakes — how you can feel so afraid of getting close to someone you could just die. But what must be slaughtered in this case is fear itself — so that same-sex desire, which has so often been pathologized and villainized, can flourish. (The trail of straight people extravagantly dispatched along the way, like so many gays before them, is one of the film’s many deranged and delightful flourishes.)

There is a potent realignment evident in the year’s period films as well, which center the desires and fates of queer characters on their own terms, rather than taking their oppression or disease as subjects unto themselves. “Elsinore” leans a bit heavily on obvious sentiment while leaving much of the thematic richness of “Hamlet” on the table. But Charleson’s determination to play the part before he dies is what drives the film, while the indignities of succumbing to AIDS are mostly a secondary plot.

Contrast that with recent period dramas on TV, like “It’s a Sin” (2021) about young people facing the AIDS crisis in London, or “Fellow Travelers” (2023) about the Lavender Scare in the U.S., and focusing on Charleson’s dream itself rather than the injustice of what threatens it marks a distinct shift.

The broad sweep of the canvas in “La Bola Negra” heralds another major turn of the page. The play of the same name by Federico García Lorca that partly inspires the movie, and appears in one of its several timelines, is about a young man denied access to an elite social club because he’s presumed to be gay. But homophobia isn’t the primary struggle (or a harbinger of death) for the film’s other gay characters. It certainly doesn’t help two doe-eyed young men (played by Miguel Bernardeau and Guitarricadelafuente) brought together and kept apart by the Spanish Civil War. But the forbiddenness of their infatuation is just one current swirling around them, the most pressing of which is, well, the Spanish Civil War.

Weaving the fates of queer characters into the broader scope of history, and suggesting a lineage of ancestry and shared desire, as “La Bola Negra” so marvelously does, feels like a kind of imaginative reparations. And it marks a bolder, more robust tactic in humanizing queer lives; the film traces generational ties and uncovers untold histories, rather than contending with acute crises like religious doctrine or deadly disease.

There is a stranger and more expansive creative palette evidenced in these films, one that suggests the unnerving climate for queer people in the real world is only furthering the reaches of the imagination. In carrying forward the legacy of queer cinema, it seems the gays presumed buried by the trope are finally rising up.

The entire Hisense U8 lineup is currently discounted ahead of Black Friday, with prices starting at $797.96 for the 55-inch model (down from $1,424.99) and going up to $2,798.99 for the massive 100-inch version (originally $3,999.99). The discounts also extend to the 65-, 75-, and 85-inch models, with savings of up to $1,200 across the lineup. Regardless of which size you choose, Amazon throws in free delivery to the room of your choice, a service that normally costs $19.99.

Brightness is the U8QG’s main advantage, with the manufacturer estimating up to 5,000 nits of peak brightness, while PCMag measured around 3,200 nits when reviewing the 65-inch model. Actual performance will vary with the picture mode and content, but either figure points to strong highlights in Dolby Vision and HDR10 video. Its Mini-LED local dimming also produces deep blacks, although some light bloom can appear around bright objects on dark backgrounds. Audio-wise, its built-in 4.1.2-channel system, which includes surround channels, a subwoofer, and upward-firing speakers, gives movies more scale than typical TV speakers, though a separate sound system can still offer clearer separation and a broader soundstage.

The U8QG also has plenty to offer gamers using a current-generation console or a capable gaming PC. It supports refresh rates up to 165Hz, variable refresh rate, and AMD FreeSync Premium Pro, with a measured 4.3 milliseconds of input lag at 1080p and 120Hz and 10.1 milliseconds at 4K and 60Hz. Those results should make controls feel responsive, even during fast-paced games. There’s also a side-mounted USB-C port that accepts DisplayPort video, while Google TV handles streaming alongside Apple AirPlay and Google Cast. The biggest inconvenience is the limited selection of three HDMI ports, since a console, soundbar, and streaming device would occupy all of them.

Yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, and we vet our deals to make sure they’re the best ones. You can also refer to guides like our live blog that have already done all of the vetting for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

#3397. 5 Actors Who Should Play Villains In Robert Pattinson's James Bond Movies

Now that we know Robert Pattinson is set to play James Bond for director Denis Villeneuve and Amazon MGM Studios, it's time to start casting the supporting characters: M, Q, Moneypenny, Felix Leiter, and so on. Then there's the question of 007's love interests and, most importantly, the villains. Because you can't make a great Bond movie without a memorable baddie.

It's important to remember that casting isn't everything. Christopher Waltz was a slam-dunk choice as Blofeld in "Spectre," but the film's script fumbled its portrayal of the character, and it wasn't his fault that Bond's arch-nemesis came off as disappointingly banal. Hopefully, Villeneuve and his group of writers (fare thee well, Neal Purvis and Robert Wade) can craft villains who present a threat that is relevant to the times in which we live. This will prove very difficult, as I'll explain later, but in the meantime, we can throw out some actors who'd make deliciously malevolent Bond villains.

But first, I need to issue a vehement ditto to my /Film colleague Nina Starner's suggestion that Pattinson's former "Twilight" co-star Kristen Stewart should absolutely be a Bond villain. I also think Florence Pugh would be dynamite as an aggressively sexual nemesis à la Famke Janssen's Xenia Onatopp in "GoldenEye." (Pugh, as you may note, was similarly one of our picks for the next Bond Girl.) Beyond that, here are five other actors I'd love to see give Bond the business. And you better believe I'm serious about the fifth name on this list.

It would be a nifty bit of symmetry if Russell Crowe, who will be seen next year in Chad Stahelski's "Highlander" reboot as Juan Sánchez-Villalobos Ramírez (a character originated by Sean Connery), could get a shot at being a Bond villain. It would also be killer casting because Crowe, at the age of 62, has acquired a burly gravitas that demands rapt attention whenever he steps in front of the camera. Bond's nemeses have typically been debonair types who travel in rarefied air and leave the skull-cracking to their henchmen.

There's an opportunity here with Robert Pattinson, who's a bruiser when he's in a Batsuit but survives on his wits (when his character has them) outside of the armor. Pit him against Crowe, who can outmuscle and outsmart all comers, and you've got a main adversary the likes of which Bond has never faced. Crowe could be the brainy version of Robert Shaw's Donald Grant from "From Russia with Love." He could use his wits to knock Bond off his game and engage him in the kind of brawl 007 can't win. And above all, watching Crowe devouring the scenery as a brilliant bully would be a treat. Crowe hasn't lost his fastball. Let him fire away.

It's going to happen for David Dastmalchian (in a bigger way than it already has). It's just a matter of how. He's equally adept at broad comedy ("Ant-Man and the Wasp") and soul-swallowing horror ("Late Night with the Devil"), but what he really needs is a character who combines these qualities. The Bond universe offers him the opportunity to amuse and horrify us. If you could rewrite Jeroen Krabbé's General Georgi Koskov from "The Living Daylights" to be a more adept operator, Dastmalchian would smash that role.

Denis Villeneuve is clearly a Dastmalchian fan. The director cast the actor as the treacherous Piter De Vries, who sets in motion the downfall of the Atreides clan, in his film adaptation of "Dune." He also cast Dastmalchian in "Blade Runner 2049" as chief medical examiner Coco (who gets his head crushed by Sylvia Hoeks' Luv). The man is a chameleon. He's slippery and very much not the type of guy who's going to get typecast. So, Villeneuve could write Dastmalchian a far-out villain, and he'd deliver with interest — and this would be a delight if Robert Pattinson is allowed to play Bond as a slightly off-kilter guy as well. And if you're thinking Dastamalchian isn't a big enough player to play a Bond baddie, please note that Mads Mikkelsen and Mathieu Almaric weren't exactly household names when they appeared in "Casino Royale" and "Quantum of Solace."

When Daniel Craig was nearing the end of his run as James Bond, people floated the idea of the franchise casting a woman as 007 for the first time. One of the most popular names when this topic came up was Rachel Weisz, which would've been amusing, given that she's married to Craig. Weisz shot this idea down in 2018, saying, "[Ian Fleming] devoted an awful lot of time to writing this particular character, who is particularly male and relates in a particular way to women. Why not create your own story rather than jumping on to the shoulders and being compared to all those other male predecessors? Women are really fascinating and interesting and should get their own stories." I agree, but would she consider entering the Bond universe as a villain?

Aside from Famke Janssen, other actors have played memorable female Bond antagonists, like Lotte Lenya's Rosa Klebb in "From Russia with Love" and Grace Jones' May Day in "A View to a Kill." Weisz has certainly flaunted her action chops in movies like "The Mummy," and she was icily effective as the manipulative Sarah Churchill in "The Favourite." She'd give Bond all he could handle and then some as a villain, one who, perhaps, is not only impervious to his charms but holds his womanizing in contempt. It all depends on whether or not Weisz is keen on making the Bond films a family affair.

Miles Teller is a legitimate leading man himself, but I think there's a load of untapped potential in his ability to play cocky, impulsive jerks. His characters are typically redeemable, but playing opposite Robert Pattinson as a hot-headed arms dealer (a riff on his character from "War Dogs") who foments bloody conflict in poor nations would set off some thespian fireworks. Just imagine these two brashly confident actors trying to outdo each other. We could see some of the best performances in a Bond movie since Daniel Craig went head-to-head with Javier Bardem in "Skyfall."

The only hurdle here is that Teller might consider himself too big of a star to play second fiddle to Pattinson. Then again, in 2026, he's co-starred as Michael Jackson's lawyer in "Michael" and received third billing under Adam Driver and Scarlett Johansson in "Paper Tiger." His ego seems to be in check at the moment. Let's get this done!

Is there a more likable actor on the planet than Paul Rudd? It's not just that he excels at playing nice guys in the movies, he's also an absolute mensch in real life. I've never heard a word against the man, which, to my mind, would make him a brilliantly unexpected choice as a Bond villain.

I'm not asking Rudd to go way out of character here. Ideally, he'd play a nefarious tech billionaire who's charmed the pants off the media and world leaders. He's Paul Rudd! People say he's up to no good, but how could this guy who's so peppy and fun be hellbent on world domination — and even if he was, would that be so bad? He's no Elon Musk, at least not on the outside. He's basically an affable Andrew Carnegie or John D. Rockefeller who self-promotes with telegenic ease. But his good deeds are all a cover for his sinister plan to create a globally unified white society. And because he was born without a moral compass, he doesn't see anything wrong with this.

On top of all that, this would be a real challenge for Bond, as he can't get the British government and MI6 to infiltrate Rudd's organization because he supports them politically. Done right, this could be Denis Villeneuve's opportunity to make a, gasp, funny movie. The only hurdle is that the film will be bankrolled by tech mogul Jeff Bezos' Amazon MGM Studios. Ergo, this is totally a pipe dream.

There are a few things you can do to make sure your packages don’t get stolen

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Porch piracy is still a major problem. 30% of American adults have had a package stolen at some point in their lives, and 49% worry more about package theft during the holidays than at other times of year, according to Security.org’s 2026 Package Theft Report. The report estimates that 47.7 million people had a package stolen in the past year, and that the stolen packages were worth $7.7 billion. And with the average adult expecting 28 deliveries between October and December, there’s simply plenty more opportunity for boxes to sit unattended.

Of course, there are things you can and should do to keep your packages safe. The best protections stop a theft before the package lands, either by arranging a verified hand-off, shortening the time a box spends outside, or sending it somewhere secure. Here are some practical ways to protect your packages from porch pirates this holiday season.

If you're looking for a deal on a video doorbell this Black Friday, the crystal-clear 2K video on Arlo's option helps you keep an eye out for holiday deliveries and feel connected to your home, even when you're away. Arlo Chime 2 offers convenient in-home audio notifications, while the Arlo Secure App provides real-time, personalized notifications and the ability to see and talk with visitors on your doorstep.

The strongest option for an expensive order is probably to require a verified hand-off. UPS Protected Delivery, which launches Nov. 16, requires the recipient to give the driver a PIN, or numeric code, before an eligible package is released. FedEx Authenticated Delivery uses a unique QR code instead. Both of these services are a little limited in how and where you can use them, and they may cost more too. The shipper, not the recipient, has to select either one, so ask the retailer before you order.

For everything else, the carrier’s tracking app is the first line of defense. Turn on notifications from Amazon, UPS, FedEx and USPS, and act on the “out for delivery” message rather than waiting for “delivered.”

Security.org identifies delivery alerts as a popular prevention method, with 39% of shoppers using delivery notifications or tracking apps. An alert alone won’t protect a box, but it at least gives you a notification you can act on relatively quickly.

“The goal shouldn’t be watching your front door all day,” says Ken Sedberry, director of Xfinity Shield. “It should be knowing when a package arrives and having a plan to bring it inside.”

Amazon’s scheduling tools can shorten that exposure further. Map Tracking shows the driver’s live position on eligible deliveries, while estimated two- to four-hour delivery windows give you something more useful than an all-day estimate. Prime members can also use Amazon Day to batch orders onto one day each week when someone is home. Security.org found that 43% of shoppers schedule deliveries for when someone will be there.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Photo on Delivery adds a record of where the driver left the package, which is especially helpful if it ended up behind a planter or at a side entrance. It doesn’t prove the package stayed there, though.

For valuable shipments, a traditional signature requirement is still worth requesting if the newer verification services aren’t available. The sender usually has to add it, and fees vary by carrier and service.

The best way to secure where packages are left is to not leave them there in the first place. That may sound silly, but there are actually a few different ways you can prevent packages from being left alone on your doorstep. Amazon Locker and Counter are free alternatives, and they’re part of a network of more than 25,000 pickup locations across the country.

“For those receiving a high volume of deliveries, especially during the holidays, giving carriers a secure place to leave packages is much more effective than simply hoping a camera discourages someone from taking them,” says Rod Sides, founder of Loxx Boxx, which makes package lockboxes.

Lockers give you three calendar days to collect a package, and size or item restrictions mean not every order qualifies. Staffed Counters at retailers offer another option if you’d rather collect from a person.

Carriers like UPS and FedEx have their own pickup locations too. UPS Access Point locations hold packages for up to seven days at no charge, although redirecting an in-flight package costs $5.99 for free Basic My Choice members. Premium, at $19.99 a year, includes it. FedEx Hold at Location keeps packages for up to seven days at FedEx Office and FedEx facilities, but FedEx says to pick up within five business days at participating retailers such as Walgreens and Dollar General. Redirecting to a retail location is free.

USPS offers free Hold for Pickup through Delivery Instructions, along with free Hold Mail for three to 30 days when you’re away. Its Smart Lockers in Post Office lobbies provide another free option with a five-day collection window. Hold windows and redirect fees change periodically, so confirm them in the carrier’s app before rerouting a valuable order.

Home parcel boxes are more convenient, but they depend on driver cooperation. Some allow you to lock packages behind a four-digit PIN — but a driver rushing through deliveries in a busy season may not take the time to do that, or may not see the request in the first place.

If you do go the route of using a drop box, it's worth anchoring it properly. An empty, lightweight lockbox can be carried away and opened elsewhere, so bolt it down or weight it properly. Then make it as hidden from the street as you can. Delivery instructions should name an exact hiding place rather than simply saying “front door.” Something like “inside the parcel box behind the side gate” gives the driver a workable instruction. It still isn’t a guarantee, and some carrier menus offer limited space for custom directions.

Some of the best home security cameras and video doorbells can help deter porch pirates as well. A battery-powered video doorbell is a pretty reasonable entry-level option. Look for higher-resolution 2K video, a wide-angle view, person and package alerts, and a choice of battery or wired power.

Prices tend to drop during holiday sales, but keep in mind that the hardware price is only part of the cost. Cloud recording, which saves clips to the manufacturer’s servers rather than in your home, typically requires a subscription.

Person and package detection makes these devices much easier to live with. AI, in this context, mostly means pattern-recognition software that distinguishes people and packages from other movement. It reduces alerts caused by passing cars, animals or swaying branches. It can make a pretty big difference.

“Delivery drivers often drop a package without ringing the bell, but a motion alert lets you know the moment someone is at your door, often before the carrier’s delivery email arrives, so you don’t have to keep watching the front door,” says Veronica Moturi, senior vice president and chief customer officer at Brinks Home.

It's worth keeping in mind the fact that cameras don't always deter theft and often document it more than prevent it. Pairing one with motion-activated lighting and a camera monitoring sign can help with the deterrence, though.

Lighting deserves special attention during the winter, when many deliveries arrive after dark. A lit entrance helps drivers find the right drop spot and removes some of the cover a thief would prefer.

“Look for a camera with clear night vision, since shorter days mean more deliveries and holiday visits happen after dark,” says Moturi.

Apartment residents have a lot more reason to plan ahead. Security.org found that 10% of apartment dwellers had a package stolen in the previous three months, compared with 3% of single-family home residents. That’s more than three times as likely. Shared lobbies, dense delivery traffic and long periods with nobody watching the entrance all create opportunities.

If your apartment building offers some kind of locked package room or front desk, it may be worth having packages left there rather than in front of your door. If you don't, there's no harm in requesting one from building management — and if there have been thefts, a request from multiple tenants could carry more weight.

Renting also makes it harder to mount security cameras and smart doorbells. Thankfully, there are plenty of battery-operated ones that don't require drilling or changing wiring, so if you are renting and want something like that, they are available.

If you do fall victim to a porch pirate, there are a few things to do. Start by verifying that the package is actually missing. Check the tracking status and delivery photo, then ask household members, neighbors or the doorman whether they collected it. Look around side entrances and other plausible drop spots. Sometimes, you might find that it wasn't stolen at all.

If you still can't find it, it's worth contacting the retailer promptly with the order number, tracking details, delivery date and any photos or footage you have. That’s usually the fastest route to a replacement before a holiday.

Amazon often asks customers to wait about 48 hours after a package is marked delivered and to file a missing-package claim within 30 days of the delivery date, but policies differ for third-party sellers and other retailers. Refunds and replacements are common, not guaranteed.

File a police report even if the retailer refunds you or sends a replacement. Only 23% of recent victims in Security.org’s survey reported their most recent theft to police. Those reports really help departments identify repeat locations, spot organized activity and decide where to assign patrols.

Purchase protection through a card such as American Express may cover eligible items for 90 days after purchase, and Amex asks for notice of a claim within 30 days of the loss or as soon as reasonably possible. Terms vary, so you’ll want to check your benefits before relying on them.

Gene Petrino, a former SWAT commander and police sergeant, offers the simplest summary of the whole problem. “Thieves can’t steal what they can’t see.”

Concealment matters, but removing the package from public view altogether is better. No single gadget covers every delivery, and paid verification won’t be available for every order. The best plan to protect your packages is to combine methods. Do what you can to prevent them from being left alone in the first place, use carrier alerts to get your packages to safety quickly, and use security cameras as a deterrent or to monitor anything that does get stolen.

#3395. David Carradine's '80s Sci-Fi Flop Is A Must-Watch For Monster Lovers

The phases of David Carradine's career vary wildly. After starting out in the short-lived '60s Western series "Shane," Carradine found fame in the 1970s by playing Shaolin monk Kwai Chang Caine in the TV series "Kung Fu." By the 1980s, he was mostly appearing in B-movies and exploitation flicks. Some of these were great. In 1983, Carradine faced off against action legend Chuck Norris in the forgotten neo-Western "Lone Wolf McQuade" (in which Norris played the lone wolf lawman who literally had a pet wolf). Then, there's "Q" or "Q – The Winged Serpent." This monster movie debuted the year prior to "Lone Wolf McQuade" and saw Carradine tangle not with a hirsute muscle man but with a giant serpent that has ensconced itself at the top of New York City's Chrysler Building.

The first clue as to what sort of tone this movie strikes, beyond the premise of a giant reptile plucking its prey from the rooftops of New York City, is the fact it's written by Larry Cohen. The B-movie legend started out in TV, working for NBC and writing for several series before creating "The Invaders." He then penned several Blaxploitation flicks before becoming known as a prolific writer of sci-fi horror movies.

Cohen is responsible for such cult classics as "It's Alive" and "Maniac Cop." Between those two movies, sits "Q," which was yet another ambitious vision realized on a relatively a small budget with impressive (for the time) results. Unfortunately, the film made very little at the box office, but like so many Cohen movies, has since become a cult favorite among monster movie enthusiasts. Carradine fans may also have missed this one, which is well worth a watch.

"Q" is written, co-produced and directed by Larry Cohen, and represents the first of many collaborations between he and actor Michael Moriarty. In the film, Moriarty plays petty crook Jimmy Quinn, who harbors dreams of being a jazz pianist. But his hopes of going on the straight and narrow are put on hold when, after a diamond heist, Quinn hides out in the spire of the Chrysler Building. Bad idea — or, if you happen to be a small-time swindler, great idea.

Turns out the winged reptilian Aztec god Quetzalcoatl has turned the inside of that same spire into his nest, from which he frequently descends to snack on unsuspecting New Yorkers. Quinn decides to use his knowledge of the creature's hideout for a payday and promises to take the police, lead by Detective Shepard (David Carradine) and Sergeant Powell (Richard Roundtree), to the lair in exchange for $1 million. Meanwhile, somebody is committing ritual murders around the city, and it turns out these killings and the giant flying reptile are linked.

The film ends with a dramatic showdown, wherein Detective Shepherd leads his men to the top of the Chrysler Building to shoot sub machine guns at Quetzalcoatl as it flies around the spire. Like much of the movie, many of the shots in this ending sequence were filmed on-location. Today, it's sort of jarring to see dodgy VFX shots interspersed with the real-world footage, but it's also incredibly charming and way better than most of the streaming slop being served up in the modern age. I would say "Q — The Winged Serpent" is a classic horror movie flop that deserves a modern remake, but it's also just great as it is.

According to Larry Cohen's "Q — The Winged Serpent" commentary track (via Film School Rejects), he tried to get access to The Chrysler Building but was turned away multiple times. Eventually, the production company offered the building management $15,000 and they gave Cohen access. That means much of the film was shot in and around the building itself, which alongside many other scenes shot around the city, makes the film yet another Cohen project that acts as somewhat of a time capsule of '80s New York.

Meanwhile, the monster effects were created using stop motion by Randall William Cook (who later worked on the 2005 "King Kong" and the "Lord of the Rings" films) and David Allen (who worked on several more high-profile projects including "Willow" and "Honey, I Shrunk the Kids"). As for Cohen and David Carradine, it turns out the former served with Carradine in the Army, and thought of his old buddy when casting "Q." In fact, prior to the movie, Carradine guest starred on the "CBS" series "Coronet Blue," created by Cohen. The winged serpent movie was their only big-screen collaboration.

Sadly, that collaboration only made $255,000 on a $1.1 million budget. But it has built a solid cult following and remains a great '80s monster B-movie. It also clearly meant a lot to Cohen, who passed away in 2019. In 2004, he spoke to The New Yorker's Amy Wallace who accompanied him on a tour of the city. When he came to the Chrysler Building he told her, "Look at that. Every time I look up at that building, I feel it belongs to me." "Q" can be seen for free on one of the best streaming services, Tubi.

#3394. Aura's Second E-Ink Picture Frame Is Much Improved, and Much Cheaper

Last year, Aura released the Aura Ink, its first digital photo frame using an e-ink display rather than the LCD screens common to the other devices that made them the major player in the market (Aura customers have already uploaded more than one billion photos this year alone). When I reviewed the original 13-inch Aura Ink last year, I recommended it, with a few major reservations. Today, Aura announced its second-generation 10-inch Ink frame, and while I wouldn't exactly say they've solved every one of my issues, the new device is significantly improved—and much cheaper.

Most digital photo frames will remind you of an iPad with a decorative border around it. They're great for displaying hundreds of your photos with vibrant color, but not everyone loves the look, or the fact that these frames always need to be plugged in. An e-ink frame, on the other hand, uses a variant of the sort of low-power screen you'd find in a Kindle Colorsoft—less bright, but more paperlike, and much closer to the look of a traditionally printed photo.The Aura Ink is a great choice if you want a digital frame that looks more like a "real" photo and doesn't need to be plugged in and doesn't light up like a tablet (though it does have a light, it's really to make up for the fact that color e-ink screens don't reflect light very well, and thus can make your pictures look way too dark without an additional boost). You'll still get all the benefits of an LCD frame like the Aura Aspen, including the ability to load photos from anywhere using the versatile Aura app (you can now even text them directly to the frame), but you'll only need to charge it once every few months.

Now for the downsides: Where most digital frames allow you to flick between photos with a swipe, the Aura Ink is much more sluggish—switching from one photo to another takes about 45 seconds. While an LCD can match the colors in your photo exactly, e-ink uses a "dithering algorithm" to blend tiny pixels together to create the illusion of different hues ("millions" of them, according to Aura). In practice, this means up close, your pictures will look rather grainy, and the colors won't be nearly as bright as what you see on your phone screen.

All of that said, the Aura Ink is a great product, provided you know what you're buying, and the new 10-inch model offers some big upgrades over the 13-inch original released in 2025:

Resolution has been bumped up from 150 ppi to 200 ppi, so your images look more detailed and less grainy. (Though the difference is hard to capture in a photo, I can definitely see the improvement when comparing them side-by-side.)

Instead of the six base colors available on the older frame, the 10-inch Aura Ink blends nine different hues to approximate the colors in your images, offering greater color accuracy and improved contrast.

The transition effect when you move between photos has been updated to look more intentional—like waves of color moving across the screen versus a series of increasingly intense flashes.

It's a heck of a lot cheaper: $349, versus $499 for the 13-inch model—though that's still significantly pricier than Aura's most popular offering, the 10.1-inch Aura Carver, which starts around $200 less.

I write a lot about e-ink devices, from e-readers to tablets, and my common refrain, especially with color devices, is that they're great at what they do, but you should understand what they do before you plunk down your money. The Aura Ink will never look as bright and colorful as an LCD frame, and if you want a frame that can switch between images every few minutes or even play video, you'll need to look elsewhere (to maximize battery life, Aura recommends swapping photos on the Aura Ink no more than 12 times per day).

But if you want to display photos that look more like the ones that hung on the walls of your childhood home, in a frame that doesn't need to be plugged in all the time, you'll probably dig it, provided you can stomach the $350 price tag.

#3393. Movie Theaters Are Back, but the Rest of Hollywood Seems to Be Crumbling

Movie theater owners have been through hell.

The pandemic forced many of them to shut their doors for months. When they could finally turn their marquees back on, Omicron and other variants made audiences skittish about returning to cinemas. Then the writers’ and actors’ strikes upended production, leaving them with fewer movies to screen. A promised moviegoing revival kept getting delayed or disrupted, often by circumstances outside of the exhibition industry’s control.

At long last, things are finally changing. Domestic ticket sales are up 20 percent year over year, and with potential blockbusters like “Dune: Part Three,” “Avengers: Doomsday,” and “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” on the horizon, analysts expect revenues to easily eclipse $10 billion for the first time since COVID. Grosses in North America currently sit at $8.76 billion through November 15, fueled by franchise fare such as “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” and “Toy Story 5,” but also by unconventional hits ranging from “Project Hail Mary” and “The Odyssey” to “Obsession” and “You Can See Everything.” Related Stories Desire, Death, and a Breakthrough Year for Queer Cinema ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Review: They Shoot Franchises, Don’t They?

Audiences are showing up for superhero movies and three-hour documentaries about a convicted felon. And media companies, which treated the theatrical business as the sick man of the entertainment industry, are finally seeing the value in cinemas, with the likes of Amazon MGM Studios and Skydance committing to making more movies for the big screen than most major studios did over the last decade. Better yet, younger viewers are driving the comeback, with studies showing that Gen Z members are the most frequent moviegoers.

That’s the good news. Elsewhere, Hollywood seems to be crumbling. Netflix, which has done more to reshape the entertainment industry this century than arguably any other company, is teetering, having jettisoned both chief content officer Bela Bajaria and film chief Dan Lin in a brutal purge. Ted Sarandos, who is clearly feeling the heat after the company’s stock has fallen 35.6 percent year-to-date, has brought in Peter Rice, a well-regarded former Fox and Disney exec whose calm demeanor and unthreatening good looks are out of c-suite central casting, to steady the ship.

As Hollywood has stumbled around trying to develop a better business model, the solution that many companies have landed on is to get bigger, fast. Thus, Fox sold to Disney, MGM was auctioned off to Amazon, and David Ellison’s Skydance bought Paramount and then quickly merged it with Warner Bros. Others, such as Comcast, spun off assets to make themselves more digestible. Has it worked? That’s the $80 billion question at Skydance, where executives have pledged to make 30 movies a year and turn a combined Paramount+ and HBOMax into a true Netflix challenger. Yet Ellison must pull this off while paying down a massive amount of debt.

So far, their early moves haven’t inspired much confidence. Executives like CBS News chief Bari Weiss have embraced the Silicon Valley ethos of “move fast and break things,” but what they’ve built instead, such as a simulacrum of “60 Minutes,” doesn’t seem better than what they’ve replaced. And if, as a recent Variety story about Skydance’s post-merger strategy suggests, part of their cost savings involves making sure executives don’t send out for “sandwiches and green juices” from Erewhon, they’re in for a world of pain. They can have Jimmy John’s cater lunch, and it won’t make a dent in their debt.

Skydance has already laid off most of Warners’ leadership and offered buyouts to the rank-and-file. Another wave of layoffs is expected at the company any day now. And across town, those types of cuts are the default move, with everyone from Disney and NBCUniversal to Amazon and Sony slashing hundreds of jobs. Are some of these layoffs in anticipation of what a leaner, AI-assisted future might bring? Probably. But with many of these companies’ share prices flatlining or falling, they aren’t being enacted out of foresight or a position of strength.

“I can’t remember a time when things have felt so scary,” an entertainment executive confessed to me recently.

And they’re right. It’s always popular to say the movie business is dying or the television industry is collapsing, and those doomsayers have been proven wrong time and time again. People want to be entertained. It’s just that making money entertaining them has never been harder for Hollywood.

#3391. Skydance Sets Film Leadership Team: Don Granger and Kira Goldberg to Head Paramount Motion Picture Group, Jesse Ehrman Promoted to WB Pictures Chief

Skydance has set its film leadership team.

Don Granger, a veteran Skydance executive, and Kira Goldberg, a leader of Netflix’s film team, have been tapped as presidents of Paramount‘s Motion Picture Group.

As part of the moves, Jesse Ehrman has been promoted to president of Warner Bros. Pictures, while Mikey Ireland will remain as president of production. Their task will be to stabilize Warner Bros.‘ film output while rejuvenating or extending franchises like “The Lord of the Rings” and “The Conjuring.” Skydance executives have been horrified by the extent of the losses racked up by Pam Abdy and Michael De Luca, with sources estimating them in the hundreds of millions of dollars. David Ellison, who orchestrated Warner Bros.’ merger with Paramount, was more diplomatic on a recent earnings call, though he said the WB film division has “underperformed this year.” Related Stories ‘Madden’ Review: David O. Russell Fumbles Again with an Unfunny and Purposeless Football Biopic Movie Theaters Are Back, but the Rest of Hollywood Seems to Be Crumbling

As part of this restructuring, Jeff Goldstein, who oversaw Warner Bros. distribution for many years, will retire, and Bill Damaschke will exit Warner Bros. Pictures Animation, which he led. Skydance said that in the interim, Jennifer Dodge and Traci Balthazor will oversee all animation across both Paramount and Warner Bros. Pictures. Richard Brener, a survivor of several mergers, will remain as president and chief content officer of New Line, where he guided hits like “Weapons.”

Others remaining include: Lia Buman, EVP, head of global acquisitions and Republic Pictures; J.D. Lifshitz and Raphael Margules, heads of the genre division, Paramount Primal; and Christian Parkes, head of the indie label Clockwork; and Charlie Tabesh, SVP and general manager of Turner Classic Movies.

Last week, Skydance announced that James Gunn and Peter Safran, who had led DC Studios, were leaving the company. Jeremy Latcham, a former Marvel executive, replaced them. It wasn’t the only overhaul at the top. Last month, as Skydance took full control of Warner Bros., Michael De Luca and Pamela Abdy were ousted. De Luca and Abdy were beloved by the creative community, but they spent liberally and accumulated too many flops, including “Digger” and “The Bride!”

Both Granger and Goldberg will report to Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein, the co-chairs of Skydance’s Motion Picture Group. Across Paramount and Warner Bros., the mandate will be to get more films into production. To get the merger over the finish line, Skydance founder David Ellison agreed to make more than 30 films annually, far exceeding the output of any traditional studio.

In a memo to staff, Goldberg and Greenstein praised Granger as “a great partner as we’ve repositioned the studio, bringing in key talent relationships and nearly doubling output.” They noted that at Netflix, Goldberg “oversaw a slate that included ‘Don’t Look Up,’ starring Leonardo DiCaprio and Jennifer Lawrence, and the upcoming ‘Bad Day,’ with Cameron Diaz, and ‘The Take’ starring Denzel Washington and Robert Pattinson. Goldberg was also an executive at Fox, working on films such as “The Greatest Showman” and “Bohemian Rhapsody.”

“Together, Don and Kira will work hand in hand going forward,” Goldberg and Greenstein wrote, adding, “We have both an incredible legacy to build upon and an enormous opportunity ahead of us: to champion the world’s best filmmakers, invest in ambitious storytelling and deliver an unparalleled slate of films that captivate audiences everywhere.”

Ehrman is a WB veteran who has worked on hits such as “A Minecraft Movie” and “Sinners.” Ireland joined Warner Bros. after years at Paramount. He left the studio after it was sold to Skydance in 2025.

“This team brings deep knowledge of our businesses, strong creative instincts and longstanding relationships across the industry,” Goldberg and Greenstein wrote. “We have tremendous confidence in these leaders and are grateful for their partnership.”

#3390. 8 Strongest Villains In The Lord Of The Rings & The Hobbit Movies, Ranked By Power (& Sauron Isn't #1)

J.R.R. Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings features some of the best villains in fantasy history. Modern fantasy often plays on humanized villains, ensuring we can empathize with the bad guy's motivation. Tolkien cared little for that; his grandest villain, Sauron, became the Dark Lord who set the pattern for every Dark Lord afterward. Smartly, though, so many of the other villains were tied to the corruptive power of the One Ring; it gave the story a wonderful thematic strength.

It's actually surprisingly difficult to rank the villains of The Lord of the Rings and The Hobbit. That's largely because there are so many different forms of "power" in this saga; physical strength, magical ability, military skill, and even political influence. Still, playing all those variables against one another, here are the eight most powerful villains of this saga.

Let's start with a character who possesses absolutely none of the traditional Tolkien powers: Grima Wormtongue. Saruman's agent, he became the "power behind the throne" for King Théoden; spinning a web of lies that ensnared the monarch and brought the entire kingdom of Rohan to the brink of destruction. It's easy to underestimate Grima, but he was a ruthless, manipulative man skilled in all the arts of manipulation. Words are his weapon, and he knows how to cut deep with them.

Interestingly, Peter Jackson's The Lord of the Rings weakens Wormtongue by suggesting he's drawing on Saruman's power. That's explicitly visible when Gandalf frees Théoden from the lies binding him, and Saruman himself experiences the backlash. Tolkien's books make Grima the mastermind in his own right, stressing how dangerous (and powerful) a manipulator he is.

Now let's move from political and manipulative power to something a little more physical: Gothmog, Sauron's senior military commander. The Orcs are far stronger than any human, and can endure a lot more punishment too. Given Orc society, we can assume he was considered one of the Orcs' greatest fighters, although we sadly never see him going up against powerful Elves like Legolos or Dwarves like Gimli.

Viewers tend to underestimate the Orcs, treating them as mindless brutes. But Gothmog's power is demonstrated by his military skills, and he is a proven master tactician. He recognizes that the capture of Minas Tirith requires more than brute force, and he adapts effectively. As formidable as the Orcs may be, they would be far less effective and dangerous without Gothmog.

The Witch-King of Angmar is probably the most powerful agent of Sauron, a mortal Man who received one of the Rings of Power and was corrupted by Sauron. He became the most dangerous of the Nazgûl, transforming him into a near-immortal spirit whose existence is tied to the One Ring. A powerful sorcerer, his very presence weakens the resolve of his opponents, and he inspires overwhelming fear in normal soldiers.

The Witch-King of Angmar is a skilled warrior, and he goes head-to-head with some of The Lord of the Rings' most skilled fighters. He is, however, not truly invincible; his eventual defeat proves there's a limit to his power and his endurance. The Witch-King remains one of Tolkien's most sophisticated villains—a blend of sorcerer, spirit, and monster—but he can be defeated.

Saruman is one of the most powerful wizards in The Lord of the Rings, an immortal Maia sent to Middle-earth by Eru (Tolkien's version of God). He's basically a fallen angel, and indeed was easily the most powerful of all the wizards until Gandalf too ascended to become a White. Aragorn gives a sense of Saruman's raw power in the books:

"Once he was as great as his fame made him. His knowledge was deep, his thought was subtle, and his hands marvelously skilled; and he had a power over the minds of others. The wise he could persuade, and the smaller folk he could daunt. That power he certainly still keeps. There are not many in Middle-earth that I should say were safe, if they were left alone to talk with him, even now when he has suffered a defeat. Gandalf, Elrond, and Galadriel, perhaps, now that his wickedness has been laid bare, but very few others."

As powerful as Saruman may be, though, note that Gandalf implies Saruman's corruption—his turn to wickedness—has diminished him. Although Saruman's ego would reject this idea, he is far less powerful than he was originally.

This next placement is actually pretty tricky, because the comparison between Saruman and the Balrog is somewhat imprecise. The Balrog is one of several Maiar who turned from the Valar and followed Morgoth, Sauron's own master. Little is known about the process by which a Maiar became a Balrog; it's unknown whether Morgoth turned all his Maiar into them, or whether he only did it with his most devoted followers. Regardless, the Balrogs were absolute powerhouses.

The Balrog possesses immense physical strength, extraordinary combat abilities, and mastery of fire and shadow. The creature's duel with Gandalf is a stunning one, pushing both to their limits (and beyond). It's difficult to say how the Balrog compares with Saruman, but I'm choosing to place it higher, given it has even more experience working with its dark magic than the fallen White.

Smaug is a Great Dragon, descended from the dragons bred by Morgoth during the First Age. He demonstrates a very different kind of power to some of the other entries on this list; he's another physical powerhouse, a being of phenomenal destructive potential. In Tolkien's lore, dragons aren't simply gigantic beasts; they are incredibly intelligent, and this allows them to use their powers—flight and breathing fire—with tremendous skill.

Smaug is large enough to destroy buildings and to crush most enemies, and he's arguably more dangerous than any other villain in the fantasy saga. I'd tentatively place Smaug above the Balrog, given his intelligence and aerial agility. But it would certainly be a fight to behold; it's just a shame Tolkien never really gave us a sense of how it would play out.

The Dark Lord is undoubtedly the most powerful villain of the Third Age, the one whose malevolent evil inspires the entire saga. Sauron is another Maia, one of their greatest, but he was corrupted by service to Morgoth back in the First Age. Sauron is not simply a powerful wizard or monster; he's a cosmic being in his own right, one even the other wizards could not stand against. He's a phenomenal sorcerer, a skilled manipulator, and (in earlier ages) was a potent shapeshifter.

It doesn't matter what form of power you're talking about; Sauron excels in it. Most significant of all, though, is the fact he is bound to the One Ring. Using this, he can exercise control over the will of others, and could easily have conquered all Middle-earth had he managed to acquire it. Sauron appears in many forms throughout this saga, each more dangerous than the last. But, surprisingly, he isn't the most dangerous character. That distinction lies with a villain who I have already mentioned, and who is discussed a great deal in The Lord of the Rings, but who was never seen.

Morgoth, originally called Melkor, was the most powerful of the Valar; the godlike beings who created the entire world. He's essentially a class above Sauron in power, which explains why Sauron became his servant after Morgoth corrupted him. "Morgoth" means "the Black Foe of the World," which gives a sense of just how monstrous he really was.

In truth, there is nothing in all of Lord of the Rings to compare with Morgoth. He's as far beyond Sauron as Sauron is beyond Wormtongue; although his powers diminished during the First Age due to grievous injuries, he'd still have far outclassed any of the other characters and creatures in the list. Sauron represents domination, but Morgoth stands for corruption; Sauron could conquer, but Morgoth could transform. He's easily the greatest villain in all Tolkien's lore.

#3389. 'GTA 6' Runs Best on This Console

Grand Theft Auto 6 might just be the most anticipated game of all time. It's been 13 years since Rockstar dropped GTA 5, and after years of rumors, leaks, and official announcements, the sixth mainstream installment in the series is nearly here. In fact, anyone who pre-ordered the game digitally can now pre-load it onto their console, if you want to ensure you're ready to play the second the game comes out.

Now, few of us will buy a game console specifically for GTA 6—unless you don't already have a current-generation PlayStation or Xbox. (The PC version of the game isn't expected until at least early 2027.) But, as it turns out, there's one specific console that can run GTA 6 better than the rest.

Rockstar confirmed as much in a post on Tuesday, which was meant to spread the news about pre-loading the game. But, interestingly, it spurred a discussion about the performance of the game itself, as well as which consoles are best to run it.

No matter which console you play GTA 6 on, Rockstar says that the game will only target 30 fps (frames per second). That's decided slow for a mainstream game in 2026. GTA 5 also shipped at 30 fps in 2013, but newer consoles can run it at higher frame rates. In fact, most games that launch on the latest generation of consoles can run at 60 fps, if not higher. While it's certainly not a dealbreaker, it is interesting that Rockstar's latest game can't run at a faster frame rate even on the PS5 Pro or the Xbox Series X.

To that point, Rockstar called out the PS5 Pro specifically in its post, announcing, "The PlayStation 5 Pro offers breathtaking visuals, with improved clarity through PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR) and ray-traced shadows only available on PlayStation 5 Pro."

PSSR is Sony's AI upscaler, similar to options like DLSS from Nvidia, which uses AI to add extra graphical information to games in real time. That allows developers like Rockstar to run the game at a lower resolution to save on processing power, but still boost the visuals to reach a higher perceived resolution. As such, it's not as ideal as running the game at a higher resolution natively, but it can help improve the visuals without pushing the hardware beyond its limits. Meanwhile, ray-tracing offers realistic lighting effects and can also be graphically intense.

While PlayStation and Xbox players alike will be stuck at 30 fps, it seems only PS5 Pro gamers will be able to play the game with ray-tracing effects and AI upscaling. It's surprising that Xbox Series X players don't have similar benefits, as the hardware is more powerful than Xbox Series S. Rockstar didn't specify why only the PS5 Pro gets these upgrades.

In the post, Rockstar also announced that the PS5 version of GTA 6 takes advantage of other PlayStation-exclusive perks, like high-fidelity haptic feedback in the DualSense controller, spatial audio rendering using the PlayStation's Tempest 3D audio, as well as improved load times—though Rockstar didn't specify what those load times would be. These perks apply to all PS5 consoles, not just PS5 Pros. Rockstar goes so far as to say that GTA 6 plays best on PlayStation 5 consoles.

That's not to say that Microsoft's consoles are totally left out of the perks. Rockstar says that GTA 6 will be available on Xbox Cloud Gaming on both Xbox Series X and S, as well as Xbox One. In addition, both PlayStation and Xbox gamers can play GTA 6 using Remote Play, so no one has to physically play on their console if they want to game on the go.

Again, there's no reason to go out and buy a specific console for GTA 6, so long as you have something that can run the game. After all, PS5 Pros are difficult to find, especially without wildly overpaying. But it's interesting that Rockstar has managed to give Sony's consoles the extra perks here, particularly since the company hasn't explained why that is.

#3387. ‘Madden’ Review: David O. Russell Fumbles Again with an Unfunny and Purposeless Football Biopic

“Madden” is technically a David O. Russell film, but all involved seem to want to downplay that fact. Amazon MGM Studios, in their infinite wisdom, has decided to emphasize star Nicolas Cage’s performance as the larger-than-life NFL coach and sports broadcaster in its scant promotional material. While the trailer includes an obligatory “From the director of ‘Silver Linings Playbook’ and ‘American Hustle’” title card, the poster features Cage and Christian Bale, who plays Oakland Raiders coach Al Davis, flashing their Super Bowl rings, and no mention of Russell. Even the PR flack at the sparsely-attended press screening introduced the film by saying, “Please enjoy Nicolas Cage’s ‘Madden’!” Related Stories Skydance Sets Film Leadership Team: Don Granger and Kira Goldberg to Head Paramount Motion Picture Group, Jesse Ehrman Promoted to WB Pictures Chief Movie Theaters Are Back, but the Rest of Hollywood Seems to Be Crumbling

To be fair, this isn’t the worst promotional strategy. Russell may be a problematic figure, but it wasn’t so long ago when starring in one of his films almost guaranteed an actor awards attention. During a brief five-year period in the 2010s, his work garnered Oscar wins for Christian Bale and Jennifer Lawrence, and nominations for Amy Adams, Bradley Cooper, and Robert De Niro. Putting aside the uneven quality of his work, Russell certainly afforded actors the opportunity to “make choices” in lavish studio productions, which often amounted to adopting broad accents and wearing flashy costumes, and receive acclaim for their efforts. It’s probably why people keep working with him in spite of the numerous incidents of on-set mistreatment (on top of a sexual assault allegation) that have continued to this day.

Russell may shifted to streaming but his commitment to allowing actors to go big or go home remains sacrosanct. In “Madden,” Cage wore 30 pounds of prosthetics on top of the 25 pounds he gained for the role. He certainly resembles the man, at least if you ignore Cage’s actual face. Ditto Bale, who adopts Davis’s Noo-Yawk accent and bold fashion sense. But it’s all in service of a film so milquetoast that it will make you beg for the sheer personality exhibited in “Amsterdam,” which at least had the decency to have a narrative and occasionally spark tension and generally be about something.

Here’s what happens in Russell’s eleventh feature: head coach John Madden leads the Oakland Raiders to finally beat their longstanding rivals Pittsburgh Steelers in the 1976 AFC Championship, after which they win the Super Bowl. Following his diagnosis of a bleeding ulcer in his stomach, Madden permanently retires from his coaching career to be with his family. Realizing he’s a stranger in his own home after spending too much time away, he quickly transitions into sports broadcasting where he becomes a television mainstay. To secure his legacy and pass on his legendary playbook, he eventually lends his likeness to EA Sports for the “Madden” video game franchise, which becomes one of the most profitable on the market. He then lives happily ever after.

If that sounds like a film with little-to-no conflict, you would be correct. Part of the problem is that Madden, while being an American institution and a legendary NFL coach, isn’t really suited to be the subject of a biopic, largely because the details of his life are fairly free of drama or intrigue. He’s the kind of figure who should be the lead of a Saturday-morning cartoon where he helps kids solve mysteries using the power of his football mind. Rather than impose a zany plot onto his life or make up outlandish shit for entertainment purposes, which he’s known to do, Russell dutifully relates the major events in his life.

The bare-bones emotional foundation of “Madden” takes the form of the two loves in the eponymous character’s life. The first is with his wife Virginia (Kathryn Hahn), who longs for John to recommit to fatherhood and their marriage, at least until it becomes clear that he needs football to be a functioning human being. Hahn’s established joie de vivre ensures Viriginia is slightly more interesting than an archetypal long-suffering wife character, but, alas, her general lack of chemistry with Cage dampens their tender scenes together, and their intermittent marital troubles are too fleeting and half-hearted to make any dramatic purchase.

The second, and arguably most pivotal, is with Davis, whose slightly-problematic bromance with Madden serves as the film’s primary source of drama. Russell’s film briefly flirts with an interesting thread by portraying Davis as a devil on Madden’s shoulder, someone who seemingly wants him to continue coaching forever, his health and family life be damned. He constantly tries to pressure Madden into returning to the league long after he retires in the vein of an old buddy who wants you to stay out for “just one more beer.” Despite his size, Madden frequently shrinks in Davis’s presence, who knows just what to say to get him to do what he wants.

But while Russell gestures towards connecting Davis’s “maverick” professional style, which made him uniquely qualified for the world of sports ownership but nevertheless created controversy within the league, and his friendship with Madden, he ultimately chickens out from characterizing him as a truly malign influence. (“Madden” just isn’t set up to be a film with a villain or an antagonist of any kind.) Instead, Russell depicts John and Virginia Madden and Al and Carol (Sienna Miller) Davis as tightknit couple friends, admittedly a type of relationship that rarely receives the big-screen treatment, whose ups and downs are manageable because, well, they really just love each other.

It’s worth noting that “Madden” is technically a comedy. It certainly presents as one, featuring well-proven settings for laughter in sports comedies like the sidelines, the locker room, and the announcing booth. Intermittent jokes pop up in these spaces, though I’m genuinely hard-pressed to remember anything specific because much of it suffocates under Cage’s affectionately-caricatured performance. Russell trusts that the sight of the actor in a full-body fat suit is enough for audiences. Granted, Cage seems to palpably enjoy embodying Madden’s flamboyant energy and imposing figure, even if his inconsistent voice acting, complete with slurred speech and vowel-swallowing, occasionally threatens to tip into outright cruelty. (“Madden” features the real article speaking at the film’s end and it’s downright absurd how much Cage exaggerates his diction.)

If there’s one semi-sophisticated bit in the film, it’s that Madden’s one-track mind sees the world entirely through football strategy. He literally can’t write “XOXO” to his future wife in their yearbook without turning it into a play design. But Russell doesn’t really develop the idea any further and instead defaults to broad humor that tends to blend together and subsequently die on the vine. These often materialize as sight gags, like Bale’s increasingly ridiculous haircuts, or John Mulaney, who plays Electronic Arts founder Trip Hawkins, costumed to resemble Steve Jobs. Sometimes it amounts to Shane Gillis delivering Shane Gillis-style lines, sometimes with a perm or donning a wizard’s outfit, or former running back Marshawn Lynch dressed like a nerd.

On paper, Russell is actually a neat fit for a film like “Madden.” He made his bones directing abrasive ensemble screwball comedies. He’s directed period biopics, including one that’s also a sports drama, and one of his most acclaimed films involves football fandom. Sadly, “Madden” features few Russellisms beyond tacky ’70s and ’80s fashion and some mild domestic discord. He’s replaced his typically messy, chaotic atmosphere for an overly genial one.

Anyone who has some familiarity with screen passes or end-arounds likely learned it downwind from Madden, who used whiteboards to make complicated play schemes accessible to the viewing public. His impact extends well into the realm of pop culture, like the Miller Lite commercial where he breaks through the wall, the custom-manufactured bus in which he drove around the country due to his well-documented fear of flying, and his famous turducken. “Madden” covers all of that material without offering any insight other than the security of the man’s legacy. The Russell who made “I Heart Huckabees” has long faded away, but it’s still a shame that he’s been reduced to directing one of the oddest and blandest examples of brand management in recent memory.

Amazon MGM Studios will release “Madden” in select theaters and on Prime Video on Wednesday, November 18.

#3386. Lifehacker's Pick for the Best TV to Gift in 2026 Isn't Actually a TV

Welcome to Holiday Office Hours From the Labs, a collaborative multimedia project in which Lifehacker, CNET, ZDNET, and Mashable harness the power of our product testing laboratory and our editors' expertise to offer the best gift-buying recommendations possible. In this episode, we're talking televisions.

I recently did a deep dive into TV development history, checked out what was on shelves for 2026, and I concluded that the best gift TV you can give this year is, actually, a pair of sunglasses. The XBX by XReal video display glasses are basically a TV you can shove in your pocket. Check them out:

I looked past traditional sets for a couple of reasons. First, because as much as we all love a great show or movie, who actually buys someone a TV set as a gift? More importantly, there's the nature of television itself. Since it was invented in the late 1920s, television quality has been measured by how big the screen is and how clear and bright the picture is, but in 2026, a nothing-special 4K television delivers an image that is pixel-invisible to a typical viewer, and most of us don't have living rooms big enough to need a display bigger than 65 inches. I think the innovation in the space is going to come from the form factor and the use case, and what better form factor is there than a pair of sunglasses?

These glasses deliver the equivalent of a 142" TV viewed from across the room. It's hard to compare resolution to traditional TVs—technically, the display is 1080p in each eye, but because the TV is just millimeters from your eye, it looks much clearer than that. The peak brightness is 1,600 nits, bright enough for most rooms, and there's a totally opaque shield if you need it. The refresh rate is a crisp 120Hz. They support HDR10 and real-time SDR-to-HDR upscaling, offer billions of colors, and it's all in a package that weighs only 62 grams.

Then there are the use cases. It can act as a separate monitor for your computer; you can watch a different show than your roommate without bothering them; but most of all, these are great for flights. There is no situation in life that calls for a big screen TV more than a cross-country airplane flight. Slip these on with a pair of headphones, and you can fly to Boise in your own private, virtual theater.

They plug right into any device that supports USB-C video, there's no battery to remember to charge, and they cost less than $300. In other words: They're the perfect TV gift for the holidays, even if they aren't technically a TV.
