#3385. 10 Longest-Running Comic Strips Of All Time

Comic strips have occupied newspaper pages for more than a century, and a surprising number have outlived the artists who created them. Some evolved from topical jokes into multigenerational family sagas, while others kept familiar characters in circulation through successive cartoonists. Their histories reveal how newspaper humor adapted to changing audiences, publishing habits and generations of readers.

This selection combines exceptionally long publication histories with some of the most recognizable comics ever created. It is not a strict statistical ranking as The Far Side, for example, had a considerably shorter original run than the century-old newspaper classics. However, its influence, alongside the 50-year publication history of Peanuts, makes both important additions to any discussion of the medium's most long-lasting titles.

Rudolph Dirks launched The Katzenjammer Kids on December 12, 1897, in the New York Journal. Inspired by German illustrator Wilhelm Busch's Max and Moritz, the strip followed mischievous twins Hans and Fritz as they tormented adults. Its early use of speech balloons, sound effects and sequential action helped establish visual conventions that later comic strips adopted.

While some works failed to secure a place in the collective memory, the most iconic comic strips shaped generations and changed pop culture forever.

The feature lasted through generations of cartoonists and changes in publishers, although a legal dispute eventually split its history. Dirks left Hearst and created a competing strip with the same characters, eventually titled The Captain and the Kids. New Katzenjammer Kids installments ended on January 1, 2006. King Features has continued circulating reprints rather than producing new episodes.

Frank King introduced Gasoline Alley on November 24, 1918, initially focusing on a group of automobile enthusiasts who gathered to discuss cars. Its premise changed dramatically in 1921, when bachelor Walt Wallet found an abandoned baby named Skeezix on his doorstep. That decision transformed a gag strip into an unusually ambitious chronicle of family life.

Unlike most comic-strip characters, the residents of Gasoline Alley age as time passes. Readers have followed marriages, children, careers and old age across generations. King's successors included Dick Moores and Jim Scancarelli, who took over in 1986. The strip remains in publication, making it one of the oldest American newspaper comics still producing new material.

Billy DeBeck began Barney Google in July 1919 as Take Barney Google, F'rinstance. Its title character was a cigar-smoking sports fan who loved horse racing, poker and betting. The strip became popular enough to inspire a hit song in 1923, but its cast and focus changed considerably when DeBeck introduced another character during the following decade.

Snuffy Smith arrived on November 17, 1934, bringing a rural setting and a different style of comic mischief. His growing popularity eventually pushed Barney into the background and gave the strip its familiar double-barreled title. Fred Lasswell, initially DeBeck's assistant, continued the comic after DeBeck's death in 1942. John Rose subsequently took over in 2001.

E.C. Segar launched Thimble Theatre on December 19, 1919, years before its most famous character appeared. The early strip centered on Olive Oyl, her brother Castor and Olive's suitor Ham Gravy. Popeye entered the story on January 17, 1929, as a supporting character during an adventure involving a voyage to an island.

The sailor quickly became the strip's biggest attraction, thanks to his distinctive speech, stubborn courage and extraordinary strength. Popeye's popularity was so overwhelming that many newspapers and readers began using his name for the feature. Segar died in 1938, but other cartoonists continued the property, keeping one of America's most recognizable comic characters in circulation.

The comic now known as Nancy began in 1922 as Fritzi Ritz, created by Larry Whittington. Ernie Bushmiller took over in 1925 and introduced Fritzi's niece Nancy in 1933. Readers quickly gravitated toward the outspoken youngster, and by 1938 the strip had been renamed Nancy to reflect its new main character.

Bushmiller developed an instantly recognizable style built around crisp lines, economical backgrounds and carefully timed visual jokes. The strip has continued through several generations of cartoonists, despite a brief pause in the early 1930s. It currently appears in more than 100 newspapers, with Caroline Cash beginning her tenure on January 1, 2026.

Chic Young introduced Blondie on September 8, 1930, as a dating comedy about a carefree flapper and her wealthy boyfriend, Dagwood Bumstead. The strip found its lasting direction when the couple married on February 17, 1933. Dagwood was disinherited, and the feature shifted toward the everyday complications of married life and raising a family.

The perspective of a mischievous six-year-old boy and his imaginary tiger has resulted in some of the greatest quotes in comic strip history.

That change gave newspapers a durable domestic comedy, complete with Dagwood's enormous sandwiches, frantic journeys to work and clashes with his boss, Mr. Dithers. Young continued the strip until his death in 1973, after which his son Dean and other cartoonists carried it forward. Blondie remains syndicated more than 96 years after its debut.

Chester Gould's Dick Tracy debuted on October 4, 1931, introducing a hard-edged detective whose cases contrasted with the lighter family humor found in many newspaper comics. Gould built the strip around elaborate criminals, high-stakes investigations, and cool police technology. One of its best-known devices, Tracy's two-way wrist radio, appeared in 1946.

Gould retired on December 25, 1977, after writing and drawing the strip for more than 46 years. Other creative teams continued the detective's adventures, preserving its combination of crime stories, unusual villains and gadgets. Dick Tracy is still in syndication, giving a character created during the Great Depression a place in modern newspaper comics.

V.T. Hamlin introduced Alley Oop on December 5, 1932, bringing a prehistoric caveman and his pet dinosaur Dinny to newspaper readers. The strip takes place in the fictional Kingdom of Moo, where Alley encounters characters including his girlfriend Ooola, friend Foozy and King Guz. Its original premise combined prehistoric slapstick with adventures involving dinosaurs and other unusual creatures.

The strip briefly lost its original syndication after Bonnet-Brown folded in 1933, but the Newspaper Enterprise Association picked it up that August. Hamlin eventually introduced a time machine, allowing Alley to travel beyond the Stone Age and encounter different historical periods. The feature passed through several cartoonists and remains a recognizable example of adventure-oriented newspaper comics.

Charles M. Schulz's Peanuts debuted on October 2, 1950, in seven American newspapers. Its small cast of children and animals turned schoolyard worries, family tensions and everyday disappointments into a comic strip with surprising emotional depth. Charlie Brown, Snoopy, Lucy, Linus and the rest of the gang gradually became familiar figures far beyond the newspaper page.

Schulz wrote, drew and lettered all 17,897 original strips himself, an extraordinary achievement across five decades. He announced his retirement in December 1999, and the final Sunday strip appeared on February 13, 2000, one day after his death. Reprints remain widely available, but no new original Peanuts newspaper strips have been produced since.

Gary Larson's The Far Side debuted in January 1980 and quickly stood apart from traditional newspaper comics. Rather than relying on recurring characters or multiframe stories, Larson usually delivered a complete joke in a single illustration. His surreal scenarios often involved animals, scientists, parents and children, with familiar situations pushed into bizarre and unexpected territory.

Gary Larson's twisted takes on pop culture were the engine that drove The Far Side; these underrated referential jokes are him at his best.

Larson announced his retirement in October 1994, and the final syndicated cartoon appeared on January 1, 1995. Its original run lasted approximately 14 years, far shorter than most comics here, but its influence was considerable: it reached more than 1,900 newspapers worldwide and inspired numerous book collections. Its continued popularity makes it one of the most recognizable newspaper comics of its era.

HBO's Harry Potter hasn't made a magical first impression

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

HBO Max has released a first look at its upcoming ‘Harry Potter’ TV show, and it’s fair to say the online reaction has been mixed. And by mixed, I mean mostly extremely negative.

The 90-second clip is presumably from an early episode (I would guess episode 2). It offers a first look at Hogwarts’ start-of-term feast, alongside a brief conversation between headmaster Albus Dumbledore (John Lithgow) and professor of Transfiguration Minerva McGonagall (Janet McTeer).

The show, which will be called “Harry Potter and the Philosopher’s Stone” for its first season (no, Sorcerer’s Stone this time), will adapt J.K. Rowling’s 1997 book of the same name across a reported eight episodes. Dominic McLaughlin will play the boy wizard, with Alastair Stout and Arabella Stanton playing his schoolmates Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger, respectively.

The first episode is due to premiere on HBO in the U.S. and HBO Max internationally on December 25, and it’s already been earmarked as one of the most anticipated (and most expensive) television projects in history. I suspect HBO was hoping this clip would be well-received…

HBO’s “Harry Potter” has faced backlash since its initial announcement in 2023. The necessity of adapting Rowling’s best-selling books a second time has been questioned, as the movie versions, released between 2001 and 2011, remain extremely popular to this day. And are seasonal staples for many.

Also, you can’t talk about Harry Potter in the current climate without acknowledging the controversy surrounding its creator, J.K. Rowling. Rowling has become an extremely divisive public figure due to her outspoken views, particularly in relation to the transgender community, which makes anything related to the Harry Potter brand controversial.

One look at my feeds, and the initial reactions to this short teaser clip haven’t exactly been magical. Over on X, the clip has been labeled “lifeless in all aspects,” and comparisons to the same scene in the 2001 movie starring Daniel Radcliffe, which is noticeably more colorful, have done few favors.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

This new Harry Potter looks so lifeless man in all aspects. https://t.co/NeLhmHNTpWNovember 15, 2026

One post from X user Matt del Rio, which has amassed more than 35,000 likes as of writing, reads, “As a millennial who spent hours upon hours reading Harry Potter growing up, I’m insulted by this,” suggesting that even viewers who haven’t turned their back on the series in the wake of Rowling’s incendiary comments are unimpressed with HBO’s first look.

As a millennial who spent hours upon hours reading Harry Potter growing up, I’m insulted by thisNovember 15, 2026

And as far as cutting remarks go, one X account states, “It’s actually so funny they spent millions of dollars to make Temu Harry Potter.” Ouch! Probably not the reaction HBO would be hoping for, considering the show reportedly cost roughly $25 million per episode to produce.

it’s actually so funny they spent millions of dollars to make Temu Harry PotterNovember 15, 2026

As one of the biggest Harry Potter fans on staff at Tom’s Guide — a label that comes with an uncomfortable degree of shame these days — my feelings on this first clip are decidedly more muted. Overall, I think, judging solely on this new 90-second clip, the show looks generally fine.

The problem is that for millions of us, myself included, we literally grew up on the Potter movies, so there is an inherent disconnect when watching a new production of “The Philosopher’s Stone.”

It’s hard to see anybody as Harry Potter but a young Daniel Radcliffe. Getting past the nostalgic fondness so many have for the movies will be tough.

I do agree with the criticism of the lack of color, but this seems to be a trend across modern TV shows and movies. The art of color grading seems to be a dying one.

Not to mention the lack of floating candles to light the Hogwarts Great Hall is a curious production design decision, considering the justification for the show’s existence has largely been that it will be more book-accurate than the movies, which jettisoned many narrative elements and characters to squeeze the increasingly lengthy novels into two-hour movies. What's up with that?

Nevertheless, there are some nice flourishes here, like the way food literally pops into existence on the tables, and the musical score from Hans Zimmer does indeed scream Potter.

Will the HBO “Harry Potter” series be any good? Will it feel completely unnecessary? Will movie nostalgia sour it with viewers? Only time will tell, but I’ll be reserving making any definitive judgements until I’ve seen the full season. Fortunately, we don’t have much longer to wait before its premiere.

"Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone" premieres on HBO and HBO Max on December 25

For all intents and purposes, Black Friday sales are already here. There are plenty of deals out already, even though we're weeks away from the actual event. One of the retailers that is making the biggest early splash is Best Buy, confirming their entire plan for the rest of the year. Here's what you need to know.

Best Buy has announced the following events:

DoorBoosters: A Halloween sale from Oct. 30 to Nov. 1.

Early Black Friday Deals and Doorbusters: The official start of early Black Friday deals on Nov. 6. New deals will drop every Friday.

Black Friday Doorbusters and Deals: Best Buy says this will be its main sale, starting on Thursday, Nov. 19 and running until Nov. 28 with deals on "computing, gaming, home theater, wearables, and more."

Cyber Sunday and Monday: Best Buy is extending Cyber Monday to five days and says you can find deals going up to 50% off select tech.

Last-minute savings: The Christmas sale will run from Dec. 18 until Dec. 24.

You don't need to be any kind of member to shop Best Buy's Black Friday in July sale; however, it is free to sign up for a My Best Buy membership, which will get you free shipping. If you join one of their paid subscriptions (My Best Buy Plus for $49.99 per year or My Best Buy Total for $179.99 per year), you'll get faster free shipping, exclusive prices and deals, an extended 60-day return window on most products, and access to select sales, like the Member Deals Days sale that is going on right now. Paid members will also earn extra rewards from both the current sale and the upcoming Black Friday in July sale.

You can find deals on TVs, laptops, headphones, video games, electric bikes, and more. There will be new deals every week in stores, on its website, and in the Best Buy mobile app. They'll offer price matching, meaning if the price drops further during the sale (Dec. 24), they will match it and offer a refund.

Here are the best deals I've found so far. I'll be updating these deals throughout the sale, so make sure to come back and see what's new. Remember that new deals drop every day.

Best Buy price matches its own products, so if a product drops in price later, you'd get those savings too, but it does not cover any deals coming from a competitor's Black Friday sale. There are some other important exceptions you can read in more detail here.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

The other major retailers doing Black Friday sales are Amazon, Target, and Walmart. Currently, Amazon has many early deals, seeing their lowest prices yet. Target has some week-long deals and a Deal of the Day. Walmart will have three Black Friday and Cyber Monday shopping events. Nowadays, large retailers and small businesses compete for Cyber Monday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, Nov. 30, 2026.

No. If you find the product you're looking for with a major discount right now, get it. It's not likely to drop any lower, but it could always run out of stock. Take advantage of price matching or guarantees instead of waiting. Remember, you can always return products later if you change your mind. For the majority of products, the deal from Black Friday will be the same one on Cyber Monday.

#3382. ‘The Other Bennet Sister’ Christmas Special Trailer: Can Mary Bennet Still Be Herself and ‘the Perfect Wife’?

#3381. Michael Connelly’s Bosch Replacement’s Next Release Is Just 6 Months Away

Cher Thompson is a Senior Staff Writer at Screen Rant, where she covers everything from explosive reality TV moments to cast interviews about the twists and turns of scripted dramas. With a background in creative writing, marketing, and teaching, Cher knows how to spot both the storytelling genius and the guilty pleasures in pop culture. Her work blends wit with insight, making readers feel like they’re chatting with a friend who just happens to know way too much about TV.

Over the past several decades, Michael Connelly has taken his time establishing Harry Bosch as one of crime fiction's most recognizable figures, but his closest replacement character's next release is sooner than you'd think. While Bosch was first introduced in the early 1990s with The Black Echo, Connelly has worked with the character and continued to build the universe for well over 30 years, bringing him into the present day. While the author's Bosch was a successful series in the literary world, nothing has helped boost the character into the cultural lexicon more than the Prime Video live-action TV adaptation.

When Prime Video began adapting Bosch into a series in 2014, the character broke containment and became one of the most popular TV investigators of the modern streaming era. With a specific point of view of policing in today's world and an incredible portrayal of the character from Titus Welliver, the series quickly rose in the rankings and stayed on the air for seven seasons before transitioning into a secondary series, Bosch: Legacy, which ran for another three seasons. With Bosch coming to a close in 2025, the decade that the series was on the air did wonders for the books, which have sold more than 92 million copies worldwide.

Connelly's tremendous character may be his most notable, and while the Bosch series continues on the page, the author's most promising replacement character has another release coming out in just six months. With his newest character in the Catalina series, Connelly's introduced his readers to a whole new detective in Steve Stilwell.

Although Bosch himself is still alive and well in the literary world, Connelly has branched out into other characters consistently throughout his career, most notably writing The Lincoln Lawyer series with Mickey Haller at the center, as well as the Ballard series, which follows detective Renée Ballard. Both The Lincoln Lawyer and Ballard have been adapted into successful TV projects as well, but his newest work is still finding its footing, despite already getting the green light for a TV adaptation of its own. The Catalina series, which follows detective Steve Stilwell as he solves cases in a sleepy California island town, is a much different swing than his previous work.

Connelly's Catalina series, which will be adapted for HBO Max by Connelly and TV legend David E. Kelley, currently consists of two novels: 2025's Nightshade, which introduced the character and brought his first intense investigation to life, and 2026's Ironwood, which introduced Stilwell to Renée Ballard. Connelly's larger interconnected universe of characters does mean that eventually, Stilwell and Bosch could come face to face. In building a very different franchise, the author has brought Stilwell to a more remote, rustic location on Catalina Island, and has made his work feel vastly different than the intensity of Bosch's, or the pace of Ballard's.

With Connelly's Catalina series kicking off on the right foot, another piece of the larger puzzle will be coming out in 2027, just six months from now. Stilwell is set to return in Daybreak, Connelly's next title within the series, which will explore another case on the island that's changed the detective's life. Daybreak is set to release on May 25, 2027, and while there hasn't been much news about what to expect from the plot, the novel will continue Stilwell's story, which is setting him up to be the prime Bosch replacement as he continues the series in sunny Catalina.

While Stilwell and Bosch share some commonalities because of their work, both investigators have a vastly different approach to what they do. With Connelly having explored Bosch as a character for decades, there's far fewer surprises on the table for readers when it comes to learning things about his past or his process. Stilwell, on the other hand, is a far newer character for Connelly to dive into. This means that novels like Daybreak are working hard to establish who he is, how he works, and why readers should invest themselves in his stories. Thankfully, Connelly's newest Bosch replacement isn't far off from releasing new material.

#3380. 10 Google Privacy Hacks Everyone Should Know

Your Gmail account doesn't just have one email address. In fact, it has unlimited addresses, but you need a hack to utilize them. When you're signing up for a new service, you can add another word to your email address, as well as the "+" symbol, to create an alias. For example, if your email is "[email protected]," and you're signing up for an Amazon account, you can use "[email protected]" as your email address. The email will still end up in your main inbox, as if you simply used [email protected]. Not only can this trick turn one Gmail address into an unlimited number of addresses, but it also helps you identify who sold your email address to spammers, because those emails will have the alias in the "To" field.

Gmail's web view has a crucial security feature that lets you view session logs. This feature is inexplicably buried at the bottom of the inbox, and the font size is tiny, so it's easy to miss. To find it, log in to Gmail on the web, and scroll to the bottom of your inbox. Click the Details button in the bottom-right corner, below "Last account activity." This will show you a pop-up that lists the devices, apps, and locations you've recently logged in from. This makes it easy to see if there's been any suspicious activity in your Google account, and you can click the Security Checkup link in the pop-up to review this data. Just note that if you use a VPN or a service like iCloud Private Relay, you might not recognize your own device's location. To check if unwanted apps have access to your Google account, you can visit this settings page.

Google wants to show you personalized search results, which initially feels very helpful, but it also ends up trapping you in an algorithmic bubble. The best way to break out of your search bubble is to periodically use other search engines, but if you wish to stick to Google, you can disable personalized search recommendations in Google Search and the Play Store on Android. Go to this settings page, and turn off Personalized Recommendations and Play Personalization.

Google tracks your web and app activity by default, which includes your search history, voice data (if you use the speak-to-search feature), and activity from sites, apps, and devices that use Google services. However, associated information, such as your location data, is also saved to your Google profile, which you might not assume gets included in "Web & app activity." Fortunately, you can disable this tracking by going to this settings page, scrolling down to "Web & App Activity," and turning off all options in this section.

Google's Timeline feature saves your location in Google Maps to create a map of places you've visited. This is useful if you want to keep track of your recent stops; however, Google can use Timeline data to help businesses see how effective their ads were, or how likely you are to visit nearby stores. Its confirmation page confirms this: "Depending on your settings, activity saved as history in your Google Account, including ad interactions, may also be connected to Timeline data to help nearby businesses estimate the likelihood that people will visit their stores. No personal information is shared with businesses."

Timeline isn't enabled by default, but in case you enabled it a while ago, and are no longer using it, you can turn it off by going to this settings page. Click Turn off, and delete your activity to remove Timeline data from your Google account.

You can't fully escape Google's ads or tracking, but you can disable personalized ads to stop the company from using your account data to show ads. To do this, go to this settings page, and turn off Personalized ads.

While Google claims that it isn't using your emails to train AI, the company does offer AI features that make your emails feel more robotic than human. One of these is "Smart Reply," which offers email reply suggestions such as "Got it. See you soon." I can type that on my own, and I feel uncomfortable with Gmail analyzing the contents of my emails and replies to offer suggestions that I wouldn't use anyway. You can disable this by going to Gmail Settings > General, or by visiting this settings page. Scroll down to "Smart features," and turn off the checkbox next to it. This will disable Smart Compose, Smart Reply, suggestions for pending replies and follow-ups, spelling, grammar, and autocorrect.

A physical security key is a great security upgrade. It's a physical barrier that prevents most ways to hack into your account remotely. Even if someone discovers your email ID and password, and has access to your two-factor authentication code, they won't get in without physical access to that key. You can check out Google's support page for physical security keys for more information on compatibility and setting up your security keys.

Google uses data from Gmail and Google Drive to target ads, which means that your emails, files, and photos could be used for monetization. To stop this, you'll need to disable Personal Intelligence. To turn it off, visit this settings page, and click Turn off Personal Intelligence.

The 2027 Audi S6 Sportback e-tron pairs its luxury aesthetics with a sporty drive that makes it fun on the road, all while remaining whisper-quiet on the inside thanks to its air-suspension ride and solid soundproofing. While its nearly $95,000 as-tested price tag is a hefty amount, it’s accompanied by premium features and surprisingly efficient for drivers who want sports-sedan thrills without sacrificing everyday versatility.

Hefty cost puts it out of the budget of most people

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

When I got into the driver's seat of the Audi A6 Sportback e-tron last year, my expectations weren’t all that high. But it ended up impressing me so much that it quickly became one of the best electric cars I’ve tested. With the 2027 Audi S6 Sportback e-tron, it’s pretty evident that Audi has dialed up the aggression and sportier flair.

While there are similarities between the two, the S6 Sportback e-tron differentiates itself with standard dual-motor quattro all-wheel drive, sport-tuned adaptive air suspension, and up to 543 horsepower. Quite simply, it’s a mid-size luxury sedan that trades some range for extra muscle.

I tested the 2027 Audi S6 Sportback e-tron Prestige for a week, which carries a $94,490 as-tested price — putting it squarely in the crosshairs of similar models I’ve tested, like the BMW i5 and Lucid Air Touring. And after seven days behind the wheel, I discovered this pricier performance variant still holds a few surprises up its sleeve.

Dual Permanent Magnet Synchronous Motors (AWD)

I drove the 2027 Audi S6 Sportback e-tron Prestige for a total of 152.4 miles and recorded an overall average efficiency of 3.6 mi/kWh. While that overall figure trails slightly behind the results I got out of the BMW i5 and Lucid Air Touring, it’s well within striking range of its main rivals.

Personally, I think it’s a valiant result given how the A6 Sportback e-tron yielded 3.7 mi/kWh in my previous test. On longer highway stretches, I’ve recorded a best mark of 3.9 mi/kWh with the A6 Sportback — while short trip efficiency reached 3.6 mi/kWh.

When plugged into a standard household outlet for Level 1 charging, the S6 Sportback e-tron added range at a rate of 4.05 miles per hour. That places it squarely in the middle of its rivals, beating the Lucid Air Touring while trailing the BMW i5 xDrive40.

I’ve always been a fan of Audi’s signature design philosophy, and the 2027 S6 Sportback e-tron takes that familiar luxury aesthetic and injects it with an aggressive, sporty edge. Between its low-slung fastback silhouette, razor-sharp LED lighting, and glossy front grille, it strikes an athletic stance that never feels overdone — and makes me feel young at heart.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Behind the wheel, the 2027 Audi S6 Sportback e-tron delivers a refined, whisper-quiet ride that glides effortlessly over rough pavement thanks to its standard sport adaptive air suspension. Yet the moment I bury my foot in the accelerator, it pins me back in the seat with blistering off-the-line speed.

That effortless torque makes overtaking slower traffic on the highway feel almost instantaneous, giving me serious passing power without ever sacrificing its composed demeanor. It actually offers a better ride than the Lucid Air and matches the BMW i5 on open roads.

One of the standout tech features on the S6 Sportback e-tron is Audi's augmented reality head-up display, which projects crisp visuals directly into my line of sight on the windshield. Beyond showing me all the usual stats — like my current speed, turn-by-turn navigation arrows, and speed limit signs — it also visualizes adaptive cruise assist and following distance in real time.

It’s one of the most comprehensive and advanced HUDs out there, even turning red when the gap to the vehicle ahead gets too short.

In 2026, it’s still very rare for any vehicle to come with an integrated dashcam, but the S6 Sportback e-tron is one of them. Ingeniously, it’s built into the auto-dimming rearview mirror — keeping the windshield free of clutter, unlike third-party camera solutions with dangling power cables. Not only does it offer automatic loop recording for convenience, but it also doesn’t require an extra fee or subscription just to work.

Another practical advantage of the S6 Sportback e-tron is its rear liftback design, which opens up a massive cargo hold that puts conventional sedans to shame. Unlike the traditional, narrower trunk openings I dealt with on the BMW i5 and Lucid Air Touring, the Audi’s entire rear glass lifts with the power tailgate — making it far easier to load bulky gear, luggage, or larger items that simply wouldn’t clear a standard trunk lid.

With roughly 26 cubic feet of space behind the second row (and even more when you fold the rear seats flat), it gives you crossover-like versatility wrapped in a sleek sport-sedan profile.

I’ll be the first to admit that its $95,000 as-tested price is hefty, but Audi compensates for it with a serious tech suite of luxury features you don’t traditionally find. Overhead, the panoramic glass roof features variable light control that electronically lets me switch between transparent and opaque at the touch of a button, while LED interior ambient lighting wraps across the dashboard and brings the cabin to life at night.

On the outside, I love small details like the animations of the LED headlights and OLED taillights, which give it a slick look when turning the vehicle on and off. There are also dual charging ports on either side of the vehicle, giving me the convenience of parking however I want for Level 1 and 2 charging — albeit with Level 3 DC fast charging only supported on the driver’s side.

Entertainment and audio get just as much attention, thanks to a crisp 10.9-inch front passenger display and a booming Bang & Olufsen 3D sound system that even builds speakers directly into the front headrests.

While the S6 Sportback e-tron’s sleek, low-slung roofline looks fantastic from the outside, it comes at the expense of a narrower rear windshield compared to its rivals. As a result, it creates a somewhat letterbox-like view.

Between the low roofline, chunky A-pillars, and the large sensor housing behind the rearview mirror, spotting overhead traffic lights can be challenging when pulling up close to an intersection.

I’m the kind of driver who religiously activates adaptive cruise control, and while I appreciate how the S6 Sportback e-tron keeps steady in its lane, it lacks automatic lane-change assist. That means I’m still forced to manually take over whenever I want to pass slower traffic on the highway — a glaring omission for a pricey $95K luxury vehicle.

Compounding that frustration is how Audi continues to put all of the adaptive cruise control functions on a dedicated stalk tucked behind the lower left side of the steering wheel, which forces me to move my hand slightly away from the wheel. I’d much rather have them integrated into one of the control pads on the steering wheel itself.

There’s a lot to love about the 2027 Audi S6 Sportback e-tron, starting with its sharp and sporty design, all the way to its genuinely practical hatchback-like utility. Add in a rich roster of high-end comfort tech — from its augmented reality HUD to its built-in dashcam — it delivers an upscale daily driving experience.

Still, at nearly $95,000 as tested, that steep price tag makes it a tough pill to swallow for most buyers, especially when smaller quirks like a narrow windshield and inconveniently placed cruise-control stalk hold it back from perfection. If you don't need the extra cargo space or blistering acceleration and are willing to go a little smaller, the 2027 Mercedes-Benz CLA 250+ delivers exceptional luxury EV value at a dramatically lower price.

#3378. All 7 Episodes Of Netflix's 10/10 Western Are Perfect From Start To Finish

While the small-screen Westerns of the 2010s might be hit-and-miss, Netflix’s seven-episode masterpiece hasn’t got a single weak episode in its entire run. Hard as it might be to believe in 2026, there was a time when Westerns were the biggest genre on TV. Admittedly, this was back in the days of Gunsmoke and Rawhide, when shows set in the Wild West produced record numbers of live-action episodes and set early TV ratings records.

However, as the decades went on, cop shows gradually replaced Westerns as the most-watched genre on TV, and the genre wouldn’t regain its mainstream popularity until the rise of the Yellowstone franchise. While the Yellowstone spinoff Marshals is CBS’s biggest show of 2026, it is important to note that the spinoff is part Western and part police procedural. Sharing many building blocks in common with cop show franchises like CSI, NCIS, FBI, and Law & Order accounts for a lot of the show’s mainstream popularity.

Even Yellowstone itself and its sequel Dutton Ranch are contemporary crime dramas as much as they are Westerns, since Sheridan’s greatest trick was selling a modern-day spin on Dynasty and Dallas as a “Neo-Western” rather than the trashy, soapy family saga that the original series really was. To find a traditional historical Western, viewers need to look to Yellowstone’s prequels 1883 and 1923, or Netflix originals like American Primeval, The Abandons, and the underrated seven-episode masterpiece Godless.

Released in 2017, Godless was inexcusably missed by many viewers upon its original release. Set in 1884 New Mexico, Godless stars Sinners supporting star Jack O’Connell as the outlaw Roy Goode, who hides out in the New Mexico town of La Belle as he attempts to avoid a murderous mob boss, his former employer Frank Griffin. In an unsettling subversion of his usual genial screen presence, The Newsroom star Jeff Daniels wows as the icy, terrifying Griffin.

However, the story of Godless isn’t defined by male characters like O’Connell’s Goode, Daniels’ Griffin, or even Scoot McNairy’s local sheriff, Bill McNue. Thanks to a mining disaster, McNue is one of the only male citizens left living in La Belle, a town that is populated almost exclusively by women. These women include Michelle Dockery’s steely wealthy widow Alice Fletcher, Merrit Weaver’s more welcoming Mary Agnes, and a host of other well-sketched heroines with complex motivations and backstories.

Thus, Godless sets up a story that functions as both a tense, gripping self-contained small town siege Western and also a daring subversion of the genre at the same time. While most traditional historical Westerns sideline their female characters in favor of stories focused on sheriffs and outlaws, Godless forces viewers to think about the women left on the margins of these old-fashioned stories.

However, no one should mistake the Netflix show for a dry, academic deconstruction of the genre. Even compared to Sheridan’s more famous Yellowstone, Godless is a dark, daring, and thoroughly enthralling Western through and through. Unpredictable and inventive, Godless is as satisfying as any earlier Western show like Deadwood or AMC’s underrated drama Hell on Wheels.

Sadly, this didn’t do anything to help the show’s performance. While Godless was a big, well-deserved hit with reviewers, the show seemingly failed to find a major mainstream audience as the series arrived shortly before the modern Western revival was kickstarted by the success of Yellowstone in 2018. As noted above, Yellowstone’s success spawned the spinoffs 1883, 1923, Marshals, and Dutton Ranch.

However, the show also helped get the green light for further Neo-Westerns from Sheridan, such as Landman, Lawmen: Bass Reeves, and arguably even the crime drama The Mayor of Kingstown. Outside of Sheridan’s work, Netflix’s Ransom Canyon proved that Godless might be better known if the iconic show had just debuted a decade later.

#3377. Garmin Cyclists Can Now Make Themselves Appear on Waze in Real Time

Cyclists who ride with Garmin gear can now appear as live, moving icons on the Waze driving app, and nearby drivers will receive an alert to slow down and watch for them on the road.

For riders already using Garmin devices, opting in costs nothing and adds a new layer of safety, particularly on roads where drivers may not expect cyclists. The feature is rolling out now, but you should be aware of its limitations.

Riders can simply opt in once through Garmin Connect. After that, sharing starts automatically when an outdoor cycling activity begins and stops when the ride ends. While a ride is underway, Waze users near the cyclist see a cyclist icon move along the road and receive a Live Cycling Alert reminding them to slow down and stay aware.

The feature runs on LiveTrack, Garmin's existing live location-sharing tool, which lets friends and family follow a rider's real-time location, speed, course, and more. Garmin says this collaboration extends that peace of mind to motorists, giving them greater awareness of their surroundings.

Garmin notes its location sharing is temporary and session-based. The rider's name, identity, and route are hidden, and no personal information is shared or displayed in Waze. Drivers see only an anonymous icon and the alert.

You'll need a few things to get this feature up and running:

A compatible Garmin Edge bike computer or Garmin watch

A phone running Garmin Connect with a data connection

An outdoor cycling activity (the feature doesn't apply to indoor rides)

The good news is using the feature is free: LiveTrack costs nothing on compatible Garmin bike computers and watches, and Waze is free for drivers.

This new feature is a great safety perk, but there are real-world caveats worth considering:

This feature is for Waze only. Alerts reach drivers only when Waze is open on their phone. Google Maps, which has far more users, is excluded, so a large portion of the drivers you share the road with won't see you this way.

It depends on your phone's signal. Your position travels from the Garmin to your phone, then to Garmin's servers, then to Waze, and finally to the driver's phone. On a patchy rural signal, a few seconds of lag could put the icon on the wrong side of a bend from where you actually are. A rider who leaves their phone at home or whose phone loses signal simply won't show up on a Waze map, as a ride without a data connection is invisible to Waze.

Finally, remember to treat this safety feature as an extra perk, not a guarantee. At the end of the day, it isn't a replacement for bike lights, bright clothing, and defensive riding.

#3376. Sean Connery Wasn’t the First James Bond: Meet Barry Nelson in the ‘Casino Royale’ You’ve Never Seen

Ever since George Lazenby first replaced Sean Connery as James Bond in 1969’s “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service,” fans have argued over who makes the best 007 — and those arguments are likely to resume once Robert Pattinson takes the screen as the latest Bond in director Denis Villeneuve’s new iteration. Although Craig has his partisans, Connery tends to be the consensus choice for the best Bond, though I’ve argued here for the merits of 1970s and ’80s Roger Moore. All the Bonds have their virtues, but Connery benefited from being there first — for anyone who discovered the series in its initial heyday, Connery simply is James Bond. Related Stories ‘The Other Bennet Sister’ Christmas Special Trailer: Can Mary Bennet Still Be Herself and ‘the Perfect Wife’? ‘Madden’ Review: David O. Russell Fumbles Again with an Unfunny and Purposeless Football Biopic

Yet Connery actually wasn’t the first actor to play Bond. That honor goes to journeyman MGM contract player Barry Nelson, who played Bond in a “Casino Royale” adaptation eight years before Connery made the character famous in “Dr. No.” Connery may have been the first 007 to grace the big screen, but Nelson established Bond on the small screen in an episode of the CBS anthology series “Climax!” opposite Peter Lorre in the Le Chiffre role that would later be inhabited by Orson Welles (in the goofy 1967 “Casino Royale”) and Mads Mikkelsen (in the 2006 adaptation that introduced Craig to the series).

The 1954 “Casino Royale” is a fascinating artifact that includes elements that would go on to characterize future James Bond movies, while also going in a few other very different directions. The key difference is in the scale, stripped down by necessity for television production. The hour-long “Climax!” episode is all interiors, taking place entirely in the hotel and casino of the title. It’s more a James Bond play than a movie, with Bond and Le Chiffre facing off in a series of verbal — and ultimately physical — jousts in confined spaces, and it’s surprisingly effective.

It’s also a very strange beginning for a franchise that would come to be known for its globetrotting locales and elaborate action set pieces. Not that this “Casino Royale” was officially part of the James Bond franchise as we know it. In fact, although there have been three adaptations of Ian Fleming’s first James Bond novel, only the third incarnation with Daniel Craig was from EON Productions, the company that controlled the character from “Dr. No” through the Craig era before selling the rights to Amazon.

The 1954 “Casino Royale” came about when producer Gregory Ratoff optioned the rights to Fleming’s novel in May of that year. The novel wasn’t yet a hit, and Fleming was sorely in need of cash, which led him to make one of the worst deals in movie-rights history when he sold the book outright to Ratoff for $6,000 after the TV episode aired. This left “Casino Royale” out of the deal when EON secured the screen rights to James Bond as a character, so Bond producers Albert Broccoli and Harry Saltzman could only sit back and grit their teeth when Ratoff turned “Casino Royale” into a comedy in 1967 and cast Peter Sellers, David Niven, Woody Allen and others as rotating Bonds.

EON ultimately made a deal to bring “Casino Royale” under their umbrella and used the novel to reboot the franchise with Craig, but in 1954 it served as the source for a much more modest affair. The biggest similarities between the 1954 “Climax!” episode and the Daniel Craig movie come in the time spent on extended gambling sequences, and the centering of a brutal torture scene. Given censorship restrictions of the time, Nelson’s torture in a bathtub is considerably less graphic than the mallet to the testicles inflicted on Craig, but it’s rough enough stuff for a 1950s TV production.

Certain aspects of Nelson’s characterization, like Bond’s mix of sexual swagger and icy indifference, would later be adopted by most future 007s, to varying degrees. The biggest difference between Nelson and future Bonds is a simple one: He’s American. Although Broccoli and Saltzman flirted with the idea of an American Bond throughout the series’ history (going so far as to cast James Brolin in “Octopussy” before Moore decided to return at the last minute), to date they’ve never actually pulled the trigger on casting outside the UK.

Nelson is probably best known to modern audiences as the affable hotel manager Stuart Ullman in Stanley Kubrick’s “The Shining,” but in the 1950s he was a sturdy character actor and occasional leading man who bounced around television after an initial sojourn as a studio contract player. As a young man, he appeared in several important MGM films, including “Shadow of the Thin Man,” “Bataan,” and “A Guy Named Joe” (the source material for Steven Spielberg’s “Always”). Later on, he popped up in “Airport” and had a successful Broadway career. He was nominated for a Tony acting opposite Liza Minnelli in Martin Scorsese’s 1977 production “The Act.”

In 1954, though, he was in the middle of a prolific and productive era as a TV stalwart, both as a series regular (on “The Hunter” and “My Favorite Husband”) and a frequent guest star. He doesn’t exhibit a ton of range as American “Combined Intelligence” agent “Jimmy” Bond, but that too is in keeping with the overall conception of the character, at least until Craig tried to bring a little more emotional depth to the role.

In Americanizing Bond, the “Climax!” edition of “Casino Royale” ends up making a number of related changes that are small but make the film feel just a bit off for fans of the EON productions. American Felix Leiter (later played by Jeffrey Wright) becomes Brit Clarence Leiter, for example. Although there’s none of the Bond gadgetry that would become famous later, there are hints of what’s to come in the form of props like a villain’s cane that hides a gun, and the opening credits for the “Climax!” series itself feature a gun barrel pointed at the viewer that predicts the iconic graphics of later Bond title sequences.

The 1954 “Casino Royale” is noteworthy for another reason: its composer, Jerry Goldsmith, who would ultimately score hundreds of major films, including “Planet of the Apes,” “Chinatown,” “Basic Instinct,” and most of Joe Dante’s work. Yet in some ways what’s fascinating about “Casino Royale” is how unremarkable it is — it’s a decent, solid piece of entertainment from an era when proliferating anthology shows provided similar programs every week.

If Fleming had his way, it would have only been the start for 007 on television; he wrote several outlines for episodes of a James Bond series before CBS canceled the project. Luckily, he repurposed most of what he wrote as short stories for his 1960 book “For Your Eyes Only,” and television’s loss was cinema’s gain. By 1962, James Bond belonged to the movies — and to Sean Connery.

#3375. 10 Movies Like ‘Interstellar’ You Should Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Christopher Nolan’s 2014 megahit Interstellar has it all: big sci-fi ideas, cool robots, ugly crying, and a Matt Damon character in need of rescuing. Grounded in the intensity of the human experience, this story of humanity’s potential extinction and the sacrifice of one man to save it doesn’t just deliver exotic planets and thrilling spaceship maneuvers; it also provides all the feels as Joseph Cooper (Matthew McConaughey) sacrifices everything he has in an effort to save the entire human race. It’s one of the best science fiction films ever made, with Nolan’s signature complexity, time manipulations, and emotional wallop. If you love this movie, here are ten more that offer a similar viewing experience.

If you loved both the special effects in Interstellar that make space travel feel viscerally thrilling (and terrifying) and the mind-blowing concepts, this is the film for you. Stanley Kubrick’s 1968 epic (written by sci-fi master Arthur C. Clarke) traces humanity’s development from mildly smart apes to spacefaring capitalists who discover a mysterious obelisk on the Moon that sparks a mission to Jupiter. While it operates in a colder emotional key than Nolan’s film, 2001: A Space Odyssey absolutely delivers on the epic side of things (and the cool—if slightly deranged and deadly—artificial intelligences). Stream 2001: A Space Odyssey on HBO Max or rent it on Prime Video.

If you’re looking for more existential missions with somewhat reluctant heroes in space, Project Hail Mary is your next stop. When the Sun begins to dim due to the interference of an alien entity, scientists identify the one nearby star that isn’t being similarly affected. Brilliant molecular biologist Ryland Grace (Ryan Gosling) winds up forced to go on what is assumed to be a fatal, one-way mission into deep space to try to find a way to save humanity, unexpectedly assisted by a charming alien he names Rocky. It’s got the same emotional volume and big ideas as Interstellar, and fans of Nolan’s film will love it. Stream Project Hail Mary on MGM+ or Philo, or rent it on Prime Video.

Part of what makes Interstellar so compelling is the stakes: The human race is slowly dying, and a handful of people must make incredible sacrifices to save it. That’s the vibe of Sunshine, set in a future where the Sun is dimming and a spacecraft is dispatched to deliver an enormous bomb designed to reignite the Sun’s fusion cycle. But the mission is the second attempt after the first ship vanished mysteriously seven years earlier, and when the new crew stumbles on the derelict wreck of the first mission, things quickly descend into violence and madness—but the crew remains determined to save the world, no matter the cost. Rent Sunshine on Prime Video.

Interstellar works in large part because of the emotional dynamics at play. McConaughey’s character leaves his children behind and is forced to witness them growing up without him, missing out on their lives and saddled with the knowledge that they resent him despite the necessity of his mission. Arrival is a First Contact story focused on language—linguist Louise Banks (Amy Adams) is drafted into an effort to understand the strange, complex language of the aliens. As she slowly builds to an understanding of how the aliens communicate and perceive time itself, her own heartbreak and loss come into play, giving this film a similarly devastating emotional punch. Stream Arrival on Kanopy or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

Family dynamics and the toll of lonely space missions fuel Ad Astra, a film with the same emotional core as Interstellar. Twenty-nine years ago, famed astronaut Clifford McBride (Tommy Lee Jones) led the Lima Project, a space station around Neptune searching for intelligent life. Thirteen years ago, Earth lost contact with him. When bursts of energy emanating from Neptune threaten to end life on Earth, his son, Roy (Brad Pitt), is dispatched to try to make contact with his father. It’s an epic journey with a powerful climax that will satisfy fans of Interstellar in every way. Stream Ad Astra on Netflix or rent it on Prime Video.

Ridley Scott’s prequel to Alien has its flaws, but if you’re looking for a sense of epic spacefaring adventure in the same key as Interstellar, it’s perfect. When two scientists discover a star map apparently left behind by ancient aliens, they secure funding from the Wayland Corporation to organize a space expedition to the indicated planet. Accompanied by a colorful crew and the android David, they discover an apparently abandoned outpost of the species dubbed the Engineers. The story wrestles with questions about humanity’s origins, purpose, and potential—but this being an Alien film, things quickly turn horrifying. Rent Prometheus on Prime Video.

Adapted from Carl Sagan’s 1985 novel, Contact follows astronomer Dr. Ellie Arroway (Jodie Foster), who becomes involved with an effort to decipher a signal originating from the star Vega. The signal turns out to be a set of instructions for constructing a one-person spacecraft of some kind, and Arroway is eventually selected as the candidate to take the journey. There’s a sense of courage in the face of the unknown that’s similar to Interstellar, as well as the thrill of strapping into a spaceship and pressing the ignition. Plus, there’s the added bonus of seeing one of the greatest trick shots in cinematic history. Rent Contact on Prime Video.

Stanislaw Lem’s 1961 novel Solaris explores what Lem saw as the impossibility of ever understanding a truly alien life. The two major adaptations—Andrei Tarkovsky's 1972 version and Steven Soderbergh’s 2002 take starring George Clooney—are both worth watching, but Tarkovsky’s film is a masterpiece of psychological horror. The story is set mainly aboard a space station orbiting a planet covered in what appears to be a sentient "ocean" and chronicles the strange haunting and inexplicable experiences of the humans living on the station. If your favorite part of Interstellar is the ending when things get trippy and weird, you’ll probably love Solaris. Stream Solaris on HBO Max, Plex, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

The story of a mission to Jupiter’s moon Europa to search for intelligent life, Europa Report has the same sense of terrifying excitement that accompanies Interstellar’s missions to the different candidate planets. Leaning into the fragility of life in an environment not designed to support it, the mission crew face a steady stream of loss and danger as they work to catch sight of alien life on the frozen, deadly moon, ultimately faced with making terrifying sacrifices in order to provide humanity with the answers that it seeks. Stream Europa Report on Netflix, Kanopy, or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

A film based on a 1956 epic science fiction poem written by a Swedish Nobel Laureate might seem like an unlikely match for fans of Interstellar, but it’s actually perfect. As the Earth becomes uninhabitable, humanity begins launching ships to colonize Mars. When one such ship, the Aniara, is damaged and veers irreversibly off course, the passengers and crew are faced with the knowledge that they will sail off into the void without hope of rescue. Within a few years, despair has driven some to suicide and madness, while others cling to the possibility that they might yet find a way back. The film offers a different perspective on the existential crisis of humanity’s extinction, exploring the worst-case scenario to its bitter, bleak end. Stream Aniara on Kanopy or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

#3374. Sony Fans Debate Major Game Awards Snub

Sony titles and The Game Awards often go hand-in-hand, as plenty of PlayStation exclusives feel tailor-made for the kind of mainstream critical appeal that makes winning awards a cinch. From The Last of Us to the modern God of War games, the company's emphasis on cinematic storytelling has resulted in plenty of nominations and wins over the years.

Of course, that's no guarantee of victory. Sony's 2024 win for Astro Bot was bookended by Marvel's Spider-Man 2 losing to Baldur's Gate 3 in 2023 and Death Stranding 2: On the Beach falling before the unstoppable Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 wave in 2025. 2026 has shaken things up to a significantly greater degree, though, leaving plenty of PlayStation fans conflicted about the nominations.

As Andy Robinson of VGC pointed out on X, 2026 marks the "first time in 11 years" that a title published by Sony hasn't landed among the Game of the Year nominations at The Game Awards. While Marvel's Wolverine followed the critically successful Marvel's Spider-Man games from developer Insomniac Games, it failed to make the same splash, instead earning nominations for Best Performance and Innovations in Accessibility.

Plenty of players seem to be perfectly fine with this snub, at least if the responses to Robinson's post are anything to go by. Jakeinvades argues that Marvel's Wolverine "absolutely did not deserve to be nominated," and FOX suggests that the publisher simply "hasn't produced a GOTY quality IP this year."

There's still some room for debate, however. Some Marvel's Wolverine fans would certainly argue for its inclusion, but the more prevelant argument seems to be in favor of SAROS, which was also released under the Sony umbrella. While X user simon agrees that the Marvel's Wolverine snub is correct, they suggest that SAROS "could've been in the conversation."

I have less affection for games like Marvel's Spider-Man and the 2018 God of War than most, so Sony breaking its nomination streak is no particular skin off my back. ScreenRant's Austin King, who provided our review of Marvel's Wolverine, also wasn't an advocate of any Game of the Year potential, awarding it a respectable but unexceptional 7/10 score.

Sadly, the absence of Marvel's Wolverine in the Game of the Year pool didn't seem to open the way for any particularly intriguing dark horse candidates, as this is a year of fairly predictable AAA inclusions. Games like Control Resonant and Phantom Blade Zero are certainly less omnipresent than Grand Theft Auto 6, but there's no upstart indie darling like 2024's Balatro in the mix.

As to whether Sony can still take home any awards, the company may not go home empty-handed. Marvel's Wolverine might not take either of its categories — Wolverine actor Liam McIntyre could have an uphill battle to take Best Performance over standouts like Resident Evil Requiem's Angela Sant'Albano, and its laudable accessibility options might be too heavily associated with its heavy hand-holding to secure a win for Innovations in Accessibility. MARVEL Tōkon: Fighting Souls in the Fighting Game category at The Game Awards 2026, though? That one could work out.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

The best of ScreenRant, directly in your inbox.

#3373. How ‘Paper Tiger’ Evolved When Jeremy Strong and Anne Hathaway Couldn’t Reprise Their ‘Armageddon Time’ Roles

Editor’s Note: The following story contains spoilers for “Paper Tiger.”

James Gray never hid that Jeremy Strong and Anne Hathaway were playing fictional versions of his real-life parents in his 2022 drama “Armageddon Time,” based on the writer/director’s experience as a sixth grader growing up in Queens in the 1980s.

“Jeremy is doing my father to such a degree that it is disturbing.  He sounds exactly like him, looks exactly like him; it’s bizarre. Annie, too, is uncanny about [playing my mother],” said Gray while a guest on this week’s episode of IndieWire’s Filmmaker Toolkit Podcast. “So I had had such a great time with them shooting ‘Armageddon Time,’ I said, ‘Well, why don’t we do this again?’” Related Stories Sean Connery Wasn’t the First James Bond: Meet Barry Nelson in the ‘Casino Royale’ You’ve Never Seen ‘Madden’ Review: David O. Russell Fumbles Again with an Unfunny and Purposeless Football Biopic

Gray knew his next film (what would become “Paper Tiger”) would be set in 1986 and once again focus on a Jewish family of four, with two sons, in Queens. In the project’s early stages, Hathaway and Strong were up for reprising their roles, but it soon became clear Gray would have to wait 18 months — after both “The Odyssey” (Hathaway) and “The Social Reckoning” (Strong) finished filming — to start production.

“You can’t wait a year and a half,” said Gray. “And then I started thinking, ‘Well, maybe this is a blessing in disguise.’ That the [film] could start to take on a new style, and so then I started to pursue it in a different way. So in the beginning, in its origin stages, it was [a sequel of sorts], but like any movie, it’s like a wild horse that’s going to get away from you.”

While Scarlett Johansson and Miles Teller’s characters in “Paper Tiger” are inspired by Gray’s parents, they are not as deeply grounded as Hathaway and Strong were in “Armageddon Time” as facsimiles of Gray’s parents in how they talked, looked, dressed, and behaved. Through this lens, Gray began to see the film as less of a straight memoir, freeing him to embrace elements of the crime genre in his storytelling.

Explained Gray, “What I tried to do was to make a film more in — for lack of a better way of really explaining — a bit more Hitchcockian in certain places. Almost — again, ‘pulpy’ is not quite the right word — a little bit more, how do I put this — more of an engagement directly with a tense idea of narrative, that it would be a driving, tense story.”

What also changed is the sympathetic lens through which Gray now saw his father. In “Paper Tiger,” Irwin (Teller) puts his family in danger when he unwittingly gets entangled (pursuing environmental consulting work for businesses along the polluted Gowanus Canal) with the Russian mob. While Irwin is guilty of pride and naivety, it is (especially compared to Gray’s previous films) a positive portrayal of a hard-working and earnest father pursuing the American dream.

In this sense, the shift from Strong to Teller was fortuitous. Strong had painted an unforgiving portrait of a miserable, strict father — tortured by generational trauma and unbending with his sons striving for upward mobility — whereas Gray saw something in Teller he could lean into for a different portrayal of his father.

“Miles has a kind of — I can’t believe I’m going to say this, he might even resist this— a softness to him, which would probably offend him, but I think that’s a great thing,” said Gray. “He doesn’t have a softness in his persona. He doesn’t have it in physical terms. It’s actually a tenderness inside. You have to embrace [that] beauty in him and hope it works for the film.”

When it came to recasting Hathaway, Gray was more practical, saying he needed three characteristics: another bankable star, who was also Jewish, and a real New Yorker. He believed the way the city seeps itself into a person’s bones is not something that even the best actors can learn to portray. Those three unnotiables made Scarlett Johansson the clear number one choice.

“I had met [Scarlett] years before on a project that never wound up happening, and quite liked her. She’s a total New Yorker through and through. Then when I found out that Annie [Hathaway] was going off to do Chris [Nolan’s] movie [‘The Odyssey’] for a thousand years, she was the first choice because you’re talking about one of the biggest stars in the world, and she’s also a Jewish woman from New York,  checks the boxes,” said Gray. “When I sent [the script] to her, I sent her a note, ‘There’s probably no chance in hell you’re going to do this, but I love you, can you read this?’ And then she texted me back very, very quickly and was like, ‘Let’s go.’”

While Hathaway’s portrayal of Gray’s mother was more open and loving than Strong’s version of his father — and therefore didn’t require as sharp a contrast in how the role was recast — Gray believed Johansson’s approach better fit the needs of “Paper Tiger.”

“It’s a more operatic idea of character than Annie’s was in ‘Armageddon Time,’” said Gray. “It’s much more a kind of high emotion. And of course, because the situation is much more tragic, and she embraced it completely.”

“Paper Tiger” opened last weekend in New York and Los Angeles, and expands on November 20.

#3372. The Apple Watch's New 'Siri Recap' Feature Is Even Creepier Than I Expected

The “Siri Recap” feature that Apple announced in September is finally available in a developer beta, and I’ve spent the last 24 hours with the feature turned on. It’s even more unsettling than the “Live Rewind” feature that launched at the same time. It listens to all my conversations, and produces summaries that are both helpful and deeply creepy.

I have a button in the watch’s Control Center that can turn the recapping abilities off, but if I forget to do so, Siri listens to everything. I’ll get a recap of my entire evening, presented in roughly hour-long chunks, including things I would have completely forgotten I had even heard about.

The recaps somberly mention silly memes my kids were laughing about, and make major bullet points out of offhand remarks from brief conversations. If a conversation sticks to a single topic, I’ll often get a reasonably good summary of it, with specific facts and numbers highlighted; but just as often, Siri will get confused and mix up several topics or completely mishear a name or phrase.

Apple has four features that it considers part of “audio intelligence":

Music recognition, better known as Shazam. We’ve had a version of this on the Apple Watch for a long time now, although it has some improvements and now identifies music automatically.

Sound recognition, which can notify you about doorbells and babies crying. A version of this launched in 2020 as an accessibility feature.

Live Rewind, which gives you an on-wrist transcript of the last 15 seconds of detected speech.

Siri Recaps, which summarizes entire conversations for you to read on your phone.

Live Rewind had the flashiest demo from the Apple event: A server rattled off the day’s specials at a restaurant, and then the Apple Watch-wearing diner checked his watch to see a readout of exactly which dishes had just been mentioned. The utility is both obvious and kind of unnecessary: Why wouldn’t you just ask the server to repeat the list while they’re standing right there?

I haven’t found myself using Live Rewind, except out of curiosity about how the feature works. I discovered that it doesn’t pick up song lyrics very well, and also that by the time I think to check what was just said in a conversation, more than 15 seconds has passed since the part I was unsure about. I haven’t yet found a reason to use it for real.

But Siri Recaps? Those are both useful and unsettling. I enabled the feature, and decided to test it out later. But since it was on, it dutifully listened in as I picked up my son from school and gave him an update on an ailing family member’s health. We stopped by the library, and along the way we chatted about a variety of things: holiday travel plans, library policies, and the possibility of humans living in space in the future. Siri was listening to it all.

At least for now, the feature is only available in a developer beta, so sign up for that now if you want to try it. You'll need an Apple Watch Series 12 (or Ultra 4) and an iPhone 16 or better, excluding the 16e. (I have a 16 Pro, so I'm good.)

After you're updated to 27.3, go into the Watch app, tap Siri, and turn on Siri Recap. You can set a schedule for when it should listen (for example, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., if you want it on for the work day but off for the evening). You'll need to set a passcode on your watch, and you'll be guided through a step to upgrade your audio connection. The control center on the watch will have a button you can use to turn Siri recaps on and off at will. To read your recaps, go to the Siri app on your phone.

But still: I feel weird publishing the contents of these recaps, because they do contain things that people said to me in what they assumed was a private setting. I had the feature on when I attended a choir practice, and Siri recapped the brief chats I had with other choir members before and after practice. (Interestingly, it did not recap any of the quiet conversations I had with fellow sopranos while the tenors were rehearsing their part. I’m not sure if the watch was unable to hear us over the music, or if Siri is programmed not to listen when music is being played.)

Because speakers aren’t identified, it seems Siri doesn’t know what to do when there is a disagreement. A human note-taker would jot down that Person A made a point in favor of something, and person B made a point against. But when my son and I disagreed about how likely space colonization might be in the future, the recap didn’t reflect the separate positions that were put forth. It summarized the conversation as including “debating the feasibility and timeline of human space colonization and asteroid mining,” which isn’t exactly accurate, but close enough.

When it comes to the content of the discussion, the recap notes a bullet point of “skepticism regarding permanent space colonies within the next 100 years.” It didn’t include my reasons for being skeptical, and didn’t mention my son’s opposing viewpoint at all. If I were using this recap to jog my memory of the conversation, it wouldn’t be all that helpful.

Details are sometimes egregiously incorrect. After a discussion about a family member’s health, the recap had notes on the prognosis of “father.” The family member we discussed is not anybody’s father. Names in general seem to be a problem; I recommended a book to my son, and the recap includes notes about the content of the book, but not its title. The book’s author appears in the introduction to the recap (sort of a summary of a summary), but not in the content of the recap itself where the book is mentioned.

I should probably turn Siri recaps off. It seems wrong to let people chat with me without letting them know that their conversation is being ... well, not technically recorded, but basically recorded.

But it’s so tempting to leave it on so that I can review my day. Some of the details in the recaps are useful, like the dates that were discussed as options for a holiday party. The recaps will be deleted in about a week (unless I save them to the notes app), so if I want to remind myself of a conversation a few days ago, I should be able to scroll back through my recaps and find it.

I would be a fool to rely on the recaps, though. The most important points of a conversation are often left out; Siri doesn’t know what’s actually important, and there’s no way to guide it as to what to pay attention to. Specific details can be wrong, as I mentioned. There’s also no way to control when a “conversation” starts or stops, unless you are turning the recap feature on and off from the watch.

And there’s more: Not only are names usually omitted (wait, who did she say I should ask about that project?), the few identifiers that make it into the recap, like names of events, are often wrong. Subjects of discussion are often conflated in really unhelpful ways: My husband mentioned paying for certain course registrations for one of our children, and later I talked to that child about an unrelated exam. The recap got all of these things mixed up with each other and was wrong about pretty much every detail. About all the recap could usefully do is to remind me that something about AP U.S. History was discussed. Reading the recaps can be like reliving your day entirely in the passive voice.

#3371. ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ Throws Netflix’s Oscar Campaign a Curveball

From a purely awards-hunting perspective, there’s a great argument to be made that Netflix could have pushed back its late November release “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” until next year. Historically, the perception of the embattled studio is that its had issues being distracted by too big an awards slate to pin down its Best Picture frontrunner. Remember in 2023 when it seemed like the streamer did not realize until the Oscar shortlists (in mid-December!) that “All Quiet on the Western Front” was its best bet at Best Picture? The Edward Berger film went on to win four Oscars, including Best International Feature. Related Stories How ‘Paper Tiger’ Evolved When Jeremy Strong and Anne Hathaway Couldn’t Reprise Their ‘Armageddon Time’ Roles Sean Connery Wasn’t the First James Bond: Meet Barry Nelson in the ‘Casino Royale’ You’ve Never Seen

This year, Netflix is running their best awards campaign yet with “La Bola Negra,” which the studio acquired out of Cannes, where its helmers, Los Javis, won the jury prize for Best Director. Come the fall festivals, it became the first Netflix film to win the People’s Choice Award at TIFF. Since then, it has fronted Netflix’s experiment in expanding the theatrical distribution of its awards slate, doing admirable business in key markets. The consensus among prognosticators is that the film is not only a lock to receive a Best Picture nomination, but is also sure to win the Oscar for Best International Feature on behalf of Spain.

If Netflix wanted to secure a second Best Picture nomination, with “Cliff Booth” out of the picture, the team could put all its energy into Lee Chang-dong’s “Possible Love.” Not only is the near-three hour film, which won the Grand Jury Prize at Venice, another Best International Feature contender (on behalf of South Korea), but it is one of this season’s most critically lauded films. If enough critics’ groups get behind it in the coming weeks, a la “The Secret Agent” last year, then a second Best Picture nomination for Netflix at the 2027 Oscars becomes highly plausible.

Somewhere along the way, “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” became something of a puzzle for Netflix. The streamer had no choice but to follow through with putting it out around Thanksgiving, because it was already set to replace the IMAX screens that had initially been secured for Greta Gerwig’s “Narnia” film. So how does a company not run an awards campaign for the sequel to a recent Best Picture nominee, directed by a three-time Oscar nominee, written by a two-time Oscar winner, and starring Brad Pitt in the role he just won a Best Supporting Actor Oscar for?

What reads as a home run on paper is more of a double or triple in execution. “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” is made by people who know what they are doing, and that expands past director David Fincher, screenwriter Quentin Tarantino, and star Pitt.

Cinematographer Erik Messerschmidt, editor Kirk Baxter, production designer Donald Graham Burt, set decorator Jan Pascale, and composers Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross have all won at least one Academy Award. Costume designer Trish Summerville was nominated for an Oscar for her work on “Mank.” Even if there is a low bar for getting the Academy excited about a late-’70s period piece set in Hollywood, “Cliff Booth” easily clears it.

But we are in a spectacle-heavy year, with “The Odyssey” and “Project Hail Mary” in the awards conversation, and “Dune: Part Three” and “Werwulf” on the horizon. Even “Digger” is a formidable contender in the craft races. So if the feeling is that “Cliff Booth” is more of a hangout movie than a cinematic event, then the focus of its awards campaign should be on categories that are more willing to embrace that, like Best Production Design or Best Costume Design. (Not so much Best Sound, which “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” did actually receive nominations for.)

In terms of the acting performances, again, Pitt is great as Cliff Booth, but there is no rush to nominate him for a performance he already won for. And there are plenty of other Best Actor contenders, like Matt Damon and John Malkovich (who have never won) and John Turturro and Andrew Scott (who have never even been nominated for an Oscar before).

The top performance of the film is with Cliff’s love interest, played by Emmy winner Elizabeth Debicki, who actually does have a shot at her first Oscar nomination, given the love for her performance in “Wicker” as well, and the lack of current consensus in the Best Supporting Actress race.

Everyone else in the film, from Scott Caan to Yahya Abdul-Mateen II to Carla Gugino, is very additive to the project but does not necessarily cross the threshold into Oscar-contender territory. In that way, it is similar to Tony Gilroy’s “Behemoth!,” another awards hopeful from this season.

Ultimately, “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” is entertaining enough to garner support from certain branches of the Academy, but falls too late in the year, in too few theaters, to truly become the last-minute surprise blockbuster that would get as many as 10 Oscar nominations, something its predecessor “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” did handily.
